This paper presents a framework for integrating quantum detection techniques into a Dual-Parallel Mach-Zehnder Modulator (DPMZM)-based Next Generation Passive Optical Network 2 (NG-PON2) communication system. We present a system model for the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system and characterize its signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), demonstrating its superiority over conventional MZM-based systems. We analyze the performance of various quantum modulation techniques, including binary phase-shift keying, quadrature phase-shift keying, and M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation. A comprehensive analytical framework is developed to evaluate the SNR, BER, and mutual information for both classical and quantum detection schemes within the DPMZM-based NG-PON2 quantum communication system. Our simulation results show that quantum detection significantly outperforms classical detection, and the DPMZM architecture further enhances the performance over the baseline MZM architecture by improving the effective modulation efficiency and receiver sensitivity.

title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
text:
Title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.

title: Beyond Tokens: Probing Higher-Order Epistasis in Learned Protein Representations
text:
Title: Beyond Tokens: Probing Higher-Order Epistasis in Learned Protein Representations
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Protein fitness landscapes contain nonlinear interactions in which mutation effects depend on other residues. We introduce ORBIT, an Order-Resolved Benchmarking of Interaction Transformations framework that separates interaction presence, representation accessibility, and functional recovery. ORBIT first validates Walsh-based diagnostics on synthetic landscapes with known interaction order, then analyzes the experimentally measured GB1 fitness landscape under the FLIP 2-vs-rest setting. We compare ridge regression, a standard MLP, independent tokens, nonlinear independent tokens, and Residual Interaction Tokenization (RIT). Across 20 paired training seeds, the primary two-hidden-layer comparison found no significant architecture differences in FLIP test R^2, third- or fourth-order functional recovery, or final-layer third- or fourth-order accessibility. However, RIT significantly increased pairwise accessibility at the token stage relative to both independent-token controls (Delta A_tok,2 = 0.2468, d_z = 1.67, Holm-adjusted p = 1.14 x 10^-5), without a detectable downstream higher-order advantage. A pre-specified depth/capacity analysis showed that deeper MLPs improved FLIP prediction, third-order functional recovery, and final-layer third-order accessibility; fourth-order accessibility also improved relative to the shallow MLP but remained below zero in absolute held-out R^2. ORBIT therefore reveals representation-level changes hidden by conventional prediction metrics and distinguishes early interaction-aware encoding from higher-order structure constructed by downstream nonlinear capacity.

title: I want to Break Free: The Positive Side of Symmetry Breaking
text:
Title: I want to Break Free: The Positive Side of Symmetry Breaking
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We study the role of internal field-space symmetries in Effective Field Theories constrained by positivity bounds. For theories with $N$ real scalar fields, we classify derivative operators according to the internal symmetries they preserve, organising them into hierarchies based on the maximal symmetry $O(N)$ and its subgroups. We find that the Wilson coefficients of operators that depart from an enhanced symmetry are bounded in terms of those that respect it. This means that departures from an enhanced internal symmetry cannot be made arbitrarily large while maintaining a standard UV completion, even when the enhanced internal symmetry was not imposed in constructing the low-energy theory. Moreover, along a cascade of progressively smaller preserved subgroups, the coefficients of operators preserving lower levels of symmetry are bounded by those preserving larger subgroups in the cascade, and are consequently subject to progressively stronger constraints. We demonstrate these results through a variety of examples involving $2-2$ and $3-3$ scattering of indefinite states formed from superpositions of multiple scalar species.

title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
text:
Title: Causal Signal Credit Assignment for Verilog Code Generation via Counterfactual Hardware Verification
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large language models have improved Verilog generation, yet functional correctness remains difficult to optimize because simulation commonly provides a coarse module-level pass/fail outcome. Such feedback discards useful evidence from partially correct RTL modules and cannot determine whether a source statement is functionally responsible for an observed output behavior. We present a new method named Causal Signal Credit Assignment (CSCA), which is a counterfactual preference-optimization framework for Verilog generation. CSCA first performs continuous signal-level behavioral verification on sampled candidate modules. It then locates output-driving assignment spans and applies five interventions while holding the remaining module and testbench fixed. The resulting changes in signal-level errors are combined with behavioral agreement to form a continuous statement credit, which is mapped to response-token weights for strict weighted direct preference optimization. This enables CSCA to learn from locally supported statements without uniformly reinforcing an otherwise incorrect response. Built on Icarus Verilog and a CodeV-derived corpus, CSCA is evaluated on VerilogEval~2.0 and RTLLM~v2.0, including both code completion and specification-to-RTL tasks. With a Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct backbone, CSCA leads the evaluated 7B-scale models and remains comparable to the much larger GPT-5.4-mini on the reported Verilog-generation benchmarks.

title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
text:
Title: UGG: Unified Generative Geometry Model
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Understanding 4D scenes is a core challenge in visual intelligence, requiring models to jointly capture scene geometry, appearance, and dynamics from partial observations. However, existing approaches are subdivided into feedforward models for direct geometric prediction, and generative models for visual synthesis. We introduce UGG, a unified framework for 4D scene understanding that jointly models RGB video and geometric representations such as depth and camera pose. By assigning different noise levels across modalities and time, UGG formulates visual generation and geometric prediction as conditional completion within a single generative model. This flexible formulation enables the model to learn from diverse, heterogeneous datasets with different subsets of geometric and visual annotations. Furthermore, our generative formulation enables inference-time search over multiple plausible scene hypotheses, using geometric evidence extracted from observed RGB frames to improve geometric prediction without ground truth geometry. We demonstrate UGG's effectiveness over non-unified baselines across camera-controlled video generation, depth estimation, and camera pose prediction, including in challenging sparse observation settings. Code and visualizations are available at https://ugg-model.github.io/

title: A Parameter-Free Few-Shot Evaluation for Elephant Vocalisation Classification
text:
Title: A Parameter-Free Few-Shot Evaluation for Elephant Vocalisation Classification
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

We present a parameter-free episodic evaluation of nearest-centroid classification of elephant vocalisations on fixed pretrained embeddings, for the Elephant Voices (EV) and Linguistic Data Consortium (LDC) datasets. We ask not which embedding yields the best classifier trained on all labelled data, but how the simplest classifier performs as the number of exemplars per class varies. There are no learnable parameters, because each class is modelled as the mean of its support embeddings and each query is assigned to the nearest centroid under squared Euclidean distance. Evaluation covers the fixed Perch (ver. 1), Perch (ver. 2) and HuBERT (base, layer 2) embeddings, alongside mel frequency cepstral coefficient (MFCC) features, $N$-way $k$-shot, under the same stratified $K$-fold cross-validation protocol as the trained classifiers. None of these embedding models was trained to distinguish elephant call types. On the smaller EV dataset the centroid classifier is markedly data-efficient. Using Perch (ver. 1) or Perch (ver. 2) embeddings it overtakes in mean average precision (mAP) the fully-trained logistic regression (LR) baseline from one or two exemplars and the recurrent baseline from two. Over the reduced set of call types on which the strongly-supervised end-to-end baseline was trained, the centroid classifier using Perch (ver. 2) embeddings overtakes that baseline in mAP as well, from two exemplars. On the larger LDC dataset the recurrent baselines retain their advantage for all considered values of $k$. Only LR is overtaken, and only in mAP. Nearest-centroid classification is therefore preferable precisely when exemplars are few and the fixed embedding already separates the call types.

title: Holographic Drag Force and the Entanglement Membrane: Geometric Reconstruction and Information Spreading
text:
Title: Holographic Drag Force and the Entanglement Membrane: Geometric Reconstruction and Information Spreading
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

A central question in holography is how different boundary observables encode and reconstruct the geometry of the gravitational dual. In this work, we uncover an exact geometric correspondence between two seemingly distinct aspects of strongly coupled dynamics: the dissipative drag force experienced by a moving heavy particle(quark) and the entanglement membrane governing the propagation of quantum information. We show that both constructions retain the same underlying structure of the geometry, leading to an invertible transformation between the finite-velocity drag force and the geometric membrane tension. This correspondence reveals that nonlinear momentum loss encodes detailed information about entanglement dynamics: the leading nonlinear correction determines the butterfly velocity, while higher-order terms successively probe the local geometry of the membrane near the horizon. We further connect this hierarchy to scalar pole-skipping, establishing an all-order relation between nonlinear dissipation and near-horizon spectral data. The shared geometric structure also has implications for quantum information recovery, with the quintic drag coefficient determining the leading dependence of information velocity on initial entanglement. Conversely, the complete information-velocity curve provides a reconstruction of the reduced bulk geometry along the physical interior membrane branch, complementing the exterior reconstruction from drag. We show that stochastic momentum broadening supplies the additional radial information needed to reconstruct the complete exterior metric up to an overall scale. Our results thus reveal how dissipation, entanglement dynamics, and spectral properties provide complementary access to holographic geometry, establishing a unified framework for understanding the geometric information encoded in distinct boundary observables.

title: Quantum advantage by designing beneficial dissipation from lossless dynamics
text:
Title: Quantum advantage by designing beneficial dissipation from lossless dynamics
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Passive loss removes probability from a system and therefore seems unable to improve an unconditional target. This intuition is exact for classical population dynamics under sink-only removal: passive killing obeys a finite-strength monotonicity principle even after optimization over the remaining controls. Here we show that coherent quantum dynamics can violate this classical monotonicity because coherent contributions to the final target can interfere destructively. We derive a trajectory-level criterion that determines when such a detrimental contribution is physically accessible to passive loss and accumulates into a net unconditional benefit. The criterion is encoded in a response operator constructed entirely from the lossless dynamics: its spectrum determines whether weak passive loss can help, while its principal eigenvector identifies the optimal environmental mode. Applying this criterion to vibronically assisted transfer, we identify a beneficial mode formed by coherently combining two individually detrimental local loss directions. The predicted mode remains near-optimal at finite loss, producing an \(8.73\%\) enhancement over the independently optimized lossless benchmark, compared with \(9.52\%\) under full finite-loss optimization. Our results establish how coherent quantum dynamics can evade classical passive-loss monotonicity and provide a general task-dependent principle for designing beneficial passive environments from lossless dynamics.

title: Medial Model of Elastic Curve Contacts, from Clasps to Knits
text:
Title: Medial Model of Elastic Curve Contacts, from Clasps to Knits
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Materials constructed from interlocking and tangled fibers are challenging to model and understand due in part to the complex interplay between fiber shape and contact mechanics. Much of our intuition about contact mechanics comes from the Hertzian description, which is based on interactions between convex bodies. However, fibers often form clasp shapes, which involve saddle-shaped contact surfaces; the ability for two interacting bodies to conform to each other along a saddle surface confounds many existing mechanical contact models. Following an observation that contact surfaces between fibers tend to look like minimal, constant mean-curvature surfaces, we seek to test this hypothesis and provide a direct link to geometric modeling methods. To do this, we leverage the medial axis transformation, which generalizes the notion of a Voronoi tessellation to generating curves and surfaces. Through computational studies on an orthogonal clasp and a simple knit structure, we find that the medial axis transformation provides a reasonable model for contact surfaces between identical curves. We also show that a generalization of the medial axis transformation based on radical Voronoi tessellations can be used to well-approximate contact surfaces between non-identical curves. We apply this ``radical axis transform'' to curves of different radii and demonstrate a trend for surfaces to adopt finite mean curvature. Our results may point the way towards more sophisticated geometric methods for modeling tangles.

title: Frank-Wolfe is Approximate Broximal Gradient Descent
text:
Title: Frank-Wolfe is Approximate Broximal Gradient Descent
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We show that the Frank-Wolfe method is an approximation of Broximal Gradient Descent (BroxGD), and hence of the ball-proximal method. For constrained minimization, the ball-proximal method minimizes the objective over the intersection of the feasible set with a ball around the current iterate. Linearizing the objective gives BroxGD, but the intersection can remain difficult to handle even when linear minimization over the feasible set alone is cheap. We therefore replace the intersection by a smaller copy of the feasible set, obtained by shrinking it toward the current iterate so that it lies inside the ball. Minimizing the linear model over this smaller set gives exactly Frank-Wolfe, with the shrinking factor as its step size. We examine what this approximation preserves and what it can lose. For smooth convex objectives on compact convex sets, Frank-Wolfe retains a linear-model decrease guarantee that gives it and BroxGD a common convergence proof, recovering the classical $O(1/k)$ bound. Among compact convex regions inside the ball chosen before the gradient is known, the smaller copy is the smallest that preserves the same linear-model decrease guarantee. Nevertheless, Frank-Wolfe can achieve much less linear-model decrease than BroxGD at the same radius. A simplex example illustrates the sparsity gained by restricting the region, while a family of triangles shows how Frank-Wolfe can lose the distance decrease guaranteed by BroxGD. We also give a computable test for recovering the distance guarantee and a refinement procedure that terminates after finitely many oracle calls on polytopes.

title: LifeLong Digital Twin: A Unified Modeling Paradigm and Agent Harness for Event-Driven Lifelong Health State Trajectories
text:
Title: LifeLong Digital Twin: A Unified Modeling Paradigm and Agent Harness for Event-Driven Lifelong Health State Trajectories
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Human health is a continuous, dynamic trajectory shaped by the cumulative interplay of biological processes, clinical events, behaviors and environmental exposures across the life course. Unifying the full breadth of lifelong health information, including longitudinal records, genetic variation, molecular profiles and environmental histories, is essential for whole-person modeling and remains a major challenge. We introduce LifeLong Digital Twin, a unified, event-driven modeling paradigm that organizes Life Events into daily Health States and accumulates them into Lifelong Health Context. An accompanying Agent Harness incorporates multimodal evidence beyond the language model's textual context. We evaluate four language models across 25 disease endpoints on three tasks: Disease Trajectory Forecasting, Disease Risk Ranking and Multi-horizon Disease Prediction. The approach yields marked gains over the reference condition: model-averaged F1 increases by 22.0% for disease identification in trajectory forecasting and 18.3% for five-year disease outcomes; thyroid-disease F1 reaches 0.669. The framework provides a foundation for whole-person digital twins and research on personalized lifelong disease prevention.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
text:
Title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Lessons from Biological World Models for Testing Action Effects
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. Taking biological experiments as the guiding case, we show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used. A second failure arises whenever many sites share one action sequence, as in world models: the pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from -17.3 to -6832 as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field (E = 1.1e10). Every single tempering factor we tried, estimated from residuals or tuned on validation data, collapsed in some setting; mixtures over a fixed grid of factors never did. In registered tests on three world-model families trained by others, the pooled test rejected in 0 of 96 units of a diffusion model in which actions mattered, and reached the registered power bar in 10 of 26 Atari games under IRIS's own token likelihood and 1 of 6 control tasks under TD-MPC2; mixtures fixed in advance reached it in all 96 units, 24 of 26 games and 6 of 6 tasks. Under exact nulls the statistics made 4 rejections in 22,848 tests.

title: Funnel-like protein energy landscapes emerge from functional evolution under thermal fluctuations
text:
Title: Funnel-like protein energy landscapes emerge from functional evolution under thermal fluctuations
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Foldable proteins exhibit funnel-like energy landscapes, but their evolution under selection for function remains unclear. We study this in a lattice protein model, defining fitness as the equilibrium probability of a fixed active-site motif and using multicanonical sequence sampling. At intermediate temperature, rare high-fitness sequences show funnel-like energy and double-well free-energy landscapes. At very low temperature, abundant high-fitness sequences retain glass-like landscapes. Thus, thermal fluctuations turn a local functional requirement into a global structural constraint.

title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
text:
Title: A Tutorial on Practical QKD Post-Processing Algorithms Using a GUI-Based Simulation Framework
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Recent experimental demonstrations of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) have attracted significant attention for their ability to establish information-theoretically secure encryption keys for next-generation communication systems. As practical deployment accelerates, the realization of compact, scalable, and high-throughput discrete-variable (DV) QKD systems has become increasingly important. While advances in photonic integration are enabling low-size, low-weight, and low-power QKD hardware, the security and performance of these systems rely heavily on efficient post-processing techniques to generate identical, secure keys. This tutorial presents a comprehensive algorithm-level review of practical post-processing techniques for DV-QKD, with particular emphasis on information reconciliation methods based on Cascade, Winnow, low-density parity-check (LDPC), and polar codes. We also analyze the theoretical asymptotic and finite-size secret key rates (SKRs) of DV-QKD and benchmark these bounds against the practical SKRs achieved using actual post-processing algorithms. Furthermore, we present a server-client model to implement the entire QKD post-processing pipeline. The performance is evaluated in terms of QBER and SKR across various system parameters, considering the complete post-processing pipeline, including sifting, information reconciliation, privacy amplification, and authentication. This tutorial also presents a graphical user interface (GUI) for the QKD post-processing methods, enabling researchers, industry practitioners, and academic users to visualize and analyze the impact of different post-processing techniques and system parameters, such as QBER, on the SKR performance of DV-QKD systems.

title: Foreground Groups and Host-Galaxy Geometry in the Dispersion-Measure Scatter of Fast Radio Bursts
text:
Title: Foreground Groups and Host-Galaxy Geometry in the Dispersion-Measure Scatter of Fast Radio Bursts
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Localized fast radio bursts (FRBs) show substantial scatter in dispersion measure (DM) about the mean cosmic DM--redshift relation, also known as the Macquart relation. Both foreground structure and host galaxies contribute to this scatter. In this work, we examine foreground tracers and host galaxy properties using a parent catalog of 136 localized FRBs with measured DMs and spectroscopic host redshifts. Among 77 FRBs within the Gfinder footprint, DM excess relative to a fixed Macquart mean increases with foreground group count excess, with a Spearman coefficient of 0.459. Adding the foreground term to a mean host baseline reduces the leave-one-out root mean square error (RMSE) and mean absolute error (MAE) in extragalactic DM by \(13.0\%\) and \(7.5\%\), respectively. For 20 of these FRBs with optical host axis ratio measurements, adding a foreground term calibrated on the other 57 FRBs to the host shape model reduces the observer-frame leave-one-out RMSE from \(76.3\) to \(64.0~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}\) and MAE from \(54.2\) to \(50.2~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}\). And the in-sample residual standard deviation in the host rest frame decreases by \(20.2\%\). Idealized galaxy models based on the Milky Way electron density distribution produce DM changes with inclination comparable to the fitted amplitude under the adopted assumptions.

title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
text:
Title: Magnolia: A Persistent-Memory Agent Framework for Computational Chemistry
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Chemistry has recently entered a high-data regime as molecular databases from high-throughput platforms or computational studies have become available. Increasing automation within the chemical sciences leads to a more digital and precision chemistry. Dedicated scientific agents are becoming central to guiding the chemist through an ever-increasing amount of data and findings, including negative ones. Here, we introduce Magnolia, a persistent-memory artificial intelligence agent framework that integrates computational protocols, from docking to quantum chemistry, lab notebooks and chat logs relying on large language models (LLMs). It relies on a three-tier memory system: session-level observations are automatically captured and distilled into structured learnings, confirmed and elevated to project-tier entries and, when human-validated, promoted to cross-project rules that actively guide subsequent work and provide direct chemical feedback. We illustrate Magnolia on four case studies: quantum-chemical evaluation of aromatic systems (COMPAS database), molecular dynamics of butane and of modified DNA, and a protein-peptide docking campaign. Across these projects, Magnolia tracked 317 runs and accumulated 116 project-tier entries, from which four cross-project rules were promoted; in controlled replays of four tasks, runs with memory passed the checks that runs without it failed (for example, ten of ten docking-configuration checks, against one to four of ten). By combining automation, reproducibility, and human-in-the-loop control, our Magnolia framework streamlines docking, molecular dynamics and quantum chemistry calculations with direct analysis and LLM-augmented feedback, offering accelerated access to computational (bio)chemistry.

title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation
text:
Title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a fundamental NLP task concerned with the identification and categorization of subjective information in text. While lexicon-based methods offer transparency, they often struggle with linguistic phenomena such as negation and intensification. Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.

title: Geometric Functional Inequalities for Markov Processes: An Invitation via the Langevin Diffusion
text:
Title: Geometric Functional Inequalities for Markov Processes: An Invitation via the Langevin Diffusion
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Functional inequalities provide a language for reasoning about the long-time properties of ergodic Markov processes in terms of their macroscopic geometry. This article offers an informal introduction to functional inequalities for readers who are more familiar with probabilistic tools based around couplings, Lyapunov techniques, and similar. The main ideas are developed through the overdamped Langevin diffusion, where various functionals related to this convergence admit particularly transparent expressions, and for which the key associated inequalities -- namely, the Poincaré and logarithmic Sobolev inequalities -- are especially well-studied. We explain the qualitative content of these inequalities, what they imply about convergence to equilibrium, how they transform and compose under natural operations, and how they interface with classical probabilistic approaches. Related inequalities are discussed more briefly, and an annotated guide is provided for readers wishing to enter the wider literature.

title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
text:
Title: SIREN: A nonlinear Rankine-source boundary element solver for the stationary motion of a marine vehicle in calm water
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

SIREN (Ship Inviscid Resistance and Elevation eNgine) is a Rankine-source panel solver for the steady wave resistance of a ship, in the tradition of Dawson's method. The free-surface condition is linearised about a base flow, and the linearisation is iterated. In the present formulation the base flow is the solution of a Neumann problem on the actual boundary: sources on the entire hull, wet and dry, and on the free surface panels, with impermeability imposed on both, so that the free surface acts as a rigid lid at the position it currently occupies. This replaces the classical double-body flow, whose image about z=0 is meaningful only for a flat surface and a hull cut at z=0, and it removes the need for desingularised free-surface panels. In the non-linear iteration the free-surface panels are moved rigidly in the vertical to the relaxed wave elevation at their centroid, the hull panels are marked wet or dry against the moved surface, and the base flow is recomputed on the moved geometry; impermeability applies to the whole hull regardless of this marking, which is used only to select which panels enter the force integral, and under-relaxation is confined to the passes where the non-linear correction accumulates without being reset. The radiation condition is imposed by a one-row upstream shift of the collocation points, and the wave resistance is obtained by pressure integration and, independently, by transverse wave-cut analysis.

title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory
text:
Title: Robust Markov Decision Processes: An Introduction Using Convex Optimization and Game Theory
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

The goal of these notes is to provide a unified and rigorous introduction to robust sequential decision-making. We offer a self-contained introduction to the main results in the field. After a concise introduction to MDPs we introduce robust MDPs with general uncertainty sets, before focusing on rectangular models of uncertainty. We make a significant effort to show connections between robust MDPs and several other popular models for sequential decision-making: MDPs with uncertain rewards, Multi-Objective MDPs and Pareto optimality, MDPs with time-varying uncertain parameters, non-rectangular robust MDPs, stochastic games, distributionally robust MDPs, and risk-averse MDPs. Having all these results in one place, within a single unifying formalism, will hopefully be useful for researchers who want to start working on this topic. The exposition combines operator and fixed point approaches, convex optimization (more specifically, duality in saddle-point problems), and game-theoretic arguments. The latter identifies robust MDPs with a certain type of two-player game; this helps build useful intuition, especially when constructing counterexamples.

title: Low-Field J-Coupling Spectroscopy Measured with a Diamond Nitrogen Vacancy Spectrometer
text:
Title: Low-Field J-Coupling Spectroscopy Measured with a Diamond Nitrogen Vacancy Spectrometer
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond (NVs) are point defects well suited to quantum sensing of magnetic fields. NV spin states can be initialized and read out optically with high spatial resolution, enabling detection of pL-scale volumes of nuclear spins. Using Coherently Averaged Synchronized Readout (CASR), standard NMR spectroscopy techniques such as free decay, spin echo, and PGSE have been performed with Hz-scale spectral resolution using NV-diamond sensors. However, using NV detection for conventional high-resolution NMR at multi-tesla fields is challenging due to the need to manipulate NV electronic spins at resonance frequencies 100 GHz or higher. Low-field J-coupling spectroscopy provides an alternative path to chemical resolution in a regime more easily accessible to NVs. Here, we demonstrate homonuclear and heteronuclear J-coupling spectroscopy using an NV-NMR spectrometer based on permanent magnets operating at $\sim$890 kHz proton Larmor frequency (bias magnetic field $\sim$21 mT). This field strength enables chemical characterization based on J-coupling using sequences such as Synchronized Echo (SyncE) and Spin-Echo Double Resonance (SEDOR), which do not require the strong chemical shift dispersion and pristine field homogeneity of high-field NMR. The frequency range is easily detected by NVs using standard XY dynamical decoupling sequences and is well-suited for applying Overhauser DNP, which can boost proton signal by two orders of magnitude. We acquire initial NV-NMR measurements of T$_1$, T$_2$, and Overhauser DNP in glycerol before advancing to SEDOR spectroscopy of methanol-$^{13}$C and a methanol-$^{13}$C/acetonitrile-2-$^{13}$C mixture at sample volumes $\sim$50 pL, in which we demonstrate measurement of $^1J_\text{CH}$ couplings and resolution between species. We also acquire a homonuclear J-coupling spectrum of a natural-abundance propylene carbonate sample.

title: Interface-Preserving ${H}_\infty$ Model Reduction of Network Systems
text:
Title: Interface-Preserving ${H}_\infty$ Model Reduction of Network Systems
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study projection-based reduced-order models that exactly retain specified input and output interfaces. Admissible projections are characterized geometrically: the retained subspace must contain every input and output direction, which fixes the minimum order. The reduction error factors into input-coupling, internal-dynamics, and output-coupling systems, giving a submultiplicative ${H}_\infty$ bound; for positively dominated factors the ${H}_\infty$ error equals a dc gain computable from linear solves. Strict dissipativity certifies the stability of every orthogonal reduction, and a Hankel singular value bounds the optimum a posteriori. These results motivate sequential graph-coarsening heuristics for networks. On a 65,566-state chip thermal network, interface-preserving coarsening yields sparse, positive lumped models that are more accurate than Kron reduction of the same interface at every order, with far fewer edges; balanced truncation is more accurate but destroys the network structure.

title: How Well Does AI Peer Review Work? A Benchmark Built from 100 Planted Errors
text:
Title: How Well Does AI Peer Review Work? A Benchmark Built from 100 Planted Errors
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

One hundred known errors were planted into 10 open-access psychology papers, and the modified papers were then run through frontier models and two commercial AI review tools. The best single system caught 71 of the 100 errors, while the worst caught 30. Pooling every system's output caught 93. Models are only partly correlated in the errors they find, which makes ensembling a big lever for finding issues in papers. Seven errors could not be caught by any system, and all seven were omissions: information deleted from a paper rather than mistakes inserted into it. Refine.ink contributes more unique catches than any other single system, though it is expensive on a per-error basis. False positives were not measured, and how this error distribution compares to the distribution of errors in real papers remains unknown. The papers, errors, model outputs, and full experiment log are public, so that others can build on this toward a comprehensive evaluation benchmark across disciplines.

title: Bi-TEAM: A Unified Cross-Scale Representation Learning Framework for Chemically Modified Biomolecules
text:
Title: Bi-TEAM: A Unified Cross-Scale Representation Learning Framework for Chemically Modified Biomolecules
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Representation learning for protein biochemical space faces a difficult trade-off: protein language models excel at capturing long-range biological semantics but often miss fine-grained chemical details. Conversely, chemical language models encode atomic information but lack broader sequence context. To address this, we introduce Bi-TEAM (Bi-gated Residual Space Modification), a general framework that injects localized chemical variation into global protein contexts. By ensuring robustness against perturbations such as non-canonical amino acids, post-translational modifications (PTMs), and topological constraints, Bi-TEAM uncovers functional chemical dependencies often missed by evolutionary baselines. Mechanistically, Bi-TEAM maps non-canonical residues to their natural counterparts and injects atomic-level data via a bi-gated residual fusion mechanism. Crucially, this process uses modification-aware prompts to ensure that local structural changes influence global functional representations without requiring alphabet expansion. We evaluated Bi-TEAM on ten datasets spanning chemically modified peptides, PTMs, and natural proteins. The model consistently outperformed state-of-the-art baselines, achieving up to a 66 percent improvement in Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) on scaffold-similarity splits and a 350 percent increase in hemolysis prediction accuracy. Furthermore, when deployed as an oracle for generative modeling, Bi-TEAM nearly quadrupled the success rate for designing cell-penetrating cyclic peptides. By unifying biological semantics with chemical precision, Bi-TEAM provides a versatile foundation for machine learning driven exploration of peptide and protein biochemical space.

title: Quaternionic Response Geometry for Proteins: Toward a Noncommutative Theory of Ordered Deformations
text:
Title: Quaternionic Response Geometry for Proteins: Toward a Noncommutative Theory of Ordered Deformations
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Protein function may depend not only on endpoint conformations but also on the ordered deformation histories through which they are reached. This distinction is relevant to allostery, conformational switching, mutation-induced rearrangements, and epistatic effects, where different perturbation sequences may produce similar visible structures while retaining distinct internal transport histories. Current state-centered or endpoint-centered representations do not always preserve this order-sensitive information. The practical motivation is therefore to provide a foundation for future descriptors of protein deformation trajectories that can distinguish ordered histories even when endpoint conformations are similar. We propose a deformation-first geometric framework based on quaternionic frame transport along the protein backbone. Local backbone frames are lifted to quaternionic variables, with infinitesimal rotation encoded by \(Ω(\ell)=2\,q(\ell)^{-1}\partial_\ell q(\ell).\) Ordered concatenation of admissible deformation paths generates a noncommutative transport algebra, recording that deformation A followed by B need not be equivalent to B followed by A. From this ordered transport layer, we construct a spectral-response layer comprising a global Dirac-type operator, local spectral germs, a renormalized spectral density, and a mixed response form. A minimal realization on an idealized \(α\)-helix shows how localized pitch and bending perturbations can yield similar endpoint descriptors while producing a nonzero endpoint-derived ordered-transport discrepancy. At the formal level, the framework separates an order-sensitive transport-memory sector, lost under a commutative shadow, from a spectral-response sector that remains visible.

title: At the EDGES of MADness: phenomenology of relic millicharged atomic dark matter
text:
Title: At the EDGES of MADness: phenomenology of relic millicharged atomic dark matter
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Millicharged dark matter lives in a corner of parameter space that has been considerably shrinking over the past decades, due to constraints from cosmology, astrophysical systems, and ground-based experiments. A particularly interesting probe is the 21-cm absorption signal at Cosmic Dawn, which attracted interest in light of the EDGES claim: the reported excess absorption can be explained by millicharged dark matter with a fractional electric charge of~$10^{-6} \lesssim ε\lesssim 10^{-4}$, but it must be a subpercent of the total dark matter abundance to remain consistent with the cosmic microwave background (CMB). We show that very low fractions of millicharged dark matter naturally arise from atomic dark matter: a dark sector model that replicates the physics of standard atomic hydrogen. Dark ions undergo the process of dark recombination, leaving a relic ionized component that, in the presence of kinetic mixing, is naturally millicharged. We modify the cosmological Boltzmann solver CLASS to incorporate this scenario, and we investigate the parameter space of millicharged atomic dark matter (MAD) that is allowed by CMB, large-scale structure, and supernovae data. We find there are cosmologically viable regions of MAD parameter space that are consistent with laboratory and astrophysical bounds and also overlap with the EDGES-defined window. Although the EDGES result is likely not a Cosmic Dawn signal, MAD leaves distinctive cosmological signatures, accessible to upcoming 21-cm observations.

title: Kardar--Parisi--Zhang density hydrodynamics in a coherent XXZ--ASEP Lindbladian
text:
Title: Kardar--Parisi--Zhang density hydrodynamics in a coherent XXZ--ASEP Lindbladian
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Coherent interactions can generate quantum correlations without changing a stationary density current. Whether that current still determines long-wavelength transport is a dynamical question. We study an XXZ chain with asymmetric Lindblad hopping, whose stationary current has the asymmetric simple exclusion process (ASEP) form although its populations do not evolve autonomously. The current curvature and static susceptibility fix the leading Kardar--Parisi--Zhang (KPZ) length and amplitude without a fitted length or amplitude conversion factor. The density-visible Liouvillian spectrum, real-space spreading, and Fourier relaxation support KPZ scaling at the finite coherent couplings studied. Central and intermediate stationary density correlations are consistent with the Prähofer--Spohn profile at this microscopic scale, with resolved finite-time corrections. Reservoir-matched classical references quantify boundary effects, while symmetric hopping recovers diffusion and reduced asymmetry produces the expected crossover. These results connect an exact nonlinear current to the observed long-wavelength KPZ transport of the physical density in an interacting open quantum chain away from the isotropic Heisenberg point.

title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
text:
Title: Features of Non-Local Quantum Correlations in Nuclei
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Classical simulation of quantum many-body systems is challenged by the combined effects of entanglement and non-stabilizerness (magic). Non-local magic, $M^{\mathrm{NL}}_α$, quantifies the component of non-stabilizerness that cannot be removed by local unitary transformations and provides a measure of quantum complexity beyond entanglement alone. It is bounded from below by the antiflatness of the entanglement spectrum, ${F}_A$. We calculate stabilizer Rényi entropies, non-local magic, entanglement-spectrum antiflatness, and entanglement entropy in shell-model ground states of more than 260 even-even, odd-even, and odd-odd nuclei, using a bipartition into proton and neutron sectors. We find that the previously established bound $4{F}_A\leq{M}^{\mathrm{NL}}_{\mathrm{lin}}$ holds for every nucleus studied and approaches saturation in the limit of separable states. Odd-odd nuclei exhibit markedly different patterns of entanglement and magic compared with even-even and odd-even systems, revealing distinctive signatures of proton-neutron quantum correlations and providing new insight into the complexity generated by nuclear interactions.

title: Auditable Algebraic Counting Field for Cryptic-Pocket Detection from Apo Structures
text:
Title: Auditable Algebraic Counting Field for Cryptic-Pocket Detection from Apo Structures
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Cryptic ligand-binding pockets are not apparent in experimentally determined apo structures, making them difficult to identify from unbound receptor geometry. A complementary challenge is to make the structural measurements and learned evidence behind each prediction directly inspectable. We introduce a supervised algebraic counting field (ACF) for predicting cryptic-pocket residues from apo structures. ACF compiles explicit geometric, physicochemical, and topological features into compact, integer-weighted lookup tables. Each prediction score can be reconstructed from feature values, training counts, table weights, and spatial aggregation, without sequence search, structural-template transfer, or a protein language model at inference. We evaluate ACF on CryptoBench and two locked external collections, separating ranking performance from the effects of residue-calling budgets. On an external set of 57 post-CryptoBench apo-holo units, ACF exceeded P2Rank by +0.044 in mean paired ROC-AUC (multiplicity-adjusted 95% CI [+0.010, +0.079]). The advantage was dataset-dependent: official-fold ROC-AUC and matched-budget F1 differences against P2Rank remained unresolved, and a second external evaluation did not confirm gains from added structural features. ACF thus provides a compact predictor with externally validated signal and an inspectable path from structural measurements and training counts to residue scores.

title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
text:
Title: Design of Self-Folding Origami Architectures for Biomedical Implants: A Finite Element Simulation Framework
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Minimally invasive brain implants require compact deployment geometries and controlled shape transformation for delivery through confined vessels. Origami-inspired structures enable large shape changes from compact to tailored deployed configurations, but implementation at microscale dimensions remains challenging, as conventional designs rely on predefined mountain and valley folds that become increasingly difficult to fabricate and assemble as unit-cell size is reduced to meet clinical requirements. To address this, we propose a self-folding methodology based on thermally induced stresses in thin-film bimetallic composites. Pairing the shape memory alloy Nitinol (NiTi) with molybdenum or stainless steel (SS316L) exploits their differing thermal expansion coefficients to generate localized hinge bending, enabling deterministic, autonomous folding into prescribed mountain and valley configurations. Using finite element simulations, we systematically optimize hinge length, layer thickness, width, and shape, identifying a hinge geometry achieving a ~50% reduction in unit-cell dimensions relative to previously reported designs. Integration into a complete waterbomb origami unit cell confirms that the strip-level folding mechanism scales to produce coordinated, self-folding deformation across the tessellated structure. These results demonstrate the feasibility of stress-induced, self-folding thin-film origami architectures built from clinically established biomaterials, providing a scalable design framework for next-generation, active neurovascular implants with integrated sensing and monitoring functionality.

title: The Energy-Momentum Tensor of a Compact Object in General Relativity to all Multipole Orders
text:
Title: The Energy-Momentum Tensor of a Compact Object in General Relativity to all Multipole Orders
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

In effective field theory approaches to compact object motion in general relativity, spin and tidal effects are encoded by operators formed from the Riemann tensor and its derivatives. Many such operators contribute degenerately to observables, with a single one often affecting several multipole moments of the body. Using the Mathisson--Papapetrou--Dixon formalism, we construct a natural basis of independent tensors which are each canonically conjugate to precisely one multipole. We find the novel exact distributional formula for the energy-momentum tensor of a compact object in terms of its reduced multipole moments and these tensors.

title: Confinement Controlled Phase-Pure 2D Layered Perovskites for Band-Edge Engineering
text:
Title: Confinement Controlled Phase-Pure 2D Layered Perovskites for Band-Edge Engineering
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Controlling the number n of connected octahedra layers in two-dimensional metal halide perovskites enables fine control of the semiconductor band gap that is highly advantageous for optoelectronic and light emission applications. Phase purity in terms of n is crucial towards narrow emission bands and the design of band structure alignment for charge carrier funneling. We present a simple and scalable synthesis method using cesium and butylammonium as A-cations to fabricate microcrystal powders of 2D lead bromide perovskites that results in samples with very high n-phase purity. The obtained microcrystals show a sharp onset in absorbance and single narrow emission peak in UV-blue spectral range, and we confirm their structure and composition with X-ray diffraction and energy dispersive spectroscopy. We show that we can tailor the spectral absorption of microcrystals samples by controlled mixing of the n-phase pure powders, and we demonstrate this capability with spectral photocurrent measurements using pellets pressed from pure and mixed powders. Both the spectral and dynamic response of the photocurrent of the pellets depend strongly on the composition of the powders, highlighting the design potential of our approach towards band-edge engineering.

title: SATE: Transferable Spin-Adapted Neural Wavefunctions
text:
Title: SATE: Transferable Spin-Adapted Neural Wavefunctions
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Accurate prediction of molecular reactivity requires both accurate and computationally efficient description of electron correlation and spin across various molecular geometries and electronic states. We introduce SATE, a spin-adapted transferable neural wavefunction architecture with effective core potentials. SATE combines a transferable neural wavefunction, the spin-adapted antisymmetrization method, and effective core potentials into a single foundation model architecture pretrained on compositions containing selected elements from hydrogen to bromine. After pretraining and adaptation, our model is able to predict 3d transition-metal spin-state gaps, bond dissociation energies, and reaction energies by addressing two key issues. First, including the core potentials into the model allows us to reduce the number of explicitly treated electrons. Second, using spin-adapted antisymmetrization enforces the prescribed total spin by construction. By testing our model with 3d transition metal chemistry, we evaluate our model's description of strong electron correlation and competing electronic states in such compounds. We find that pretraining improves most tested component energies at matched adaptation budgets, while improvements in spin-state gaps, dissociation energies, and reaction energies remain system dependent. Ultimately, our work lays the foundation for more accurate and transferable modeling of molecular systems by combining the computational efficiency of effective core potentials with explicit control over total spin.

title: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation
text:
Title: RipplePLM: Structural and Property Decoupling for Protein Mutation Effect Generation
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Protein mutation effect generation asks a model to describe the functional consequence of a point mutation in natural language. Existing protein-to-text systems typically encode mutation information into undifferentiated representations, overlooking the organization of mutation-induced evidence across structural and biochemical factors. We propose RipplePLM, a mutation-aware generation framework centered on Direct-Distal Cross-Attention (DDCA). By constructing a residue-level Mutation Perturbation Field from pre-trained protein language models, DDCA leverages predicted contact maps to organize mutation representations into two pathways: the mutation site's immediate contact neighborhood and its multi-hop distal context. To complement this structural decomposition, we further introduce the Property Latent Chain (PLChain), which injects expert-guided supervision of biochemical property changes (e.g., thermostability and optimal pH) into the LLM hidden-state pathway through latent property tokens. On MutaDescribe, RipplePLM improves over mutation-specific baselines on temporal and structural splits; under a matched-backbone comparison, average structural-split ROUGE-L increases from 22.23 to 35.65. Expert evaluation further shows a higher proportion of biologically accurate or relevant descriptions than the mutation-specific baseline. Additional ablations, representation diagnostics, and low-$N$ fitness regression experiments further support the effectiveness of the learned mutation-aware representations. Code: https://github.com/Lyu6PosHao/RipplePLM.

title: Controlling the Sign and Magnitude of the Thermoreflectance Coefficient of Gold-MoS$_2$ Metamaterials
text:
Title: Controlling the Sign and Magnitude of the Thermoreflectance Coefficient of Gold-MoS$_2$ Metamaterials
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Heating a material changes how much light it reflects. This effect, quantified by the thermoreflectance coefficient $C_\mathrm{TR}$, enables temperature sensing, while it is a nuisance for situations where constant reflection is crucial. Whereas temperature detection requires a large $C_\mathrm{TR}$, the latter situation demands it to be as close to zero as possible. Controlling the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ has so far relied on the selection of materials and wavelengths, rather than engineering the coefficient itself. This work demonstrates that the $C_\mathrm{TR}$ of a 50 nm thin gold film on SiO$_2$/Si can be controlled in sign and magnitude by an ultrathin ($<$8 nm) MoS$_2$ film underneath it. Time-resolved thermoreflectance measurements reveal suppression, sign inversion, and revival of the thermoreflectance signal, controlled by three knobs: ($i$) the buried MoS$_2$ thickness, ($ii$) probe wavelength, and ($iii$) ambient temperature. Transfer-matrix simulations using temperature-dependent dielectric functions of gold and MoS$_2$ reproduce all experimental observations, demonstrating an optothermal metamaterial platform with controllable properties. In particular, these (anti-)thermoreflective metamaterial mirrors bring $C_\mathrm{TR}$ under the same interference design rules previously applied to the optical response itself, opening ways to maximize or minimize the temperature dependence of the optical reflectance, tailored to the specific application.

title: MIRAGE: Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization
text:
Title: MIRAGE: Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Deep learning now underpins structure-based drug design, from complex and affinity prediction to ligand ranking and pose generation. Recent co-folding models reportedly approach free-energy-perturbation accuracy at far lower cost. Yet standard evaluation, a single held-out correlation or pooled pose-success rate, cannot separate transferable binding principles from repeated exposure to related protein families in public databases, and practical success depends on genuinely novel targets. We introduce MIRAGE (Measuring Interpolation and Redundancy in Affinity GEneralization), a plug-in benchmark treating historical public family support (through 2019) as an explicit variable, applying a family-support axis to affinity and pose prediction via matched strata, family-disjoint controls, ligand-only baselines, and temporal evaluation. Co-folder affinity accuracy rises sharply with family support, while shallow controls that cannot exploit the test family stay flat, large for co-folders and near zero for every family-disjoint or trivial control. For Nesso-1 it survives covariate, conditioning, balancing, and clustering checks; Boltz-2's endpoint is limited by coverage. It localizes to family support rather than ligand chemistry, approaching a level from family identity alone. Rankings reverse on novel families, where a family-disjoint random forest leads both co-folders, significantly vs Nesso-1. On one external low-support target, neither co-folder beats molecular weight, corroborative rather than population-level evidence. gnina shows significant support dependence in rescoring whereas smina does not; MSA-free pose engines show larger gaps than smina redocking. This redundancy-driven inflation differs from conventional leakage. We propose reporting performance across family support plus excess over a support-insensitive baseline, and release MIRAGE as an installable benchmark and dataset.

title: Generative AI for Enzyme Design and Biocatalysis
text:
Title: Generative AI for Enzyme Design and Biocatalysis
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Sparked by innovations in generative artificial intelligence (AI), the field of protein design has undergone a paradigm shift with an explosion of new models for optimizing existing enzymes or creating them from scratch. After more than one decade of low success rates for computationally designed enzymes, generative AI models are now frequently used for designing proficient enzymes. Here, we provide a comprehensive overview and classification of generative AI models for enzyme design, highlighting models with experimental validation relevant to real-world settings and outlining their respective limitations. We argue that generative AI models now have the maturity to create and optimize enzymes for industrial applications. Wider adoption of generative AI models with experimental feedback loops can speed up the development of biocatalysts and serve as a community assessment to inform the next generation of models.

title: Large deviations for random walks generated by countable groups: a unified approach
text:
Title: Large deviations for random walks generated by countable groups: a unified approach
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We present a unified treatment of various large deviation principles in the context of random walks induced by actions of countable groups. The fundamental notion undergirding the global perspective is that of weakly almost additive random walks, inspired by earlier works on the metric geometry of group actions as well as by recent developments in the theory of nonadditive thermodynamic formalism. We treat large deviations of the renormalized vector-valued distance function from the origin for groups acting simultaneously, by isometries and in a weakly almost additive fashion, on an arbitrary number of metric spaces. The foremost class of examples is provided by group actions with contracting elements, which encompasses, among others, actions on Gromov-hyperbolic spaces and mapping class group actions on Teichmüller spaces. We further establish large deviation principles for quasimorphisms on countable groups, and for random walks generated by compositions of Euclidean isometries; also, we discuss extensions and streamlining of known large deviation results for singular values of random matrix products. Finally, in all the contemplated cases, we investigate the analytic properties of the rate function, leveraging its expression as the Fenchel-Legendre transform of a pressure function for certain nonadditive sequences of potentials on shift spaces.

title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations
text:
Title: Evaluation of upper-scale mechanical parameters of particulate aluminum-based nanocomposites from molecular simulations
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

This paper focuses on the numerical and analytical determination of the mechanical parameters of aluminum-matrix nanocomposites using atomistic-scale simulations within a multiscale modeling framework. Molecular statics simulations were employed to evaluate the tensile and compressive behavior of Al based composites reinforced with nanosized alumina particles. Two classes of atomistic models were investigated. First, a unit-cell model containing a single Al2O3 monocrystal embedded in an aluminum matrix was used to examine the influence of the volume fraction of the ceramic inclusion on the effective mechanical properties. Second, a polycrystalline RVE model comprising an alumina particle was analyzed to assess the effect of the number of Al grains on effective properties. For each case, the mechanical response was characterized by stress-strain curves, enabling the identification of upper-scale material parameters associated with the elastic regime (bulk, shear and Young's modulus) and the damage stage (ultimate strength, ultimate strain, and failure strain). The isotropized elastic constants evaluated from molecular simulations were compared with classical Voigt-Reuss-Hill bounds to assess their applicability in the elastic regime. Finally, atomistic-scale simulation outputs provided insight into the dominant deformation/damage mechanisms (brittle versus ductile) and fracture modes (transgranular versus intergranular).

title: Background Effects on Thermal Free Energy in Conformal Field Theories
text:
Title: Background Effects on Thermal Free Energy in Conformal Field Theories
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We compute background corrections to the thermal free energy of free conformal field theories (CFTs) with a global abelian symmetry defined on a box with all sides infinitely long by turning on a flat gauge field in general dimensions. This result is applied to the U(N) maximally supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory, the ABJ(M) theory, and the free U(N) vector model in four, three, and two spacetime dimensions, respectively. In these examples, the thermal free energies monotonically increase as the background field does, and cross a zero within the valid range. We argue that the systems undergo a phase transition at the zero, where the effective degrees of freedom fall off similarly to the color-confinement one, and that it always occurs if the number of matter fields is greater than a critical value. We comment for this phase transition to circumvent the Mermin-Wagner-Coleman theorem in two spacetime dimensions.

title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
text:
Title: When does text encoding matter for language modeling?
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

UTF-8's role as the de facto encoding standard in language models introduces cross-lingual inequities due to its variable-length design. However, the effect that this encoding choice has on model performance remains largely unexamined. In this work, we investigate how text encoding impacts the performance of byte-level language models, comparing UTF-8 with a wide range of other encoding strategies, including other Unicode-based approaches, language-specific encodings, and our own customized encodings. To facilitate our analysis, we propose Aether: a hybrid encoding scheme that uses script-specific encodings for our target setting while maintaining full Unicode coverage through UTF-8 fallbacks, using this framework to model four orthographically diverse languages. Surprisingly, we find that while languages with information-dense characters (Chinese, Korean) significantly benefit from compressive encodings, languages whose characters carry less information individually (Georgian, Tamil) are largely insensitive to encoding choice. In light of these findings, we argue that text encoding should be a language-specific design decision, rather than a universal default.

title: GENIE: Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics
text:
Title: GENIE: Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic highlighted the ongoing risk infectious diseases pose to society and the value of reliable information on the likely future burden. When forecasting an epidemic at fine spatial resolution, traditionally used mechanistic compartmental model struggle to capture highly complex granular transmission dynamics, resulting in inaccurate and overconfident forecasts. However, detailed Agent-Based Models (ABMs), are challenging to calibrate and are too computationally expensive to use in real-time. Amortized simulation-based inference promises to overcome this difficulty by exploiting the power of machine learning (ML) to perform approximate forecasting at near-real-time using arbitrarily complex models of epidemics. In this work we introduce Generative Neural Inference for Epidemics (GENIE), a spatio-temporal ML-based framework for high-resolution forecasting of the burden of respiratory pathogens. GENIE is designed to reflect two key characteristics of outbreaks: (i) shared biological mechanisms across locations and (ii) location-specific characteristics affecting transmission dynamics. This results in the model architecture having two modules: (i) a Local Infection Encoder - which learns to represent disease dynamics shared across all locations and (ii) a Local Profile Encoder - which learns location-specific representations. Using simulations from a high-resolution spatio-temporal ABM, GENIE is trained to generate samples from an approximate posterior predictive distribution of future epidemic trajectories. Benchmarked against established statistical and ML models, GENIE demonstrates superior performance across a range of measures including the timing and magnitude of peak hospitalisations.

title: Unraveling phenotypic variation in multiscale behavioral dynamics
text:
Title: Unraveling phenotypic variation in multiscale behavioral dynamics
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Behavioral variability reflects differences in internal and external parameters and provides a substrate for natural selection. However, uncovering its structure is challenging because behavior evolves nonlinearly across multiple timescales. Our goal is to reconstruct phenotypic variation from finite behavioral observations without prescribing the scales at which individuals should be compared. To achieve this, we introduce a multiscale dissimilarity that compares dynamics across all statistically resolvable resolutions by constructing reduced transfer operators at progressively finer scales and weighting their differences by finite-sampling uncertainty. This dissimilarity defines a geometry of dynamical phenotypes, which we reconstruct using diffusion maps. We show that the resulting phenotypic coordinates locally follow the parameter directions to which dynamics are most sensitive. We validate our approach in a stochastic model and apply it to bacterial and larval zebrafish behavior. In bacteria, we identify run speed as a major component of inter-individual variability, associated with the chemotaxis protein CheB. In zebrafish, we find that prior prey experience reshapes behavioral dynamics and phenotypic variability, with paramecia experience concentrating fish in a prey-capture-associated region of phenotypic space. Together, these results provide a framework for identifying internal and environmental variables that structure dynamical phenotypes across scales.

title: samQEq: universal charge equilibration for molecules and conductors
text:
Title: samQEq: universal charge equilibration for molecules and conductors
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Charge equilibration assigns atomic charges by equalizing an atomic chemical potential built from electronegativity, hardness and the Coulomb interaction. Under one global constraint it lets charge flow without limit between molecules, which fluctuating-charge models prevent with one neutrality constraint per molecule. A metal needs the opposite: a global constraint and a hardness near zero, and there the charge operator becomes indefinite unless it includes each charge's own self-energy. Here, we present samQEq (solids-and-molecules QEq), a unified charge-equilibration package for LAMMPS that combines the two constructions in one energy functional and one matrix-free solve. An orthogonal projector imposes one neutrality constraint per molecule, and the finite-width self-energy of a Gaussian charge on designated conductor types, narrower than the conductor's own Gaussian, keeps the conductor's part of the operator positive definite at any hardness. On a gold slab carrying a water film, the operator stays definite down to the conductor limit of the model, the metal screens a point charge by a constant amount at every height beyond 4 Å, and the film's charges stay bounded under dynamics. Reciprocal-space electrostatics is evaluated inside the matrix-vector product, and three distinct shielding kernels are run-time settings. We verify the implementation by reproducing a published fluctuating-charge water model without refitting, and the native ReaxFF charge-equilibration step to approximately $10^{-9}\,e$. On a single four-V100 node the largest tested systems run at approximately twice the throughput of a 128-core CPU node. samQEq thus provides one charge-equilibration layer for molecules, conductors and the interfaces between them.

title: AMPERe: an exactly divergence-free quadrature-by-expansion evaluator for near-surface Biot--Savart and virtual-casing fields in fusion geometries
text:
Title: AMPERe: an exactly divergence-free quadrature-by-expansion evaluator for near-surface Biot--Savart and virtual-casing fields in fusion geometries
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Accurate magnetic-field evaluation on and near current-carrying surfaces is a recurring computational bottleneck in magnetic-confinement fusion. As targets approach the source surface, Biot--Savart and virtual-casing kernels become singular, causing standard Gauss--Legendre and upsampled trapezoidal quadratures to lose accuracy. We introduce AMPERe, a quadrature-by-expansion (QBX) evaluator for vector magnetostatic kernels on general three-dimensional, non-axisymmetric tokamak and stellarator geometries. The method develops a spherical-harmonic QBX formulation for the vector Biot--Savart and virtual-casing (Stratton--Chu) fields and expresses the resulting magnetic field as the analytic curl of a regular-solid-harmonic vector potential. This construction yields a divergence-free discrete field at every expansion order, provides analytic derivatives, and enables an a priori separation of truncation, quadrature, and geometric errors. On the rotating-ellipse benchmark of Malhotra et al. [1], QBX maintains a relative error of 2--5 x 10^{-6} throughout the near-surface regime at distance-independent cost, whereas upsampled trapezoidal quadrature exhibits O(1) errors and requires node counts scaling as (h/d)^2. AMPERe is implemented as a header-only, performance-portable Kokkos library supporting CPU and GPU backends, with target-specific and local-correction accelerations validated against the baseline. The method is further demonstrated on realistic Wendelstein 7-X configurations, including sheet-current and virtual-casing field evaluations.

title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
text:
Title: Federation Is Nearly Free, Reasoning Is Not: Tradeoffs for AI Co-Scientists in Protein Characterization Workflows
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Natural language driven autonomous co-scientist workflows involve a fundamental trade-off between flexibility and reasoning at the expense of determinism, reproducibility, and observability. Such agents increasingly must communicate across institutional boundaries, where federation topology can shape latency and cost. We systematically evaluated these tradeoffs using a controlled ablation on a production agentic platform for science. We use a verifiable task: given a protein sequence, we ask an agent to confidently characterize its function by routing across common tools. We compare federation topology, classic RL vs LLM-driven harnesses, language model, and prompt expertise. We also stratify results by protein novelty. We find that the choice of LLM dominated prediction quality far more than topology or prompting (Opus ~92%-94% vs o4-mini ~40%-50%). The PPO policy was nearly as accurate as the best LLM (88%) at zero token cost, fastest latency, and perfect consistency, but yields no reasoning trace. Expert prompted LLMs reached the highest accuracy but were high-cost and less consistent; prompt dependence was largest when the task was hardest. Federation imposed a negligible penalty on performance. These results offer actionable guidance for deploying agents for scientific workflows: for routine, verifiable tasks, a cheap deterministic policy delivers near-frontier accuracy with complete reproducibility, while flexible LLM reasoning is best reserved for open-ended discovery.

title: Benign population landscapes do not transfer to empirical risk minimization in nonsmooth optimization
text:
Title: Benign population landscapes do not transfer to empirical risk minimization in nonsmooth optimization
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Benign landscapes provide a geometric explanation for the success of iterative methods on nonconvex problems arising in data science. The landscape is benign if every local minimizer is global and every other critical point is a strict saddle. For methods that avoid strict saddles, convergence to a critical point therefore implies convergence to a global minimizer. For smooth stochastic optimization, a common strategy for establishing such landscapes proceeds in two steps: $(i)$ establish benign geometry for the population objective---which is often easier to analyze---and $(ii)$ transfer this geometry to the empirical objective using concentration of gradients and Hessians. Recent work has extended saddle-point avoidance guarantees to weakly convex nonsmooth optimization through the notion of active strict saddles. We show, however, that benign population geometry need not transfer to empirical objectives in this setting. Specifically, for robust phase retrieval with Gaussian measurements---a well-studied and highly structured problem---the population objective is benign. Nevertheless, the empirical objective has sharp spurious local minima with probability bounded away from zero as the sample size tends to infinity. This asymptotic probability lower bound is independent of the dimension.

title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
text:
Title: PeptSol: A Translational Benchmark for Protected-Peptide Solubility in Drug Manufacturing
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Liquid-phase peptide synthesis (LPPS) offers a scalable route to peptide manufacturing, but route development still depends on empirical solvent screens because each protected intermediate must be soluble for reaction and recoverable for purification. The protecting groups, terminal modifications, and noncanonical residues that govern this behaviour are poorly represented in existing peptide property benchmarks, limiting the ability to develop and rigorously evaluate molecular representation models for LPPS-relevant prediction tasks. We introduce PeptSol, an open benchmark of 1388 hand-curated protected-peptide solubility measurements with chemistry-aware splits. The measurements span only 84 parent sequences and 101 protected structures, and 92.5% come from a single historical programme. Across seven frozen molecular encoders, the best macro-F1 is 0.843 on binary solubility for the historical subset under a peptide-held-out split; the harder three-class ordinal task reaches 0.614 in that cell.
