In this paper, we set out to demonstrate that the further introduction of two additional latent losses to LeWorldModel, a backward dynamics predictor and an inverse dynamics action predictor, enforces further structure on the latent embedding, leading to further gains in both performance and planning efficiency. These are critical properties for improving the applicability of such methods to real-time model-based control of real-world robots. We demonstrate these gains on standard world model benchmarks and two simulated robot manipulation tasks.

title: Local Convergence of Triadic Closures of Sparse Random Graphs
text:
Title: Local Convergence of Triadic Closures of Sparse Random Graphs
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Triadic closure is a natural mechanism for modeling the clustering phenomenon observed in many real-world networks. Given a possibly random undirected graph $H$, we consider pairs of non-adjacent vertices that have a common neighbor. Conditional on $H$, each such pair is joined by an edge independently and simultaneously, with a probability depending on the degrees of its endpoints and on the number of their common neighbors. The resulting graph is called a triadic closure of $H$. We study the effect of this operation on local convergence. More precisely, we prove that if a sequence of potentially random finite undirected graphs of $\left( H_n \right)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ converges locally in probability to a rooted graph $H^*$, then the corresponding sequence of triadic closures converges locally in probability to the same triadic closure of $H^*$. As a consequence, we obtain a general limit theorem for the clustering coefficients of triadic closures. In particular, we show that the triadic closures can have a strictly positive limiting clustering coefficients even when the limiting clustering coefficients of the parent graph sequence is zero. Finally, we apply our results to several classical sparse random graph models including Erdős-Rényi, configuration, preferential attachment models and compute the limiting clustering coefficients of their triadic closures.

title: Optimal last-iterate rates for the projected decentralized stochastic subgradient method
text:
Title: Optimal last-iterate rates for the projected decentralized stochastic subgradient method
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study the projected decentralized stochastic subgradient (PDSG) method for minimizing the average of convex, possibly nonsmooth local objectives over a common closed convex constraint set and a fixed connected undirected network. We focus on the finite-time expected suboptimality of the last local iterate generated at each node, which is the actual output locally available without time averaging or network averaging. Under the standard stepsizes $α_t=α/\sqrt{t}$ and $α_t=2/(μt)$, we establish $\mathcal{O}(\log T/\sqrt{T})$ and $\mathcal{O}(\log T/T)$ last-local-iterate rates for PDSG when each local objective is convex and the aggregate objective is strongly convex, respectively. To eliminate the logarithmic loss, we introduce a general horizon-dependent stepsize framework, termed cooldown stepsize, that combines a base stepsize with segmentwise scaling over a multistage partition and includes the dyadic construction (Jain et al, SIAM J. Optim., 2021) as a special case. For adapting to decentralized settings, we propose a long-range variation condition to make the stepsize schedule compatible with network contraction. Under this cooldown stepsize, we obtain $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ and $\mathcal{O}(1/T)$ last-local-iterate rates for PDSG in both problem classes, matching the optimal centralized dependence on $T$. Experiments on a lower-bound instance and constrained hinge-loss problems illustrate the predicted terminal behavior of local iterates and the control of consensus error under the cooldown stepsize.

title: Elliptic master integrals and the one-loop cosmological wavefunction
text:
Title: Elliptic master integrals and the one-loop cosmological wavefunction
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Loop corrections to the cosmological wavefunction involve similar integrals to those required for scattering amplitudes. For the one-loop triangle of a conformally coupled scalar, the master integrals are elliptic, and so the triangle wavefunction coefficient was expected to be elliptic as well. Using a bootstrap approach, we compute this triangle coefficient exactly and show that it is not: the elliptic periods cancel, and the flat-space wavefunction coefficient is a combination of dilogarithms. The cancellation occurs because the residue of the loop integrand on the elliptic sector is a flat-space amplitude, rational in the loop momentum. The one-loop box, by contrast, is not polylogarithmic, even with a single external leg at each site. Its threshold discontinuity involves elliptic integrals, which we also give in closed form. For regular-tetrahedron momenta the periods of a K3 surface enter its loop integrand.

title: Confirming HSC strong lens candidates with DESI Spectroscopy. II. Analysis of 80 galaxy-scale systems with lens redshifts above 0.8
text:
Title: Confirming HSC strong lens candidates with DESI Spectroscopy. II. Analysis of 80 galaxy-scale systems with lens redshifts above 0.8
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The total mass distribution of galaxies provides a sensitive probe of the fundamental physical processes governing galaxy evolution, including gas inflow/star formation, AGN/SN feedback, galaxy merging, and the nature of dark matter. State-of-the-art cosmological simulations have therefore made extensive predictions for the evolution of the total-mass density slope. Interestingly, their predictions diverge significantly at high redshift, primarily due to differences in how these key physical mechanisms are implemented. However, measurements of the total-mass structure evolution have been largely confined to low and intermediate redshifts, leaving the regime where model predictions differ most significantly (z>0.8) largely unexplored. In the first paper of this series, we reported the discovery of 84 candidate strong-lens systems with lens redshifts above 0.8. In this work, we perform lens modeling of the 80 galaxy-scale systems to assess their lensing nature. Of these, 71 systems (approximately 90%) exhibit clear lensing features that are well reproduced by our lens models and are therefore classified as secure strong lenses. Another eight systems are classified as probable (5) or possible (3) strong lenses, based on the prominence of their lensing features and the quality of the lens modeling. One system lacking reliable lensing features in current imaging data is classified as a non-lens. Our analysis nearly triples the number of known galaxy-scale strong lenses at z_lens > 0.8, making statistical studies of the total mass structure of high-redshift galaxies possible for the first time. This expanded sample provides an unprecedented opportunity to test the predictions of cosmological simulations and discriminate between competing physical prescriptions.

title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
text:
Title: Recalibration-Aware Optimization of ZEFOZ Operating Points in $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ for Quantum Memories
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Erbium-doped solids like $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}:\mathrm{Y}_2\mathrm{SiO}_5$ have properties that make them suitable for quantum-network memories, however, their unquenched effective electronic spin causes rapid magnetic decoherence. Operating at Zero First-Order Zeeman (ZEFOZ) points allows us to mitigate this, where we evaluate the ZEFOZ landscape for Site-2 $^{167}\mathrm{Er}^{3+}$ by incorporating a full-Hessian spin-Hamiltonian treatment with the anisotropic magnetic-field covariance derived from the native $^{89}\mathrm{Y}$ crystal lattice directly. Operating-point screening criteria were adopted to devise a Pareto-optimal frontier of four transition pairs to balance modeled Y-only magnetic pure-dephasing lifetimes ($T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}$) against microwave control authority. The $ε_{14}\leftrightarrowε_{15}$ transition exhibits the longest modeled Y-bath-induced quadratic pure-dephasing time, $T_{φ,Y}^{(2)}>2.2\times10^5~\mathrm{s}$, while the $ε_{12}\leftrightarrowε_{13}$ transition stood out, achieving a Rabi frequency coefficient of $1.248 \times 10^5~\mathrm{Hz/mT}$. An assumption-based Hamiltonian-uncertainty analysis demonstrates that while uncompensated deviations shift the ZEFOZ condition away from its nominal magnetic-field coordinate, the shifted operating points can be recovered via numerical vector-field recalibration. The Pareto-optimal coordinates were mathematically recovered for all sampled Hamiltonian perturbations, and the $84.1^{\mathrm{st}}$-percentile field relocations ranged from $10.95$ to $27.97~\mathrm{mT}$. The intended operation near $10~\mathrm{mK}$ must be taken into account for the suppression of Er-induced spectral diffusion through electronic-spin polarization, while the extended Y-bath pure-dephasing timescales also remain conditional on the adopted temporal-correlation model.

title: Benchmarking open-source tools for in silico antiviral drug discovery
text:
Title: Benchmarking open-source tools for in silico antiviral drug discovery
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Antivirals are uniquely positioned to be deployed quickly during a new outbreak, especially when repurposed from approved drugs. Yet there are no FDA-approved antivirals for the majority of viral families with pandemic potential. Here we lay out the case for investing in technologies and techniques for antiviral drug discovery and designing antiviral combinations. We present a survey of open source datasets and computational tools for in silico antiviral drug discovery, with a particular focus on the latest AI-based systems and docking tools. We then present our custom dataset of 43,005 viral protein-ligand binding measurements that we curated from BindingDB and other sources. Importantly, we found that 31% of viral protein binding data in BindingDB required polyprotein sequences to be carefully split before the data were suitable for training or testing ML models. Using our custom dataset we fine-tuned the DrugFormDTA binding affinity prediction model (Khokhlov et al. 2025). We then benchmarked 15 open-source binding affinity prediction tools on a custom test set of 853 antiviral compounds spread across 16 different protein targets from 10 virus species. Models tested include Boltz-2, GNINA, FlowDock, Interformer, AutoDock-GPU, and others. We found that Boltz-2 and DrugFormDTA ranked highest overall among ML-based approaches, and GNINA did best among docking approaches, with notable variance across specific viral proteins. Fine-tuning DrugFormDTA on our custom cleaned antiviral dataset boosted performance from $r=0.5$ to $r=0.7$. As part of this work we also compiled a library of approved drugs and a comprehensive list of investigational and approved antiviral drugs that can be viewed at https://antivirals-database.radvac.org. Together, this work provides a foundation for future work towards new tools and platforms for rapid drug repurposing and rapid design of antiviral combinations.

title: Packing and covering random trees
text:
Title: Packing and covering random trees
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study the sizes of optimal packings and coverings of conditioned branching processes by balls with growing radii. We find a universal limiting constant, and thereby establish universality of packing and covering numbers across different scales and different offspring distributions. To be precise, for $μ$ an offspring distribution with mean $1$ and finite variance $σ^2$ we let $T_n$ be a Bienaymé tree with offspring distribution $μ$ conditioned to have size $n$. We prove that the packing number (resp. covering number) of $T_n$ with balls of radii $1\ll γ_n \ll n^{1/2}$ is asymptotically equivalent to $\mathfrak{C} n /(σ^2 γ_n^2)$ (resp. $\mathfrak{C} n /(4σ^2 γ_n^2)$), for a universal constant $\mathfrak{C}$. We also show that the order of limits can be exchanged and that the same limit occurs when we first consider the limiting covering number of $T_n$ by balls of fixed radius $R$, and thereafter let $R$ tend to $\infty$. We then extend these results to the Brownian continuum random tree conditioned to have mass $1$. For this model, we prove that the packing (resp. covering) number with balls of radii $\varepsilon$ are asymptotically equivalent to $\mathfrak{C}/\varepsilon^2$ (resp. $\mathfrak{C}/(4\varepsilon^2)$), for the same constant $\mathfrak{C}$, in contrast with a conjecture by Aldous. Finally, our results answer a question by Devroye, Eide and Pralat on the asymptotic burning number of mean $1$ finite variance Bienaymé trees of size $n$, by showing that it lies between $(c+o(1)) n^{1/3}$ and $(2c+o(1))n^{1/3}$ with high probability, for a constant $c$ that only depends on the offspring variance.

title: Orbital Hall effect from the Wannier function approach
text:
Title: Orbital Hall effect from the Wannier function approach
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Using the Wannier function approach, we develop a gauge-covariant formalism for the orbital angular momentum (OAM) operator and the orbital Hall conductivity (OHC). The Wannier function formulation resolves the position-operator ambiguity inherent to Bloch states, providing a transparent and rigorous theory of orbital transport. Our formalism is validated through a finite-lattice calculation of the Haldane model, where the OAM operator is evaluated exactly from its real-space definition. Our results are also relevant to other orbital phenomena in solids such as the orbital Edelstein effect, orbital torque generation, and the like, where the OAM plays a crucial role.

title: Emergence of the transformer architecture as the score of entropic laws of random measures
text:
Title: Emergence of the transformer architecture as the score of entropic laws of random measures
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We show that the transformer architecture emerges as the score of last-token laws in a natural statistical model of language, where sentences are empirical measures of tokens, a language is a law on $P(S^d)$, and our prior belief is that sentences carry no structure at all. By the maximum-entropy principle, we select the law closest to this prior in relative entropy among those reproducing an observed sentence-level statistic. We discuss the relevance of the statistic in the posterior interaction between tokens and we build a statistic, able to capture that interaction, with Luce's choice axiom truncated at the lowest relational order. This procedure gives the softmax choice rule, with the attention cross-moment as its mean parameter. The query--key matrix is then the Lagrange multiplier of a maximum-entropy problem inside each sentence, and the value matrix the multiplier of the constraint over the language, so that the two are untied. Under the optimal entropic law we then show that a transformer head appears in the score of the last-token law. For ordered sentences, causal masking follows from the masked reference choice rule, and with a next-token cross-moment the score equals one causally masked attention head. We also discuss multi-head attention, weight-tied unembedding, and a heuristic reading of residual blocks as projected Langevin steps.

title: Hydration Free Energies from Local Electronic Structures
text:
Title: Hydration Free Energies from Local Electronic Structures
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Free energies of solvation are crucial to our understanding of chemical reactions, particularly when these take place in water. However, computing changes in free energies associated with the process of immersing arbitrary molecules in an aqueous solution both accurately and efficiently with the use of one universal method remains challenging. By means of atomic decompositions of total (bulk) energies from Kohn-Sham density functional theory in a basis of spatially localized molecular orbitals, the present study enables the computation of hydration free energies from local electronic-structure objects derived in the condensed phase. Specifically, our protocol computes an enthalpy of hydration as the sum of the decomposed change in internal energy of a solute upon solvation and a newly developed term that accounts for the response of the environment, which may then be combined with a standard expression for the corresponding change in entropy. In applications to eight neutral solutes in water, internal energies are all found to converge rapidly and in a smooth manner upon an increase in the size of the solvated cluster, and the corresponding enthalpies and free energies of hydration are likewise found to agree with experimental references within statistical uncertainty.

title: Mean-field BSDEs with jumps under quadratic-exponential growth
text:
Title: Mean-field BSDEs with jumps under quadratic-exponential growth
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

This paper studies the well-posedness of mean-field backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs, for short) with Poisson jumps, where the generator has quadratic growth with respect to $Z$ and exponential growth with respect to $U$, where $(Y,Z,U)$ denotes the solution of this BSDE. First, we prove the existence and the uniqueness of local solutions to mean-field backward stochastic differential equations with jumps (BSDEJs, for short) by using a fixed-point argument. Then, based on these local results, we discuss the solvability of global solutions in the following two cases: in the first one, the generator has linear growth with respect to $Y$ and the corresponding marginal distribution $μ_1$; and in the second one, the generator has subquadratic growth with respect to the marginal distribution $μ_2$ and linear growth with respect to the marginal distribution $μ_3$, corresponding to $Z$ and $U$, respectively. Finally, by employing a Girsanov transformation we establish a comparison theorem for mean-field BSDEJs under quadratic-exponential growth conditions.

title: Particle-loss error correction using $2^l$-step states generated via particle-number-resolving measurement schemes
text:
Title: Particle-loss error correction using $2^l$-step states generated via particle-number-resolving measurement schemes
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We present an iterative scheme for generating finite superpositions of Fock states whose photon numbers differ by $2^l$ ($2^l$-step states). We derive an upper bound on the probability of generating such states. Based on the proposed class of states, we construct several bosonic encodings and compare their performance in correcting particle-loss errors. Our results identify the most efficient encoding, which achieves a higher channel fidelity than previously studied bosonic encodings.

title: Integrals of motion for the deformed $W$-algebra $W_{q,t}(D_l)$
text:
Title: Integrals of motion for the deformed $W$-algebra $W_{q,t}(D_l)$
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

The deformed $W$-algebra $W_{q,t}(D_l)$ of type $D_l$ possesses an infinite family of commuting elements that can be viewed as a two-parameter deformation of the classical Hamiltonians for the KdV hierarchy of type $D_l$; these conserved charges are termed local integrals of motion (IMs). Concurrently, the quantum toroidal algebra $U_q(D_l^{"})$ of type $D_l$ admits four distinct representations via free field realizations, each corresponding to one of the four end nodes of the affine Dynkin diagram. Utilizing these representations, we associate an infinite set of commuting operators with each node, which we define as non-local integrals of motion. Both local and non-local integrals of motion act simultaneously on a shared Fock space consisting of $l+1$ free fields. We provide a direct, computational proof demonstrating that these local and non-local integrals of motion mutually commute.

title: Stochastic evolutionary dynamics in structured populations: Network degree governs evolutionary stability
text:
Title: Stochastic evolutionary dynamics in structured populations: Network degree governs evolutionary stability
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Stochasticity shapes evolutionary dynamics in finite populations beyond the reach of infinite-population theories. Using a stochastic birth--death framework on random regular networks, we establish evolutionary stability criteria for finite structured populations playing three-strategy games and identify critical degree thresholds governing invasion dynamics. Our framework goes beyond two-strategy evolutionary games to reveal that the initial composition of multi-type mutants, together with population structure and stochasticity, shapes the evolutionary fate of the resident population.

title: Maximizing Reaction via Spatial Localization: The Reaction-Flux Landscape and Maximizing Sequences
text:
Title: Maximizing Reaction via Spatial Localization: The Reaction-Flux Landscape and Maximizing Sequences
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We continue our study of a PDE-constrained variational model for maximizing the total reaction flux by optimizing the spatial distribution of catalytic materials, such as enzymes. The total amount of enzyme is fixed, and the substrate concentration is governed by a reaction-diffusion equation with prescribed boundary values. We consider both linear and nonlinear Michaelis-Menten reaction kinetics. In previous work, we constructed a maximizing sequence, computed the first and second variations of the reaction functional, and established the nonexistence of local maximizers. Here, we conduct a more comprehensive analysis. We prove that the functional is strictly concave for linear kinetics but need not be concave or convex for nonlinear kinetics. We also show that no critical points exist. We then characterize maximizing sequences and identify all their possible limiting measures. Our analysis reveals the mechanism of reaction maximization through spatial localization: maximizing sequences concentrate enzymes near the portion of the boundary where the substrate concentration is largest. Moreover, the landscape of the functional defining the total reaction differs between the linear and nonlinear cases, a point less emphasized in applications. Consistent with existing biophysical studies, these findings motivate the development and analysis of regularized models.

title: Reproducibility and Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of Machine-Learning Models for Chronic Kidney Disease Classification
text:
Title: Reproducibility and Leakage-Controlled Evaluation of Machine-Learning Models for Chronic Kidney Disease Classification
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Near-perfect classification of small clinical datasets can hinge on preprocessing, data leakage, missing-data handling, and the evaluation sample. We reproduced a published chronic kidney disease (CKD) classification study on the UCI CKD dataset (400 records, 24 predictors) under explicit leakage controls. A stratified 70:30 development-holdout partition was fixed before any learned preprocessing; imputation, encoding, scaling, supervised feature selection, and PCA were fitted only within training folds. Nine classifiers, three feature representations, and three missing-data strategies were compared by 5x3 repeated stratified cross-validation and ranked on training cross-validation only (ties reported); a frozen set of finalists was evaluated once on the holdout (discrimination, calibration, Brier score), treated as a locked historical internal sample. Ablation, grouped SHAP values, three further seeds, and post hoc sensitivity analyses examined robustness. The top-ranked selected-feature pipeline (KNN imputation, Extra Trees) reached a repeated cross-validation accuracy of 0.9869 and a holdout accuracy of 0.9833 (exact 95% interval 0.9411-0.9980). PCA (27 components, 95.96% of variance) gave only a marginal, seed-dependent advantage over interpretable original-feature representations, and several pipelines were statistically indistinguishable. Nested resampling of the selection procedure gave an outer accuracy of 0.9845, 0.0095 below the top-ranked pipeline on the same folds; missingness indicators alone yielded a ROC area of 0.85-0.88, and removing renal, urinary, and hematologic fields cut accuracy to 0.89. High internal performance persisted after leakage controls but appears driven largely by clinically proximal laboratory and urinalysis variables and CKD-associated missingness; it is not clinical validation, and external, prospective evaluation remains necessary.

title: Observation of light-induced topological state in graphene
text:
Title: Observation of light-induced topological state in graphene
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Driving quantum materials with light can reshape not only their electronic band structures but also the geometry of their electronic wavefunctions. In graphene, circularly polarized light is predicted to open gaps at the Dirac points and induce a pseudospin texture and Berry curvature characteristic of the Haldane model, realizing a Floquet Chern insulator. Transport and all-optical measurements have provided evidence for a light-induced anomalous Hall response, but cannot resolve the underlying electronic states in both energy and momentum space. Time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy has revealed Floquet-Bloch sidebands and hybridization gaps at crossings between Floquet bands. However, these experiments used linearly polarized driving, which preserves time-reversal symmetry and thus does not induce a topological phase. Here, we combine circular-dichroic time-resolved extreme-ultraviolet momentum microscopy with ab initio theory to investigate graphene driven by circularly polarized light. We observe a pump-induced photoemission circular dichroism near the Dirac point that reverses sign with pump helicity and across the Dirac energy, in agreement with our calculations. These results link the measured dichroic response to the light-induced pseudospin texture and its associated Berry curvature, providing spectroscopic evidence for the Floquet-engineered topological insulating state in graphene.

title: Covariance Eigenspace Provides Latent Attribution of Longitudinal Effects in Brain Age Gap
text:
Title: Covariance Eigenspace Provides Latent Attribution of Longitudinal Effects in Brain Age Gap
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Brain age gap is a promising machine learning (ML)-driven bio\-marker of accelerated biological aging and is derived from neuroimaging data. Recent works on coVariance neural networks (VNN) for brain age gap prediction have provided an explainable and anatomically verifiable framework for brain age gap prediction. Notably, VNN outcomes are derived by filtering inputs along covariance eigenvectors, providing a mechanism for explaining their decisions in terms of latent (orthogonal) vectors. In this paper, we investigate the longitudinal brain age gap effects in a Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) cohort using a VNN-driven brain age gap prediction framework. Specifically, using Integrated Gradients (IG) as the attribution mechanism, our results demonstrate that the eigenspectrum of the anatomical covariance matrix explains the different longitudinal effects observed in brain age gap in amyloid positive vs amyloid negative subcohorts more prominently than individual brain regions ($83.2\%$ with the leading eigenvector versus a maximal value of $7.7\%$ for any brain region). Therefore, the covariance-based latent explanation identifies a key coordinated input pattern that carries most of the observed longitudinal effect in brain age gap.

title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
text:
Title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.

title: Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
text:
Title: Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

title: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction
text:
Title: Syn2DRE: Synergistic Dual Teacher-Student Framework for Document-level Relation Extraction
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Document-level Relation Extraction (DocRE) aims to identify relations between entities across a document but typically relies on costly large-scale annotations. While pseudo-labelling enables the use of low-quality data, existing methods often suffer from inefficiency and confirmation bias. To address these challenges, we propose Syn2DRE, a semi-supervised framework that combines self-supervised learning with cross-supervision in a lightweight teacher-student architecture to produce more reliable pseudo-labels. Additionally, we introduce a unified end-to-end training strategy to further improve efficiency of the framework. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that Syn2DRE consistently outperforms prior state-of-the-art semi-supervised DocRE methods.

title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
text:
Title: OpticalRAG: Pixel-Space Compression for Token-Efficient Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is bottlenecked by the token budget of large language models: feeding long documents into the context window is expensive, while aggressive textual compression discards fine-grained information that is irreversibly lost in a one-dimensional token sequence. We argue that this bottleneck is not fundamental to information density but to the choice of compression \emph{modality}. Modern visual encoders can pack the contents of a rendered text page into roughly a hundred visual tokens with little semantic loss, opening a new compression-fidelity tradeoff that purely textual methods cannot reach. We present \textbf{OpticalRAG}, a framework that renders documents as page images, encodes them with a frozen vision encoder, and distills the retrieved visual tokens into as few as $16$ injected tokens before passing them to the LLM. Two ingredients make this work without expensive cross-modal training: (i) \emph{Encoder-Bridged Retrieval}, which projects text-query states into the visual feature space of the frozen encoder, through a projection shared with the compressor, to retrieve visual tokens from a text query, with no contrastive training; and (ii) \emph{Query-Driven Distillation}, a lightweight cross-attention compressor that condenses the retrieved visual tokens into a small set of query-conditioned prefix tokens. On LongBench-v2, BAMBOO, and LooGLE-v2, OpticalRAG achieves the best compression-aware accuracy (CAP) on all three benchmarks while injecting only $16$ tokens, and improves the closed-book Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbone by $5.17$ points on LongBench-v2.Code is available at https://github.com/brighterr/OpticalRAG.

title: Existence of the thermodynamic limit for the Hopfield model
text:
Title: Existence of the thermodynamic limit for the Hopfield model
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We prove that the quenched pressure of the Hopfield model with $K\simαN$ i.i.d. symmetric Rademacher patterns has a thermodynamic limit at every load $α\in(0,\infty)$, finite inverse temperature and uniform external field, with no replica-symmetry, order-parameter concentration or non-condensation hypothesis required. The limit is the supremum over $r$ of limiting pressures of mixed models with $r$ binary patterns in a Gaussian bulk. Via the Hubbard--Stratonovich representation we extract the finitely many patterns whose hidden coordinates exceed $δ\sqrt N$; a collective interpolation replaces the other binary patterns by Gaussian ones with error $O(δ^2)$ uniform in the volume, and convex concentration on the discrete cube controls the disorder-dependent choice of retained patterns. For the mixed models we prove a Gaussian hidden-spin truncation bound uniform in the volume and in an arbitrary Ising potential, and convergence for Gaussian bulks with finitely many site-field types, reducing to results of Ho and of Chen, Ho and Issa on non-convex vector spin glasses with compact spins. For Gaussian patterns we give an alternative proof of the existence result announced by Camilli, Contucci and Mingione, extended to a uniform field and an extra binary pattern. In both cases the pressure has exponentially small deviation probabilities and converges a.s.; internal energy and entropy converge wherever the limit is differentiable. An extra binary Mattis pattern admits a scalar variational reduction. At zero field the Rademacher pressure dominates the Gaussian one with an extra binary pattern, which dominates the pure Gaussian one. No explicit formula is given. The proofs were generated through extensive interaction with the AI models Claude (Opus~5.5) and ChatGPT (Sol~6.1), based on the problem formulation and guidance of the authors.

title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method
text:
Title: Efficient quantum ultraspherical transform and a well-conditioned quantum spectral method
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Solving differential equations is a promising application of quantum computing. Spectral methods, where the solution is represented by coefficients in a basis, are particularly well suited to quantum solvers because their structured discretizations can enable efficient linear-algebra operations while providing rapid convergence. Their quantum implementation, however, requires an efficient transform between amplitudes encoding function values and amplitudes encoding expansion coefficients. This work develops two key components of a quantum spectral method. First, we construct the quantum ultraspherical transform (QUT) for orthonormal ultraspherical polynomials, a basis that supports sparse and well-conditioned discretizations of differential equations. For the basis parameters $m=0$ and $1$, this transform reduces to the discrete cosine and sine transforms with known efficient circuits. Our contribution covers every fixed integer $m\geq2$: for dimensions $N$ with $N+m=2^n$, where $n$ is the number of qubits, the QUT achieves error at most $\varepsilon$ using a gate count polynomial in $n$ and $\log(1/\varepsilon)$. The construction builds on the quantum Fourier transform, augmented by approximations whose accuracy guarantees are independent of $N$. Second, we develop a quantum spectral solver for regular linear ordinary differential equations based on the QUT. Under suitable boundary conditions and data-access assumptions, preconditioning keeps condition numbers bounded independently of the basis size, allowing the solution state to be prepared at polylogarithmic cost in system size and inverse error. Together, these contributions provide a framework for quantum spectral methods with the potential to solve linear differential equations efficiently.

title: CoRA-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation by Context Selectors Under Token Budgets
text:
Title: CoRA-Bench: Evaluating Evidence Preservation by Context Selectors Under Token Budgets
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Context selection can reduce input length during long-input inference but can remove evidence required to answer a query. We introduce CoRA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating evidence preservation under shared token budgets. We compare head and tail truncation, BM25, dense retrieval, dense retrieval with reranking, LLMLingua-2, and Provence across BABILong, LOONG Financial Spotlight, a custom NoLiMa diagnostic, and LongMemEval. Evidence-preservation results reveal task-dependent tradeoffs: BM25 achieves 0.921 supporting-fact recall on BABILong at 128K, dense retrieval and dense reranking each achieve 0.908 needle recall on NoLiMa at 64K, and dense retrieval achieves 0.993 answer-bearing-turn recall on LongMemEval at 64K. Evidence, token retention, and complementary reader evaluations use the same selected contexts. Reader evaluations use dataset-native answer metrics and three runs on the same questions, with paired bootstrap confidence intervals. At a 32K budget, BM25 achieves 46.20% BABILong answer accuracy and dense retrieval achieves 71.13% LongMemEval accuracy. The results show that method rankings vary across evidence types and between evidence recall and downstream accuracy.

title: Replication of Thermal Comfort Cohort Models: No Support for Improved Thermal Preference Prediction
text:
Title: Replication of Thermal Comfort Cohort Models: No Support for Improved Thermal Preference Prediction
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Cohort comfort models (CCMs) aim to overcome the extensive individual data requirements of personal comfort models (PCMs) by grouping occupants based on demographic and psychometric characteristics (cold start) or similar thermal preferences (warm start). We evaluated the validity of the reported CCM performance gains through (i) a methodological assessment of the original study, (ii) a replication using one of the two original datasets (DORN: 20 participants, 6 months) under a revised experimental protocol, and (iii) a replication using an independently collected dataset (PersonAI: 72 participants, 4 weeks). Classification performance was evaluated using F1-micro, as in the original study, and F1-macro to account for class imbalance. Under F1-micro, a trivial baseline that always outputs the majority class performed on par with cohort models. Under F1-macro, all cohort models achieved lower median scores than a simple baseline that makes random predictions based on the estimated distribution of thermal preferences. In our methodological assessment we identified the following key issues: Limited data per participant and per minority class, reliance on a metric insensitive to class imbalance, missing trivial baselines, inadequate cross validation strategy, and multiple occurrences of information leakage. Our findings challenge the original study's conclusion that CCMs improve thermal preference prediction. CCMs did not outperform simple class-distribution baselines. Future studies should improve experimental designs, including controlled thermal conditions, to obtain sufficient observations across thermal preference classes.

title: Structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operators for Long-time Cahn-Hilliard Dynamics under Coarse Temporal Supervision
text:
Title: Structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operators for Long-time Cahn-Hilliard Dynamics under Coarse Temporal Supervision
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Accurate long-time prediction of Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, particularly in the late-stage coarsening regime, is computationally demanding because it requires simulations over extended physical time. Various machine learning approaches have been developed to speed up the simulations through efficient surrogate evaluations. While the learned map can be accurate over a single learned interval, small prediction error will accumulate when the map is repeatedly applied in a long-time prediction, leading to large numerical errors. In this work, we identify the structure function for the coarsening dynamics of the Cahn-Hilliard equation and propose a two-stage structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learning framework. Stage~I introduces a bound-conforming FNO (bcFNO) with a soft, magnitude-dependent amplitude penalty. Stage~II retains the bound-conforming objective and supplements it with structure-function regularization, yielding a structure-preserving FNO (spFNO) that corrects late-stage coarsening statistics. Numerical experiments on the various spatial resolutions and reference-solver time steps suggest that the bcFNO stabilizes the long-time prediction by suppressing large amplitude excursions, without changing the low online cost of the FNO. Furthermore, the structure-function term consistently reduces discrepancies in the normalized structure function and provides further correction in associated late-stage coarsening quantities, including the $L^3(t)$ growth trend and the scaling collapse. These results indicate that our multi-stage implementation of physical principles in operator learning could be applied to other multiscale systems with statistical scaling, such as the functionalized Cahn--Hilliard equations and turbulence, provided that the state constraints and statistical observables are adapted to the governing dynamics.

title: Inversion-Free High-Dimensional Counterfactual Inference
text:
Title: Inversion-Free High-Dimensional Counterfactual Inference
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Counterfactual inference is the task of answering hypothetical "what-if" queries about a unit, given an observational dataset, modeling assumptions, and a causal graph. This enables a modeler to reason about hypothetical scenarios that cannot otherwise be answered without assumptions or a causal graph. The simpler case involves a causal graph with scalar 1-D variables that denote different attributes in the data-generation process. While the literature is clear in the 1-D case, extending this to settings with high-dimensional nodes (e.g., images) remains challenging. Conventionally, in the literature, methods recover the latent state from the factual image (inversion), generate counterfactual attributes from the graph, and render the counterfactual image from the latent state using the updated attributes. In our work, we investigate the necessity of the inversion step in computing high-dimensional counterfactuals. We first discuss moving from the scalar 1-D case to the higher-dimensional case. Secondly, we discuss the relevance of the inversion step and evaluate an inversion-free counterpart repurposed from the image-editing literature. Finally, on image datasets such as CelebA and ADNI, we benchmark our approach using two measures: namely, effectiveness and identity preservation. While effectiveness is a measure of how faithfully the counterfactual attribute is rendered, identity preservation measures whether the same unit (image) is being rendered, both of which are crucial for high-dimensional counterfactual inference. We present the tradeoffs of using inversion-based and inversion-free approaches in our work.

title: First-Principles Investigation of Multimodal Toxic Gas Sensing in Carbon-Tuned hBN-Graphene Alloys: Chemiresistive, Work-Function, and Optical Responses
text:
Title: First-Principles Investigation of Multimodal Toxic Gas Sensing in Carbon-Tuned hBN-Graphene Alloys: Chemiresistive, Work-Function, and Optical Responses
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Compact, reliable, and cost-effective gas sensors have become a highly demanding subject for safety management in the medical sector, chemical manufacturing, food quality monitoring, agriculture, and industrial safety. Hazardous gas emissions need to be controlled and monitored with fast-responsive and highly sensitive sensing devices. A first-principles study employing density functional theory (DFT) was used to investigate the adsorption behavior of Cl2, CO, CO2, NO, NO2, and HCN gas molecules with our proposed alloys, which consisted of hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) and graphene (Gr). The alloy consisting of 22% carbon (BNGr-2) was found to be most competent for sensing Cl2, CO, CO2, and HCN with sufficient adsorption energy, charge transfer, and bandgap alteration. However, NO and NO2 gas molecules showed more engagement with 33% carbon-proportioned alloy (BNGr-3) in terms of adequate gas sensing properties. NOx gases exhibited the most chemiresistive sensitivity towards the adsorbents. Other gases also showed significant chemiresistive sensitivity and distinct selectivity ratios, which would facilitate these alloys as chemiresistive sensors. Besides, noticeable work function variation (~20%) of these systems manifested potential as work function based sensors. Cl2 and NO2 showed strong physical adsorption, while the rest of the gases were weakly to moderately physisorbed, resulting in very short recovery times (10-1 ~ 10-6 seconds). Additionally, the distinctive absorption spectra observed for the gas analyte systems highlighted the potential of the proposed alloys as optical gas sensors. Temperature variation revealed that all gas molecules can be freed from the adsorbent BNGr-2 at 425 K. These findings imply hBN-Gr alloys as promising gas sensors for pollution auditing.

title: Static Vacuum Geometry Encodes Gravitational Collapse and Cosmology
text:
Title: Static Vacuum Geometry Encodes Gravitational Collapse and Cosmology
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We show that, within covariant Hamiltonian gravity in spherical symmetry, a prescribed one-parameter family of static vacuum geometries uniquely determines the local dynamics of gravitational collapse coupled to irrotational dust, despite the nonuniqueness of the underlying gravitational Hamiltonian. We further derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which the resulting dynamics admits a homogeneous and isotropic cosmological sector. These conditions establish a two-way correspondence between static vacuum geometries and modified Friedmann dynamics and impose a universal restriction on the spatial-curvature dependence of the latter. Our results provide a criterion for determining whether independently proposed black-hole and cosmological models can arise from a common covariant gravitational theory.

title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
text:
Title: FERN: Cross-Benchmark Table Retrieval for Text-to-SQL with Frozen Retrievers and Learned Ranking
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Text-to-SQL systems over large pooled catalogs must first retrieve the tables a question needs. We compare against the published table recall of RASL, which uses Claude 3.5 models to extract keywords and select tables, on pooled BIRD, Spider, and Fiben catalogs. FERN (Feature-Engineered Ranking with No generative LLM) instead fuses three frozen retrievers into 100 candidates, describes each with up to 120 features, and reorders them with LightGBM rankers fitted once on BIRD's training questions. On Spider, where it was not fitted, its candidate pool alone reaches RASL's published recall at fifteen tables (98.0), and the ranker raises the share of questions with every gold table in the top five (complete@5) from 83.9% to 95.6%. At five tables, FERN's recall is within one point of RASL's on Spider (96.7 vs 97.0) and on BIRD with its evidence hints (96.6 vs 97.5), and 8.2 points below on BIRD without them (89.3). On 121 real BEAVER questions, without BEAVER fitting, its recall at fifteen (82.1) falls between two BEAVER-trained retrievers (80.8, 84.5), but its complete@15 is below both (49.6 vs 54.5 and 62.0). On Fiben, it falls far short at fifteen tables (54.2 vs 69.2, different question sets), although its recall at fifty is numerically close to RASL's question-only retrieval result (80.7 vs 79.4). On BIRD dev with evidence, non-retrieval features raise complete@5 by 7.7 points over retrieval signals alone. On BIRD dev, median latency is 208 ms per question on one A100, without hosted model calls.

title: CARM: Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking for Reliable Scientific Super-Resolution
text:
Title: CARM: Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking for Reliable Scientific Super-Resolution
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Deep learning-based super-resolution (SR) can reconstruct fine-scale Earth-observation fields from coarse observations, but reconstruction accuracy alone does not provide a calibrated rule for identifying reliable spatial regions. Conformal Mask Calibration (CMC), built on conformal risk control, converts a spatial uncertainty score into a trust mask and controls the expected worst-case local distortion under exchangeability. However, its fixed threshold can become miscalibrated in Earth-observation streams affected by seasonality and episodic events. We propose $\textit{CARM}$ (Conformal Adaptive Risk Masking), a statistical framework for adaptive spatial risk control under temporal distribution shift. CARM maintains experts with heterogeneous update rates and aggregates their threshold proposals online using an asymmetric surrogate loss, balancing rapid adaptation to distribution changes against stability during relatively stationary periods. All updates are causal and use only mature feedback available after a fixed delay, allowing CARM to operate with any SR model that provides a spatial uncertainty score. We prove that the time-averaged mask-conditioned risk converges to at most $α$ at an $O(1/T)$ rate, without distributional assumptions and for any choice of aggregation weights across experts. On a daily South China Sea chlorophyll-$\textit{a}$ SR stream, CARM reduces the empirical violation rate from $43.49\%$ to $9.38\%$ and the moving-average exceedance frequency from $47.29\%$ to $1.22\%$ at $α=0.10$, while retaining a non-trivial trusted region. Experiments on ERA5 wind and OSTIA sea-surface temperature further show consistent relative improvements across multiple SR backbones.

title: acousticHelmholtzFoam: an MPI-parallel unstructured finite-volume solver for frequency-domain acoustics in heterogeneous two-phase media with perfectly matched layers
text:
Title: acousticHelmholtzFoam: an MPI-parallel unstructured finite-volume solver for frequency-domain acoustics in heterogeneous two-phase media with perfectly matched layers
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

acousticHelmholtzFoam is an OpenFOAM application that computes time-harmonic acoustic pressure fields in heterogeneous gas-liquid media on unstructured polyhedral meshes. The complex pressure is stored as real and imaginary volume fields, the material coefficients are constructed from a volume-of-fluid phase fraction with geometric face-fraction averaging, and open boundaries are truncated by Cartesian perfectly matched layers (PMLs) whose damping tensor is generated by the companion utility setPMLFields. The two coupled real-valued equations are discretized with the cell-centred finite-volume operators of OpenFOAM and assembled explicitly, including processor couplings and boundary contributions, into a distributed PETSc matrix that is solved by default with the MUMPS sparse direct solver. The solver writes pressure amplitude, complex velocity, acoustic radiation pressure and time-averaged momentum flux for acoustic-force evaluation. This paper documents the implemented equations, the case interface, the assembly and solution algorithm, the build procedure and the test infrastructure. A layered gas-liquid-PML case with an analytical solution serves as an end-to-end regression: on 8000 cells the whole-domain relative complex-pressure error is $1.197\times10^{-3}$, and serial and MPI solutions on up to eight ranks agree to within $10^{-12}$ in relative $L_2$ norm. A single-axis acoustic-levitator height sweep with constant-volume spheroidal drops demonstrates the two-phase material input and the force output, and strong- and problem-size-scaling measurements characterize the direct-solver workflow. The numerical formulation and its verification are presented in a companion paper (arXiv:2610.01593).

title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems
text:
Title: Bi-FORK: Generative Modeling of High-Dimensional Bifurcating Systems
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Bifurcations are ubiquitous in physical systems, from structural buckling to fluid and climate dynamics, yet they remain largely unexplored in deep learning. At a symmetry-breaking bifurcation, a single input admits multiple equally valid solutions, violating the one-to-one assumption underlying most learned physical surrogates. We introduce Bi-FORK, a generative framework for learning these one-to-many solution maps in high-dimensional systems. Bi-FORK generates complete trajectories through latent flow matching, preserving space and time coherence, and uses repulsion-guided sampling to recover distinct solution branches in a single amortized pass. We evaluate Bi-FORK on buckling beams, mechanical metamaterials, and Allen-Cahn phase separation, spanning continuous, discrete, and field-valued bifurcations with discretizations up to 260,000 points. Bi-FORK recovers the multimodal solution structure while scaling several orders of magnitude beyond prior approaches, opening generative modeling to high-dimensional bifurcating physical systems.

title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. II. Adsorption of nonmetal atoms (N, P, As, and Sb) on Ga-terminated surfaces
text:
Title: Universal model of the growth of III-V tetrahedral semiconductors on polar surfaces: pyramids and glue atoms. II. Adsorption of nonmetal atoms (N, P, As, and Sb) on Ga-terminated surfaces
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Ab initio calculations were used to simulate the adsorption processes on Ga-terminated surfaces of tetrahedral semiconductors: GaN, GaP, GaAs and GaSb. The considered adsorbates are nonmetal species, i.e., nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, and antimony on wurtzite gallium nitride, i.e., GaN(0001) surfaces, zinc blende gallium phosphide, i.e., GaP(111), gallium arsenide, GaAs(111), and gallium antimonide, GaSb (111) surfaces. The cases investigated include single adsorbed nonmetal atoms and full coverage, i.e. theta=1 of these surfaces. The calculated results include the stable sites and the energies of the single adsorbed atoms: located at H3 sites at low coverage and in on-top positions at high coverage for GaP, GaAs and GaSb. At high nitrogen coverage, the N2 admolecules are formed, weakly attached to the surface. The calculated electronic properties of the single-adatom systems include the band diagrams of the slabs in real and momentum space, the energies of the quantum states. In addition, the overlaps of the quantum states of the nonmetal adatoms and the nearest topmost surface Ga atoms are given. The full coverage data include the atomic configurations and the bond energies of the adsorbed layers. The electronic properties include the above-mentioned data for single adatoms, together with additional properties related to interactions between adsorbed atoms. The evaporation stability analysis confirms that the adatoms stabilize the topmost Ga atoms against detachment because of the high energy barrier of DE > 3 eV which is further increased to DE > 4 eV by coverage located at H3 sites. Thus, growth simulations should employ unreconstructed Ga-terminated surfaces covered by nonmetal atoms located at on-top positions.

title: Penguin data reanalyzed via Computational Taxonomy
text:
Title: Penguin data reanalyzed via Computational Taxonomy
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

We employ Computational Taxonomy (CT) to reanalyze the penguin data set penguins_lter by validating and addressing two biological issues: Sexual Size Dimorphism (SSD) and mate-selection criteria. Via Scientific Data Analysis (SDA) computing, CT constructs a Taxonomic Hierarchy by splitting Species first and then Sex, without involving Island, to achieve less complexity. This Taxonomic Hierarchy validates SSD as a branch comparison: (Species, Sex = Male)-vs-(Species, Sex = Female), upon which SDA explores all potential pieces of associative information from all covariate feature-sets, including interacting effects from order-2 to order-4, and then confirms them via their idiosyncratic reliability checks. The collective of confirmed information pieces are displayed on a heatmap platform to manifest underlying dynamics of SSD with explicit block-structured heterogeneity found within males and females. SSD dynamics is explained through mechanistic dependence pertaining to one chief factor consisting of up to 8 feature-sets: Body-Mass coupled by combinations of {Culmen-length,Culmen-depth, Flipper-length}, and two minor factors consisting of low-order combinations of {Culmen-length,Culmen-depth, Flipper-length}. Such Intra-Sex heterogeneity invalidates all Logistic regression modeling on SSD in the original paper. Further, we explore potential mate-selection criteria through the data-frame of Nest-ID within-species homogeneity.

title: When AI Generates Covariates: Causal Typing and Estimand Drift in Sequential Experiments
text:
Title: When AI Generates Covariates: Causal Typing and Estimand Drift in Sequential Experiments
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

AI-generated covariates from notes, conversations, images, and wearable streams can change the causal question when their roles are left unspecified. A generated feature may represent a treatment version, pre-action state, history, design variable, mediator, outcome proxy, observation process, or intercurrent event; these roles are not interchangeable. We formulate a causal type discipline for sequential experiments: a versioned representation map, a causal role classifier, a claim-status filter, and an estimand lock. The lock fixes a standardized proximal effect before generated covariates enter the analysis. Under audit correctness and standard identification assumptions, admissible role assignments preserve this estimand. We apply the established conditional-covariance characterization of compression bias to substitution of generated representations for design-relevant states. A standardized decomposition separates compression, conditional-law, and standardization drift. Further results cover mediator adjustment, post-action leakage, marker-intervention conflation, outcome-guided discovery, and state-measurement error. Cluster-level orthogonal estimators distinguish empirical and superpopulation targets under repeated sessions and missing outcomes. Simulations show that refinement helps when it retains design-relevant information, whereas design erasure, leakage, and same-data marker selection can produce bias or undercoverage. The framework places causal semantics and claim status before confirmatory inference with generated representations.

title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation
text:
Title: The Cost of Working Memory in Streaming Mean Estimation
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

A streaming estimator must compute from the evidence that fits in memory. We determine when storing an accurate mean is easier than computing it. For Gaussian mean estimation over the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we establish the minimax rate under squared error with $K$ persistent states, a known horizon, and a public time index: $\min\{1, K^{-2/d}+\frac{d}{n} (1+\frac{\log(ed)}{1+(\log K)/d})\}$. Unrestricted computation followed by $K$-level encoding has rate $\min\{1,d/n+K^{-2/d}\}$. At a fixed sufficiently small error, statistically optimal sample size therefore requires order $d\log d$ working bits, while order $d$ bits suffice to store the answer. The lower bound tracks repeated state compression through an entropy potential obtained by Gaussian smoothing. A matching construction combines a multiscale modular counter with workspace reused across coordinate groups. In one dimension, it attains the terminal rate $n^{-1}+K^{-2}$. Any fixed confidence requirement that the realized loss not exceed the zero baseline preserves these rates. Increasing confidence creates a further memory requirement: at fixed nontrivial risk in every fixed dimension, failure probability $e^{-γn}$ requires and permits order $\log n$ working states for sufficiently small fixed $γ>0$. In the scalar problem, a fixed terminal alphabet suffices under the same protection. These bounds separate the memory needed to represent an answer from the memory needed to accumulate evidence and validate a decision.

title: GPU acceleration of the numerical-atomic-orbital DFT code OpenMX with GEMMul8: performance and numerical agreement on consumer and HPC GPUs
text:
Title: GPU acceleration of the numerical-atomic-orbital DFT code OpenMX with GEMMul8: performance and numerical agreement on consumer and HPC GPUs
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We integrate GEMMul8, a library that emulates FP64 matrix multiplication on INT8 Tensor Cores, into the GPU version of the numerical-atomic-orbital first-principles code OpenMX 4.0. The GEMMul8 configuration is compared against the cuBLAS FP64 configuration within each of two environments, a consumer GeForce RTX 5080 and an HPC-oriented H100 PCIe, for the four computational paths formed by collinear (CL) or noncollinear (NCL) spin and band or $Γ$-point-cluster solvers. In fixed-work measurements that completed 25 SCF iterations, the diagonalization section of a 384-atom CL band calculation on the RTX 5080 is accelerated by a factor of 2.1 and the total run time by 1.8; a 512-atom CL cluster calculation, which uses only real matrix products in contrast to the CL band calculation, still gains a factor of 1.5 in the diagonalization section. On the H100, GEMMul8 provides little additional acceleration of the diagonalization section. In an accuracy test on a 216-atom Si system in which one atom was displaced by 0.05 angstrom, all 24 configurations were converged using an SCF convergence criterion of $10^{-8}$; every configuration converged at the same iteration within each path, and the differences between GEMMul8 and cuBLAS are at most $2\times10^{-12}$ Ha in the total energy and $7\times10^{-12}$ Ha/Bohr in force components.

title: From Gaussian to stable and back: Non-Pareto points in growing dimension
text:
Title: From Gaussian to stable and back: Non-Pareto points in growing dimension
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study the number of non-Pareto points in two high-dimensional models: a homogeneous Poisson point process and a fixed-size sample of independent uniform points in the unit cube. A point is non-Pareto if some other sample point is coordinatewise less than or equal to it. As the dimension grows on the logarithmic scale of the intensity or sample size, the asymptotic behavior exhibits a surprising sequence of transitions: from Gaussian to stable fluctuations, back to Gaussian, then to a Poisson limit at the sparsity threshold, followed by the eventual disappearance of non-Pareto points. We identify the critical thresholds, normalizations, and limiting laws in both models. Notably, the return to Gaussianity occurs while the stability index remains strictly below $2$ and is driven by a change in the dominant fluctuation mechanism. Moreover, in part of the returning Gaussian regime, the natural normalization is the square root of the expected count rather than its standard deviation. At the stable--Gaussian transition, the two mechanisms can coexist, giving rise to a sum of independent stable and Gaussian random variables.

title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
text:
Title: Persistent Retrieval for Conversational Agents: A Study of Retrieval Efficiency
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Conversational agents can retrieve information directly or delegate retrieval to a subagent. This design choice affects how retrieval history is maintained, what context each model call receives, and what information must be re-retrieved in follow-up questions. We compare three designs: skill-based retrieval in the main agent, a non-persistent retrieval subagent that generates a findings response, and our persistent retrieval subagent, which maintains retrieval history across turns and returns retrieved evidence directly to the main agent. Our approach also allows the main agent to request corrections from the same subagent. We evaluate the three designs on enterprise questions posed independently, within shared conversations, and as dependent follow-ups. Across five multi-turn settings, our approach uses 43.3% fewer recorded agent-model tokens and incurs 45.0% lower estimated API cost than skill-based retrieval, while reducing average response time by 9.1%. Compared with non-persistent retrieval, it reduces response time by 15.6 seconds per question, while using 65.1% more tokens and incurring 29.1% higher estimated API cost. Our approach shifts the retrieval subagent from producing synthesized responses to maintaining retrieval state and supplying evidence that the main agent can directly evaluate and use for answer generation.

title: Analysis of Transient Microscopy Data in Reciprocal Space
text:
Title: Analysis of Transient Microscopy Data in Reciprocal Space
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Transient microscopy has evolved to include a family of well-established techniques for studying the spatiotemporal dynamics of excited states in a variety of materials systems. In these methods, a laser pulse is focused to locally excite a material, and the subsequent evolution of the excited species is visualized to extract transport parameters such as diffusivities. Typically, transport coefficients are extracted from experimental datasets using curve-fitting methods to analyze the change in the mean squared displacement (MSD) of the spatial profiles over time. However, this approach can lead to inaccurate or misleading diffusivity values under many common experimental conditions, and is only formally accurate for the case of a single diffusing species. In this work, we introduce a new approach to the analysis of transient microscopy data based on the evolution of profile shapes in reciprocal space. We use simulated datasets to quantitatively analyze the performance of our proposed methods and compare them to current state-of-the-art analysis techniques. We demonstrate that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods have the highest overall performance in terms of accuracy and precision for normal diffusive transport over a range of realistic initial conditions and signal-to-noise ratios. Furthermore, we highlight the limitations of using MSD alone to characterize anomalous transport in materials, and we show how analysis of spatial frequencies can yield a more comprehensive understanding of complex excited-state dynamics and their underlying physical mechanisms. Our results show that reciprocal-space-based analysis methods are powerful tools for characterizing and quantifying many different types of transport behaviors.

title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
text:
Title: Non-Unitary Quantum Butterfly Effect: Theory and Experiment
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We present a generalization of the out of time order correlator (OTOC) for non-unitary systems. For a Haar-random brickwork qudit-circuit, peppered with local, projective measurement, we calculate the infinite-temperature, ensemble-average OTOC. Utilizing transfer matrix machinery, we find that the OTOC asymptotically decays exponentially and that the decay depends on the rate of measurement. In the thermodynamic limit, with sparse measurement, the OTOC approximately exhibits a Gaussian shape. Phenomenologically, this corresponds to the development of a causal scrambling front where unlike the unitary case, the signal decays in the bulk of the causal cone. We develop a Monte Carlo framework to compute the OTOC. We then estimate the OTOC directly via quantum simulation and on Quantinuum's trapped-ion quantum computer. We resolve the unitary and non-unitary OTOC phenomenology despite the presence of hardware noise. Our analytic results characterize how local nonunitary channels affect OTOC decay, providing a quantitative benchmark for the cumulative effects of a broad class of hardware noise on many-body dynamics.

title: A Mathematical Theory of Redox Biology
text:
Title: A Mathematical Theory of Redox Biology
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Redox biology underpins signalling, metabolism, immunity, and adaptation, yet lacks a unifying theoretical framework capable of formalising structure, function, and dynamics. Current interpretations rely on descriptive catalogues of molecules and reactions, obscuring how redox behaviour emerges from constrained biochemical organisation. Here, we present a mathematical theory of redox biology that resolves this gap by treating redox systems as finite, compositional, dynamical, and spatially embedded objects. We define a structured redox state space in which admissible molecular transformations form a neutral algebra of possibilities. Biological function emerges when this structure is embedded within a wider molecular network and interpreted through weighted flux distributions. Time-dependent reweighting of these transformations generates redox dynamics, while spatial embedding enforces locality and causality, yielding a distributed redox field. Within this framework, context dependence, nonlinearity, hysteresis, and memory arise naturally from bounded state spaces and irreversible transformations, without requiring ad hoc assumptions. This theory provides a working, predictive interpretative basis for redox biology: it constrains admissible states and trajectories, clarifies the meaning of redox measurements, and links chemical transformation to biological behaviour. Redox biology emerges as a geometric, dynamical process governed by lawful organisation.

title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
text:
Title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp$ reaches $10^8$ to $10^{10}$. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by $\|r_0\|_{L^+}(χ_\parallel-χ_\perp)^{-1/2}$, where the numerator does not depend on $χ_\parallel$. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as $χ_\parallel^{-1/2}$, which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp=10^9$, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives $1.3\times10^{-5}$. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of $7.0\times10^{-6}$ with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to $1.2\times10^4$ shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.

title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
text:
Title: Solubility of poorly soluble species in bulk and nanopores from grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Poorly soluble species can have mean populations below one in small systems such as nanopores. In this regime, the grand-potential minimum, which identifies the most probable particle number, differs from the ensemble-averaged solute loading. We use grand-canonical Wang-Landau sampling (GCWLS) to calculate the density of states $Ω(N_\mathrm{A}, N_\mathrm{B})$ for a binary Lennard-Jones mixture of solute B in solvent A, both in bulk and in slit pores. One set of GCWLS simulations gives ensemble averages over a range of chemical potentials, whereas conventional grand-canonical Monte Carlo (GCMC) simulation requires a separate simulation at each state point. Independent GCMC simulations confirm the GCWLS ensemble averages. The solvent number distribution is nearly Gaussian, whereas the dilute solute distribution is skewed and Poisson-like. The most probable solute number therefore lies below the ensemble-averaged loading $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle$ and is zero whenever $\langle N_\mathrm{B}\rangle<1$. Reading the solute loading from the grand-potential minimum underestimates it and can falsely indicate that no solute is present. Defining the oversolubility as $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}=x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{conf}}/x_\mathrm{B}^{\mathrm{bulk}}$, where $x_\mathrm{B}$ is the solute mole fraction, we find $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}\approx12$ in a pore of 3.5 particle diameters width when both wall interactions are repulsive. Adding wall-solute attraction moderately raises it to $\approx13$, whereas wall-solvent attraction lowers it to $\approx3.4$. This comparison shows that the wall-solvent interaction controls most of the enhancement. As the pore widens, $\mathcal{O}_\mathrm{B}$ decreases toward unity. In bulk and in nanopores alike, the solubility of poorly soluble species should be obtained from ensemble averages rather than from grand-potential minima.

title: MERGE-RNA: a physics-based model to predict RNA secondary structure ensembles with chemical probing
text:
Title: MERGE-RNA: a physics-based model to predict RNA secondary structure ensembles with chemical probing
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

RNA function is tied to secondary structure, operating through dynamic and heterogeneous structural ensembles. While current analysis tools typically output single static structures or averaged contact maps, chemical probing methods like DMS capture nucleotide-resolution signals representing the full structural ensemble, which remain difficult to interpret structurally. To address this, we present MERGE-RNA, a framework that describes and outputs RNA as a structural ensemble. By modeling the physics of the experimental pipeline, MERGE-RNA learns a small set of transferable and interpretable parameters, enabling the integration of measurements across different molecules, probe concentrations, and replicates in a single optimization to improve robustness. Our model employs a maximum-entropy principle to predict thermodynamic populations, with the minimal adjustments necessary to align the ensemble with experimental data. We validate MERGE-RNA on diverse RNAs, showing that it achieves structural accuracy surpassing standard pseudo-free-energy methods and yields ensembles better recapitulating measured DMS reactivity. Applied to the V. vulnificus adenine riboswitch, MERGE-RNA recovers the NMR-resolved conformations and their ligand-induced rearrangement, with population shifts matching the NMR-derived K_d. In a designed RNA construct for which we report new DMS data, MERGE-RNA deconvolves mixed states to reveal transient intermediate populations involved in strand displacement, dynamics invisible to methods based on enumerating a small number of structures.

title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
text:
Title: SGA-Sparse: Training Native SwiGLU Gates for Activation-Sparse and Low-Bit LLMs
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Activation sparsity can reduce FFN weight traffic during single-user LLM decoding, but active channels must be identified early enough to avoid fetching unused weights. In pretrained SwiGLU models, training-free routing with the native gate performs substantially worse than routing with the up activation at high sparsity. We show that this ordering reverses after sparsity-aware training. Based on this insight, we introduce SGA-Sparse, which converts pretrained SwiGLU LLMs into fixed-budget activation-sparse models by training the existing gate projection directly as a top-k router. SGA-Sparse updates all model parameters end-to-end while preserving the original SwiGLU activation and introducing no auxiliary router parameters. After approximately 30B training tokens, LLaMA models from 1B to 8B achieve uniform per-token 75-85% FFN channel sparsity while remaining within 0.2-2.7 pp of their original dense checkpoints in average zero-shot accuracy. Because post-training quantization degrades sparsity-trained checkpoints, we further study two complementary quantization-aware training (QAT) recipes: continued-QAT largely recovers performance at 4-bit weight quantization, while joint-QAT performs better for the more aggressive sub-4-bit target. To compare activation sparsity with dense low-bit quantization, we translate the sparsity-induced reduction in weight traffic into an equivalent bit-width.
