title: Modeling and Interpreting Correlations, Null Distributions and Significance Levels in Neural Tracking of Natural Stimuli
text:
Title: Modeling and Interpreting Correlations, Null Distributions and Significance Levels in Neural Tracking of Natural Stimuli
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Neural tracking - the time-locking of neural responses to continuous stimuli such as speech, music, and video - is widely used to study how the brain processes natural input. Tracking strength is typically quantified as the correlation between the recorded neural response and the stimulus, decoded and/or encoded through data-driven models, and this correlation is routinely used to compare stimulus features, models, or settings. However, its magnitude depends not only on how strongly the brain tracks the stimulus, but also on the statistical properties of the signals being correlated. For example, a smallband speech envelope carrying almost no information about speech content yields among the highest correlations, simply because it is easier to reconstruct. Meaningful interpretation therefore requires comparing each correlation to its null distribution: the correlations expected without any stimulus-response relationship. We show that the randomization procedures commonly used to construct this null distribution are not interchangeable: each implicitly encodes a different null hypothesis, and we motivate stimulus-response misalignment as the most practical and appropriate choice. Because reliable null distributions require many permutations, we introduce a semi-parametric model using the normal distribution after the Fisher transform that yields accurate significance levels from only 3-5 min of data and predicts them across analysis window lengths. Building on this, we propose the null-normalized tracking score, an interpretable measure placing features and models on a common scale, which relates directly to the widely used match-mismatch accuracy. Applied to EEG from 121 participants listening to continuous speech, the framework reverses conclusions drawn from raw correlations, providing an efficient and principled methodology for interpreting neural tracking correlations.

title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
text:
Title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Attention-based time series forecasters commonly group consecutive observations into patches. Patch length is known to have a substantial impact on forecasting performance, yet its selection remains largely empirical. We develop a theoretical framework that explains why patch length matters for forecasting accuracy and provides a principled basis for its selection. For linear state-space models, we derive an exact factorization of the forecasting coefficient matrix that separates forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics. We show that dominance of a single forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation. This explains why longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. We combine the factorization with estimation bounds to develop a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors under temporal dependence. Our analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified and clarifies how predictive structure, head count, training sample size, and long-run dependence enter the selection criterion.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
text:
Title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Deep Neural Networks: Methods, Frameworks, and Perspectives
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Deep neural networks underpin fundamental tasks in a wide range of signal domains, such as image, audio, and language processing. However, their internal mechanisms are notably difficult to interpret. Internal activations are structured signals transformed across layers that may encode a multitude of interdependent relationships, as individual neurons frequently represent multiple underlying concepts. Mechanistic interpretability aims to uncover the internal mechanisms of neural networks by identifying components whose activations are causally responsible for specific behaviors. In such a context, this article provides an overview of advances in mechanistic interpretability for the analysis of causal inference in deep neural networks.

title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
text:
Title: Learning inexact alternating minimization for convex problems with quadratic coupling
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Alternating minimization is a standard tool for optimization problems with two coupled variable blocks. Its cost is dominated by the inner subproblem solvers, which rarely have a closed-form solution. In this paper, we propose to learn an inexact alternating scheme in which neural networks approximate the subproblem solution at each iteration. For convex problems with quadratic couplings between the variable blocks that satisfy a quadratic growth condition, we derive a worst-case bound on the optimality gap that exposes the per-iteration error that each network is trained to minimize in a greedy fashion. Combining the bound with a PAC-Bayes argument, we obtain a fixed-horizon, high-probability bound on the expected optimality gap over the distribution of problem instances. We apply the learned scheme to robust matrix completion and low-dose CT reconstruction with dictionary regularization where we achieve a 5x-13x speedup over the inexact first-order baseline at matched accuracy. A brief end-to-end fine-tuning stage extends this up to 30x and outperforms other learned schemes. The code is available at https://github.com/paulhausner/learned-alternating-minimization.

title: Exploiting chemical shift variability enables recovery of overlapping metabolites from 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectra
text:
Title: Exploiting chemical shift variability enables recovery of overlapping metabolites from 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectra
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Overlapping peaks and sample-dependent chemical shift variability prevent reliable metabolite recovery from complex biological spectra. This problem is critical in one-dimensional proton (1D 1H) NMR which has become the standard method providing fast acquisition and information-rich spectra in metabolomics and foodomics. This study demonstrates how chemical shifts can be utilised as a strength in 1D 1H NMR, when suitably modeled through the proposed Bayesian Shift-Invariant Non-negative Matrix Factorization (BSI-NMF) procedure. We find that BSI-NMF accurately recovers the underlying chemical signals in 1D 1H NMR spectra missed by existing analyses approaches across simulations, laboratory created datasets, and a large urine dataset obtained from 2439 people across Europe. Our study highlights how shifts in the chemical signatures - until now perceived as a nuisance - can in fact when suitably modelled be instrumental for unique recovery of metabolites. This creates an opportunity to experimentally induce chemical shifts changes to facilitate unique recovery of spectra.

title: Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo
text:
Title: Static Response of the Strongly Coupled Electron Gas from Diffusion Monte Carlo
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The local field factor $G(q)$ of the HEG describes how exchange and correlation modify the response to a static perturbation, and enters dielectric screening, effective electron--electron interactions, and the xc kernel of TDDFT. Accurate zero-temperature data for $G(q)$, however, remain limited to metallic densities, $r_s\leq10$. In this work, we present diffusion Monte Carlo calculations of the static density response function $χ(q)$ and of $G(q)$ for $2\leq r_s\leq100$, and describe and discuss the methodological steps that enabled these calculations. We show how optimization of the perturbing potential in the trial wave function has an important effect, as a poor choice can reverse the sign of the response. A closed-form expression is provided for its optimal value, together with the density dependence of the linear-response window. We further show that backflow correlations leave $χ(q)$ unchanged and that $G(q)$ depends only weakly on system size even at very low density, so that Slater--Jastrow wave functions and modest system sizes suffice. Together, these results provide a practical guide for future QMC calculations of response properties of the electron gas and real materials. Our results agree with previous DMC data at metallic densities for $q>k_F$, and extend them below $k_F$. They also agree with diagrammatic QMC at $r_s=2$. At lower densities, our results show that $G(q)$ develops a nonmonotonic structure at intermediate-$q$, where the response approaches that of the noninteracting gas. Quantitative agreement is seen with finite-temperature path integral Monte Carlo, suggesting that the previously reported finite-temperature structure is inherited from the ground state. Using a parametrization of $G(q)$ that reproduces our data throughout the liquid phase, we relate this structure to short-range order in the pair correlation function and the static structure factor.

title: Localized Hybrid Analytical-Finite-Element Thermal Modeling for Laser Powder Bed Fusion
text:
Title: Localized Hybrid Analytical-Finite-Element Thermal Modeling for Laser Powder Bed Fusion
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Hybrid analytical--finite-element methods support scan-resolved, part-scale thermal simulation of laser powder bed fusion, but their analytical evaluation cost grows as scan-line contributions accumulate. This work develops a space--time localized hybrid formulation that restricts where and how long each contribution is evaluated analytically. Residual terms and boundary conditions derived from the heat equation allow the finite-element correction to account for the thermal effect of contributions removed from the analytical field. The formulation is assessed using a single-line benchmark against an independent full finite-element solution and multiline comparisons with the conventional hybrid formulation. Localization limits the number of analytical contributions retained while maintaining close agreement with the conventional solution. A comparison with uncompensated temporal truncation demonstrates the importance of the residual correction in retaining the thermal effect of removed contributions. In the 500-line case, analytical and total simulation times are reduced by factors of approximately 25.5 and 3.92, respectively, with a relative nodal 2-norm difference of 0.139%.

title: Non-Markovian Cosmology with Causal Memory Kernels
text:
Title: Non-Markovian Cosmology with Causal Memory Kernels
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We investigate a non-Markovian extension of Friedmann cosmology in which the present expansion rate retains information about the past cosmic evolution through a causal memory kernel, with \LCDM{} recovered in the limit of vanishing kernel amplitude, $A\to0$. We show that five kernels (Linear, Power Law, Exponential, Gaussian and Oscillatory) arise as cosine transforms of the spectral densities of an unresolved hidden sector, and that the Exponential and Linear kernels also follow independently from Israel-Stewart causal viscosity and from Deser-Woodard non-local gravity, respectively. We constrain the kernels with 30 Cosmic Chronometer (CC) measurements and with $H(z)$ derived from the DESI DR1 and DR2 baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) data, using multi-start $χ^{2}$ minimisation followed by Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling, and compare them with \LCDM{} through the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. The Linear amplitude is consistent with zero ($A=0.002\pm0.030$ for CC+DR2). The Power-law, Exponential and Gaussian kernels are observationally degenerate: the data select sharply peaked kernels that constrain only an integrated amplitude $\Aeff\simeq0.01$--$0.03$, equivalent to a uniform $0.5$--$1.5\%$ rescaling of $H(z)$, and they are disfavoured relative to \LCDM{} ($Δ{\rm AIC}=+2.5$ to $+3.6$). Only the Oscillatory kernel improves the fit appreciably ($\dchi=4.5$--$8.1$), but it requires a negative damping rate, which is incompatible with the causal derivations, and it is not favoured once CC data are included ($Δ{\rm BIC}=+4.4$ to $+6.2$)

title: SwitchCraft: A Programmatic Framework for Designing State-Switching Proteins
text:
Title: SwitchCraft: A Programmatic Framework for Designing State-Switching Proteins
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Multistate mechanisms underlie many of the complex functions observed in natural proteins. The ability to rationally design multistate proteins would have transformative implications for many areas of biotechnology, yet lies beyond the capabilities of existing deep learning frameworks for protein design. To address this gap, we introduce SwitchCraft, a versatile and programmatic framework for designing state-switching proteins based on backpropagation through compositional design constraints parameterized by structure prediction models. In silico evaluations demonstrate success on a wide range of state-switching functional primitives, from allosteric regulation of motifs to discrimination of bound ligand identities. Using these primitives, we demonstrate an in silico strategy for de novo design of fluorescent biosensors to arbitrary small molecule analytes. These results position SwitchCraft at the inception of a powerful paradigm for higher-order functional protein design. Code is available at https://github.com/bjing2016/switchcraft.

title: Relative-Error Composite Federated Optimization with One Server-Side Proximal Step per Round
text:
Title: Relative-Error Composite Federated Optimization with One Server-Side Proximal Step per Round
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We consider deterministic composite federated optimization, in which distributed smooth client objectives are combined with a shared, possibly nonsmooth, regularizer. We propose Relative-Error Composite FedDyn (REC-FedDyn), an inexact method that supports partial participation, with one server-side proximal evaluation per communication round. REC-FedDyn employs a directly testable relative-error criterion that allows each client to independently control the accuracy of its local subproblem, without a server-side acceptance test. We establish almost-sure iterate convergence for strongly convex and convex problems, almost-sure asymptotic stationarity for nonconvex problems, and communication and parallel gradient-evaluation complexity bounds, all under partial participation and without assuming bounded data heterogeneity. Experiments on image inpainting, fMRI prediction, and neural-network classification with structured regularization demonstrate efficiency and robustness across levels of data heterogeneity and client participation.

title: Two-Phase Rapid Simulation-Based Inference with Differentiable Simulators
text:
Title: Two-Phase Rapid Simulation-Based Inference with Differentiable Simulators
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We introduce Rapid Simulation Based Inference (RSBI), a diffusion-based variational approach to likelihood-free Bayesian inference that achieves high sampling efficiency under large prior-to-posterior volumes. RSBI builds on advances in Schrödinger Bridge (SB) diffusion sampling to handle multi-modal posteriors, with an initial likelihood supplied by a distance measure via a differentiable simulator. The key innovation of this initial surrogate likelihood is that it gives a highly efficient proposal distribution, replacing sequential rounds of other methods with an efficient one-shot proposal. Subsequent refinement then transports the proposal to the true posterior as specified by the simulator and the original prior. The SB sampler is warm-started from the proposal, and its energy is corrected by a neural likelihood ratio that is learned only where the proposal places mass. As a variational method, RSBI does not suffer from prior leakage commonly observed in standard sequential posterior estimation methods. To improve mode coverage we optionally utilize the well-tempered meta-dynamics framework, which also encourages exploration of the prior volume. We observe strong performance on standard SBI benchmarks, particularly when the prior volume is increased relative to the ground truth posterior, achieving a performance degradation of only $\sim5\%$ on Two Moons under a highly constrained simulation budget. Additionally, we evaluate RSBI's performance for gravitational wave ring-down posterior estimation, in a real-world physics benchmark inspired by black hole spectroscopy.

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
text:
Title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

title: High-order fractional linear differential equations do not describe stochastic processes with finite state space
text:
Title: High-order fractional linear differential equations do not describe stochastic processes with finite state space
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

The replacement of the classical derivative in the governing equation of a continuous-time Markov process with finite state space by a fractional derivative of arbitrary order $α>1$ produces solutions that are mathematically incompatible with the theory of stochastic processes.

title: Surface Charge--Potential Relation for Spherical Particles in Electrolyte Solutions
text:
Title: Surface Charge--Potential Relation for Spherical Particles in Electrolyte Solutions
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Predicting the relationship between surface charge density and electrostatic potential for spherical particles remains a fundamental challenge in colloid science. Because the governing non-linear Poisson--Boltzmann equation lacks a general exact analytical solution, researchers typically rely on numerical calculations or various semi-empirical approximations. In this paper, we overcome these limitations by developing a dual-asymptotic framework that provides explicit, closed-form expressions for this surface charge--potential relationship across the entire spectrum of particle curvature. For weakly curved systems, where the Debye length $λ_D$ is much smaller than the particle radius $R$ ($λ_D/R \ll 1$), a formal mathematical derivation rigorously establishes the Ohshima--Healy--White formula as an exact regular perturbation expansion. Conversely, for highly curved spheres ($R/λ_D \ll 1$), we employ singular perturbation analysis using the scaled particle radius as the small parameter. This approach provides a first-principles mathematical justification for the spherical Debye--Hückel theory, proving that its leading-order expansion remains asymptotically exact within the full non-linear Poisson--Boltzmann framework due to the geometric deactivation of non-linearity. Crucially, we map the exact limits of this geometric regulation, demonstrating how non-linear screening re-emerges as the particle radius increases, with the breakdown threshold governed by the interplay between curvature and surface charge density.

title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
text:
Title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.

title: Actions Should EARN Their Credit: Test-Time Adaptation and Route Consolidation for Frozen LLM Agents
text:
Title: Actions Should EARN Their Credit: Test-Time Adaptation and Route Consolidation for Frozen LLM Agents
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

LLM agents can use feedback from repeated attempts to improve their decisions without updating model parameters. However, positive action credits can continue to favor actions that repeatedly achieve the same score, even when higher scores are achievable. Under a fixed interaction budget, trying new actions in the final attempts can also lower performance. We introduce EARN, a method that uses past experience to guide further progress and retain earlier performance through conditional reuse of effective action sequences. EARN reduces action credits for reaching scores repeatedly attained in earlier episodes and assigns larger credits to action segments that reach higher scores. These credits adjust the probabilities of LLM-proposed actions. During the final episodes, EARN directly replays stored actions when the current context matches the recorded context and the actions remain available, bypassing LLM candidate generation. We evaluate performance at the end of the interaction budget using the average score over the final four episodes. Across Jericho, ScienceWorld, and Crafter, EARN achieves the best score on this metric in 31 of 33 task--budget settings among the evaluated methods, including ties. Across the evaluated Jericho budgets, replay bypasses 78.9--86.3\% of candidate-generation calls in the final four episodes, averaged across games.

title: Genetic weight of a mutant in a biparental Moran model with infinite selection
text:
Title: Genetic weight of a mutant in a biparental Moran model with infinite selection
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study, after Coron Le Jan (2024), the genetic contribution of a single strongly advantageous mutant in a biparental Moran model under infinite selection. We prove a functional limit theorem for the entire beneficial mutation spreading period: after normalization by \(\sqrt N\), the contributions carried by the advantaged and disadvantaged subpopulations converge jointly in law to a non-degenerate random multiple of an explicit deterministic profile. Randomness is generated during the initial microscopic growth of the mutant lineage and subsequently propagated through the population along a deterministic macroscopic trajectory. At the heart of this phenomenon is an eigenmode martingale that measures the imbalance between the mean genetic weight of the founding ancestor within the two classes; its limiting value provides precisely the random amplitude of the macroscopic profile and is characterized by a smoothing equation.

title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
text:
Title: SpecValley: Aggregation as Spectral Valley in Dense Heterophilic Graphs
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Node classification in heterophilic graphs remains an open problem: aggregating over neighbourhoods can damp precisely the part of the signal that carries the labels. The field has answered with ever more expressive propagation operators, leaving the aggregation step that precedes them fixed by degree normalisation. However, degree normalisation acts as a spectral valley in its own right, attenuating a fixed middle band whose position at lambda equal 1 is set by the normalisation rather than by the data, exactly where the eigenvalues of dense graphs accumulate. We therefore begin with the representations rather than the propagation, in two stages: a learnable aggregation followed by an ordinary spectral filter. The first, SpecValley learns the position, sharpness and flank gains of the valley for every graph. We show formally how the aggregation operator and downstream filter interact. We establish that the response 1 minus lambda of degree normalisation vanishes exactly at that accumulation point. A spectral energy budget shows that what aggregation removes from a band, no linear spectral filter can recover. Crowding alone says nothing about the benefit. That is decided by how much label energy the valley removes, which we measure for every graph. SpecValley achieves strong results across heterophilic benchmarks, and a controlled ablation over aggregation operators and downstream filters attributes the gain to aggregation rather than the filter.

title: A Lighter QCD-Axion from Small Instantons
text:
Title: A Lighter QCD-Axion from Small Instantons
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We propose models where the QCD axion mass can be much smaller than the standard expectation. We show that this is possible in models where both QCD and the Standard Model flavor structure get modified in the ultraviolet (UV). In these models, both the axion mass and the up-quark Yukawa can receive sizeable non-perturbative contributions from instantons in the UV. If both these effects are carefully taken into account, the QCD axion is not necessarily heavier than usual expectations and can, in fact, be much lighter. We show that if small instanton contributions account for a large fraction of the up-quark Yukawa, the QCD axion can be lighter than standard expectations whereas it is heavier otherwise. We propose two different models where this condition is realised: (1) one where the QCD gauge group emerges as a subgroup from a product of $SU(3)$ groups in the UV; and (2) a composite Higgs model that also implements partial compositeness. In both these models the QCD axion can lie not only in the region to the right of the QCD axion band but also far to its left. This is especially relevant for a range of proposed haloscope and helioscope experiments that will probe a region mostly to the left of the QCD band.

title: virasoro_blocks: Software for the 2d bootstrap
text:
Title: virasoro_blocks: Software for the 2d bootstrap
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We introduce virasoro_blocks, software that computes Virasoro conformal blocks at any central charge in a form suitable for the numerical bootstrap. At each finite order in the elliptic nome, Zamolodchikov's recursion gives the block as a positive prefactor times a rational function of the exchanged weight. However, its many Kac poles make it difficult to use in semidefinite programming approaches to the bootstrap. In this software we use optimal interpolation to reduce the number of poles while keeping high accuracy. The software works in arbitrary precision and handles singular central charges, including the minimal models and $c=1$. It also computes global blocks, $N=1$ superconformal blocks, torus characters, and torus one-point blocks. We illustrate it with two applications. Assuming only scalar Virasoro primaries, we compute bounds on the scalar gap that approach the window of Liouville solutions between $(c-1)/16$ and $(c-1)/12$. We also bound the average exchanged dimension in four-point functions of identical scalars at several central charges. These bounds have a rich structure, and many known 2d CFTs lie on or near their boundary.

title: Atom-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for 3D Atomistic Systems
text:
Title: Atom-JEPA: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for 3D Atomistic Systems
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Large-scale self-supervised pretraining has reshaped modern machine learning, substantially advancing the ability of language and vision models to generalize across downstream tasks. While deep learning has driven considerable progress in modeling atomistic systems in recent years, self-supervised pretraining in this domain has not yet achieved comparable downstream generalization. To address this, we introduce Atom-JEPA, a self-supervised pretraining framework that learns latent representations from unlabeled 3D structures through complementary atom-level and substructure-level objectives inspired by joint-embedding predictive architectures. We pretrain Atom-JEPA on large-scale molecular and crystalline datasets and evaluate its transfer performance by fine-tuning on a diverse set of downstream property prediction tasks. Atom-JEPA achieves state-of-the-art performance on molecular ADMET and quantum-chemical property prediction tasks, and is highly competitive in predicting the physical properties of crystalline materials. These results demonstrate the potential of latent-space predictive pretraining to support broad downstream generalization from structural data alone. Code and pretrained model checkpoints are publicly available at https://github.com/khelverskovp/atom-jepa

title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
text:
Title: Fairness in Explainable AI Narratives: Decomposing Social Disparities in LLM-Generated Explanations
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate technical explainable AI (XAI) artefacts such as SHAP into explanatory narratives (XAINs) for lay users. In high-risk domains, these explanations are often the main resource through which individuals can understand and contest adverse decisions. Yet LLMs are known to reproduce social bias, even from proxy variables alone, and fairness in XAINs remains unstudied. Because XAINs are bound to a ground-truth artefact, fairness concerns not only what a narrative says and how, but also whether it is equally faithful across social groups. We introduce fairness in XAINs as a new field of research and propose a framework that generates narratives under three conditions (protected attribute disclosed, withheld, or counterfactually swapped), allowing five comparisons that pinpoint the cause of disparities. We apply it to adversely classified instances from four datasets in credit scoring, education and employment, generating narratives with five LLMs, and evaluate faithfulness, feature coverage and sentiment. We find significant disparities across all datasets, metric families and models, arising in two ways. Faithfulness disparities result from feature values: LLMs make plausible but false statements, triggered by values that are unequally distributed across social groups. Feature coverage and sentiment disparities stem from the protected attribute itself: once it is disclosed, LLMs give less explanation to, or frame more negatively the narratives of, groups that have historically been discriminated against or are stereotypically associated with worse outcomes. A more faithful model removes the faithfulness disparities, and withholding protected attributes mostly removes the others, but neither suffices on its own. Fairness in XAINs should therefore be audited separately from the predictive model and its XAI artefact.

title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
text:
Title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.

title: Strictly proper scoring rules for node selection tasks on graphs
text:
Title: Strictly proper scoring rules for node selection tasks on graphs
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

In node selection tasks, the goal is to identify a single unknown target node in a graph. We consider probabilistic supervised node selection, where the estimator outputs a probability distribution over the nodes of the graph and the ground-truth node is available for evaluation. Classical evaluation metrics for such tasks are either statistically ill-conceived or blind to the graph structure. To fill this gap, we introduce two strictly proper scoring rules that are explicitly graph-aware: the Resistance score, which is parameter-free, and the Diffusion score, which operates at an adjustable coarse-graining resolution. We show that the Diffusion score interpolates between the multi-category Brier score and a cluster-level weighted Brier score. The Resistance score generalises two classical scoring rules: the multi-category Brier score and the Ranked probability score. Applied to rooted trees, it also serves as the strictly proper version of the improper Hierarchical error distance used in hierarchical classification. In the same setting, we furthermore establish strict propriety of the Hierarchical cross-entropy family, a recently introduced separate class of hierarchy-aware scoring rules. Experiments on epidemic source detection and on ImageNet classification confirm that the proposed scores detect meaningful differences in estimation quality that classical metrics miss.

title: Fast, training-free simplification of spinor-helicity amplitudes
text:
Title: Fast, training-free simplification of spinor-helicity amplitudes
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We present a training-free method that simplifies massless spinor-helicity expressions by a greedy best-first search over on-shell identities, and test it at four, five, and six points. Applied to the color-ordered five-gluon MHV tree-level amplitude, the search derives the Parke-Taylor formula from all 1024 Feynman-diagram expressions with different polarization reference spinors and up to 228 numerator terms. On public test sets used by previous machine-learning methods, the search solves every case and generally outperforms these methods in solve rate. Its mean wall-clock time per case is 0.02-0.3 s on one CPU core. With longer searches and an alternative ranking of candidate expressions, it also solves all 21,600 cases of a new suite of larger test expressions. Each result comes with an explicit derivation and is independently checked over finite fields at on-shell kinematics. For the classes studied here, the method effectively compresses long expressions produced by identity scrambling or Feynman-diagram calculations into compact forms. This is a first step toward extracting physics from amplitudes by relating distinct compact expressions, selecting representations with preferred factors and poles, and guiding the discovery of new amplitude structures.

title: Practical Ellipse Fitting for Atom Interferometry
text:
Title: Practical Ellipse Fitting for Atom Interferometry
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

In differential atom interferometry, it is necessary to extract the differential phase shift between two interferometers that are individually noisy. A variety of techniques can be used for this purpose, under the general label of ellipse fitting. We compare several methods for ellipse fitting, considering parameters and performance relevant to atom interferometry. Statistical, algebraic, geometric and Bayesian methods are discussed, and we describe a novel "reciprocal" geometric method that offers some benefits. Each method has advantages and disadvantages that depend on the use case required. Supplemental material includes basic Python and Matlab code for each method.

title: Graphlets as structural fingerprints of complex networks
text:
Title: Graphlets as structural fingerprints of complex networks
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Complex networks are often compared using selected graph-theoretical measures that capture a selected set of properties with effects ranging from local to global, such as degree, clustering or betweenness centrality. Here we introduce a structural fingerprinting framework based on graphlets: small rooted subgraphs whose distributions provide a systematic description of local-to-mesoscale topology. Across synthetic networks generated from several random graph models, graphlet fingerprints capture parameter-dependent structural differences, outperform standard graph-theoretical measures, and identify even subtle local patterns driving discrimination. We then apply the framework to empirical resting-state functional connectomes, documenting that while graphlets show superior sensitivity also to controlled topological perturbations of brain connectivity, specifically in schizophrenia-control classification they perform only comparably to classical graph-theoretical features. This is in line with the notion that schizophrenia-related alterations are dominated by spatially localized connectivity changes rather than general topological reorganization. Altogether, the generative modeling, targeted perturbations and real-world neuroimaging classification challenge position graphlets as flexible structural fingerprints of complex networks, while carefully outlining their strength and weaknesses compared to more classical graph theoretical features.

title: Isothermal-Isobaric Molecular Dynamics with a Foundation Interatomic Potential in LAMMPS across NVIDIA and Intel GPUs
text:
Title: Isothermal-Isobaric Molecular Dynamics with a Foundation Interatomic Potential in LAMMPS across NVIDIA and Intel GPUs
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer one model for many chemistries, but their deep, globally coupled architectures do not fit the spatial decomposition that scales classical and short-ranged MLIPs. We present pair_style uma, a LAMMPS pair style that evaluates the Universal Model for Atoms (UMA) through LibTorch on NVIDIA and Intel GPUs from a single source tree. It reimplements FairChem's edge-sharded graph parallelism in C++ over exported TorchScript modules, with one MPI rank per device, NCCL or oneCCL collectives, and the whole energy and force path in double precision. The strain-gradient virial is carried through the exported modules and the cross-device reductions, so that fix npt runs on both vendors' hardware. We measure NPT capacity and cost on one 4xA100-40GB node, one 8xH200 node, and one 12-tile Intel node, and on up to 32 Intel nodes. Without activation checkpointing, one node holds NaCl cells of about 8,000 atoms (A100, 0.21 ns/day), 22,000 atoms (Intel, 0.10 ns/day), and 47,000 atoms (H200, 0.16 ns/day). Graph parallelism raises the capacity of a single device by 8.0x on H200 and 4.6x on A100. Across nodes, capacity grows to about 779,000 atoms on 32 Intel nodes, with a slower speed at 0.007 ns/day. On H200 and A100, a FLOP count of FairChem's graph-parallel predictor gives lower bounds of 31% and 51% of FP64 peak. From one omat checkpoint and with no refit, nine 100 ps NPT heating ramps (NaCl, equiatomic Pt-Ru, and equiatomic (HfNbTaTiZr)N, on all three node types) ran to completion.

title: On Solvability of Irregular Infinite-Dimensional Differential-Algebraic Equations
text:
Title: On Solvability of Irregular Infinite-Dimensional Differential-Algebraic Equations
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

This paper investigates the solvability of infinite-dimensional differential-algebraic equations (DAEs) on Hilbert spaces. We focus on irregular systems for which the operator pencil is not surjective onto the full state space, but only onto a subspace determined by the algebraic constraints. We establish a Lumer-Phillips-type generation result for this class of systems, showing that dissipativity together with a partial surjectivity condition yields a contraction semigroup on the dynamic subspace. The resulting wellposedness conditions are compared with existing solvability results. We further extend the analysis to systems in which hidden algebraic constraints restrict the dynamics to a proper closed subspace of the dynamical subspace. Under an additional structural condition, we show that the resulting constrained system is $E$-radial on suitably chosen spaces. We also demonstrate that semigroup generation does not, in general, imply $E$-radiality on the original state spaces. This provides a Weierstraß-type decomposition useful for controller design. The framework is illustrated by some examples.

title: Images of Regular Black Holes with Hedgehog Scalar Hair Embedded in Radiatively Inefficient Accretion Flows
text:
Title: Images of Regular Black Holes with Hedgehog Scalar Hair Embedded in Radiatively Inefficient Accretion Flows
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

How a black hole's geometric critical scale manifests in an accretion-flow image is governed by photon propagation, plasma radiative processes, and instrumental resolution. In this work, we investigate radiatively inefficient accretion flows (RIAF) surrounding geometrically regular black holes with hedgehog scalar hair. Adopting the mass and distance of $\mathrm{M87}^*$, we generate total-intensity synchrotron images and systematically explore the viewing inclination, disk thickness, and observing frequency. For the fiducial setup at $230\,\mathrm{GHz}$, raising $L/M$ from $0$ to $0.9$ contracts the critical curve diameter by $4.78\%$, shrinks the half-flux radius by $4.07\%$, and lowers the required electron-density scale by $9.15\%$. At $84\,\mathrm{GHz}$, the primary brightness peaks shift farther outside the critical curve due to enhanced synchrotron self-absorption, whereas the sharper emission rings at $230$ and $345\,\mathrm{GHz}$ closely trace the critical curve. Ultimately, we find that although the regular core systematically contracts the emission ring and alters the required plasma density, resolving these deviations from a Schwarzschild black hole demands angular resolution finer than that achievable with current baselines.

title: English Calibration Erodes Lithuanian in Expert-Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
text:
Title: English Calibration Erodes Lithuanian in Expert-Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Expert pruning compresses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models by removing the experts that a calibration set marks as unimportant. Studies of high-resource languages largely find that English calibration transfers well to other languages. We test this for Lithuanian: we pruned four MoE models with REAP, removing 25% or 50% of the experts with English, Lithuanian or mixed calibration, and evaluated both languages on reading comprehension, translation and language modelling. English calibration does not transfer to Lithuanian: at 25% pruning, English comprehension fell by a median of 1.7 points but Lithuanian by 21.4. The transfer is asymmetric. Lithuanian calibration removed most of the Lithuanian loss and never significantly hurt English comprehension, which was on average 2.5 points better than under English calibration; only English language modeling got slightly worse. Routing suggests why: in the last layers, Lithuanian sends 55-72% of its expert selections to just eight experts, against 19-39% for English, and English calibration removes some of these experts. Compressed models should be calibrated, and evaluated, in every language they must serve.

title: Solvent Fluctuations Enable Photoionization of Aqueous Nitrite Microdroplets
text:
Title: Solvent Fluctuations Enable Photoionization of Aqueous Nitrite Microdroplets
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Nitrite photochemistry in atmospheric aerosols and natural waters is a major source of hydroxyl radicals and reactive nitrogen oxides. Contrary to the prevailing view that in the environment aqueous nitrite photochemistry proceeds exclusively through photoexcitation followed by homolytic bond cleavage, we show that visible light directly ionizes aqueous nitrite in individual micron-sized droplets. Although the photoionization cross section is exceptionally small, this pathway is observable at the high photon flux densities accessible in single-droplet experiments. Molecular simulations reveal that this is because photoionization absorption has an exceptionally long wavelength tail due to the large solvent reorganization energy in aqueous solutions. Kinetic modeling of an aqueous-phase reaction mechanism quantitatively accounts for the observed chemistry and predicts the formation of nitrate, hydroxyl radicals, and solvated electrons. The overlap of the predicted broad photoionization continuum with the visible solar spectrum further suggests that visible-light photoionization is an overlooked source of nitrogen oxides, solvated electrons, and oxidants in atmospheric aerosols, snowpack, and natural waters. Under dilute conditions, where dissolved oxygen is the main sink for solvated electrons, photoionization is expected to be the dominant photochemical loss pathway for nitrite.

title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
text:
Title: From Sound to Occupancy: Privacy-Aware Audio Sensing for Buildings
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Occupancy-based controls regulate lighting and HVAC according to whether a space is in use. Passive infrared (PIR) sensors, the most common choice, respond to motion and can report an occupied room as vacant when its occupants remain still. Sound offers an alternative cue, since seated occupants type, turn pages and cough, but microphones raise privacy concerns. We therefore study a two-stage design: an on-device encoder maps each second of audio to a short embedding, and a server-side temporal model turns the stream of embeddings into an occupancy state. To our knowledge, no publicly available dataset pairs office audio with occupancy labels, so we evaluate the two stages separately on public data. The encoder is trained on synthetic scenes that mix empty-room recordings, room impulse responses, office sounds and read speech, and tested on unseen rooms, recordings and speakers for whether a second contains a sound made by a person. On 11 real office recordings (DCASE 2013) it reaches an AUC of 0.87, against 0.76 for log-mel statistics. Attacks on the transmitted embeddings recover at most 1% of the spoken words, against 94% from log-mel frames, but still identify the speaker among 40 in 69 to 77% of the utterances. Noise-floor normalization with adversarial training, an 8-dimensional embedding, or sending only class probabilities lowers this to 38 to 55% without hurting detection. On HPDmobile, which pairs home occupancy labels with an amplitude envelope of the audio, a causal temporal model pretrained with a hierarchical contrastive loss matches hand-crafted features (AUC 0.75) and does better when only one labelled day per home is available. These results make the two-stage design a practical basis for privacy-aware acoustic occupancy sensing, with speaker identity as the one leak still to close.

title: MetaARIMA: Configuration-Level Transfer Learning for ARIMA Models
text:
Title: MetaARIMA: Configuration-Level Transfer Learning for ARIMA Models
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Time Series Foundation Models have demonstrated that pretraining on diverse datasets enables effective transfer to new forecasting tasks. Classical methods like ARIMA, however, remain configured and trained independently for each series, discarding knowledge from previous experiments. Consequently, selecting and training an ARIMA configuration remains challenging and often relies on heuristic approaches based on in-sample goodnessof-fit measures. We propose MetaARIMA, a pretrained configuration policy based on metalearning that brings transfer learning to classical statistical forecasting at the configuration level rather than the model level. The policy learns from historical experiments which ARIMA configurations achieve top-quantile performance, and recommends promising candidates for new series while preserving interpretability and local estimation. At inference, it selects a diverse set of candidates via maximal marginal relevance and efficiently identifies the final configuration using successive halving. Experiments in a transfer learning setting, training on M4 and evaluating on M1, M3, and Tourism, show that MetaARIMA outperforms AutoARIMA and other classical methods while being more dataefficient. In a comparison with recent zero-shot foundation models, MetaARIMA remains competitive with Chronos2, Moirai2, and TimesFM. The experiments are publicly available at https://github.com/vcerqueira/experiments-metaarima.

title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
text:
Title: Flexible Intensities Matter: A Comprehensive Re-evaluation of Hawkes Processes and Neural Temporal Point Processes
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Temporal point processes (TPPs) are the canonical model class for event sequences in continuous time, with applications ranging from seismology to electronic health records. Recent benchmarks report that neural TPPs substantially outperform their classical counterparts, such as Hawkes processes. However, these comparisons set flexible neural models against Hawkes processes in their most restricted forms and covered only a narrow range of domains. We revisit this comparison under autoregressive next-event prediction, evaluating Poisson and Hawkes processes of increasing flexibility against neural TPPs on five established benchmarks and two large-scale medical tasks derived from UK Biobank disease histories and MIMIC-IV ICU records. First, once Hawkes processes are equipped with flexible, learnable baselines and kernels, the previously reported gap to neural TPPs largely closes. Second, neural TPPs are likewise limited by their intensity parametrization: a Transformer with a spline-based intensity head outperforms previous intensity-based neural TPPs and matches or exceeds the intensity-free model. Decomposing the log-likelihood into time and type terms shows that this gain lies almost entirely in modeling when events occur (log p(t)) rather than which type occurs (log p(d|t)). Third, only on MIMIC-IV do neural TPPs retain an advantage in predicting event types, underscoring the value of complex datasets for evaluating TPPs. We release TorchPP, an open-source PyTorch framework with unified implementations of classical and neural TPPs.

title: Variance Reduction Note 3: The Convergence of PAGE
text:
Title: Variance Reduction Note 3: The Convergence of PAGE
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

The probabilistic gradient estimator (PAGE) alternates randomly between an accurate gradient refresh and a cheap recursive correction. This third expository note on recursive variance reduction explains the algorithm and gives a self-contained convergence proof for smooth nonconvex optimization. A Lyapunov function combines objective decrease with estimation error, turning the refresh probability into an explicit contraction parameter. The resulting expected oracle complexity is $O(n+\sqrt n\,ε^{-2})$ for finite sums and $O(ε^{-3})$ for online problems, with the other problem parameters fixed. Initialization, refreshes, and both evaluations in each gradient difference are counted. The presentation is pedagogical and makes no claim of a new algorithm or convergence rate.

title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
text:
Title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations. Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.

title: Quantum error correcting codes from quiver moduli: Grassmannians, cyclic monodromy, and argyle collision divisors
text:
Title: Quantum error correcting codes from quiver moduli: Grassmannians, cyclic monodromy, and argyle collision divisors
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Building on aspects of a recent diagrammatic field-theory programme for quantum error correction put forward by the first-named author (arXiv:2607.08911), we construct exact finite-dimensional codes from twisted cyclic and argyle quiver moduli on the projective line. A regular fibre of the node-labelled cyclic Hitchin map records the ways to distribute simple spectral zeroes among the arrows with prescribed degrees. The Hilbert space spanned by these allocations is a Young permutation module. Root monodromy acts on its Specht factors and leaves their multiplicity spaces noiseless. Resetting the Specht factor therefore recovers the encoded state for every channel in the monodromy noise model. We prove that the largest Kostka multiplicity is the optimal dimension of a subspace code correcting the full monodromy algebra, even among codes spanning several isotypic blocks. Quantizing an argyle master space recovers the cyclic sheet space as a weight sector of a tensor power, with the identification preserving monodromy. For the balanced three-cycle with $t$ zeroes per arrow, the multiplicity of a partition $(a,b,c)$ of $3t$ is $1+\min(a-b,b-c)$. The optimal logical dimension is thus $t+1$, attained uniquely by the block indexed by $(2t,t)$. At $t=1$ we give explicit codewords for a qubit on six sheets. The commuting right action generates its full logical algebra, yielding errors outside the monodromy model that leave the measured footprint statistics unchanged yet require different recoveries. We also compute collision-parity ranks, give a higher-rank Grassmannian example, and derive a conditional criterion for recovery across splitting types.

title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
text:
Title: An Energy-Based Perspective on Machine Learning
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Energy-based models (EBMs) define a distribution through a scalar energy, $p_θ(x)\propto\exp(-E_θ(x))$, and are usually presented as one model family among many. This tutorial has a broader goal: beyond introducing EBMs, it uses them as a single lens that connects the different aspects of machine learning. Any EBM is specified by three choices, the energy, which determines what the model represents; the inference procedure, which samples from or optimizes the energy; and the learning method, which fits the energy to data. We first develop these components, including sampling, variational inference, and learning by maximum likelihood, noise contrastive estimation, pseudolikelihood, score matching, and adversarial training, and show that the learning methods share one contrastive structure. We then show that discriminative models, generative models such as GANs, normalizing flows, diffusion and autoregressive models, representation learning methods such as contrastive learning, word2vec, BERT, denoising auto-encoders, and diffusion representations, reinforcement learning with EBM policies and world models, inverse reinforcement learning, and planning, as well as inference-time computation with verifiers, are all EBMs that differ in these three choices, mostly in how they handle the partition function and sampling. This view explains existing methods, organizes them into a common framework, and suggests new algorithms by replacing one component while keeping the others, with composition of energies as a principled way to combine learned models at inference time.

title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
text:
Title: LawKAN: Group-Law Layers for Composition -- When Imposing a Known Law Pays Off
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Many tasks compose transformations by a known rule: chained rotations in robotics and navigation. Learned models relearn it, compounding error; classical estimators hardcode it and miss hardware deviations. We impose the known structure and learn only the remainder: an exact non-commutative group law sits in the node of a self-contained layer, its edges learn local increments, and a zero-initialized correction psi learns unknown deviations of the law. A pre-training criterion predicts exact representability. On fixed-angle SU(2) composition, a 54-parameter dense edge is the most accurate dense model, at 27x fewer parameters than the strongest fixed-matrix baseline, and lies 0.05 deg above the Bayes floor. On real robot arms, an isolated 306-parameter psi reaches 1.12-1.14 mm versus 1.29-1.33 mm for Gauss-Newton at N >= 60, and the recipe transfers across three vendors and two protocols. The recipe matches classical fits where the data obey the law and loses where the imposed law is not the task's.

title: Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Federated Unsupervised Visual Recognition
text:
Title: Harnessing Vision-Language Models for Federated Unsupervised Visual Recognition
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Federated learning (FL) is a promising research paradigm that enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without data sharing. To handle unlabeled data in local clients, existing unsupervised FL research has primarily focused on tasks like clustering and self-supervised representation learning, leaving the critical problem of unsupervised visual recognition largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce FedUR, the first framework designed for unsupervised recognition by leveraging the zero-shot capabilities of pre-trained vision-language models like CLIP. Specifically, FedUR addresses data heterogeneity through a pseudo-labeling mechanism with a class-aware data selection strategy. This strategy first estimates a global pseudo-label distribution, then allocates pseudo-labeled data to clients accordingly. To handle the uncertainty of conventional positive pseudo-labels, FedUR further incorporates class weights and a negative pseudo-labeling strategy. Furthermore, FedUR proposes a personalized prompt aggregation protocol where general visual prompts are aggregated on the server, and personalized text prompts encoding local knowledge are retained on clients. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FedUR consistently outperforms baseline methods under both label-level and feature-level distribution shifts. We believe this work paves the way for further advances in federated unsupervised recognition. Code will be available at {github.com/tim-learn/FedUR/}}.

title: Coupled dark energy and apparent phantom crossing: a potential-independent lower bound
text:
Title: Coupled dark energy and apparent phantom crossing: a potential-independent lower bound
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Baryon acoustic oscillation measurements from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), combined with the cosmic microwave background (CMB) and type Ia supernovae, prefer a dark energy whose equation of state was below $-1$ in the past and is above $-1$ today. A canonical scalar field cannot cross this line, but it can appear to do so if it is coupled to dark matter, and we ask how strong this coupling must be, for any potential. We show that the apparent crossing requires the dark matter to lose a minimum fraction of its mass after recombination, fixed by the expansion history $H(z)$. For a constant coupling $β=d\ln m/dφ$, the mass can change only as fast as the field moves, and the speed of the field is itself set by $H(z)$, so that the coupling must be larger than a minimum value $β_{\rm min}[H(z)]$. This bound holds for any potential, applies to the largest value of the coupling when the coupling depends on the field, and is reached exactly when the field comes to rest within the observed range. For the DESI DR2 best fits, the dark matter must lose about 5-7% of its mass by $z\simeq 0.8$, which requires $β_{\rm min}=0.047$-$0.058$; including the uncertainties of the data, the public DESI DR2 chains give the 95% lower limit $|β|>0.025$-$0.038$. We also apply the bound to published fits of coupled quintessence: all of them respect it, and those with a constant coupling reproduce only a shallow version of the crossing. Since the coupling cannot be smaller than $β_{\rm min}$, two known effects of the coupling have a minimum size: an extra attraction between dark matter particles of at least a few tenths of a per cent of gravity, and a lensing signal at least a few per cent weaker than the clustering of dark matter would suggest.

title: Generalizing Density Functional Theory with a Particle-Hole Expansion
text:
Title: Generalizing Density Functional Theory with a Particle-Hole Expansion
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Strong electron correlation remains difficult to describe within conventional density functional approximations, particularly when natural-orbital occupations become strongly fractional. We introduce a systematic particle-hole expansion that generalizes density functional theory (DFT) through an explicit functional of the one-electron reduced density matrix. The previously derived cumulant-based correction emerges as the leading term and the thermal (entropic) correction as an infinite-order member whose coefficients are fixed by a single parameter. The expansion can be formulated as a moment problem solved by semidefinite programming with computational scaling comparable to DFT. We show that both the first- and second-order corrections yield closed-form natural-orbital occupations. Applications to periacenes and Fe-porphyrin demonstrate that the second-order correction substantially reduces excessive orbital fractionalization, yielding natural-orbital occupations and fundamental gaps in improved agreement with correlated calculations.

title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
text:
Title: Is Persona Generalization Predictable?
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Persona generalization occurs when fine-tuning a language model in one domain induces behavioral changes in others -- for example, the broadly unsafe behavior observed in emergent misalignment. We discover a surprising "on-the-line" phenomenon in persona generalization: in-domain and out-of-domain persona rates across various fine-tuning hyperparameters follow an approximately probit-linear relationship, and the specific probit-linear relationship is surprisingly shared even across model families and model sizes, including Qwen and Llama. Training choices that leave the set of trainable parameters unchanged, such as learning rate, weight decay, and training duration, largely move models along the same line, reducing transfer mainly by weakening in-domain learning. Changing which layers are fine-tuned, however, can change the slope. For unsafe behavior, fine-tuning only later layers yields shallower slopes, retaining strong in-domain learning while reducing out-of-domain misalignment. This "on-the-line" phenomenon unifies unexpected, isolated observations of persona generalization within a quantitative framework for predicting and controlling behavioral transfer.

title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
text:
Title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.

title: JUMP-lite: Compact, reproducible benchmarking of cell representations
text:
Title: JUMP-lite: Compact, reproducible benchmarking of cell representations
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Image-based profiling captures rich phenotypic signatures for drug discovery and functional genomics. Large public datasets like JUMP Cell Painting now provide millions of images for systematic study. However, JUMP alone occupies 115 TB, and fragmented evaluation practices make systematic comparisons of representation methods impractical for many researchers. Here we present Nahual, an open-source framework for reproducible model deployment, and JUMP-lite, a 92.0 GB subset of JUMP that is approximately 1,250-fold smaller, selected to cover genetic modalities and compound annotations and reduced via lossy JPEG XL compression. Using these resources, we benchmark five representation methods, including classical features (CellProfiler) and deep learning models (MorphEM, OpenPhenom, SubCell, DINOv2). Moderate compression broadly retains signal relative to uncompressed images. Standardized phenotypic activity and consistency metrics reveal meaningful performance differences across methods. Together, JUMP-lite and Nahual provide a foundation for accessible, reproducible benchmarking of image-based cell representations.

title: Latin American Studies since the 1980s: From Apocalyptic Dreams to Assimilationist Consolidation
text:
Title: Latin American Studies since the 1980s: From Apocalyptic Dreams to Assimilationist Consolidation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

We investigate how Latin American Studies (LAS) has evolved since 1982 in three leading LAS journals. Using network analysis, text mining, and bibliometrics, we trace transformations in disciplinary positioning, authorship, and citation patterns. Our main claim is that LAS has undergone an assimilationist consolidation. The field is now institutionally recognisable, with core LAS journals occupying central positions in disciplinary networks and acting as bridges across fields. Yet this consolidation has reinforced hierarchies privileging Anglophone academic norms. Journals based in Latin America, once central, have been marginalised. The share of Latin American authors has grown, but their profiles converge towards Northern standards.

title: Critical Branching Systems with General Lifetimes: Hunt Motions and Applications to Semilinear Equations
text:
Title: Critical Branching Systems with General Lifetimes: Hunt Motions and Applications to Semilinear Equations
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We consider a critical monotype Bellman-Harris branching particle system on $E=R^d$ or $E=[0,\infty)^d$, started from a homogeneous Poisson field with Lebesgue intensity. Particles follow a conservative Hunt process with transition semigroup $(P_t)_{t\ge 0}$, have independent lifetimes with distribution $Γ$, and reproduce at death with generating function $f(s)=s+c(1-s)^{1+β}$. We assume Lebesgue invariance and uniform bounds $P_t1_K=O(t^{-q})$ for compact $K$. We also impose a localization condition: the expected number of particles in a fixed compact set at time $t$ descended from ancestors initially outside suitable regions of volume $O(t^q)$ can be made arbitrarily small, uniformly for $t\ge 1$. For spread-out lifetimes of finite mean, the system converges to a nontrivial limit of Lebesgue intensity when $qβ>1$ and becomes locally extinct when $qβ\le 1$. For nonarithmetic lifetimes satisfying $\barΓ(t)\sim c_1t^{-γ}$, $0 0$ in the absorption term $-v^{1+β}$.

title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering
text:
Title: Controlling nitrogen incorporation in (Eu,Ba,Ca)TiO$_3$-derived perovskite-type oxynitrides through Fermi Level Engineering
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Defect states directly influence not only functional properties, but also oxynitride formation during ammonolysis. Along with structural stability and charge balance, these defects can cause non-uniform nitrogen incorporation. To address this, the recently proposed Fermi Level Engineering concept provides a powerful alternative of rationalising oxynitride synthesis. By using the electron chemical potential, i.e., the Fermi level, as a unique descriptor, this approach can predict, understand, and manipulate defect formation enthalpies and charge transition levels, subsequently allowing to incorporate defect-property correlations to the concept. This work combines theoretical modelling and experimental characterisation of barium titanium oxynitrides to explain an intrinsic, self-limiting nitridation process. Progressive nitrogen incorporation causes a Fermi level downward shift, leaving further nitrogen substitution on oxygen sites energetically unfavourable, up to 0.03 N per unit formula. We demonstrate that A-site cation substitution in Eu$_{1-x}$Ba$_x$TiO$_3$- and Eu$_{1-x}$Ca$_x$TiO$_3$-derived oxynitrides can be applied to control compensation of the additional negative charge from N$^{3-}$ and keep the Fermi level high. The Eu$^{2+/3+}$ redox couple enables substitution of oxygen by nitrogen through pinning of the Fermi level at the europium charge transition level, at $\sim$ 2.9 eV above the VBM. This allows for higher nitrogen uptake of up to 0.65 per formula unit (taken from hot gas extraction) through a more controlled process. Further incorporation is then limited by an intra-Ti(O,N)$_6$ octahedra distortion due to internal bond-angle variance. These findings demonstrate that Fermi Level Engineering provides a pathway to predict and overcome intrinsic synthetic and thermodynamic limitations in oxynitride synthesis.

title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
text:
Title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

title: A Note On Lattice Definition of Gauge Theories With Chiral Fermions
text:
Title: A Note On Lattice Definition of Gauge Theories With Chiral Fermions
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Because of the fermion doubling problem, it has been a longstanding challenge to describe a lattice algorithm for studying four-dimensional gauge theories coupled to chiral fermions. Recently, an algorithm to do so has been described by Craig, extending partial results in the previous literature. Here we describe a variant of this algorithm, based on interpolating a lattice gauge field over the continuum (as in Craig's work) and coupling the interpolated gauge field to continuum chiral fermions. The same variant was also proposed recently by Hsu. In any dimension and for any anomaly-free representation, this approach can be implemented on a computer in principle, but not in practice by Monte Carlo methods because the chiral fermion path integral is not positive.

title: What Transfers Across Protein Pockets? Experience Reuse in Molecular Optimization for Agentic Structure-Based Drug Design
text:
Title: What Transfers Across Protein Pockets? Experience Reuse in Molecular Optimization for Agentic Structure-Based Drug Design
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

LLM agents optimize a ligand in a protein pocket by editing it step by step and docking each edit. Recent agents first spend extra dockings probing the complex with controlled edits; guidance induced from these probes is reported to help more than the chemical knowledge the model already carries. The probes are then discarded with the instance that produced them, so the obvious next step is to keep them in an experience base, letting a new pocket inherit what earlier ones already paid for. Such a base is read through a \emph{key}: the record properties under which past edits are pooled and a new one is looked up. Using the full log of one such run over the CrossDocked2020 test-set pockets, we ask whether its keys recur on a pocket the base has never seen and still separate improving from worsening edits. \crchange{Using} the contacts at the site being edited, the action, and the round as \crchange{a} key, the base separates them sharply. Within our analysis, this separation is largely explained by how much the edit changed the molecule's size, the action, and the round, none of which describes the target.
