To assess the performance of the proposed method, we compared TractSpLearn with the original TractLearn in three cohorts: (i) healthy controls (HC), (ii) athletes with persistent post-concussive syndromes (PPCS), and (iii) athletes with repeated head injuries (RHI), with abnormalities particularly evident in axial kurtosis (AK) and mean diffusivity (MD). In RHI, TractSpLearn highlighted recurrent abnormalities across patients. In the PPCS cohort, the overall group-level differences were more modest, potentially reflecting both limited statistical power due to the small sample size and partial normalization of white-matter alterations during recovery. Still TractSpLearn identified abnormality evidence in more patients and across more affected tracts than TractLearn.

title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
text:
Title: Defects and Structural Evolution in CrSBr: Machine-Learning Potentials for Atomistic Simulations
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

The layered van der Waals semiconductor CrSBr combines intrinsic magnetic order with semiconducting and optical properties, making it a promising material for multifunctional electronic and photonic applications. Understanding how defects and structural transformations affect its properties under experimentally relevant conditions, however, remains challenging for first-principles simulations due to the relevant length and time scales. Here, we develop and benchmark machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) for the Cr-S-Br system, enabling large-scale atomistic simulations of CrSBr with accuracy approaching that of density functional theory (DFT). The charge-aware variant qNEP achieves near-DFT accuracy in predicting lattice constants, formation enthalpies, vacancy energetics, and the anisotropic pressure response of o-CrSBr. Nudged elastic band calculations reveal that pre-existing S vacancies lower the Cr Frenkel-pair migration barrier by up to 1.1 eV, providing an atomistic mechanism for beam-induced Cr redistribution and structural transformations. Displacement threshold calculations further show that Br is the most susceptible species to electron-beam-induced displacement, identifying the relative ease of removing different atomic species. Together, these results establish a validated computational framework for investigating atomic-scale disorder and structural transformations in CrSBr, providing a basis for defect engineering in materials for future magneto-optoelectronic applications.

title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
text:
Title: SU(2)-Equivariant Spinor Message Passing for Molecular Magnetism
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Predicting molecular magnetic properties often requires costly electronic-structure calculations that account for spin-orbit coupling. Inspired by the spinor nature of the underlying electronic states, we introduce eSpinor, an SU(2)-equivariant graph neural network that propagates spinor features alongside the integer-rank tensors used in conventional equivariant models. We initialize spinors from eigenvectors of an approximate Hamiltonian that includes spin-orbit coupling. The network preserves their rotation laws and makes predictions independent of arbitrary eigenbasis choices. Comparisons with geometry-only and Hamiltonian-informed baselines assess the benefit of this architecture beyond supplying electronic information. On cobalt single-molecule magnet candidates, eSpinor improves magnetic anisotropy predictions, including for unseen ligands. It also improves excitation-energy predictions for dysprosium candidates with unseen ligands, extending the benefit to rotationally invariant scalar targets. For a dysprosium magnetic resonance imaging probe, it predicts real electron-spin correlations and low-field nuclear relaxation rates more accurately despite static crystal-field errors similar to the Hamiltonian-informed baseline. This dynamical advantage extends from water to methanol without retraining. These results support spinor message passing as a useful inductive bias for molecular magnetism in the tested systems and show why model selection should be guided by accuracy on the intended physical observables.

title: Local limit Theorem for Directed polymers in a random environment in the full weak disorder regime
text:
Title: Local limit Theorem for Directed polymers in a random environment in the full weak disorder regime
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

For directed polymers in random environment, we provide a short and mostly self-contained proof of the local limit theorem in the full weak disorder phase, including the critical inverse temperature $β_c$. That is, the point-to-point partition function is well approximated by the product of two independent point-to-line partition functions (one starting from each endpoint of the system) multiplied by the simple random walk transition kernel. The approximation is valid in the $L^p$ sense for an optimal range of $p$. The result is new at $β=β_c$ and for $p>2$, and in all cases the proof is significantly simpler, technically and conceptually, than what can be found in the literature. As a consequence of the result we establish an invariance principle for the polymer measure with fixed end-point, valid for all $β\in [0,β_c]$.

title: Conditioned free-energy density of proteins using unbalanced solutions to constraint satisfaction problems
text:
Title: Conditioned free-energy density of proteins using unbalanced solutions to constraint satisfaction problems
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

We show that computing the log-partition function (free-energy) of conditioned inhomogeneous Curie--Weiss spin Hamiltonians reduces to an unbalanced $2 \to 1$ norm computation, and design a polynomial-time SDP algorithm for this problem with a lower bound proof for the amount of unbalance achieved. Applied to the protein Ubiquitin, the framework starts from a known crystal structure, explores alternative backbone conformations across the free-energy landscape, and identifies flexible regions of the protein while preserving its native secondary structure.

title: A Unified Interface Neural Network for Elliptic Interface Problems
text:
Title: A Unified Interface Neural Network for Elliptic Interface Problems
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We develop a Unified Interface Neural Network (UINN) framework for elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients. A single shared network provides a unified representation of the solution in both subdomains, while a projection--correction construction embeds the solution and flux jump conditions directly into the neural trial space. This design aligns with the classical numerical principle of incorporating interfacial physics into the approximation basis to construct interface-unfitted numerical methods. The jump conditions are therefore satisfied exactly for any network parameters. Compared with methods based on separate phase networks and numerical formulations with interface penalty terms, UINN provides a unified representation with exact enforcement of interfacial jump conditions and interface-penalty-free optimization. Those features streamline the numerical formulations and can enhance training robustness. Numerical experiments on smooth interfaces at modestly large and high coefficient contrasts demonstrate UINN's solution accuracy, near-machine-precision satisfaction of the interface jump conditions, and enhanced robustness.

title: Galactic warps constrain equivalence-principle violation in the dark sector
text:
Title: Galactic warps constrain equivalence-principle violation in the dark sector
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Current measurements of the expansion of the Universe allow for the presence of evolving dark energy, distinct from a cosmological constant, with an equation of state that seems to violate the null energy condition. One notable explanation for this behaviour is that the dark energy interacts with the dark matter, violating the equivalence principle yet evading conventional laboratory and astrophysical constraints. Such models produce fifth forces acting only on dark matter. We show how such forces separate halo and stellar disk centres, creating a potential gradient across the disk that warps it into a cup shape. Measuring the warps of $4\times10^3$ edge-on disks in Sloan Digital Sky Survey images and modelling the fifth-force signal together with competing baryonic effects, we find no sign of the predicted correlation between the measured warps and the fifth-force field. This constrains the fifth-force strength relative to gravity to $ΔG/G_N<7.7\times10^{-4}$ at 95% credibility (or $<1.7\times10^{-3}$ once systematic uncertainties are included) for force ranges of 8 Mpc and above. In the infinite-range limit of a scalar rolling today, even the conservative bound is three times stronger than the tightest cosmological bound (which, unlike ours, depends on the scalar's cosmological evolution) and about two orders of magnitude below other astrophysical bounds. It disfavours at 2-3$σ$ the couplings preferred by recent fits of interacting dark energy to cosmological data unless gravitational screening is invoked.

title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
text:
Title: Exploiting floating point emulation in tensor contractions in relativistic coupled cluster theory
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

In this manuscript we outline a computational strategy to leverage a vendor-optimized implementation of the Ozaki scheme I for floating point emulation as part of an implementation of the Transpose-Transpose-GEMM-Transpose (TTGT) pattern for tensor contractions, and assess its potential to accelerate two of the most expensive tensor contractions appearing in relativistic coupled cluster theory in high-end accelerators such as the NVIDIA Blackwell B200 system in which there is a strong differential in the performance of computations for double and lower precision datatypes. Our results indicate that this emulation-based TTGT strategy can provide significant speedups compared to runs without emulation, and can be competitive with state-of-the-art, vendor-optimized tensor contraction libraries using native double precision as compute datatype. More importantly, our scheme provides a path towards easily allowing users to tune the desired accuracy in the tensor contraction steps, including cases where precision between single and double is sufficient for the application.

title: MoleCode unlocks structural intelligence in large language models
text:
Title: MoleCode unlocks structural intelligence in large language models
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Molecules are graphs, but large language models~(LLMs) are usually asked to reason about them through linear strings. The most popular molecular representation, SMILES, compresses atoms, bonds, branches and rings into a compact sequence in which topology is implicit, forcing LLMs to reconstruct molecular structure before performing the requested chemical operation. Here we introduce MoleCode, an LLM-native, training-free, graph-explicit molecular language in which all molecular components are represented as typed entities with persistent identifiers and explicit relations. MoleCode makes molecular topology directly readable, editable and auditable within the language context, allowing an LLM to operate on structure rather than recover it from syntax. Across molecular reasoning, editing, generation and analysis tasks, this representational shift improves frontier LLMs most strongly when structural access is limiting: unfamiliar molecules, topology-sensitive operations, larger structures and repetitive polymers. It also changes how inference is allocated, replacing long reasoning traces devoted to implicit structural reconstruction with shorter, more chemically directed reasoning over explicit atoms and bonds. In molecular optimization, this enables localized, property-aligned edits that preserve structural similarity to the starting compounds. The same Subgraph--Node--Edge grammar extends beyond small molecules to polymers, Markush structures, mechanism-style transformations and interleaved scientific documents, including research articles and patent disclosures in which chemical information is distributed across text and images. These results suggest that the interface between scientific objects and LLMs should not treat structure as something to be decoded from text. When the object of reasoning is relational, the structure itself should be part of the language.

title: Amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line
text:
Title: Amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Propagating spin waves have emerged as promising candidates for signal processing and information transmission. We present a theoretical investigation of the generation, propagation and collection of spin-wave wave packets in micrometer-wide magnetic conduits, highlighting their potential for analogue frequency demultiplexing in space and time. We clarify the roles of the excitation duration and of the spin wave dispersion relation, as well as the influence of the spin-wave linewidth in setting the spatio-temporal evolution of propagating spin-wave wavepackets excited by Gaussian field pulses. We issue rules for the spatio-temporal separation of wavepackets that carry different frequencies. We finally propose an amplitude-conserving frequency demultiplexer based on a spin wave delay line of 60x5 $μ$m$^2$ footprint.

title: Integrative modelling of protein-glycan interactions with HADDOCK3
text:
Title: Integrative modelling of protein-glycan interactions with HADDOCK3
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Glycans are structurally diverse and flexible biomolecules that play key roles in many biological processes. Their conformational variability makes the modeling of their interactions with proteins particularly challenging. This chapter presents a step-by-step protocol for modeling protein-glycan interactions using HADDOCK3, an integrative modeling platform that supports the inclusion of experimental or predicted interaction restraints and allows for flexible refinement of the solutions. The workflow is illustrated using the interaction between a linear homopolymer glycan, 4-beta-glucopyranose, and the catalytic domain of the Humicola grisea Cel12A enzyme, for which an experimental X-ray structure is available as a reference. Detailed instructions are provided for input structure preparation, restraint definition, docking setup, execution, and result analysis. Application of the protocol starting from unbound structures yields models of acceptable to medium quality, with interface-ligand RMSD values below 3 angstroms. Although illustrated on a specific system, the protocol has been optimized and benchmarked on multiple protein-glycan complexes and is broadly applicable to similar systems, providing a framework for integrative modeling of protein-glycan interactions.

title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
text:
Title: Unifying Central Flow, Rod Flow, and the Edge Coupling
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

At the edge of stability, the iterates of gradient descent oscillate along the sharp directions of the Hessian. This poses a significant challenge for continuous-time models as the usual continuous-time approximation -- the gradient flow -- admits no oscillations. Several continuous-time models have been proposed to capture the behavior at the edge of stability, among them central flow and rod flow. Although both models can be interpreted as performing a coarse-graining in time, the connection between them remains poorly understood. Here we show that both flows can be derived from a third object, the edge coupling: a functional on consecutive iterates whose critical points are the fixed points and period-two orbits of gradient descent. It is revealed that the two flows correspond to coarse-grainings at different time scales. Rod flow coarse-grains over only the fastest time scale, while central flow coarse-grains over both the fast and intermediate time scales. Furthermore, using the edge coupling, we derive rod flows and central flows for momentum methods such as heavy ball and Adam. We verify the derived flows experimentally on representative neural network architectures, where they track the discrete iterates throughout all phases of training -- including the transition from the stable regime to the edge of stability.

title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
text:
Title: MicroLens: Read, Trace, and Rewire the Residual Stream with Two Lenses
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Lenses that decode hidden states into words are a popular way to look inside language models, but a heatmap of decoded words only shows what a vector reads as and cannot distinguish whether, or how much, the model uses the information. We present an interactive viewer that puts reading, tracing and editing on the same layers-by-tokens grid of the residual stream. In the viewer, every cell can be decoded with two lenses, the logit lens and the Jacobian lens (J-lens), traced back to the tokens it drew from, and edited, with the rest of the model rerun on the spot. We demonstrate three usage scenarios on Gemma-3-4B-it, backed by sweeps over a few hundred prompts, to show what this tool can discover. First, the two lenses give different directions to write with, each suiting a different edit: the logit lens's word direction sets what a token outputs, while the J-lens's direction changes what later tokens read. Second, in two-hop trivia questions (the capital of the state or country containing a given city), the state or country is readable at the city token from as early as layer 7, and swapping it there can redirect the answer 92-98% of the time; however, at the answer position, the state or country information is not used. Third, when a chat model answers questions with a step-by-step reasoning prompt, the correct answer is often already the top word in the residual stream before any reasoning is written: for 89-92% of retrieval questions and 39-63% of multi-hop and serial ones, far above their respective distractors (at most 5%). However, ordering puzzles are an exception, as the model works them out only once it writes its final reasoning steps. Furthermore, for answers that are visible in the residual stream, the J-lens reads them a layer or two earlier than the logit lens across the different types of question.

title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
text:
Title: Underdamped Stochastic Optimal Transport with Landauer boundary conditions: machine learning and analytical solution
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Finding optimal transport protocols for underdamped stochastic processes is a difficult yet important problem in control theory. In this paper we develop a direct method, based on machine learning, to find the optimal solution of the problem in the presence of non-linear boundary conditions, including those modelling the Landauer bit-erasure problem. The dynamics is steered from a single-peak to a double-peak distribution in position space, by only acting on a controllable external potential. The problem is highly non-linear, and analytical solutions are not available in general. We benchmark our numerical results with a perturbative expansion, which is expected to hold in a suitable overdamped limit.

title: Analytic criteria for criticality of subordinated Schrödinger operators
text:
Title: Analytic criteria for criticality of subordinated Schrödinger operators
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

For a subordinated Schrödinger operator, we introduce a quantity that plays a role analogous to the bottom of the spectrum of a Schrödinger operator, and establish analytic criteria for subcriticality, criticality and supercriticality of a subordinated Schrödinger operator.

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
text:
Title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
text:
Title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.

title: Collider-observable curvaton
text:
Title: Collider-observable curvaton
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We study a technically natural realization of the curvaton mechanism, in which decay is mediated through the superrenormalizable interaction with the Higgs. We compute the quantum and thermal corrections to the curvaton potential and show that they remain under control throughout its cosmological evolution. For high inflationary scales, the curvaton dissipates through off-shell processes in the Standard Model plasma. The viable parameter space is broad, and the region in which the curvaton mass and dimensionful Higgs-portal coupling are closest in scale lies within the discovery reach of proposed searches for light Higgs-mixed scalars.

title: Two-loop matter power spectrum from FFTLog and kite integrals
text:
Title: Two-loop matter power spectrum from FFTLog and kite integrals
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We present a fast and accurate method for computing the two-loop matter power spectrum in the Effective Field Theory of Large-Scale Structure (EFTofLSS). Using FFTLog, we decompose the linear power spectrum into complex power laws, reducing the two-loop corrections to cosmology-independent massless Feynman integrals of kite topology. A central numerical challenge is the evaluation of these integrals for complex powers with large imaginary parts, where the highly oscillatory integrands make accurate numerical evaluation particularly challenging. We overcome this difficulty using a Mellin--Barnes representation summed over a uniform lattice, achieving approximately ten digit precision even for large imaginary powers, with an error estimate for each integral. The resulting precomputed matrices allow the two-loop power spectrum to be evaluated for a new cosmology in a few milliseconds. Comparing with direct numerical integration, we find agreement at the $10^{-4}$ level relative to the power spectrum up to $k=0.2$ $h$Mpc$^{-1}$ after accounting for EFTofLSS counterterm contributions and FFTLog decomposition errors. The same framework extends to biased tracers and redshift-space distortions, providing the building blocks for general two-loop calculations in EFTofLSS. We make the code for evaluating the kite integrals publicly available, together with precomputed matrices and an implementation for the two-loop matter power spectrum as a concrete application. Our results can be directly incorporated into existing FFTLog-based codes for large-scale structure, extending their current one-loop capabilities to two loops within the same computational framework.

title: A Polynomial-Scaling PDE Solver with Entanglement-Basis Tensor Networks
text:
Title: A Polynomial-Scaling PDE Solver with Entanglement-Basis Tensor Networks
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We develop a finite element method (FEM) for partial differential equation (PDE) solver based on the entanglement-basis representation introduced in our companion work. By lifting non-linear finite-element equations into an augmented coefficient space, the governing PDE together with boundary, initial, and inter-element constraints can be expressed through a unified quadratic residual minimization. Although this augmented space grows exponentially with the number of elements, its tensor-product structure allows it to be represented efficiently using tensor networks. Using the matrix product state (MPS) as a concrete example, we show that density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) sweeps enable element-by-element optimization without explicitly constructing the full augmented space. For bounded bond dimension, the resulting computational cost scales polynomially with the number of finite elements. We extend the framework to time-dependent problems through implicit temporal discretization and demonstrate convergence under both mesh and polynomial refinement using diffusion equations.

title: Enhancing Cryo-EM Density Map Segmentation in Phenix for Improved Atomic Model Building
text:
Title: Enhancing Cryo-EM Density Map Segmentation in Phenix for Improved Atomic Model Building
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

We introduce PhenixCraft, a fully automated pipeline for building atomic models from cryo-EM density maps. By integrating AlphaFold predictions, we enhance the map-segmentation step in Phenix during model building, addressing challenges posed by noise and artifacts that traditionally hinder this step. Our results demonstrate PhenixCraft's superior performance in TM-scores and sequence accuracy, significantly improving upon the limitations and inefficiencies of traditional model building using Phenix.

title: Coherent detector responses to quantum-controlled spherical-shell geometries
text:
Title: Coherent detector responses to quantum-controlled spherical-shell geometries
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

A detector inside a static spherical shell samples globally matched field modes even though its local geometry is flat. We construct the response of a compactly switched Unruh-DeWitt detector on a quantum-controlled pair of transparent spherical-shell spacetimes with common Arnowitt-Deser-Misner mass. A stipulated common-incoming scattering identification places the branch excitations in one Hilbert space. Their positive Gram matrix determines joint, conditional, and dephased detector responses at a finite common readout, retaining the physical detector-clock phase in the uncompensated protocol. An additional coherent phase-gate protocol compensates free detector-clock propagation while preserving the shell interaction response. For concentric shells the centered response is exactly $s$ wave. A common incoming direction basis extends the construction to a lab-fixed detector and displaced shell centers, preserving common-translation covariance. The equal-radius benchmark exhibits conditional changes of order $25\%$ without dark-port amplification. Combining radius and position produces an assignment-odd response that reverses under reflection and vanishes at the relational midpoint. The relative normalized-state contrast reaches $34.15\%$ among the computed samples; the relative clock-resolved probe-influence contrast reaches $8.09\%$ for the declared readout, while larger values belong to its separate shared-phase envelope. These effects already occur in the dominant-energy-condition-compatible core. They are relational, model-dependent detector responses, not a background-independent witness of quantum geometry. First-order coefficients have finite pointlike limits; finite-coupling statements are made only at a fixed shared regulator.

title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
text:
Title: Dynamics of thermalization in classical three-dimensional many-body systems: Non-Maxwellian distributions and the role of anisotropic trapping
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The physics of interacting baths is of interest in a variety of contexts, ranging from ultracold atoms to ionized gases. While many features can already be captured in a one-dimensional model, others are specific to the situation of two or three-dimensional systems. In this paper, we focus on three-dimensional features of a model for thermalization between two baths that we have explored in earlier publications. In contrast to the one-dimensional situation we show that, en route to thermalization, deviations from the Maxwell-Boltzmann energy distributions more akin to $κ$-distributions are observed. In three dimensions, these can be seen in changes at the peak of the distribution, which is precluded by the expected monotonic behavior of the energy distributions in one dimension. Furthermore, we consider thermalization for anisotropic trapping and explore its role in the onset of anomalous scaling with respect to the particle number. These results may be pertinent to the understanding of the interplay between turbulent behavior and nonlinearities for a variety of many-body classical systems.

title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model
text:
Title: Mean Field Game Problem with Kantorovich Potential Coupling: An Attrition model
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

In this work we address a class of Mean-Field Game (MFG) systems on the flat torus $\mathbb{T}^{d}$ in which individual agent incentives arise from macroscopic, distribution-dependent objectives governed by the Wasserstein-2 ($W_{2}$) distance. Taking the first variation (Lions derivative) of the Wasserstein-based macroscopic functional yields a coupled forward-backward system of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) and Fokker--Planck (FP) equations featuring a nonlocal coupling driven by the Kantorovich optimal transport potential. As a primary case study, we formulate a large-scale attacker-defender attrition model aimed at protecting High-Value Units (HVUs). By defining population-wise attrition rates via the $W_{2}$ metric and casting the defense strategy as a Pareto-optimal McKean--Vlasov control problem, we derive a concrete HJB--FP system with a Kantorovich potential coupling. We prove the local-in-time existence of classical solutions for this system using Schauder's fixed-point theorem. Finally, we compute the MFG dynamics by combining the Sinkhorn algorithm with ResNet-based Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), and simulate two-dimensional attacker-defender engagements across diverse attrition parameters, control costs, and multi-HVU configurations.

title: Empirical approximation of $L_p$ norms for $p\in (2, \infty)$
text:
Title: Empirical approximation of $L_p$ norms for $p\in (2, \infty)$
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

For $p>2$ and an $N$-dimensional subspace $X\subset L_\infty(μ)$ satisfying \[ \|f\|_\infty\le (KN)^{1/p}\|f\|_{L_p(μ)} \quad\forall f\in X, \] we show that $m\ge C(p)KN \bigl(\varepsilon^{-p} +\varepsilon^{-2}\log_2(2N)\bigr)$ independent samples $ξ^1,\ldots,ξ^m$ with distribution $μ$ satisfy \[ (1-\varepsilon)\|f\|_{L_p(μ)}^p \le\frac1m\sum_{j=1}^m|f(ξ^j)|^p \le(1+\varepsilon)\|f\|_{L_p(μ)}^p \quad\forall f\in X \] with probability at least $1-\exp(-c(p)\frac{m\varepsilon^2}{KN})$. This gives the optimal sample-size order $N\log_2 N$ for independent random sampling with fixed $K$, $p$, and $\varepsilon$. This result follows from a more general empirical moment estimate over unit balls of $p$-convex norms.

title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
text:
Title: Trained, Frozen, or Absent: Identifying What a Quantum Layer Contributes to Cross-Sectional Equity Ranking
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Hybrid quantumclassical models are increasingly proposed for nancial prediction, but reported gains are rarely separated from the classical components around them. We study a hybrid quantum temporal convolutional network for daily cross-sectional ranking of 2000 Tokyo Stock Exchange equities under a protocol built to make the quantum contribution identiable: six conditions (circuit trained, frozen or absent, a parameter-matched classical surrogate, and the circuit alone, trained or frozen) through one code path; four walk-forward folds with ve seeds; bootstrap intervals, Deated Sharpe Ratios, backtest-overtting probabilities and family-wise error control; ve classical baselines including a gradient-boosted tree; and a locked holdout. On 500 out-of-sample days two one-sided tests place the trained-versus-frozen dierence inside 0.03 annualised Sharpe (p = 0.0055, minimum detectable eect 0.02): the circuit is equivalent to a frozen one, not merely indistinguishable from it. With the circuit as the head's only input the two are equivalent inside 0.25; against the network with no circuit the design resolves only 0.50. No condition is distinguishable from zero (best De-ated Sharpe Ratio 0.17). The holdout reproduces the ablation on a protable window, and 2000 US equities reproduce it where every condition loses money.

title: Out-of-equilibrium selection pressure enhances inference from protein sequence data
text:
Title: Out-of-equilibrium selection pressure enhances inference from protein sequence data
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Homologous proteins have similar three-dimensional structures and biological functions that shape their sequences. The resulting coevolution-driven correlations underlie methods from Potts models to AlphaFold, which infer protein structure and function from sequences. Using a minimal model, we show that fluctuating selection strength and the onset of new selection pressures improve coevolution-based inference of structural contacts. Our conclusions extend to realistic synthetic data and to the inference of interaction partners. Out-of-equilibrium noise arising from ubiquitous variations in natural selection thus enhances, rather than hinders, the success of inference from protein sequences.

title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
text:
Title: Right for the Wrong Reasons? Evaluating Plausibility and Behavioral Change in Explanation-Guided Learning
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Explanation-Guided Learning (EGL) promises models that are not only accurate but also rely on task-relevant evidence. However, whether improved agreement between model explanations and human-provided rationales also implies a changed decision strategy remains unclear. We study this tension under controlled synthetic shortcut introduction using a constructed shortcut dataset. Inspired by real-world applications, our benchmark covers shortcuts of different kinds, including localized, background-based, and global cues. This allows us to evaluate whether different EGL objectives produce behavioral changesand explanatory changes. Across these axes, we find that the effects of EGL are strongly objective-specific. Rationale-based data augmentation provides the clearest robustness gains when shortcut evidence can be separated from task-relevant foreground information, reaching average accuracy improvements of up to +4.8 percentage points (pp) together with increased foreground reliance. Attribution-constraining objectives primarily improve explanation plausibility, increasing Importance Mass by up to +14 pp on average, but provide weaker and less consistent behavioral correction, with average accuracy gains of at most +1.6 pp. Moreover, neither improved robustness nor improved plausibility reliably implies higher perturbation-based fidelity. Overall, our results show that EGL can be useful, but its success cannot be inferred from rationale agreement alone and should instead be evaluated along complementary behavioral and explanation-level axes. We publicly release all experimental results to enable further analysis (https://right-for-wrong-reasons.dfki.de/).

title: First-principles-based search for emergent topological spin textures in transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers
text:
Title: First-principles-based search for emergent topological spin textures in transition-metal dichalcogenide monolayers
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Topological spin textures such as skyrmions and bimerons offer rich physical functionalities and strong potential for future spin-based technologies. Identifying materials that host such emergent magnetic states, however, remains challenging due to the complex interplay between microscopic magnetic interactions and large-scale spin textures. Here, using a multiscale first-principles discovery framework, we identify a broad class of two-dimensional materials that stabilize nontrivial spin textures. The framework integrates relativistic density functional theory, magnetic force theory, and atomistic spin-dynamics simulations, enabling a direct connection between electronic interactions and emergent magnetic textures and allowing efficient screening of systems with large magnetic unit cells and competing exchange interactions. Applying this approach, we systematically screen 312 monolayer transition-metal dichalcogenides across 1T and 2H phases of 3d, 4d, and 5d transition metals. We uncover a diverse set of emergent spin textures, including skyrmions, bimerons, and complex domain states, and clarify their distinct stabilization mechanisms driven by exchange interactions, Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions, and magnetic frustration. These results identify promising candidate materials for topological spin textures and establish a transferable computational framework for accelerating materials discovery of complex magnetic states in two dimensions.

title: Thermal Field Theory for General Equilibrium Density Matrices
text:
Title: Thermal Field Theory for General Equilibrium Density Matrices
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Thermal field theory (TFT) is the combination of statistical mechanics and relativistic quantum field theory. This (book) chapter provides a pedagogical introduction to (and a review of) TFT for general equilibrium density matrices, which allow arbitrary values not only of temperature and chemical potentials, but also of average angular momentum. A general technique to compute ensemble averages is illustrated. Path-integral methods are developed to study the partition function and the thermal Green's functions of general operators, with an arbitrary number of points, in all field theories of physical relevance.

title: AlphaFunctor: Bridging The Gap Between Protein Function Annotation and Property Prediction
text:
Title: AlphaFunctor: Bridging The Gap Between Protein Function Annotation and Property Prediction
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

The fundamental relationship among protein sequence, structure, function, and physicochemical properties is a central principle in biology. While in principle protein function and properties should be able to be derived directly from protein sequence, in practice protein function and property prediction methods have been designed around specific datasets and specific property or function subsets, leading to an enormous gap between function annotation and property prediction. To address these challenges, we introduce AlphaFunctor, a category theory based foundation model-like platform to bridge the gap between protein function annotation and property prediction. Based on the hypothesis that protein function and properties can be directly derived from protein sequence, AlphaFunctor predicts protein functions as represented by Gene Ontology terms directly from sequence. Using these function predictions, AlphaFunctor further maps protein functions using topological spectral theory, path-complex neural networks, and protein domain analysis onto downstream property prediction. AlphaFunctor is (pre)trained in nearly 0.6 million protein function data points to deliver the state-of-the-art protein function annotation on three benchmark datasets. Without task-specific network redesign, AlphaFunctor maps qualitative protein function annotation to various qualitative and quantitative protein property predictions, outperforming other dataset-specific and task-specific competing predictors.

title: A Self-Interacting Dark-Matter Route to Supermassive Kerr Black Holes via Super-Eddington Bondi Accretion: Mass-Spin Evolution
text:
Title: A Self-Interacting Dark-Matter Route to Supermassive Kerr Black Holes via Super-Eddington Bondi Accretion: Mass-Spin Evolution
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Recent JWST observations motivate mechanisms for rapid black-hole growth in the early Universe. Extending our previous Schwarzschild study, we show that critical relativistic Bondi accretion of repulsively self-interacting dark matter remains an efficient super-Eddington channel for Kerr black holes with rotating inflow. Within a stationary equatorial quasi-spherical framework, smooth critical solutions exist over a finite range of inflow angular momentum set by the Kerr marginally bound capture values. Rotation changes the sonic structure and accretion efficiency, while the critical density cancellation and dark-sector/halo matching retain their Schwarzschild form. The resulting rapid growth persists until the finite halo supply becomes limiting. Because the inflow also carries angular momentum, stellar-mass seeds can grow and spin up simultaneously; illustrative population evolutions therefore provide a joint mass--spin route to early supermassive Kerr black holes.

title: Gravitational Particle Production and Locality of the Wavefunction-Squared
text:
Title: Gravitational Particle Production and Locality of the Wavefunction-Squared
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We show that no particle production due to the background geometry implies the locality of the wavefunction-squared for free heavy masses on expanding cosmologies. On global de Sitter of odd dimensions these two stem from the same identity, whereas in the Poincare patch neither occur under any condition. These two phenomena both depend on the behaviour of the out modes at far future and we show that they almost always come together for systems with an out mode that has a phase with separated time and momentum dependency at far future. This will be true for most expanding cosmologies. We comment on how the discussion can be connected to Green's functions and on some previous results in the literature that are seemingly contrary to our conclusions.

title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
text:
Title: Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions for the Spectral Difference method on simplex elements
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Unsteady compressible simulations with high-order methods on unstructured meshes require boundaries that let acoustic, entropy and vorticity waves leave the domain without spurious reflection. For the spectral difference (SD) method, the Navier-Stokes characteristic boundary conditions (NSCBC) have only been formulated on quadrilaterals and hexahedra. Their strong-form formalism relies on a line of flux points normal to the boundary face, which does not exist on triangles and tetrahedra. This paper extends the NSCBC to the SD method on simplex elements, including multi-species reacting gases. The characteristic analysis is performed in the physical frame of each flux point of the boundary face, and the normal derivative of the normal flux is evaluated using the Raviart-Thomas divergence operator. The boundary fluxes are recovered from a linear system local to each boundary element, whose matrix depends on the geometry only. The treatment is compared with the tensor-product formulation at a comparable number of degrees of freedom on a series of test cases covering acoustic, vortical, viscous and reacting flows on triangles and tetrahedra. In all cases, the results are in close agreement with those obtained on quadrilaterals and hexahedra, so that the NSCBC become available for the SD method on simplex meshes, which are well suited to complex geometries.

title: Topological Enhancement of Protein Kinetic Stability
text:
Title: Topological Enhancement of Protein Kinetic Stability
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Knotted proteins embed a physical (i.e., open) knot within their native structures. For decades, significant effort has been devoted to elucidating the functional role of knots in proteins, yet no consensus has been reached. Here, using extensive Monte Carlo off-lattice simulations of a simple structure-based model, we isolate the effect of topology by comparing simulations that preserve the linear topology of the chain with simulations that allow chain crossings. This controlled framework enables us to isolate topological effects from sequence, structure and energetic contributions. We show that protein kinetic stability, defined as resistance to unfolding at a fixed temperature, is higher in knotted proteins. Additionally, kinetic stability increases significantly with knot depth, whereas foldability (or folding efficiency) is comparatively less affected. By considering a simple model of protein evolution in which amino-acid alphabet size is used as a proxy for evolutionary time, we find that increasing primary-sequence complexity through the addition of biotic amino acids predominantly enhances kinetic stability. Taken together, these results indicate that kinetic stability is a functional advantage conferred by protein knots and suggest that evolutionary pressure for kinetic stability could contribute to the persistence of knotted proteins.

title: Fermionic Kaluza-Klein Reductions
text:
Title: Fermionic Kaluza-Klein Reductions
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We work out the Kaluza--Klein (KK) compactification on a general product spacetime for free spin-1/2 and spin-3/2 fields in arbitrary dimension. The analysis is performed at the level of the action, and the resulting lower-dimensional theory describes infinite towers of massive particles whose masses are related to the eigenvalues of the Dirac and Rarita--Schwinger operators on the internal space. A Hodge-like decomposition is used to write down a KK ansatz for spin-3/2 fields, and the fate of gauge invariance is discussed.

title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
text:
Title: Safe Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Turn Clinical Agents: When Dense Rewards Beat Outcome Rewards
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is increasingly used to improve language model reasoning, yet its effects on sequential decision procedures remain poorly understood. We study this problem in clinical multi-turn agents that must decide what information to request, when to stop gathering evidence, and which action to take. We introduce three controlled environments: medication refill triage, acute diagnostic work-up, and dosing titration, each with hidden clinical states, query costs, exact adaptive oracles, and deterministic outcome verifiers. Across these tasks, outcome-only group relative policy optimization often improves aggregate reward while producing undesirable procedures, including premature commitment, one-question collapse, and failures on rare high-risk cases. In diagnostics, assigning dense credit to questions that reduce uncertainty improves held-out value and moderate-case support across three training seeds relative to outcome-only reinforcement learning, without the high-risk seed collapse observed under outcome-only training. Separating exploration from exploitation further increases high-risk support at its best checkpoint, but at the cost of excessive information gathering on low-acuity cases. Additional experiments show that the optimal strength of process credit is task-dependent; that after a supervised warmup that already gathers carefully, reinforcement learning raises aggregate reward by trimming questions while degrading high-risk performance; and that reinforcement learning does not reliably repair rare behavior gaps inherited from biased supervised data. Verifiable final outcomes are therefore insufficient for training reliable multi-turn agents: reward design must account for the procedure used to reach an answer, and evaluation must distinguish adaptive information gathering from reward-exploiting shortcuts.

title: PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets
text:
Title: PathFinder: Joint Decompositions of Linked Multimodal Datasets
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Low-rank matrix decompositions can uncover patterns and structure in data and have a number of different applications across many disciplines. Extensions to "joint" low-rank decompositions have been proposed to link datasets from different modalities. While these methods enable the discovery of common patterns across modalities, they require that all the multimodal data share one or more dimensions. We propose a new analysis method, PathFinder, that enables co-analysis of datasets that do not necessarily all share a dimension. The key insight is that as long as pairs or subgroups of matrices do share some dimension, and that there are one or more paths that link across the data matrices, a global joint decomposition can be sought out. This enables the joint estimation of common patterns across different modalities, species, or scales, where a one-to-one mapping across all data along some dimension is not necessarily available. We show that PathFinder is a general umbrella under which many matrix decomposition methods fall as special cases. It can be used to discover common patterns across disparate datasets and to make predictions for missing data or modalities.

title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
text:
Title: Quantum Spin Wave Theory with Multi-Spin Interactions for Magnetic Materials Modeling
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

In the field of magnetism within condensed matter physics, magnetic systems are microscopically described by a spin Hamiltonian. Its parameterization is accessible through both ab initio calculations and fits to experimental data. Frequently, this is achieved via multi-stage calculations that either relate the parameters to observable material properties or map a Kohn-Sham Hamiltonian onto an effective spin model. In this realm, accurate and flexible methods are essential for simulating the physical properties of the latter. The present study focuses on one such method: spin wave theory. The approach is applied to a new formulation of the spin Hamiltonian, named polynomial localized spin model (PLSM), which includes terms of arbitrary order in the spin operators. This enables the direct application of linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to the analysis of the energy landscape and spin-wave spectrum of arbitrary collinear and non-collinear phases in any realistic magnetic material. Moreover, the classical and quantum parts of the PLSM are cleanly separated. Finally, an open-source implementation of LSWT, named Magnopy, is presented. It interfaces with modern parameterization software, supports arbitrary collinear and non-collinear systems, and is designed for both scripting and standalone use.

title: Covariant Calculus and Hamiltonian Flows for Nonlocal Wasserstein Metrics
text:
Title: Covariant Calculus and Hamiltonian Flows for Nonlocal Wasserstein Metrics
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In this paper, we study nonlocal metrics on smooth positive probability densities on a closed manifold, induced by symmetric jump kernels and density-dependent mobilities. First, we introduce the density-variation operator to express the density derivatives of the Dirichlet form and kinetic energy. Second, we construct density and velocity-field representations of the tangent space and prove their isometric equivalence. We use the generator's pseudoinverse to derive Levi-Civita connections and covariant differentials in both representations. Third, we establish mechanical Hamiltonian dynamics in both tangent representations; an action principle and Legendre duality identify the Hamilton--Jacobi and covariant Newton equations; smooth negative gradient flows admit a zero-energy Hamiltonian lift. Entropy diffusion, nonlocal mean-field equations, Keller--Segel dynamics, and a nonlocal Vlasov equation illustrate the resulting calculus. For geometric-mean mobility, the Hopf--Cole transformation of the nonlocal Schrödinger bridge system and the Madelung transformation of the nonlocal Schrödinger equation yield hyperbolic and trigonometric phase energies, respectively. At zero momentum, both recover the metric kinetic energy to second order.

title: Probing the Spatial Coherence of Chiral-Imbalance Fluctuations with Hyperon Spin Correlations
text:
Title: Probing the Spatial Coherence of Chiral-Imbalance Fluctuations with Hyperon Spin Correlations
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Topological fluctuations in the quark-gluon plasma can generate local chiral imbalances whose spatial coherence remains difficult to access with conventional charge-separation measurements. We propose differential hyperon-pair spin correlations as a probe of both the strength and spatial organization of these fluctuations. Fluctuations of the axial chemical potential $μ_5$ can induce pair correlations even when the mean helicity polarization vanishes. Using the AMPT model, we find that the magnitude of the hyperon spin correlation probes the magnitude and spatial coherence scale of $μ_5$, while the ratio of short- and long-range correlations varies strongly with the spatial coherence scale, but only weakly with $μ_{5}$ over the range of explored parameters. These observables provide an experimentally testable strategy for constraining the spatial structure of chiral-imbalance fluctuations.

title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
text:
Title: An Accelerated Proximal Gradient Method for Bures-Wasserstein Space
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study composite optimization over the Bures--Wasserstein (BW) space of Gaussian measures. Our main observation is that a useful class of BW problems can be lifted into the Euclidean space of affine transport maps, such that the lifted problems can be solved efficiently using accelerated proximal gradient methods. For objectives whose smooth and nonsmooth components admit convex smooth and convex proximable affine lifts, respectively, our algorithm BW-FISTA achieves minimax-optimal objective gap $O(k^{-2})$ after $k$ iterations. We verify these regularity conditions for potential and interaction energies together with common spectral regularizers, and we treat stochastic gradients under a suitable noise model. As a principal application, we consider Gaussian variational inference with a log-concave, log-smooth target. Here, the resulting entropy term is handled by an efficient, exact proximal step, and we improve the previous rate of $O(k^{-1})$ to $O(k^{-2})$. We numerically verify this predicted boost with synthetic experiments.

title: Can we constrain the binary neutron star merger time from kilonova light curves?
text:
Title: Can we constrain the binary neutron star merger time from kilonova light curves?
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The joint observation of gravitational waves (GWs) from a binary neutron star (BNS) merger (GW170817), together with a short Gamma-Ray Burst (GRB 170817A) and a kilonova (KN, AT2017gfo), marked the birth of multimessenger astronomy with GWs, and demonstrated the informative power of multimessenger observations. More BNS merger and KN detections are expected , thanks to the increasing sensitivity of GW detectors and the advent of new electromagnetic facilities such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. However, the association between a BNS merger and a KN might not be trivial: the detection of a KN might not coincide with the onset of the EM emission, making it difficult to define a temporal window to assess the coincidence with a GW event. In this work we investigate the possibility to constrain the BNS merger time from KN light curves, exploring different observing conditions and with focus on the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. We used different KN models and different inference frameworks to simulate and fit KN light curves. We explored different cadences and wavelength coverages for observations, to investigate how the different observing conditions can affect the capability to recover the BNS merger time. The tests performed also include real data related to AT2017gfo, plus a few GRBs that have been associated to possible KN candidates. We find that, under realistic observing conditions with the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, the BNS merger time can be recovered with a precision of 5.5 days (90\% CI) with a best-case scenario with an accuracy of 0.18 day and a precision of 0.74 day (90 \% CI). Results can slightly improve (by $\sim$ 5 \%) if the source redshift is available. Upper limits near the merger time can also improve the results, reducing the width of the posterior by $\sim60$ \%. The BNS merger time estimate could also benefit from EM follow-up observations with other telescopes.

title: Constructive Probability, Foundations and Numerical Analysis for mathematical finance and machine learning
text:
Title: Constructive Probability, Foundations and Numerical Analysis for mathematical finance and machine learning
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

This monograph sets out a constructive theory of stochastic processes in the continuum, in the sense of constructive field theory: the continuum is not postulated but reached as the limit of a sequence of lattice approximations, with the renormalisation the limit requires exhibited rather than assumed, and the limit controlled by estimates that can be checked. The primitive object is not a sigma-algebra but de Finetti's prevision, the price of finitely many gambles at a fixed resolution, which coherence turns into a conditional expectation. The theorem at the centre of the book, called plainly the fundamental theorem, is at once de Finetti's fundamental theorem of probability, the fundamental theorem of Bayesian statistics, and the one-period fundamental theorem of asset pricing; the financial vocabulary is a convenience only. The applications are two, mathematical finance and machine learning, and they are one mathematics read in opposite directions: an assessment is a price in the one and a prediction in the other, and both are computed by one adjoint recursion, the adjoint of a propagation in the first case and backpropagation in the second. Carried through, the two directions give sharp rates of convergence rather than asymptotic orders: for the moments of Ito diffusions, for the value function of Feynman-Kac semigroups, and for the measure changes of the fundamental theorem, the last as a limit theorem for reweighted generators, under a condition keeping the reweighting well behaved. A measure change is thus calculated, not postulated: a lattice approximation with Farkas' lemma computes it, completeness makes it unique, and the passage to the continuum is earned by the regularity of what is computed. Sixty-seven Python scripts regenerate every numerical table, and much of the finite-dimensional core of the argument has been verified in Lean 4.

title: Goldstone theory of gluon saturation in high energy QCD: From color glass to color superfluid condensate
text:
Title: Goldstone theory of gluon saturation in high energy QCD: From color glass to color superfluid condensate
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

In the high energy Regge asymptotics of QCD, the rapid overpopulation of gluons leads to gluon saturation, characterized by nonperturbative semi-classical lumpy configurations of size $1/Q_S$, where $Q_S\gg Λ_{\rm QCD}$ is a dynamical semi-hard saturation scale. We discuss here a generalization of the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework describing this phenomenon that is obtained by carefully treating the breaking of global symmetries by the condensate. In particular, we show that the breaking of a global subgroup of color results in a Goldstone effective field theory (EFT) whose dynamics is characterized by a Goldstone decay constant $f_G = \sqrt{N} Q_S$, where $N=O(1/α_S)$ is the phase space occupancy of the condensate, which is large for $α_S(Q_S)\ll 1$. Further, the coupling of these colored Goldstones to collinear gluon modes leads to a depletion of the condensate, thereby modifying the static shockwave scattering framework of the CGC on timescales controlled by $f_G$. The CGC EFT on these longer time scales is a novel color superfluid. Low frequency modes with $ω\leq α_S Q_S$ in an external probe of the CGC are sensitive to superfluid dynamics, with interesting physical consequences for deeply inelastic scattering and ultrarelativistic nuclear collisions.

title: Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
text:
Title: Observation of strong electric dipole-dipole interactions between two atoms
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We have prepared pairs of atoms at densities exceeding $ 10^{16}/\rm{cm}^3$ corresponding to $n\lambdabar^3>10$ and studied how they interact with light. In this regime, the coherent part of the electric dipole-dipole interaction is larger than the dissipative part, and a single photon emission can transfer large momenta (larger than ten times the single photon recoil) to the atoms. For off-resonant laser light, the atoms are dressed with an electric dipole moment of $\approx$ 1 Debye and interact coherently. This light-induced dipole-dipole interaction has been previously observed only in the far-field mean-field regime. For two atoms, the resonance is shifted by the two-body Lamb shift which is dominated by the near-field part of the dipolar interaction. Dipolar resonance shifts have been observed before only for many atoms interacting with the far-field part of the dipolar interaction. Our work sheds new light on photoassociation processes and paves the way for studying driven quantum systems with strong electric dipole-dipole interactions.

title: How much data does a memory kernel need? Measurement requirements for fractional models of battery and corrosion degradation
text:
Title: How much data does a memory kernel need? Measurement requirements for fractional models of battery and corrosion degradation
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

How much data does a memory kernel need before a fit is meaningful? For a distributed-order model, the answer is about 3.1 decades of observation, more than standard battery-degradation tests provide. Battery capacity fade and corrosion-film growth depend on their history, so they are often modelled using general fractional calculus (GFC), where memory is described by an arbitrary Sonine kernel rather than a single power law. We tested this using two mechanistic models without fractional operators and de Levie's porous-electrode model, whose high-frequency order is exactly 0.5; our estimator recovered 0.500. A single aging curve can recover an effective order, alpha, to within 5% noise using a weak formulation, while separating the tempered parameters (alpha, lambda) requires several Arrhenius conditions, with errors improving from (0.25, 0.43) with one condition to (0.04, 0.07) with four. A distributed-order memory needs 3.1 decades of data to be resolved to 90%; below that, a two-order memory can collapse into one intermediate order that fits the data better than the true spectrum. For saturating passivation, however, a general kernel improves the fit substantially, raising R2 from 0.862 to 0.998. Across 20 cells from two public datasets, observation windows span only 1.23 to 2.24 decades, making the 3.1-decade result a practical design rule: it defines what must be measured before fitting a memory kernel, not only what cannot be fitted.

title: Distilling Instructions into Weights: Closed-Form Edits Fix a Robot Policy's Misreading
text:
Title: Distilling Instructions into Weights: Closed-Form Edits Fix a Robot Policy's Misreading
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Generalist robot policies often fail at one step of a task they can otherwise perform. We ask whether such a failure can be repaired by editing the policy's weights directly, without gradients, training data, or a change to the instruction. Told to put the cube then the banana in the bowl, a zero-shot $π_{0.5}$ vision-language-action policy in RoboLab releases the cube before it reaches the bowl. Replaying 21 of these decisions under rewordings shows that it binds "in the bowl" to the wrong object. Closed-form instruction distillation copies the per-layer effect of an explicit rewording into the language model's MLP weights. On 128 held-out seeds, success rises from 27 to 106 episodes, with 81 fixed and 2 broken ($p=7\times10^{-22}$), while an update of the same size in random directions leaves success unchanged. The edit also lifts two other tasks without detectable harm on the remaining 13, and a variant that stores 0.16% of the parameter count keeps most of its effect. Placed in the action expert or action head instead, the same distillation helps less or not at all. Our released tool reproduced the fix end to end on new held-out seeds, from 8/64 to 36/64. Edits aimed at perception, a missing grasp, contact physics, or the gripper threshold did not help, and of seven blind Claude Opus editors, only the one given the misread instruction produced an edit that passed held-out scoring. These results suggest that weight edits work best when a known-good input already exists to distil. Because reruns with unchanged weights flip about a third of paired outcomes, evaluations should pair seeds, rerun the unedited policy, and confirm gains on held-out seeds.

title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
text:
Title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.

title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
text:
Title: Transactional Data Change for Real-Time Analytics in Lakehouses
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Real-time data analytics has become a key demand for lakehouses. It requires propagating data changes from the data source to the lakehouse in real time, while ensuring ACID guarantees and minimizing resource consumption and impact on analytical query performance. This is highly challenging for a data system according to the RUM conjecture, especially given the read-optimized immutable file storage layer in lakehouses. Existing lakehouses offer only git-style catalog version control on a single table, and they trade data freshness, query performance, and/or resource efficiency to achieve a barely acceptable data-change throughput. In this paper, we propose a novel data synchronization framework, Retina, that enables real-time, cost-efficient, query-performant, and fully transactional data changes in lakehouses. We implement and open-source Retina. Evaluations show that Retina delivers 10-millisecond-level data freshness and over 3.2 million row/s linear-scalable data-change throughput with low resource consumption and query-performance overhead, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art lakehouse systems and lake-compatible HTAP databases.

title: The kernel mean embedding of a random probability distribution and its principal components
text:
Title: The kernel mean embedding of a random probability distribution and its principal components
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Given a random probability distribution \(F\), whose realizations are defined on \(\mathbb R^d\), and a kernel \(k\), our aim is to analyze the properties of the kernel mean embedding, \(μ_F\), of \(F\) as a random element of the corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\). This establishes a rigorous framework in which kernel statistical techniques for distributional data can be stated both in the sample and population settings and, thus, the asymptotic properties of sample procedures can be properly established. As an illustration of this approach we focus on the principal components of \(F\). We obtain a general convergence result and the explicit expression of the spectral decomposition for the uncentered covariance operator of a normal probability distribution with a Gaussian distributed expectation. The performance of this kernel principal components procedure is illustrated with simulations and the analysis of the intensity distribution in synthetic aperture radar images.

title: In-Band Boundary Resonances from Coalescing Zero-Group-Velocity Points
text:
Title: In-Band Boundary Resonances from Coalescing Zero-Group-Velocity Points
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Boundary states generally reside in band gaps, whereas in-band confinement typically requires exact decoupling from propagating modes. We demonstrate an alternative mechanism in reciprocal, topologically trivial Hermitian lattices arising from the coalescence of two zero-group-velocity (ZGV) points. At coalescence, the group velocity and inverse effective mass vanish simultaneously, and the corresponding Bloch root acquires higher multiplicity. The coalesced root remains propagating, whereas nearby root splitting yields weakly evanescent channels that, together with a bulk-matched termination, generate a boundary-weighted resonance within the propagating spectrum. The mechanism is realized analytically in a two-leg ladder model through the coalescence of time-reversal-related ZGVs and extends to distinct ZGVs produced by longer-range interactions. Finite-size scaling distinguishes the resulting resonance from extended and defect-bound states. Scanning laser Doppler vibrometry on a 3D-printed elastic ladder reveals boundary enhancement in a nearly flat band region, consistent with operation slightly below criticality. ZGV coalescence thus provides a bulk framework for in-band boundary resonances in reciprocal Hermitian lattices.

title: Wavelength-Resolved Timing of Near-Infrared Scintillation in Gaseous Xenon
text:
Title: Wavelength-Resolved Timing of Near-Infrared Scintillation in Gaseous Xenon
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

The near-infrared (NIR) scintillation signal of xenon has the potential to enhance the performance of xenon-based detectors, but a robust understanding of its properties is a prerequisite for its application. In this work, we measure the NIR time response for $α$-particle interactions in gaseous xenon in 12 wavelength bands spanning approximately $(950-1620)\,$nm. The time response is decomposed into a fast (ns-scale) component and a dominant slow ($μ$s-scale) component. The fast-component spectrum coincides with strong atomic emission lines, predominantly 6p$\,\to\,$6s, whereas the slow-component spectrum follows the broad continuum centred around $1.3\,μ$m. The pressure dependence of the continuum can be described by a two-step kinetic model in which the emitting state is formed by a three-body process and depopulated by a two-body collisional process, with density-independent terms in both rates. Interpreting the slower of these as radiative decay yields an intrinsic lifetime of $\sim3\,μ$s. Theoretical calculations identify a neutral-excimer transition $0_u^- \rightarrow 0_g^-$ and an ionic-dimer transition $1/2_{u} \rightarrow 1/2_g$ as plausible candidates for the continuum emission, with the ionic-dimer transition showing better overall agreement with the measurements.

title: Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
text:
Title: Conditions for Normality of Pontryagin's Maximum Principle in the Absence of State Constraints
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Pontryagin's Maximum Principle is said to be "normal" for the problem at hand when it has a solution (maximizer u*) that explicitly involves the problem's cost function, making the maximum principle helpful (while in the opposite situation it is of no help). The aim of the present paper is, for Lagrange optimal control problems without state constraints, to identify classes of problems for which the Principle is normal. General conditions are introduced that guarantee normality, and classes of problems that satisfy these conditions are identified. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the control values) "augmented" reachable set, with cost along an upward vertical axis, has a convex lower-boundary function and the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the reachable state set, with the terminal constraint within the affine hull of that set. Such classes include problems for which the constrained (by bounds on the values of the control signal) "augmented" (with the cost value along an upward "vertical axis") reachable set has a "convex" lower boundary for which the optimal terminal state lies in the relative interior of the set of reachable states. Special attention is given to Lagrange steering problems: sufficient conditions are obtained on a nested sequence of sub-classes of such problems, culminating with the class of steering problems with scalar control signal and linear time-invariant (LTI) state dynamics and objective integrand, for which normality is guaranteed whenever all eigenvalues of the state dynamics matrix A are real (e.g., if A is symmetric or triangular or the system is overdamped) or have small enough imaginary parts; simple 2 x 2 examples show that, in contrast with the situation in the finite-dimensional case, this property does not extend to arbitrary A matrices.

title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium
text:
Title: Strain Controlled Hydrogen Interstitial Site Preference and Hydride Phase Suppression in Epitaxial Vanadium
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Understanding hydrogen behavior in transition metals is crucial for energy storage and sensing technologies. Here we combine density functional theory (DFT) calculations with in-situ electrical measurements to reveal how epitaxial strain governs hydrogen interstitial site selection and phase stability in vanadium. Our calculations demonstrate a robust thermodynamic preference for tetrahedral (T) over octahedral (O) sites, with the energy difference modulated by lattice anisotropy through strain-tunable H 1s-V 3d orbital hybridization. Experimentally, epitaxial V films on MgO(001) exhibit a critical thickness-dependent crossover: 50 nm films show characteristic first-order alpha-beta hydride transitions, while 10 nm films display continuous solid-solution behavior with complete transition suppression. This crossover is governed by the progressive relaxation of epitaxial strain with increasing film thickness: the 10 nm films retain strong coherent strain that flattens the free-energy landscape and suppresses hydride nucleation, whereas the 50 nm films approach the strain-relaxed bulk limit where long-range elastic interactions restore first-order phase behavior. Finite-size truncation of elastic fields and interfacial electronic reconstruction further reinforce this dimensional crossover. Our work establishes a unified framework connecting atomic-scale orbital physics to mesoscopic phase thermodynamics, providing design principles for strain-engineered metal-hydride systems.

title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
text:
Title: BioMem: Agentic Memory for Biomedical LLM Agents
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)
