A key empirical result of the theory is that high assembly index combined with high copy number constitutes a signature that cannot arise abiotically, and this has been validated experimentally in application to molecular biosignatures. The foundational theoretical concept underlying these results is the assembly space, which encodes the causal possibilities determinable from observed objects, with the assembly index the shortest path to them given the physical constraints of a given substrate. Here, we provide a generalized formalism to describe assembly spaces and tools for assembly index approximations. We begin by reviewing the applications of assembly theory across molecules, minerals and atmospheres, and then introduce a general, substrate-independent formal definition of assembly spaces and assembly indices. We develop a unified path hierarchy framework to clarify relationships among the various representations of assembly spaces and assembly paths that appear in the literature on molecular assembly. Finally, we show how formal grammar algorithms can be adapted to efficiently bound assembly index calculations and provide clarification on the utility of such approximations, with the goal to increase the accessibility of tools to explore this emerging area for a broader group of researchers across chemistry, biology, and complexity science.

title: On the information rate of phones, syllables and words
text:
Title: On the information rate of phones, syllables and words
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Which linguistic units minimise the bitrate required to encode speech content: phones, syllables, words, maybe larger units, or something in between? This question has implications for the development of speech and language systems and theories of human language processing. Using a transcribed corpus of 960 hours of English audiobooks, I compare the information rates of phones, syllables, words, multi-word combinations and intermediate tokenisations. While all units are equivalent under a perfect language model, it makes sense to compare these under limited modelling budgets; I use $n$-gram and transformer language models. The lowest bitrates are achieved using words, with slightly longer units sometimes performing best. The results show that, when modelling capacity is limited, units larger than syllables but smaller than long multi-word phrases provide the most efficient representation in terms of information rate.

title: Colossal magnetoresistance in narrow-gap magnetic semiconductor Eu$_2$CdAs$_2$
text:
Title: Colossal magnetoresistance in narrow-gap magnetic semiconductor Eu$_2$CdAs$_2$
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Discovering antiferromagnetic materials with a sizable colossal magnetoresistance (CMR) effect and precisely tuning their responses remain significant challenges in materials science. This work reports the synthesis, phase transitions, and magnetotransport properties of the narrow-gap Zintl arsenide Eu$_2$CdAs$_2$. The compound undergoes antiferromagnetic ordering at $T_\mathrm{N} = 9$ K and exhibits semiconducting behavior with a low-temperature activation energy of 3.2 meV, achieving a large CMR effect of $-10^4\%$ at 9 T. Below $T_\mathrm{N}$, a distinct butterfly-shaped magnetoresistance hysteresis emerges without any macroscopic ferromagnetic order, revealing a transport anomaly likely dictated by AFM domain dynamics and/or the formation and percolation of localized magnetic polarons. Furthermore, a systematic survey of reported Eu-based Zintl phases uncovers a nearly exponential scaling trend between the maximum CMR magnitude and the low-temperature activation energy. This correlation demonstrates that bandgap engineering serves as an effective strategy for tailoring magnetotransport, establishing Eu-containing Zintl phases as a versatile platform for exploring and manipulating CMR effects.

title: ERGO-ML and how to directly infer the multi-temperature nature of intra-cluster gas: simulation-based inference with TNG-Cluster
text:
Title: ERGO-ML and how to directly infer the multi-temperature nature of intra-cluster gas: simulation-based inference with TNG-Cluster
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Though galaxy clusters are virialized and mostly in thermodynamic equilibrium, their internal gas thermodynamics are complex. The hot gas is multiphase and spatially inhomogeneous. The exact state of the gas contains important information about the internal physics governing clusters, however, measuring the multiphase distribution of the X-ray emitting gas is hard if not impossible with current observational methods. In this work (part of the ERGO-ML series), we present a direct inference method of the multiphase temperature distribution of the gas in the intra-cluster medium (ICM), applicable over a large range of spatial and mass scales. It works using different spectral resolutions (XRISM-like and Chandra-like) and realistic photon noise. Our method is an application of simulation-based inference. We train a neural-network on X-ray spectra in the range 0.1-10 keV, generated for $\approx 10^5$ sightlines of massive clusters ($M_{\rm 200c} = 10^{14.2-15.2}~\mathrm{M_\odot}$) from the TNG-Cluster cosmological MHD galaxy simulation. We show that our method recovers the mass-weighted temperature of both individual sightlines and entire clusters with an average prediction error of $< 0.01 ~\mathrm{dex}$, and the total gas mass within $0.04 ~\mathrm{dex}$. On top of that it gives accurate measures of the fraction of sub- and super-virial gas. Our method is capable of extracting the cooler gas phase even if the flux contribution is 3 orders of magnitude below that of the virial gas phase. We then show that we can accurately recover the spatial distribution of multi-phase gas both in relaxed and merging systems. This opens the way to studies of the multiphase nature of the ICM and the violent physics of feedback, accretion and merging.

title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
text:
Title: A Fully Polynomial Approximation Algorithm for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Montanari's incremental approximate message passing (IAMP) algorithm [FOCS 2019; SIAM J. Comput., 2025] and the zero-temperature formulation of El Alaoui, Montanari and Sellke (AMS) [Ann. Probab., 2021] find a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation to the maximum Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) energy in $C(\varepsilon)N^2$ operations for fixed accuracy, with probability tending to one as $N\to\infty$, under their respective full-support and access-model assumptions. However, it was unknown whether this approximation could be achieved with work polynomial in both $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$, together with quantitative guarantees at finite dimension. Under the same assumptions as AMS, we introduce grouped IAMP with exact Gaussian query outputs (GEG-IAMP), which is the first SK approximation algorithm with total work polynomial in $N$ and $1/\varepsilon$ and a finite-size guarantee above a dimension threshold polynomial in $1/\varepsilon$ and $\log(1/α)$. More precisely, for every $α\in(0,1/2)$, it returns a $(1-\varepsilon)$ approximation with probability at least $1-α$ whenever $N\ge \mathsf{K}\varepsilon^{-2}\log^2(e/\varepsilon)\log(\mathsf{K}/α)$, using $O(N^2/\varepsilon)$ work and $O(N^2)$ storage. GEG-IAMP replaces the Onsager correction by Reeves's coupling construction [arXiv:2508.10782] and groups Euler-Maruyama steps into $O(1/\varepsilon)$ matrix-vector products. We also prove a relative guarantee for AMS IAMP with $O(N^2\varepsilon^{-3}\log^2(e/\varepsilon))$ work but a sufficient dimension exponential in inverse accuracy. By returning a fixed configuration below its dimension threshold, GEG-IAMP also provides an asymptotic fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme (AFPRAS), with an additive error independent of dimension.

title: Weak and strong discretization errors for signatures of Gaussian processes
text:
Title: Weak and strong discretization errors for signatures of Gaussian processes
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Let $X$ be a continuous Gaussian process in $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d\ge2$, with independent components of roughness $H\in(\tfrac14,1)$, possibly with a linear drift, and let $X^n$ be its piecewise-linear interpolant on a mesh of width $δ$. We study how well the truncated signature of $X^n$ approximates that of the natural lift of $X$, in mean (the weak error) and in $L^2$ (the strong error). Over a class of drivers defined by quantitative regularity conditions, the weak error at every fixed truncation level is $O(δ^{γ(H)})$ with $γ(H)=\min(2H,4H-1)$, uniformly over the class, and for truncation levels $M\ge4$ fractional Brownian motion attains this rate. For centred drivers the weak error vanishes at levels $1$ to $3$, Gaussian or not. It first appears at level~$4$, where we compute its leading constant for independent fractional Brownian motion in $d=2$: on $(\tfrac12,1)$ it is $1/(2\sqrt3)$, independent of $H$, and on $(\tfrac14,\tfrac12)$ it is given by a $ζ$-series. For fractional Brownian motion with drift, a level-$3$ error of the same order appears for $H\ge\tfrac12$. Below $\tfrac12$ the drift reaches the rate only at levels $\ge5$ (proved for $d\ge3$). The strong error is of exact order $δ^{2H-1/2}$ for fractional Brownian motion with $H\in(\tfrac12,1)$, so in mean square the weak error lies a full power of $δ$ below it. For $H\le\tfrac12$ the strong error is $O(δ^{\vartheta})$ for every $\vartheta<2H-\tfrac12$, uniformly over the class, and the exponent $2H-\tfrac12$ cannot be improved. Finally, we construct pairs of laws in the class whose mesh data have the same law but whose expected signatures differ by order $δ^{γ(H)}$. Hence no quantity computed from the mesh data has mean within $o(δ^{γ(H)})$ of the expected signature uniformly over the class.

title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
text:
Title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
text:
Title: HistoTx: Early fusion of H&E images and spatial transcriptomics at varying spatial transcriptomics resolution with self-supervised learning
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Spatial transcriptomics maps gene expression across tissue sections and, when integrated with whole slide images, jointly captures both morphological architecture and molecular activity to provide a rich, multimodal view of tissue biology. ML approaches combining spatial transcriptomics and WSIs typically learn a mapping from morphological features to molecular profiles via contrastive alignment or supervised fine-tuning of pathology foundation models. In both cases, transcriptomics serves as a training signal rather than a true input modality, leaving inference fundamentally image-driven. We propose an early-fusion vision transformer architecture in which transcript tokens are constructed at arbitrary spatial resolution, merged with image patch tokens, and jointly processed through a shared transformer stack for deep cross-modal interaction. Starting from a pretrained vision-only pathology foundation model, we train HistoTx by continuing self-supervised pretraining on paired image and spatial transcriptomics data and demonstrate that: 1) at inference with image only, performance remains on par with the baseline on most tasks while improving on tasks that inherently benefit from molecular knowledge, such as gene expression prediction; 2) when both modalities are available at inference, jointly providing image and transcript inputs outperforms either modality alone.

title: Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
text:
Title: Optimization Frameworks & Learning Algorithms for Discrete-Time Mean Field Games
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

This monograph introduces discrete-time mean field games with finite state and action spaces, emphasizing optimization formulations and learning algorithms. Starting from Markov decision processes and finite-player stochastic games, it develops the notion of mean field Nash equilibrium, establishes existence and uniqueness results under suitable assumptions, and explains how mean field equilibria yield approximate equilibria in large finite-player games. Building on the linear programming formulation of Markov decision processes, occupation measures and primal-dual formulations connect equilibrium computation with mathematical optimization. The monograph presents fixed-point iterations, fictitious play, online mirror descent, and optimization-based methods, discussing their convergence properties and limitations. Numerical examples illustrate crowd motion, traffic routing, epidemic management, and the computation of multiple equilibria. It combines examples, theoretical results, and implementable algorithms, with bibliographic notes providing connections to the broader literature.

title: Random waves on sub-Riemannian $SU(2)$
text:
Title: Random waves on sub-Riemannian $SU(2)$
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Random spherical eigenfunctions for the Lalplace-Beltrami operator are well understood and their local behavior, after renormalization, is described by Berry's random wave model. In this paper we construct a family of random fields on the sphere $\mathbb{S}^{3}$, identified with the group $SU(2)$, endowed with a sub-Riemannian structure. These fields are random eigenfunctions for the sub-Laplacian and they are constructed from matrix elements of unitary irreducible representations of $SU(2)$. We prove that the local behavior of such fields is the same as the Berry-Heisenberg random field on the Heisenberg group introduced in [10].

title: Unraveling Primary Energy Conversion Dynamics in Intact Cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica
text:
Title: Unraveling Primary Energy Conversion Dynamics in Intact Cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Photosynthetic bacteria have evolved specialized light-harvesting structures to efficiently capture sunlight. Here, we investigate the ultrafast dynamics in intact cells of Gemmatimonas groenlandica, featuring unique double-ring LHh-LH1 photosynthetic complexes containing bacteriochlorophyll a. Two-dimensional electronic spectroscopy with lock-in detection allows us to directly observe primary energy-conversion processes, from excitation-energy transfer within the antenna system to the formation of a charge-separated state in the reaction center, taking place on 50 ps time scale. Through comparison with Rhodospirillum rubrum, which lacks the outer antenna ring, we use a combination of global analysis and nodal/center line slope analyses to resolve LHh-LH1 excitation energy transfer which occurs on a ~1-2 ps timescale in Gemmatimonas groenlandica.

title: An Open Reliability Atlas of Sensitivity and Failure Modes in the Pulse Physiology Engine
text:
Title: An Open Reliability Atlas of Sensitivity and Failure Modes in the Pulse Physiology Engine
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Pulse is an actively maintained open-source adult-physiology simulator, yet its maintainers report no formal sensitivity analysis of its operational inputs. We present the first open reliability atlas across its critical-care envelope: Morris elementary-effects sampling of seven inputs, four severity scenarios, male and female bodies (1,280 simulations). Sensitivity is skewed: three inputs carry a median 93% of each output's total. A four-flag classifier reveals failure modes: two operator-actionable, one sex-stratified. Tidal-volume oscillation (20.6% of runs) is consistent with patient-ventilator dyssynchrony; locking the VC-AC trigger to -2 cmH2O collapses that variability. At FiO2 = 1.0, transient hyperoxia makes 120-second runs underestimate plateau PaO2; 300-second healthy-lung reruns give a median 643 mmHg. Solver divergence was all-male in an input-extreme regime (20/1,280); reducing the male blood-volume baseline to the 4,082 mL floor eliminated it. Runs and flags are released openly, showing users which regions need checking before training on Pulse output.

title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
text:
Title: Preconditioned Implicit Midpoint Langevin Sampling for Non-Smooth Bayesian Imaging
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We introduce P-IMLA, a preconditioned implicit-midpoint Langevin sampler for high-dimensional log-concave targets with non-smooth regularization. The obstruction is that the large steps enabled by matrix preconditioning are precisely where preconditioned Euler-Maruyama inflates stationary variance. Implicit midpoint removes this surplus via a Cayley-transform identity, making P-IMLA Gaussian-exact at any step size. Beyond Gaussians, whitening transfers the sharp IMLA contraction rate to $κ_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and backward-error analysis gives drift-only rather than Euler-type diffusion bias under explicit smoothness assumptions. An $M$-norm Moreau envelope yields a proximal non-smooth variant with a three-term error budget. Controlled Gaussian and TV-regularized imaging experiments confirm the predicted separation: the unpreconditioned midpoint scheme retains long transients as $κ_f$ grows, whereas P-IMLA remains $κ_{\mathrm{eff}}$-governed and near variance-exact.

title: Improving the accuracy of the momentum-exchange method in lattice Boltzmann methods
text:
Title: Improving the accuracy of the momentum-exchange method in lattice Boltzmann methods
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

In the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), the momentum-exchange method (MEM) is widely used to evaluate hydrodynamic forces at fluid-solid interfaces due to its computational efficiency and geometric flexibility. However, when mapping complex geometries onto structured Cartesian grids, the physical boundary rarely intersects the lattice links exactly at their midpoints. This discrepancy violates an implicit assumption inherent to the conventional momentum-exchange (CME) formulation. In this study, we systematically analyze this geometric deficiency and demonstrate that it induces significant force inaccuracies, even in elementary flows where the solid boundary deviates from the midway position. To resolve this, we propose a modified momentum-exchange (MME) method that explicitly accounts for the exact boundary location along the lattice links, demonstrating enhanced accuracy for both flat and curved geometries. Furthermore, we address another critical issue with the interpolation-supplemented bounce-back (ISBB) schemes, and that is their inherent violation of local mass conservation. This mass leakage induces unphysical pressure buildup in the system, which compromises the accuracy and stability of the LBM. We propose a mass-conservative remedy for ISBB schemes that eliminates this leakage. Through a series of benchmark simulations of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that combining the proposed MME with the mass-corrected ISBB scheme drastically improves the fidelity of hydrodynamic force evaluations, establishing a robust framework essential for moving boundary problems and fluid-structure interactions.

title: Compatibility of Pauli Observables
text:
Title: Compatibility of Pauli Observables
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Given an arbitrary finite family of Pauli observables, how sharply can they be approximated by a single measurement? We derive an exact state-space correspondence that characterises the resulting sharpness tradeoffs, establishing a link between incompatibility and preparation uncertainty. In particular, suitable ensembles of quantum states determine the full compatibility region and generate explicit parent measurements through Pauli conjugation and classical randomisation. The compatibility region depends only on the anti-commutativity graph and determines all nonuniform tradeoffs under standard noise models, including depolarising, probabilistic and generalised noise. We show that optimal sharpness tradeoffs are determined by spectral problems for signed Pauli Hamiltonians, whose ground states supply the seeds for optimal parent measurements. The correspondence also shows that magic is necessary to attain the full compatibility region of every noncommuting Pauli family. We quantify the resulting sharpness advantage and relate it to the reduced robustness of magic. Finally, we apply the framework to several structured Pauli families, obtaining exact compatibility characterisations and explicit optimal parents.

title: Finite-temperature adiabatic-connection reduced density-matrix functional theory: a unified framework for i-DMFT and TAO-DFT
text:
Title: Finite-temperature adiabatic-connection reduced density-matrix functional theory: a unified framework for i-DMFT and TAO-DFT
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Accurately describing chemical bond breaking requires capturing strong/static electron correlation, a major challenge for single-reference self-consistent-field methods such as Hartree--Fock and Kohn--Sham density-functional theory (DFT). Fractional occupations substantially improve this situation, as demonstrated by information-density-matrix-functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation DFT (TAO-DFT). Although useful, they are formulated within rather different theoretical frameworks, are somewhat semi-empirical, and their relationship remains unclear. Here we introduce finite-temperature adiabatic-connection reduced density-matrix functional theory (FT-AC-RDMFT), in which i-DMFT and TAO-DFT emerge as different reductions of a unified framework. The effective eigenvalue equation for natural orbitals and the Fermi--Dirac occupation numbers follow directly from the variational principle, while a thermal adiabatic connection relates the empirical entropy coefficient of i-DMFT to a characteristic temperature of the auxiliary non-interacting system. Within this framework, i-DMFT is the exact-exchange-based reduction, whereas TAO-DFT results when exact exchange is replaced by a density-based exchange-correlation functional. Numerical calculations confirm that i-DMFT, apart from a constant, coincides with the exact-exchange realization of the framework, and show that the improved dissociation behavior from finite-temperature occupations extends beyond exact exchange to hybrid and semilocal density functionals. For strongly correlated V2O3, finite-temperature occupations substantially reduce the severely overestimated non-magnetic LDA bulk modulus, bringing it close to experiment. These results establish FT-AC-RDMFT as a common theoretical foundation for finite-temperature occupation-based electronic-structure methods in molecular and solid-state systems.

title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
text:
Title: The scale of homogeneity in DESI Data Release 1
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We present measurements of the scale of cosmic homogeneity using the first data release (DR1) of the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), the largest publicly available spectroscopic extragalactic survey to date. Using a counts-in-spheres estimator applied to nearly 5 million galaxies and quasars across six independent redshift bins spanning $0.1 < z < 2.1$, we measure the correlation dimension $D_2(r)$ and define the homogeneity scale $R_H$ as the point at which the galaxy distribution reaches within 1\% of the homogeneous asymptotic value. We find that all tracers clearly transition to homogeneity, with the galaxy homogeneity scale ranging from $93.8^{+0.9}_{-0.7}$ to $142.6^{+1.4}_{-1.4}$ $h^{-1}$Mpc depending on the tracer redshift, galaxy bias, and modelling used to extract the scale. Using a cosmology-dependent model, we reconstruct the underlying matter homogeneity scale, finding it decreases monotonically with redshift in excellent agreement with $Λ$CDM predictions. We identify a systematic offset of up to $\sim 10\%$ between measurements in the North and South Galactic Caps, largely due to fiber assignment effects reproduced in our simulations. Accounting for this, and with a complementary demonstration using toy models that our methodology correctly identifies inhomogeneous universes in all but rather finely-tuned observer configurations, this hence provides strong evidence in favour of the cosmological principle across our full redshift range. Our matter homogeneity scale measurements are consistent with, and substantially more precise than, previous constraints from WiggleZ and SDSS, demonstrating the power of DESI data for precision tests of the cosmological principle.

title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
text:
Title: What to randomize matters: a controlled study of volume, axis and representation in low-data molecular generation
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Chemical language models can struggle to generate new molecules when trained on small datasets, where a model may reproduce training examples rather than learn a useful generative distribution. Randomized SMILES augmentation varies atom traversal, whereas Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding (SAFE) also allows the order of fragment blocks to vary. How these distinct sources of representational variation affect low-data molecular generation has not been clearly studied. Here, using 1,000 seed molecules to train an autoregressive sequence model, we compare canonical SAFE with randomized SAFE at increasing corpus sizes, isolate atom-order and fragment-order axes of SAFE randomization, and compare fully randomized SAFE with randomized SMILES at molecule-by-molecule matched training corpora. Three findings emerge. First, randomization of SAFE alone raises the genuine yield of novel molecules more than 450-fold, turning a model that merely reproduces its training set into a practical molecular generator. Second, the two axes of randomization act jointly rather than additively: atom order alone reaches a tenth, and fragment order alone a seventh, of the genuine yield obtained when both vary, which is four times their combined contribution. Third, at matched corpus size and compute, randomized SAFE delivers 2.8 times the genuine yield of randomized SMILES. Welch tests with Games-Howell post-hoc comparisons resolve every difference on the primary outcomes. In the low-data regime, thus, what one randomizes rather than only how much determines whether augmentation produces new molecules or merely new spellings of the training set.

title: Fluctuation-induced ionic friction at solid-electrolyte interfaces
text:
Title: Fluctuation-induced ionic friction at solid-electrolyte interfaces
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

In this article, we explore how transport at a solid--electrolyte interface is affected by the internal fluctuations of the solid and quantify the role of solid excitations on ionic friction. Combining molecular dynamics simulations with theoretical modeling, we show that the presence of ions enhances the dynamical response of the electrolyte compared to pure water. This leads to an ionic contribution to the fluctuation-induced interfacial friction. We show that collective ionic modes dominate the dissipation, such that ionic friction arises from many-body effects rather than from individual drag forces. Furthermore, high-frequency molecular modes are found to be ion-specific, suggesting possible routes toward spectral separation of ions, with implications for desalination, filtration, and energy conversion.

title: Strong Borel-Cantelli laws and clusters of visits for random intermittent maps
text:
Title: Strong Borel-Cantelli laws and clusters of visits for random intermittent maps
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Near the neutral fixed point of an intermittent map, a single entrance into a small target can be followed by a long run of consecutive visits, so the number of visits need not follow its mean. We study targets $[0,u_n]$ for iid random compositions of Liverani-Saussol-Vaienti maps with a bounded parameter law that is regularly varying at its minimum $α\in(0,1)$; this includes a single map. For $u_n=cn^{-g}L(n)$, where $c>0$, $0<g\leq1$ and $L$ is slowly varying, the visit count is almost surely asymptotic to its mean if and only if $\sum_n n^{-1}(nu_n)^{-(1-α)/α}<\infty$. Under the stationary law, the count divided by its mean converges to one in $L^1$ exactly when $nu_n\to\infty$. Thus clusters of visits separate these two modes of convergence.

title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem for independent triangular arrays
text:
Title: Necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem for independent triangular arrays
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

For a rowwise independent triangular array $\{X_{n,i}:1\le i\le n\}$, put $S_n=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}$ and $V_n^2=\sum_{i=1}^nX_{n,i}^2$. We prove that $S_n/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm d}{\mathrm N}(0,1)$ implies $\max_{i\le n}|X_{n,i}|/V_n\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}0$. The same assumption gives $V_n^2/b_n^2\xrightarrow{\mathbb P}1$ for any choice of medians $b_n^2$ of $V_n^2$. Combined with the results of Shao (2018), this yields necessary and sufficient conditions for the self-normalized central limit theorem and resolves his conjecture for independent sequences. The proof identifies the joint limits of the sum and its sum of squares, then uses the standard normal ratio to remove every non-Gaussian component.

title: OmniST: Topology-Invariant Spatiotemporal Forecasting with Guaranteed-Coverage Uncertainty at Unseen Sensor Locations
text:
Title: OmniST: Topology-Invariant Spatiotemporal Forecasting with Guaranteed-Coverage Uncertainty at Unseen Sensor Locations
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Standard spatiotemporal graph convolutional networks need a fixed-size adjacency matrix, coupling model weights to a specific sensor count N; they cannot produce any output at a sensor absent from training. We present OmniST, a topology-invariant forecaster whose computation has zero structural dependency on the number of nodes, and which, composed with inductive split-conformal calibration, gives distribution-free, coverage-guaranteed prediction intervals at arbitrary (including never-seen) sensor locations, preserving that guarantee as sensors are added or removed. Topology invariance follows from coordinate-based tokenization, k-nearest-neighbor attention from geographic coordinates at each forward pass, and per-node temporal processing via a bidirectional GRU. On real Delhi air-quality data (37 stations, 2019-2023), OmniST attains a 30-day PM2.5 MAE of 31.0 ug/m3 and degrades at most 1.1 percent when 40 percent of stations are removed. Its inductive forecasts at unseen stations beat nearest-neighbor interpolation (about 12 percent) and a learned kriging GNN (IGNNK, about 21 percent), and, unlike either, carry a finite-sample coverage guarantee. The guarantee holds at 90 percent or above under 30-50 percent node dropout across four real datasets over three domains (Delhi and Beijing air quality, NOAA GHCN weather, Caltrans PeMSD7-M traffic), and still holds at 325 real sensors (full PeMS-BAY). We also fix a temporal-drift failure: static conformal under-covers over time (about 0.50 late), but a rolling adaptive-conformal estimator restores target coverage (0.89 overall, 0.96 late) at the cost of wider intervals.

title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
text:
Title: SeqFold: Timestamp-Addressable Compressed States for User Action Sequence Backbones
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Existing sequential user modeling methods mainly focus on improving the backbone encoder or learning task-specific user representations for a single prediction objective. We instead study how to export the multi-layer user states of a frozen long-history backbone as compact, timestamp-addressable representations for downstream training backfill and serving. In this setting, the user state at a given timestamp summarizes the user's actions before that time, so downstream systems need only the state aligned to each target timestamp rather than the full hidden-state timeline. To this end, we present \texttt{SeqFold}, a compressed-state interface that combines learned multi-channel fusion, channel-specific temporal decay, and Lookup-Free Quantization (LFQ) to produce compact discrete codes from frozen backbone states. Task-specific decoders then map these shared codes into flexible embedding spaces for downstream models. To make timestamp-addressable export practical at scale, we further develop a fused streaming implementation that updates the fusion recurrence after every action while materializing states only at target timestamps. On large-scale proprietary datasets, SeqFold reduces per-state representation storage by $3{,}400\times$ while preserving most of the downstream ranking performance of the uncompressed model, showing that SeqFold is an effective interface for reusing long-history sequence backbones in downstream models.

title: Wireless AI Networks: Co-Adapting Communication Resources and Distributed Intelligence
text:
Title: Wireless AI Networks: Co-Adapting Communication Resources and Distributed Intelligence
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly relies on wireless networks, where communication and computing resources shape how AI tasks are configured and executed. However, resource availability alone does not determine how effectively these tasks can be supported, since different information selections and transmission strategies may yield different AI performance under the same resource constraints. To address this challenge, this article presents Wireless AI Networks as a unified design perspective for bidirectional adaptation between wireless communication and distributed intelligence. Specifically, an AI-executable resource budget characterizes candidate AI configurations, while task-level information value guides their selection and wireless resource allocation. Building on these principles, a wireless-AI co-adaptation framework coordinates resource abstraction, joint configuration and allocation, and execution feedback. Two complementary experiments illustrate this perspective: update selection and statistical correction improve federated learning under identical model-update payload budgets, while sensitivity-aware power allocation reduces model accuracy degradation under the same average transmit-power constraint. Together, these results highlight the importance of coordinating resource feasibility and task-level information value in distributed AI execution.

title: Estimating LuSEE-Night's Sensitivity to Cα Radio Recombination Lines
text:
Title: Estimating LuSEE-Night's Sensitivity to Cα Radio Recombination Lines
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Carbon radio recombination lines (CRRLs) arising from the cold neutral medium (CNM) of the interstellar medium are potential foregrounds in the 1-50 MHz band that LuSEE-Night will observe from the lunar far side. CRRLs are sensitive probes of the temperature, density, and radiation field of the CNM, and LuSEE-Night will provide sky-averaged measurements in a poorly explored frequency range. We model CRRLs across this band, accounting for doppler, collisional, and radiation broadening, and we estimate line strengths using two independent methods - fixing either the peak or the frequency-integrated optical depth - applied both uniformly across the sky and with region-dependent values informed by prior low-frequency observations. We simulate LuSEE-Night's expected response to these CRRLs and further convolve the beam-diluted spectra with LuSEE-Night's polyphase-filter-bank spectrometer response, including its zoomed-mode frequency resolution of $\sim$390 Hz, to obtain the expected observed brightness temperature. Using these simulated spectra, we estimate the integration time required to detect individual CRRLs at SNR=5 across the six sky models considered. Required integration times range from as short as 30 hours (in the most optimistic model where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-3}$) to 27.6 years (in the most conservative models where the optical depth across the sky is $\sim$10$^{-4}$). Stacking the 361 simulated C$α$ lines between 10 and 50 MHz reduces the integration time needed for an SNR=5 detection to $\sim$11 minutes and $\sim$151 hours respectively, indicating that LuSEE-Night has realistic chances of making a stacked detection of C$α$ RRLs within a realistic mission lifetime, even under the most conservative optical-depth assumptions.

title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
text:
Title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.

title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
text:
Title: Robust and Private Swarm Learning via Zero-Knowledge Validator Admission and Consensus Aggregation
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Swarm Learning improves resilience and removes the need for a single trusted coordinator by distributing model aggregation and validation across participating nodes. However, it also delegates the validation of model updates to peers whose private data may be biased, unrepresentative, or adversarial, and existing Swarm Learning protocols generally do not attest that data, leaving decentralized validation as an attack surface. We present a robust, privacy-preserving Swarm Learning framework that makes verifiable data quality the condition for admission to the learning task. A validator joins only after a zero-knowledge attestation proves, without revealing any raw sample, that a reference model ran correctly on its private data. The attested outputs also yield a label-free class profile, so the network assembles a collectively IID validator pool from individually skewed validators as accurately as an oracle with the true labels (total-variation distance to uniform 0.025, against 0.021 for the oracle and 0.21 for random selection). Admitted validators score client updates and, through a Tendermint-style Byzantine Fault Tolerant consensus, agree on a gradient mask and a quality-derived aggregation weight for each submission, replacing dataset-size weighting with a quality-aware signal. Adapting the cut-layer idea of Split Learning, a challenge-based audit lets peers re-verify that a mask was computed on the attested data without an expensive end-to-end zero-knowledge proof. Across four benchmarks under non-IID partitions the framework matches FedAvg on clean data; under a gradient-scaling attack that collapses FedAvg to random chance, it retains 94% of clean accuracy on CIFAR-100 and over 99% on FashionMNIST, where FedAvg achieves only 2.1% and 11%. The result is a private, robust, and auditable foundation for decentralized learning.

title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
text:
Title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Is a chromosome a miniature of its genome, with the same mix of functional elements as the whole? We ask this of eight annotated genomes: human, mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize. Elements are classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements (TEs), pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) down to finer classes. Units are chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. We compare each unit with the genome and with other units, call compositions homogeneous when they differ by less than 5%, and score each against a random sample of the same size. The first finding is a surprising homogeneity. The level-1 compositions of the major chromosomes match each other and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast and C. elegans, and in fly down to the major arms. Finer classes can be homogeneous too: protein function in Arabidopsis, and the Wicker TE orders in maize. Enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable between chromosomes in all eight genomes. The second finding is a structured heterogeneity. Where a unit departs from its genome, it does so in one of three ways: clusters of named elements, such as rRNA genes or immune receptor loci; megabase-scale compartments, such as TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin; and lineage-specific gene families, visible only at the finest levels. Corrected for chance, the genomes fall into groups. For protein function and gene families, composition is more uniform in plants and fly than in vertebrates, and least uniform in C. elegans. For the major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows where each genome places its repeats, along the arms (maize, zebrafish) or around the centromeres (Arabidopsis, fly), not its lineage.

title: Spectral Diffusion for Protein Dynamics
text:
Title: Spectral Diffusion for Protein Dynamics
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Generative models present a promising alternative to expensive molecular dynamics for computationally querying protein dynamics, yet many existing approaches treat ensembles as unordered snapshots rather than temporally coherent trajectories, or scale poorly with protein size. We present a new physics-informed representation using Fourier transforms as an inductive bias for the multiscale temporal nature of protein dynamics. Diffusion in the spectral domain allows for disentangling of dynamics into slow conformational modes and fast atomic jitter, enabling rapid and improved prediction of dynamics across a range of temperatures. This is facilitated by denoising of structure and temperature conditioned spectral volumes where the low frequencies directly encode per-residue flexibility. Trained on the mdCATH dataset, we evaluate our model, DynaMode, on a held-out test set achieving strong performance across a set of ensemble-based metrics including a Root Mean Squared Fluctuation (RMSF) pearson $r$ of $0.844$. Code is available at https://github.com/HPuntu/DynaMode.

title: Query-Efficient Quantum Multi-Objective Optimization for Materials Configuration Search via Bayesian Weight Selection
text:
Title: Query-Efficient Quantum Multi-Objective Optimization for Materials Configuration Search via Bayesian Weight Selection
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Materials design is a multi-objective problem, and recent advances in quantum optimization make it possible to bring quantum solvers to bear on such problems. The realistic near-term win, though, is not raw quantum advantage but making an expensive, noisy quantum solver usable by spending its calls wisely. Quantum Approximate Multi-Objective Optimization (QAMOO) traces a Pareto front by solving a family of scalarized Ising problems, one per objective-weight vector, with QAOA --- but chooses those weights \emph{non-adaptively}, sampling them at random, blind to what it has already found. We recast weight selection as \emph{multi-objective Bayesian optimization}: our method, BW-QAMOO (Bayes-Weighted QAMOO), picks each next weight by expected hypervolume improvement (EHVI) under a Gaussian-process (GP) surrogate over the weight-to-objective map. On a frustrated alloy-configuration benchmark across $m\in\{3,4\}$ objectives and $n\in\{10,11,12\}$ sites, BW-QAMOO reaches the same Pareto hypervolume as QAMOO's random sampling with a median 33% fewer scalarized solves across the 90/95\% targets and 60--74\% fewer than a uniform-grid baseline), on a genuine (simulated) QAOA solver; a paired Wilcoxon test confirms the saving is significant, and the advantage grows with the objective count m as the weight simplex expands and blind sampling wastes more of the budget. This is a \emph{query-efficiency} result, and we close with the open challenges on the path to real alloy data and hardware.

title: Visualizing Three-Dimensional Quantum Fluctuations of Ground-State C$_3$H$_4$ via Deep Sub-Angstrom Coulomb Explosion Imaging
text:
Title: Visualizing Three-Dimensional Quantum Fluctuations of Ground-State C$_3$H$_4$ via Deep Sub-Angstrom Coulomb Explosion Imaging
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Coulomb explosion imaging (CEI) is a powerful tool for determining static geometries of isolated gas-phase molecules. In this work, taking allene and propyne as prototype, we demonstrate sub-angstrom resolution achieved with highly charged ion-induced CEI. Using 41.9 keV/u Xe$^{20+}$ beam, minute variations of CC single, double and triple bond lengths are clearly visualized, indicating that an ultrahigh resolution of 0.1 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ is achieved. This unprecedented resolution not only makes it possible to distinguish CC bonds with different bond orders, but also lays a solid foundation for direct observation of quantum fluctuations inherent to 3D structure of a ground-state molecule. Notably, the coupled collective motion of the two CH$_2$ moieties spaced by a central carbon within allene is unambiguously visualized in our measurements.

title: Warm inflation beyond the Gaussian limit: primordial black holes and induced gravitational waves
text:
Title: Warm inflation beyond the Gaussian limit: primordial black holes and induced gravitational waves
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

In warm inflation, the primordial fluctuations are driven by random kicks from a hot radiation bath. Two features of these kicks matter: how long the bath remembers them, which shapes the power spectrum, and how their strengths are spread, which controls the rare, extreme fluctuations. In this paper, we investigate how primordial black holes and the accompanying induced gravitational waves can be used to discriminate between these two features. We use a simple model inspired by warm inflation, in which independent kicks of random strength add up to a narrow peak in the power spectrum. At leading order, the induced gravitational wave depends only on the power spectrum and is therefore insensitive to how the kicks are distributed. However, the black holes are very sensitive to these rare large fluctuations. Hence, two baths can yield the same gravitational wave signal while forming black holes at very different rates. A modest kurtosis range of 0.1 to 0.3 enhances black-hole formation by factors of ten to a million at fixed gravitational-wave amplitude, the larger factors for the rarer black holes. Counting peaks rather than all points, or widening the spectrum, lowers the enhancement by at most a factor of about four. In general a change in the power affects both phenomena, while the kurtosis affects only the black hole production.

title: Rotational Doppler Effect and Helimagnon Frequency Comb in Sliding Magnetic Spirals
text:
Title: Rotational Doppler Effect and Helimagnon Frequency Comb in Sliding Magnetic Spirals
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Collective spin motion can reshape magnon spectra by providing a dynamical magnetic background. Magnetic spirals offer a particularly clean setting, as they simultaneously host propagating helimagnons and a gapless Goldstone mode, i.e., the sliding of the spiral. Here, we show that once a helimagnon is excited and the spiral slides, the motion, which rotates the local spin frame, produces a thresholdless rotational Doppler shift of the helimagnon spectrum, with even winding for the linear mode and odd winding for its second harmonic. Stronger excitation generates one finite-momentum phason. Mixing of that phason with the helimagnon produces a helimagnon frequency comb only inside a finite driving window, spaced by the phason frequency fixed by the spiral length rather than by the sliding rate. These two scales are separable in a microwave experiment: the Doppler offset tracks the sliding velocity, whereas the comb spacing scales inversely with the length of the spiral.

title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
text:
Title: AVCORP: Identifying and Resisting Deception via Communication Theory and Theory of Mind
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Today's LLM-based agents are vulnerable to deception by users and other agents. Defending against deception requires Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning to infer the beliefs and goals of others as well as modeling tactics based on communication theory. To enable training models to detect deception, we adopt the well-known deception game, Avalon. We present a corpus, AVCORP, of 5,000 annotated utterances from 250 games of Avalon. AVCORP includes (1) 37 tactics mapped to a 4x4 behavior matrix, and (2) reasoning traces capturing abductive hypotheses, suspicion levels, and nested ToM beliefs. We train Qwen3-8B on AVCORP and evaluate it on 25 held-out games and 20 games played by humans. On held-out games, our best trained detector outperforms its untrained baseline and frontier models (GPT-5.6 Sol, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro), matching Claude Opus 5.5. On human games, every trained detector exceeds the untrained model in F1 score across all rounds.

title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
text:
Title: Multirobust Control Pulses Designed by Iterative Quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser Algorithm
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We introduce a multi-robust quantum control strategy designed to suppress multilevel leakage outside the computational qubit space while simultaneously ensuring robustness against unknown inhomogeneities in control parameters. It is based on a reformulation of the Derivative Removal by Adiabatic Gate (DRAG) technique which allows for the full incorporation of control pulses originally designed for two-level models by using the iterative quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser (KAM) algorithm. We apply it for optimal robust control designed by inverse optimization (RIO), referred to as RDK pulses. We analyze the performance of RDK pulses on various durations, iterations, and robustness types. We show that the two-level robustness is restored after only a few iterations with an asymptotic exponential approximation (i.e. as a superasymptotic series), even for relatively short pulse durations and that the resulting pulses are near optimal in terms of energy compared to the optimal RIO pulses defined in the qubit subspace. Such pulses are well suited for superconducting transmons as well as other forms of qubits embedded in a multi-level structure. By effectively reproducing a two-level dynamics within a multi-level system, this approach is versatile thanks to its compatibility with two-level control strategies under conditions (smoothness, duration) that are analyzed.

title: Primordial Power Spectrum from the Lensed CMB Temperature Spectrum using Iterative Delensing and Fourier Denoising
text:
Title: Primordial Power Spectrum from the Lensed CMB Temperature Spectrum using Iterative Delensing and Fourier Denoising
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The CMB power spectra are a strong probe of the primordial power spectrum (PPS) of the initial inflationary scalar perturbations. There are many proposed models, from the simpler power law form to various well motivated physical models that predict features in the PPS beyond the power law. Given the large parameter space of possible models, it is necessary to have model independent searches for such features. Weak gravitational lensing alters the CMB temperature power spectrum and can bias free form reconstructions of the primordial power spectrum (PPS) if not accounted for precisely, such as when using estimators like the Richardson-Lucy (RL) deconvolution algorithm. We build on our design of the Non linear Iterative Richardson Lucy (NIRL) estimator that updates the lensing contribution using the freeform PPS recovered at the previous iteration, making it truly model independent in the PPS domain while accounting for lensing. Inspired by signal processing and Fourier filtering techniques from radio interferometry, we also design a Fourier space iterative low pass filter (FLIP) to suppress noise overfitting in NIRL reconstructions. We demonstrate the performance of NIRL-FLIP on a range of simulated PPS models with bootstrap estimates of reconstruction uncertainty obtained from simulated realizations, and show that both our estimator and regularization are robust, accurate and precise, and are able to both reduce lensing induced reconstruction bias and suppress noise overfitting by a significant factor in Fourier space. We provide a detailed description of these results and recommend its utility for future model independent searches for hints of novel physics in the form of deviations from a power law PPS. This can further assist in precise and accurate testing of inflation models, in conjunction with joint cosmological parameter estimation.

title: On Superconformal Index Degenerations and Half-Indices in S-Confining Gauge Theories
text:
Title: On Superconformal Index Degenerations and Half-Indices in S-Confining Gauge Theories
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We study the $p \rightarrow 0$ limit of four-dimensional $\mathcal N=1$ superconformal indices and its relation to half-indices of three-dimensional $\mathcal N=2$ theories. At the level of special functions, this limit reduces elliptic hypergeometric integrals to basic hypergeometric integrals. The scaling of the flavor fugacities determines the Neumann and Dirichlet boundary conditions of the chiral multiplets. The gauge multiplet has Neumann boundary conditions. We apply this prescription to s-confining theories with gauge groups $SU(2)$, $USp(2N)$, $G_2$, and $SU(N)$, and recover the half-index identities of several boundary confining dualities, expressed through the Nassrallah-Rahman and Gustafson integrals. For $SU(N)$ with a rank-two antisymmetric chiral, four fundamentals and $N$ antifundamentals, we obtain an analytic proof of the half-index identities proposed by Okazaki and Smith for all $N \geq 5$.

title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
text:
Title: How Many Candidates Does a One-Step World Model Need? A Random-Codebook Account of Nearest-of-m Training on Frozen DINO Tokens
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

One-step stochastic world models avoid the mode averaging of deterministic feature predictors without the tens of network evaluations per step that diffusion and flow matching require. The simplest such objective is nearest-of-m matching (conditional implicit maximum likelihood estimation, IMLE): draw m candidate futures and pull only the one closest to the observed outcome. Recent work conjectures that a small m suffices for feature-space world models and that a strictly proper energy score should replace the hard minimum. We test both claims with one-step world models on frozen DINOv2/v3 patch tokens, using benchmarks whose futures can be enumerated. Under mode-like uncertainty, nearest-of-m with m=16 covers the enumerated futures better than 50-step flow matching (at about 1/30 of its latency), one-step flow generators and an energy-score generator at matched parameter counts, and its rollouts stay on the token manifold where flow rollouts drift. One quantity governs the choice of m: the nearest-of-m objective is the expected distortion of a random codebook of m draws from the generator. This view yields three predictions, recorded before the corresponding runs: (i) memorization of the realized outcome in contexts that never repeat, whose strength is governed by the codebook's miss distortion I(m) rather than its miss probability, and which an energy-score generator does not escape by raising m; (ii) a flattening of mode probabilities with m, matching a known optimum within 0.01; and (iii) under-dispersion on continuous high-dimensional outcomes, which bounds the method on real robot video. Per-step matching on self-rollouts cuts long-horizon error by a third on a stochastic Push-T variant; an ablation separates its manifold and coverage benefits. Planning success does not improve despite accurate risk estimates, a negative result we report with its diagnosis.

title: Poisson boundaries of lattices in locally compact groups
text:
Title: Poisson boundaries of lattices in locally compact groups
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

For a random walk on a general locally compact group we provide a discretization procedure transforming the walk to one on a lattice of the group, preserving the Poisson boundary and some finiteness of moments.

title: CRAFT-ε: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
text:
Title: CRAFT-ε: A Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for the Static Relative Permittivity of Pure Organic Liquids
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

The static relative permittivity is an important property in thermodynamic modeling, electrochemistry, and solvent design, but predicting it directly from molecular structure remains challenging because both electronic polarization and molecular dipole orientation contribute to the measured response. Here, we introduce CRAFT-ε (Conformer-Resolved Atom- and Fragment-based Theory for ε), a conformer-resolved molecular descriptor model for predicting the static relative permittivity of neutral pure liquids. Conformer free energies, molecular dipoles, and atom-resolved polarizabilities are obtained from a GFN2-xTB/ALPB 10 workflow. The molecular dipole is decomposed into chemically defined polar-fragment vectors, allowing fitted corrections to retain both the magnitude and relative orientation of local dipolar contributions. Electronic and orientational polarization are combined with a group-contribution molar volume in the Onsager-Kirkwood-Fröhlich relation. A staged parameterization with 41 parameters is applied to nonpolar, polar, and hydrogen-bonding compounds. For 1393 liquids with permittivities between 1.5 and 183, CRAFT-ε reaches a five-fold cross-validated average absolute deviation of 2.40 ({R^2} = 0.93). Conformational averaging 15 is essential for liquids with several polar groups. Compared with an established fragment-based model with 139 parameters, it reaches a similar cross-validated RMSE (3.65 versus 3.41) with about a quarter of the parameters and applies to every liquid of the dataset. The resulting framework provides a computationally inexpensive route from molecular structure to liquid dielectric response and forms a basis for later application to solvent mixtures and electrolyte systems.

title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification
text:
Title: Convex Regression at Scale: Geometry-Preserving Constraint Sparsification
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Convex regression provides a flexible nonparametric estimation framework while incorporating appropriate shape information. However, its standard least-squares formulation has $O(n^2)$ supporting-hyperplane constraints creating a computational bottleneck as the sample size $n$ increases. We study a $K$-nearest-neighbor (KNN) localized relaxation for convex regression where we for each sample, we only maintain the $K$ nearest hyperplane constraints. Under mild regularity conditions, we establish statistical guarantees for our modified estimator in every fixed dimension $d\ge2$. In particular, for $d>4$, the population risk of our modified problem can be shown to have equivalent convergence rates as the original least square convex regression estimator of $\widetilde O(n^{-2/d})$ using neighborhoods sizes (i.e. $K=K_n$) of order $\widetilde O(n^{2(d-1)/(2d-1)})$ for general convex functions and $\widetilde O(n^{(d+1)/(d+2)})$ for strongly convex functions. To corroborate our theory, we implement iterative optimization methods to compare the prediction accuracy of the KNN relaxation with those of the full estimator across synthetic convex benchmarks. Our experiments demonstrate that KNN prediction risk approaches the full-estimator prediction risk at neighborhood sizes matching the theoretical scale.

title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
text:
Title: Plumbline: When the Loss Lies, Validating LLM Training Correctly
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Correctness is a prerequisite for training large language models (LLMs) at scale, yet it is hard to ensure: a fault can sit in any part of a run, and how it shows differs across frameworks and the libraries they depend on. Some failures are loud and some are silent, and both take time to detect and trace. A single fault can waste a long run: the run crashes late, or the model scores lower only at the final evaluation. We present Plumbline, a correctness validation system for LLM training, used in production at Amazon. Plumbline checks each part of the training lifecycle, from the data a run trains on to the model it serves, down to the new layers each model brings and up to whole runs. Its diagnosis reuses these checks to trace failures to their root causes. Both rest on a systematic correctness methodology designed to carry across models and frameworks. Plumbline supports two agentic use cases: Day-0 onboarding, which validates the training of a newly released model before teams rely on it, and root-cause tracing of training failures. Across 3 frameworks and 5 models, it found 61 problems, 32 of them silent. Of these, 42 are fixed or reported upstream, 8 of them first raised by us. We further group the 61 into seven failure patterns that show where training breaks, and report how problems recur across frameworks and models.

title: Electrochemical Molecular Dynamics within the Finite-Field Framework
text:
Title: Electrochemical Molecular Dynamics within the Finite-Field Framework
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Electrochemical processes at charged interfaces lie at the heart of modern technologies and their continued improvement depends on insights into the relevant atomistic processes. However, the necessary tools to impose constant-voltage conditions in molecular dynamics (MD) simulations typically directly target the electrode charge, making their extension to methods that go beyond an empirical description of metals more cumbersome. In this work, we propose an MD protocol to realize a thermodynamic ensemble in which voltage control is attained, but which is formulated purely within the framework of finite-field simulations in 3D periodic boundary conditions. We show a derivation and implementation of such a control device, which we coin an electrostat, in the ELECTRODE package within LAMMPS. Our simulations systematically benchmark the derived theory against other established approaches, for example, showing its equivalence to a potentiostat, and quantify the importance of properly accounting for ensemble fluctuations. We find that for systems of several thousands of atoms, one obtains the same equilibrium properties with the electrostat as with a simpler constant-field simulation. The difference between the two methods only manifests itself at smaller length scales, thereby establishing practical limits for the inclusion of voltage fluctuations in atomistic simulations of electrochemical systems. The strength of this framework also lies in its simplicity of extension to first-principles ab initio and reactive machine-learning potentials.

title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
text:
Title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The propagator of one-dimensional diffusions has relevant applications in statistical inference and across many disciplines. Yet it is obtained in closed form only for very few simple models. Here we analyze an importance sampling strategy based on a bridge change of measure to estimate propagators: paths are generated under an auxiliary diffusion whose bridge between the two fixed boundary points is easy to generate, and the target propagator is recovered through a Radon-Nikodym derivative or likelihood ratio correction derived from Girsanov's theorem. This method overcomes the main limitations of the crude Monte Carlo estimator, which relies on binning in state space, introducing bias and becoming inefficient with rare transitions. We apply the method to a range of benchmark processes and show that the bridge-based estimator matches the accuracy of crude Monte Carlo with orders of magnitude fewer sample paths. Finally, we elaborate on discretization schemes for the Radon-Nikodym derivative and on approximations to the best-in-class change of measure, both of which increase the efficiency of the method.

title: Modeling and Experimental Validation of Bubble-Induced Performance Losses in Microstructured Copper Electrodes for Alkaline Water Electrolysis
text:
Title: Modeling and Experimental Validation of Bubble-Induced Performance Losses in Microstructured Copper Electrodes for Alkaline Water Electrolysis
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Water electrolysis is a promising technology for sustainable hydrogen (H$_2$) production. However, gas bubble formation significantly degrades the electrochemical surface area ($A_{\rm EC}$) and the electrocatalytic activity of microstructured electrodes in water electrolyzer cells. Existing theoretical models fail to connect computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and electrochemistry to analyze how bubble dynamics affect the performance of gas-evolving microstructured electrodes. This work develops a multiphysics-based theoretical model that couples two-phase CFD with Butler-Volmer and Faradaic kinetics, incorporating exchange current density, cell current, gravitational acceleration, surface tension, and fluid properties such as density and viscosity. The model quantifies essential electrochemical parameters, such as the enhancement in $A_{\rm EC}$ and the overpotential ($η$), which deviate by less than 7\% and 15\%, respectively, from the experimental results. Evaluations of the fabricated microstructured electrodes using polarization curves, cyclic voltammetry, electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, and linear polarization resistance techniques demonstrate reduced $η$ by 2.49--21.39\% and 9.55--24.32\% for oxygen (O$_2$) and H$_2$ evolution, respectively. Furthermore, the model reveals the interplay between enhanced geometric surface area and bubble-transport limitations, facilitating the optimization and analysis of structural parameters. These findings establish a physics-informed roadmap for designing optimal, robust, and industry-scalable microstructured electrodes for efficient H$_2$ generation via water electrolysis.

title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
text:
Title: Where, When, and How Many Bits? Scaling Laws for SGD with Stochastic Rounding
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Low-precision training reduces computation but introduces additional rounding error. We theoretically study how stochastic rounding (SR) affects prediction risk as model size, training time, and precision change. We consider a two-layer linear network with a fixed random first layer, trained by mini-batch SGD on fresh Gaussian data with power-law spectra. At each SGD step, the features used in forward and backward computations are rounded independently. We prove matched upper and lower bounds on prediction error for the final model and for uniform parameter averaging, with general learning-rate and precision schedules chosen before training. For fixed precisions and constant learning rates with parameter averaging, we derive how the smallest prediction error decreases with compute, and we identify model sizes and training times that achieve this optimal-compute scaling. Rounding only the forward features preserves the compute scaling of exact arithmetic, while rounding backward features changes it. Averaging parameters can change which computation needs higher precision and when higher precision is useful. Our results also give bit requirements for a given accuracy tolerance and show how backward rounding can change learning-rate schedule design. At a fixed compute budget, lower precision can improve prediction when the benefit of a larger model or longer training outweighs the additional SR-induced error. Model simulations illustrate these tradeoffs, and experiments with an MLP and a small transformer examine rounding choices beyond the theoretical model.

title: State Evolution and Universality of Iterated Linear Programs for the Binary Perceptron
text:
Title: State Evolution and Universality of Iterated Linear Programs for the Binary Perceptron
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

The binary perceptron is a random constraint satisfaction problem that asks for a sign vector satisfying a system of random linear inequalities. Its solution space has a strikingly extreme geometry: at every positive constraint density, all but a vanishing fraction of the solutions are isolated. Yet polynomial-time algorithms find solutions at small enough constraint density, which raises the question of how efficient algorithms navigate such a landscape. Linear programming is a natural algorithm to study here, but its analysis has so far been limited to a single round. Li, Schramm, and Zhou (STOC 2025) analyzed one linear program followed by iterative rounding. In this work, we overcome this limitation and give a precise analysis of iterated linear programming for the binary perceptron. (1) For Gaussian matrices and any fixed number of rounds, we characterize the iterated linear programs exactly through a deterministic state-evolution recursion. (2) Adding a final rounding step, we obtain a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for the binary perceptron. Numerical evaluations of the recursion provide evidence that it succeeds at constraint density $α=0.60$ with zero margin, well beyond the range $α\le0.1$ guaranteed by the single-LP analysis and $α\approx0.327$ (Jo and Lee, 2026), the best guarantee so far. (3) We establish universality, showing that the same characterization holds for matrices with i.i.d. entries drawn from any centered, unit-variance subgaussian law. The key idea of our proof is that, although conditioning on earlier rounds makes the matrix non-Gaussian, its conditional law can be computed explicitly and remains close to a Gaussian law, so the convex Gaussian min-max theorem applies in every round. For universality, we compare Gaussian and subgaussian matrices through the Lindeberg principle, using a regularized version of each linear program.

title: A Visual Understanding of Circular Dichroism Spectroscopy: The Case of Interacting Chromophores
text:
Title: A Visual Understanding of Circular Dichroism Spectroscopy: The Case of Interacting Chromophores
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Exciton coupling shapes the photophysical and chiroptical properties of molecular aggregates, but a microscopic, real-space understanding of how intermolecular interactions generate circular dichroism (CD) remains incomplete. Here, we computationally investigate the microscopic origins of CD in coupled molecular dimers to separate intermolecular (topological) from intramolecular (intrinsic) chirality. A combination of time-dependent density functional theory and transition chiral tensor (TCT) analysis provides a quantitative, visually intuitive framework showing how electronic coupling strength, intermolecular separation, and relative angular orientation govern chiroptical response. We find that pairs of individually achiral chromophores exhibit robust, topological chiroptical signals which give rise to the conventional Cotton effect, a standard interpretation of derivative features in circular dichroism spectra. We next establish that intrinsically chiral chromophores, on the other hand, disrupt the Cotton effect due to the competition between intrinsic chirality and topological chirality. This work establishes a foundation for interpreting exciton-coupled CD spectra in molecular aggregates, supramolecular assemblies, and nanostructures using the TCT approach, which offers an attractive tool for analyzing chiroptical responses in complex multi-chromophore systems relevant to emerging quantum technologies.

title: Theoretical Prediction of Superconducting 2D Hydrogenated Janus V2CSH and Nb2CSH MXenes
text:
Title: Theoretical Prediction of Superconducting 2D Hydrogenated Janus V2CSH and Nb2CSH MXenes
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Two dimensional hydrogenated Janus MXenes represent a new frontier in superconducting materials, where asymmetric surface terminations enable tunable electronic and vibrational properties. In this work, we present the first comparative study of hydrogen or sulfur terminated V2CSH and Nb2CSH monolayers using density functional theory and density functional perturbation theory. Both compounds are structurally and thermally stable, exhibiting isotropic in plane elasticity and nonmagnetic multiband metallic states dominated by transition metal d orbitals. The asymmetric S or H terminations generate nonequivalent surface potentials and intrinsic out of plane dipoles. Electron phonon coupling constants of 0.39 (V2CSH) and 0.53 (Nb2CSH) yield superconducting transition temperatures of 2.36 K and 5.27 K, respectively, within the Allen Dynes framework. Low energy lattice vibrations, primarily involving metal and sulfur atoms, account for 77% of the coupling in both MXenes. These findings establish metal substitution as a design principle for tuning superconductivity in Janus MXenes and highlight Nb2CSH as a promising candidate for low temperature superconducting applications.

title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
text:
Title: Stochastic dynamics of cosmological inflation in general relativity
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The theory of Inflation, supplemented by fluctuations of the quantum vacuum, is the leading paradigm to explain the correlations of inhomogeneities at very large distances in the Universe. Particle physics methods fail when strong non-linearity and non-perturbativity are involved, leaving a whole landscape of untestable scenarios of inflation. Starobinsky's stochastic inflation can in principle treat inflationary inhomogeneities nonlinearly and classically as the Hubble radius becomes smaller than their wavelengths, but it was never formulated in full general relativity, which motivates this thesis. Using the Keldysh formalism of nonequilibrium quantum field theory, we first develop a validity criterion for the use of classical computations, and thus simulations, to probe inflationary interactions, finding analytically that the bispectrum can be extracted from slightly sub-Hubble scales in quasi-de Sitter spacetimes. We then provide the first analytical solutions to the constraints for inhomogeneous initial conditions of numerical relativity simulations of inflation, and use them to explore its nonperturbative regime. Our main contribution is to obtain stochastic equations for the full set of inflaton equations in general relativity: this description incorporates the full nonlinear and backreacting evolution, is small-gauge-invariant, and is free of historical assumptions such as the gradient-free separate universe approximation. We implement these equations in the BSSN formulation of numerical relativity, demonstrating their correctness in slow-roll and ultra slow-roll scenarios via the satisfaction of the constraints, with a first look at eternal inflation.
