To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

title: Dipolar boson stars as static two-body systems: an effective-one-body description
text:
Title: Dipolar boson stars as static two-body systems: an effective-one-body description
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Dipolar boson stars consist of two scalar-field lumps held in static equilibrium by the balance between gravitational attraction and scalar repulsion. The repulsion stems from a $π$ phase difference between the harmonically varying complex scalar field sourcing each lump. We construct sequences of these configurations numerically and describe them analytically as bound states of two boson stars within the effective-one-body (EOB) formalism. We map the EOB potential previously derived for the scattering of two boson stars onto an energy-dependent Schwarzschild-like radial potential. We find that the EOB-based analytical prediction for the binding energy of the system agrees remarkably well with the numerical values. The analytical prediction for the critical gravitational coupling beyond which no static equilibrium exists is also consistent with the numerical results.

title: Multichannel Phonon Interconversion Drives 90 Polarization Rotation for Stable Domain Walls in Hafnium Oxide
text:
Title: Multichannel Phonon Interconversion Drives 90 Polarization Rotation for Stable Domain Walls in Hafnium Oxide
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Polarization rotation is a fundamental mechanism in ferroelectric materials, yet how such rotation arises microscopically in fluorite ferroelectrics and gives rise to distinct domain walls (DW) remains unresolved. Phonon modes offer a microscopic route to such structural transformations, as geometric orientations can modify their frequencies, dispersion relations, and vibrational eigenstates when their characteristic wavelengths become comparable to relevant physical dimensions. Here, by combining condensed phonon mode decomposition with first-principles calculations, we investigate the origin of 90 polarization rotation in the ferroelectric phase of HfO2. Using the cubic parent phase as reference, we show that polarization rotation originates from multiple symmetry equivalent phonon modes of distinct eigenstates at different wavevectors in the Brillouin zone, whose coupling and cooperative reorientation continuously evolve to generate distinct 90 Pca21 variants and switching pathways. Among the 90 variants, the lowest-energy switching pathway through the Pmn21 exhibits an energy barrier comparable to, but slightly lower than, that of the 180 polarization reversal pathway through the P42/nmc phase, indicating that 90 polarization rotation is an energetically accessible alternative switching route. We further analyze 90 DW and find that frustrated phonon modes emerge at the wall center, where the coexistence and competition of condensed modes promote local reconfiguration of the lattice distortions, contributing to the elevated DW energies. Importantly, experimental observations with STEM imaging provide direct evidence of atomic mode distortions in stable 90 DW, consistent with the theoretically identified low-energy DW. These findings provide the fundamental structural mechanism underlying 90 switching dynamics, competing domain-wall physics, and macroscopic ferroelectric behavior.

title: Ion Redistribution and Lattice-Distortion-Modulated d-Electron Correlation in Layered Multiferroic ABP$_2$S$_6$ Probed by X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy
text:
Title: Ion Redistribution and Lattice-Distortion-Modulated d-Electron Correlation in Layered Multiferroic ABP$_2$S$_6$ Probed by X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Ferroelectric phase transitions are driven by ion displacement-induced symmetry breaking, yet their chemical signatures are rarely probed directly at the atomic level. Here, we establish temperature-dependent X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) as a powerful and quantitative probe of ferroelectric phase transitions by tracking ion migration-induced changes in local chemical environments. Using van der Waals (vdW) layered ABP$_2$S$_6$ materials as a model system, we systematically compare CuCrP$_2$S$_6$ (CCPS), which undergoes a ferroelectric phase transition, with AgCrP$_2$S$_6$ (ACPS), which remains paraelectric over the same temperature range. While ACPS exhibits only smooth trivial thermal broadening and shifts in core-level spectra, CCPS shows pronounced and enormously large temperature-dependent XPS anomalies across the ferroelectric transition, demonstrating that XPS is intrinsically sensitive to ferroelectric order. Detailed analysis of the Cu 2p spectra reveals that these anomalies originate from temperature-driven Cu$^+$ ion migration associated with polarization switching, whereas concurrent changes in the Cr core levels reflect secondary lattice squeezing and modulation of d-electron correlation induced by Cu displacement. Supported by a ferroelectric structural model, we further correlate XPS binding-energy shifts with the magnitude of Cu-ion migration, enabling a quantitative estimation of ionic displacement directly from spectroscopic observables. This work also highlights the rich information provided by temperature-dependent XPS for detecting and quantifying ferroelectric phase transitions and ion migration, offering a general chemical probe for ferroic materials and ion-displacement-driven phase transitions.

title: Approximating graphic TSP by b-matchings
text:
Title: Approximating graphic TSP by b-matchings
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We give a polynomial-time algorithm for graphic TSP that returns a tour of length at most $\frac{89}{64}=\frac{7}{5}-\frac{3}{320}$ times the value of the subtour relaxation. This improves the long-standing ratio $\frac75$ of Sebő and Vygen and shows that the integrality gap of the subtour LP on graphic instances is at most $\frac{89}{64}\approx 1.3906$. We optimize a non-linear objective function over an odd-join polytope, which uses (i) a new removable system of edges, and (ii) reconnection of subtours if the graph is disconnected. This approach gives a $\frac{13}{10}$-approximation algorithm for $4$-regular $4$-vertex-connected graphs, improving the $\frac43$ of Newman, and a $\frac43$-approximation for $k$-vertex-connected graphs of maximum degree at most $k+1$, for every $k\ge 3$. For the general graphic TSP, we construct a feasible point in the odd-join polytope, using an optimal vertex from the Subtour linear programming relaxation of TSP, which helps us bound the approximation factor by 89/64.

title: Neutral-atom quantum features as complementary structural encodings for graph learning
text:
Title: Neutral-atom quantum features as complementary structural encodings for graph learning
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Structural descriptors provide graph neural networks (GNNs) with positional and topological inductive biases. However, widely used classical encodings based on random walks or Laplacian spectra emphasize specific structural statistics of a graph, leaving room for alternative descriptors. Neutral-atom quantum processing units (QPUs) can realize graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonians, allowing graph topology to be probed through dynamical correlation measurements. In this work, we use these measurements as quantum graph features (QGFs), providing a complementary, hardware-derived family of structural encoding that is not accurately described by classical features derived from Laplacian and adjacency matrices, even when supplemented with an extended set of random-walk, geometric descriptors and classical physical models. By appropriately selecting the quench parameters of the Hamiltonian, we access two characteristic correlation regimes with distinct structural signatures: antiferromagnetic-like and ferromagnetic-like. On an intrinsic information benchmark of 15 topological and spectral probing tasks, quantum and hybrid quantum-classical features match or surpass classical descriptors on local topological properties. When supplied to message-passing, attention, and graph-transformer backbones, hybrid quantum-classical features yield improvements that are within cross-fold noise on most cells but sign-consistent across architectures. When comparing noiseless, shot-sampled emulation-derived quantum features with a neutral-atom QPU implementation, the downstream hybrid results with compressed hardware features match their emulated counterparts within $0.01$ F$_1$ on all backbones. On a synthetic family of ladder graphs, QGFs distinguish two specific classes, outperforming the strongest classical structural descriptors by a margin exceeding cross-fold variability.

title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
text:
Title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. The resulting objective and its analytic gradients can be evaluated using low-rank factors, diagonal quantities, and small dense matrices, without forming the full kernel matrix or its derivatives. The complete training procedure is implemented in single precision and evaluated on nine large-scale regression datasets. Across these problems, the method reaches the reference predictive accuracy while substantially reducing training time, although the required approximation rank varies across datasets. We also study the numerical behavior of the full-kernel predictive solve and show that single precision can become limiting for ill-conditioned problems. Finally, we investigate further reducing selected matrix operations to fp16 or TF32. These lower-precision variants provide only modest additional speedups and can become unreliable when the reduced system is poorly conditioned.

title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
text:
Title: Curie's Jarvis: Autonomous Robotic Chemistry Experiments from Printed Protocols
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

A person running a bench experiment works from a printed instruction sheet, tells identical containers apart by the labels written on them, and looks at the bench again before each step. Lab automation usually works the other way around: the procedure is written as a script, and containers stand at fixed positions or carry fiducial markers. We present Curie's Jarvis, a system that lets a robot arm carry out a chemistry experiment on a bench set up for people. It reads the steps from a photo of the printed sheet, finds containers on an ordinary bench with no fixed positions or markers, tells identical-looking containers apart by reading their labels in four camera views, locates its target again before every step, and sets how each step is carried out, including its speed, from what is being handled. On a Franka Panda arm, Curie's Jarvis completed 5 of 5 runs of one protocol from a children's chemistry kit and 4 of 5 runs of another, with no human intervention, and in 160 locates on printed and handwritten labels it identified every container correctly. This brings robots a step closer to doing bench chemistry the way people do.

title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
text:
Title: Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Microscopic simulations resolve spatial patterns but are feasible only over small domains and short timescales, whereas bulk descriptions erase those patterns through spatial averaging. Mesoscopic fields preserve this spatial organisation, but their effective equations are known only for selected microscopic systems and scaling limits. We introduce Deep Mesoscopic Dynamics (DeepMesoD), which uses neural networks to learn an effective mesoscopic field equation from microscopic trajectories at a prescribed coarse-graining scale. For the nonconserved dissipative dynamics studied here, DeepMesoD learns the free-energy functional with a spatial interaction kernel and a state-dependent dissipation operator constrained by the fluctuation-dissipation relation. We first validate the construction in the Ising-Kac model, where the learned mesoscopic equation recovers the known hydrodynamic limit and rollouts remain stable far beyond the training horizon. We then treat two systems without closed-form mesoscopic descriptions. For a two-dimensional Heisenberg ferromagnet governed by atomistic spin dynamics, DeepMesoD learns a mesoscopic model whose predictions match atomistic references up to 1 ns, and a rollout with an unseen initial condition remains bounded up to 25 ns. For layered CrBr$_3$, the learned kernel captures the suppression and sign reversal of interlayer coupling at a stacking fault whose location and strength are not supplied as inputs. Controlled changes to the learned interaction show how fault number and placement shape multistep magnetic responses, complementing our magneto-photoluminescence measurements. Across the two atomistic systems, DeepMesoD achieves a three-to-four-order-of-magnitude reduction in wall-clock time compared with atomistic spin dynamics.

title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking
text:
Title: Weight-Space Programming of Policies and Their Verification via Model Checking
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Large language models (LLMs) can write the weights of small neural networks directly, without gradient descent. This weight-space programming creates policies for sequential decision-making from a task description alone, but nothing guarantees that a written policy behaves as intended. We combine weight-space programming with probabilistic model checking. Given an environment modeled as a Markov decision process and a requirement in probabilistic computation tree logic (PCTL), an LLM writes all weights of a policy network, optionally repairs them on a dataset of optimal actions, and receives model-checking feedback until the requirement holds or a round limit is reached. The model checker Storm computes, rather than estimates from simulations, the probability that the policy satisfies the requirement, so every returned policy is verified. With two LLMs on three environments, the created policy of each of the 18 runs attains the optimal probability, before any dataset or model-checking feedback. Four of six policies programmed for two transporter jobs also complete three jobs with probability 1, so they generalize to a task that the LLM never saw. The pipeline also programs a policy that satisfies a complex safety requirement expressed with the PCTL until operator in all six runs. In one of them, dataset repair raised the accuracy to 98.4\% but broke the requirement, and one round of model-checking feedback restored it.

title: Clique Constraints for Exact Causal Structure Learning
text:
Title: Clique Constraints for Exact Causal Structure Learning
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Exact score-based causal structure learning supports explicit structural constraints and optimisation certificates, but its branch-and-cut search can be computationally demanding. We augment exact causal structure learning methods with an upper bound on the maximum clique size of the learned undirected skeleton, enforced at integer candidates through lazy cycle and clique constraints. On static linear-Gaussian Erdős-Rényi and scale-free DAGs, we evaluate callback order, alternative clique-cut policies, incumbent repair, fractional separation, and Big-M bounds. We report causal-recovery metrics jointly with optimality gaps, primal and dual bounds, node throughput, MIPSOL events, and callback cost. Two variants receive particular attention: B3 selects the most violated minimal (k+1)-clique inequality at each callback, whereas C3 repairs an infeasible integer candidate by deleting violating edges and refitting affected regression columns using QR-based least squares. The results do not indicate that clique constraints uniformly accelerate optimisation. However, their benefit depends on graph density, sample size, and cut-management policy, while large collections of correlated constraints can reduce node throughput. Tighter valid Big-M bounds reduced the fixed-budget optimality gap in most tested settings, without necessarily changing SHD or F1 at a fixed time limit. These findings characterize the computational trade-offs of clique-constrained exact causal learning, and identify selective separation and incumbent repair as promising directions.

title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
text:
Title: DiffSequence-Q: Diffusion Design with Quantum Assistance for Biologically Active Proteins
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Designing protein sequences that satisfy both secondary structure requirements and solubility targets remains challenging. We present DiffSequence-Q, a hybrid multinomial diffusion model conditioned on secondary structure at each residue and a continuous solubility target. To introduce quantum auxiliary supervision during training, we employ a quantum neural network (QNN) or quantum Kolmogorov-Arnold network (QKAN) as an auxiliary solubility prediction head over shared Transformer representations. The auxiliary prediction loss is jointly optimized with the diffusion objective, allowing quantum auxiliary supervision to influence the learned denoising model. Once trained, protein sequences are generated entirely through classical reverse diffusion. On the CATH benchmark, DiffSequence-Q achieved the highest secondary structure recovery among the four evaluated models for complete sequence generation. Evaluation with a separately trained solubility prediction model showed that the best QNN and QKAN configurations achieved mean predicted solubility scores 14.0% and 22.7% higher than the multilayer perceptron (MLP) baseline, respectively. Experimental characterization further demonstrated biological activity across three distinct protein families. Selected defensins exhibited pronounced inhibitory activity against Aspergillus niger, while xylanases and short-chain dehydrogenases exhibited substantial enzymatic activity. Together, these results support DiffSequence-Q as a framework for integrating structural requirements and solubility targets in protein generation, with experimentally demonstrated biological activity.

title: Learning on-the-fly quasi-stationarity diagnostics from low-dimensional surrogates
text:
Title: Learning on-the-fly quasi-stationarity diagnostics from low-dimensional surrogates
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Accelerated dynamics methods, such as parallel replica dynamics, require estimates of the decorrelation time, after which a process trapped in one of its metastable states is distributed according to the quasi-stationary distribution (QSD). In a method proposed by Binder, Lelièvre and Simpson, decorrelation times are defined by coupling a particle approximation of the non-linear conditioned probability flow of the process with MCMC-inspired diagnostics. We explore an alternative to MCMC diagnostics, based on coarse-graining of non-linear probability flows and simulation-based inference. We first develop a coarse-graining framework for killed Markov jump processes conditioned on survival, proving uniform-in-time, non-asymptotic estimates approximating the non-linear probability flow of the true process by the non-linear flow of a surrogate process, defined with a collective variable. The framework does not assume reversibility of the true process, and also gives bounds which scale explicitly in an adiabatic regime. Motivated by these results, we then construct a quasi-stationarity diagnostic using simulation-based inference: a recurrent neural network (RNN), trained on particle approximations of non-linear effective flows, estimates posterior probabilities of decorrelation. The learned diagnostic is then transferred to collective-variable traces of high-dimensional particle approximations. We investigate the behavior and robustness of this diagnostic on a set of numerical experiments, comparing it to the MCMC diagnostic of Binder et al.\ on both synthetic examples and a molecular system, in and out of its training prior distribution. When its prior assumptions hold, the RNN diagnostic outperforms the MCMC diagnostic in ROC analysis, is less conservative, fails less often, and has an interpretable decision threshold.

title: HyInv Technical Report
text:
Title: HyInv Technical Report
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Inverse folding designs amino-acid sequences for a given protein backbone, and screening needs many candidates that are both diverse and well folded. We present HyInv, a 1.96-million-parameter backbone-conditioned graph network with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained by Hyra 2.0, the research agent developed by our team: pretrained with random-order autoregressive sequence modeling, followed by structure-reward reinforcement learning. At inference, a grouped draft-and-rewrite sampler that uses separate draft and rewrite temperatures improves refolding TM-score at matched diversity. An optimized implementation with BF16 numerics designs 128 sequences for a 402-residue backbone in 50.6 ms on a single NVIDIA H20 GPU, about 52 times faster than the reference sampler, and an exact FP32 path that returns the reference sequences is 8.7 times faster. Across five benchmark datasets and seven dataset-predictor combinations, HyInv reaches a higher average scTM than all ten external baselines at comparable or higher sequence diversity, with large margins over ProteinMPNN and ProteinZero V2. The same default setting supports de novo backbones, pocket-constrained libraries, enzyme redesign with the catalytic site kept, and loop redesign. We have released our code and model at https://github.com/Tencent-Hunyuan/Hyra-results/tree/main/AI4Science/hyinv.

title: Latest $ν$s from the Earliest Galaxies: Probing neutrino self-interactions with JWST
text:
Title: Latest $ν$s from the Earliest Galaxies: Probing neutrino self-interactions with JWST
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Our Universe serves as a complementary laboratory for particle physics interactions. One intriguing possibility is that neutrinos may have beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) self-interactions, which can delay their free streaming and have an observable effect across different redshifts. Such interactions can induce scale-dependent changes in the matter power spectrum. The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has opened up a new window onto the early Universe by discovering a large population of high-redshift galaxies up to $z \sim 15$ and various probable galaxy candidates at even higher redshifts, between $z \sim 15-30$. Such high-redshift observations can probe the matter power spectrum on small scales, since structure formation is hierarchical and the structures hosting these high-redshift galaxies are therefore expected to be small. We, $\textit{for the first time}$, use the UV luminosity function data from JWST and combine them with the $\textit{Planck}$ CMB data to probe neutrino self-interactions ($ν$SI). If only one neutrino flavor experiences such BSM interactions, then $\textit{Planck}$ + JWST data give a 95% C.L. upper limit on $\mathrm{Log}_{10}(G_{\mathrm{eff}}/\mathrm{MeV}^{-2})$ $\approx$ $-2.75$ and when all three flavors are interacting, the corresponding constraint becomes $\lesssim -3.41$; both stronger than those obtained using only $\textit{Planck}$ data. Our results highlight the power of this new observable, the high-redshift UV luminosity function from JWST as a complementary probe to terrestrial experiments, showing that small-scale observables can open a new window onto smaller neutrino self-interaction strengths.

title: SEISMO: Explanation-Aware, Trajectory-Conditioned LLM Agents for Sample-Efficient Molecular Optimisation
text:
Title: SEISMO: Explanation-Aware, Trajectory-Conditioned LLM Agents for Sample-Efficient Molecular Optimisation
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Optimizing molecules to achieve desired properties is a central bottleneck across the chemical sciences, particularly in the pharmaceutical industry, where it underlies the discovery of new drugs. Since molecular property evaluation often relies on costly and rate-limited oracles, such as experimental assays, molecular optimization must be highly sample-efficient. To address this, we introduce SEISMO, an LLM agent for inference-time molecular optimisation that turns information routinely available alongside the oracle score, but discarded by existing methods, into an explicit guidance signal. Rather than treating the oracle as a scalar black box, SEISMO conditions each proposal on a natural-language task description, the full optimization trajectory, and machine-readable feedback derived from post-hoc explainability methods and sub-score decompositions. Across a wide range of drug-discovery-relevant tasks, this consistently improves sample efficiency over existing optimisers as well as zero-shot LLM generation, with gains growing as explanatory feedback is enriched. In practice, medicinal chemists can inspect the agent's reasoning and intervene to steer generation in natural language, keeping them central to molecular optimisation projects.

title: Open Quantum Time Crystals without External Thermodynamic Resources: Go and No-Go Theorems
text:
Title: Open Quantum Time Crystals without External Thermodynamic Resources: Go and No-Go Theorems
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Time crystals are phases of matter that spontaneously break time-translation symmetry. They have been ruled out in the ground and Gibbs states of isolated systems with only short-range interactions, yet they have been proposed and observed experimentally in nonequilibrium settings such as Floquet and open systems. However, existing proposals for time crystals in open quantum systems require an external supply of thermodynamic resources, such as work or energetic coherence. Whether coupling to an environment, without any such resource supply, can induce a time crystal absent in the isolated system remains open. Here, we answer this question systematically. We first construct an explicit model and prove that coupling to an environment can activate a time crystal absent in the isolated system, even without such resource supply. We consider Lindblad master equations with (i) time-independent Hamiltonian and jump operators, (ii) time-translation covariance, and (iii) detailed balance---conditions that hold in standard derivations unless thermodynamic resources are supplied externally. Our model satisfies these conditions, and the activation occurs in a stationary state of both the isolated and open systems. We give several implementations of this dynamics with a zero-temperature Gibbs environment, a time-independent, energy-conserving interaction, and only short-range Hamiltonians, one of which exactly reproduces the time-crystalline periodicity. We then prove a no-go theorem: under (i)--(iii), activation can arise only from an environment-induced Hamiltonian term, not from dissipation. Our results show that time crystals can be activated in open systems without external resource supply and identify the physical requirements on the system and environment for this activation through our general no-go theorem.

title: Epitaxial Displacement-etched GaAsSb Quantum Dots Emitting at Telecom Wavelengths
text:
Title: Epitaxial Displacement-etched GaAsSb Quantum Dots Emitting at Telecom Wavelengths
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are essential components for integrated photonic and quantum information systems, yet current epitaxial growth techniques face significant limitations in complexity of growth, material selection, and density tunability. Here we report a displacement etch technique that enables controlled formation of GaAsSb QDs with emission at telecommunications wavelengths. Our approach uses arsenic molecular flux (As$_2$) to react with antimonide surfaces through thermodynamically favorable displacement reactions, creating three-dimensional quantum confined nanostructures without requiring strain-driven growth or complex droplet-based processes. Density functional theory shows the two competing As-for-Sb exchange pathways to be nearly equivalent in both reaction energy and activation barrier, which places morphological control in the subsequent adatom kinetics rather than in the surface reaction itself. A single process parameter, the As$_2$ exposure, sets the QD areal density across three orders of magnitude, from 10$^2$ to 10$^5$ $μm^{-2}$, covering both isolated emitters and dense gain media. Structural analysis reveals well-defined GaAsSb QDs with a mixed GaAs/GaSb composition and no extended defects. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements confirm emission at 1550 nm (0.8 eV) within the telecommunications C-band, with characteristic QD-like temperature dependence. Because the QDs form on a lattice-matched GaSb surface in a single growth step, the technique offers a practical route to C-band emitters built into the GaSb/AlGaSb device family already used for mid-infrared sources and detectors.

title: Advances in Machine Learning for Directed Evolution: A Five-Year Retrospective
text:
Title: Advances in Machine Learning for Directed Evolution: A Five-Year Retrospective
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

The last five-plus years have seen many protein engineering disciplines transformed by advances in machine learning (ML), but the same cannot be said for directed evolution. Reflecting on a previously co-authored perspective, I discuss why I believe this to be the case, arguing that a disconnect between the goals of machine-learning-assisted directed evolution (MLDE) researchers--"identify an optimal protein"--and the goals of directed evolution more broadly--"identify a sufficient protein given time and resource constraints"--is a principal culprit. As an example, I highlight how nearly all current MLDE methods neglect to account for the cost of DNA synthesis, resulting in strategies that have limited practical applicability regardless of the underlying models' capabilities. I close by discussing recent works that are exceptions to this overarching trend, and emphasize that the last five years of efforts in ML-assisted protein engineering and the prescribed reframe of MLDE objectives need not be mutually exclusive.

title: A Study of Side Jet Interactions over a Hypersonic Cone Flow using Kinetic Methods
text:
Title: A Study of Side Jet Interactions over a Hypersonic Cone Flow using Kinetic Methods
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The interaction between the hypersonic flow over a cone and a side jet creates complex multiple recirculation regions as well as separation, reattachment and bow shocks known as Edney-Type IV shock-shock interactions. The interactions between these multi-scale structures are shown to be well captured with the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method, a particle-kinetic approach. This computational technique was used because even though the free stream conditions were continuum-like, sufficiently strong gradients in the shock and jet expansion were observed to cause continuum breakdown. The time-accurate DSMC approach has been shown in previous work to capture the multi-scale structures and unsteadiness in the shock structure that occurs in such flows, as was also observed in this work. These sources of unsteadiness in the shock system are shown to locally affect surface parameters such as heat transfer and skin friction as well as predict a low frequency unsteadiness consistent with earlier values in the literature.

title: Gravitational-Wave Microlensing as a Probe of Compact Object Population
text:
Title: Gravitational-Wave Microlensing as a Probe of Compact Object Population
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The abundance of compact objects ranging from stellar to intermediate masses ($\sim 1 - 10^{5}M_{\odot}$) remains poorly constrained, particularly for populations such as primordial black holes and dark matter subhalos that emit little or no electromagnetic radiation. Gravitational-wave (GW) microlensing provides a complementary way to probe these populations through wave-optics effects imprinted on the GW signals, with implications for astrophysical and cosmological inference. We develop a hierarchical Bayesian framework to infer the population properties of microlenses from an ensemble of microlensed GW events, constraining the slope of the power-law lens mass function ($α_{\rm ML}$), the lens number density ($n_0$), and the fraction of dark matter in compact lenses ($f_{\rm DM}$). Using simulated microlensed GW signals drawn from a realistic binary black hole population, we find that $\sim 100$ detected microlensed events are able to constrain both $α_{\rm ML}$ and $n_0$, although a degeneracy between the two remains. For a low-mass-dominated lens population ($α_{\rm ML}=2$) with $n_0=10^6~\mathrm{Mpc}^{-3}$, a three-year observation at the O4 sensitivity yields $\sim 130$ detectable microlensed events and recovers the injected dark-matter fraction, $f_{\rm DM}\simeq 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$, with a 90% credible interval of $7.3 \times 10^{-5} \lesssim f_{\rm DM} \lesssim 1.8 \times 10^{-4}$.

title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
text:
Title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral $v$-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen

title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures
text:
Title: A Unified Framework for Training-Dataset Aggregation and Exact Machine Unlearning via Gibbs Probability Measures
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

In this paper, three operations on Gibbs probability measures are studied: renormalization, normalized log-linear combination, and nesting. The resulting measures are shown to be Gibbs probability measures with explicit expressions for their objective functions, reference measures, and regularization factors. These measures are further characterized as unique solutions to optimization problems involving linear combinations of the original objective functions, subject to either relative entropy regularization or relative entropy constraints. When the reference measures are probability measures, geometric interpretations of these three operations are established involving Pythagorean identities and exponential geodesics.A central result is the equivalence between nesting and normalized log-linear combinations of Gibbs probability measures. These results are then applied to supervised machine learning with Gibbs algorithms, which are represented by Gibbs probability measures. In this context, either through nesting or log-linear combinations, Gibbs algorithms trained on local datasets are used to form new Gibbs algorithms trained upon the aggregation of all local training datasets. Interestingly, the parameters of such operations, determine the weights of each training data point on the aggregated dataset. %Operations on local Gibbs probability measures are shown to control the contributions of training data. This observation is leveraged for achieving: (a) exact machine unlearning in centralized, decentralized, and federated learning systems; and (b) centralized-equivalent performance, in the sense of producing algorithms trained on the aggregation of all local datasets in decentralized and federated learning .

title: Tunneling from an oscillating state in quantum field theory
text:
Title: Tunneling from an oscillating state in quantum field theory
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

How does a scalar field oscillating about a metastable minimum decay? For a coherent state with $\langle q(t) \rangle = a \cos mt$ we find two results. When $mR \ll 1$, with $m$ the mass and $R$ the bubble radius, the decay at time $t$ is a Coleman bubble in the frozen potential $U_t(η) = U(\langle q \rangle +η)-U(\langle q \rangle)-U'(\langle q \rangle)η$, for any amplitude. At small amplitude but any $mR$, $B(t)=B_0 - a \mathcal{M} \cos mt+O(a^2)$, with $\mathcal{M}$ set by the tail of the vacuum bounce; for a thin wall $\mathcal{M} \propto e^{mR}$, so exponentially small oscillations change the rate significantly. Both results follow from a Euclidean source construction. The same method computes the tunneling rate of a field slowly rolling in one direction and metastable in another.

title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
text:
Title: Automatic Generation of Novel Highly-Functional Molecular Sequences
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

While multiple methods now exist to generate functional sequence variants from existing annotated examples, it is unclear how well such methods can be used to generate sequences that exceed the functionality of those contained in the example set. Using two complete fitness landscapes, we quantify how effectively generative tools can search sequence space and find rare, novel, highly functional sequences, focusing on variational auto-encoders and information-theoretic methods. We find that an information-theoretic method that does not require training and runs significantly faster than standard Machine-Learning/Artificial Intelligence (ML/AI) methods also is significantly more effective in finding rare highly-functional sequences. We discuss the application of this novel method to discover rare polypeptides with anti-bacterial properties that are specific to bacterial, but not eukaryotic, cell membranes.

title: FocusBranch: Combinatorial Branch-and-Bound for $\ell_0$ Neural Network Robustness Verification
text:
Title: FocusBranch: Combinatorial Branch-and-Bound for $\ell_0$ Neural Network Robustness Verification
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Verifying the local robustness of neural networks under $\ell_0$ perturbations is inherently combinatorial, as it must reason over all sparse subsets of $ε$ perturbed pixels. This paper presents FocusBranch, a combinatorial branch-and-bound framework for $\ell_0$ robustness verification. The key insight is to make the $\ell_0$-ball decomposable and branchable using a node abstraction, which consists of a focus pixel set $\mathcal{S}$ and a level $l$, permitting at most $ε-l$ pixels outside $\mathcal{S}$. This abstraction unifies two branching mechanisms: concrete nodes branch through upper shadows to fix additional perturbed locations, while super nodes branch through covering designs to cover many perturbation cases with fewer child nodes. FocusBranch proves node safety by concretizing linear relaxations over node-constrained $\ell_0$-balls and recursively branches on unknown nodes. Rather than relying on a fixed verification plan, it samples nodes across levels to estimate safe rates and costs, then selects a starting level and branching strategy predicted to minimize verification time. Experiments on fully connected and convolutional classifiers for MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 show that FocusBranch verifies $\ell_0$ robustness effectively across architectures and outperforms state-of-the-art verifiers. The code is available at: https://github.com/simpl-group/FocusBranch.

title: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
text:
Title: A Cooperative Game-Theoretic Framework for Real-Time Deviation Settlement in Local Energy Communities
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

This paper proposes a cooperative game-theoretical framework for the financial settlement of real-time deviations in Community-Based Local Energy Markets (CB-LEMs). The real-time settlement process is modeled as a transferable-utility cooperative game, and the resulting Real-Time Local Energy Market (RTLEM) game is shown to be superadditive and balanced. We analyze two game-theoretical allocation mechanisms, the Shapley value and the nucleolus, and evaluate their efficiency, individual rationality, coalitional rationality, and temporal-aggregation properties. We subsequently compare these mechanisms with a settlement rule based on proportional imbalance responsibility. The three mechanisms are efficient and individually rational, but only the nucleolus is guaranteed to satisfy coalitional rationality for every RTLEM instance. The proposed framework is demonstrated using real-world data from a residential energy community in Amsterdam, showing the trade-offs among the three allocation mechanisms in terms of surplus distribution, coalitional stability, interpretability, and computational requirements.

title: A Bayesian Framework for Safe Optimal Control of Unknown Systems from Input-Output Data
text:
Title: A Bayesian Framework for Safe Optimal Control of Unknown Systems from Input-Output Data
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

As control engineering is applied to increasingly complex systems, learning-based control, which uses empirical data to reduce the reliance on first-principles models, has emerged as a promising paradigm. However, such approaches must cope with nonlinear and stochastic dynamics, the absence of state measurements, and scarce data, while ensuring safe operation under constraints, which requires rigorous uncertainty quantification. Whereas existing methods treat these challenges in isolation, this article proposes a Bayesian framework that jointly addresses them. A prior in state-space form is updated from input-output data using particle Markov chain Monte Carlo methods, yielding a representation of joint uncertainty over dynamics and latent states. Building on this representation, a validation procedure is developed that provides probabilistic guarantees for constraint satisfaction under arbitrary causal control laws. For control synthesis, a formulation penalizing the conditional value-at-risk of the constraint function is proposed, together with an adaptive calibration mechanism that adjusts the performance-robustness trade-off to achieve a desired robustness level. The probability of successful certification is characterized theoretically. The framework is extended to a receding-horizon setting, where posterior updates from new measurements allow the controller to progressively reduce uncertainty and improve performance. The approach is demonstrated on the optimal control of a vertical farm.

title: LAFA: A Framework for Reproducible Longitudinal Assessment of Protein Function Annotation Models
text:
Title: LAFA: A Framework for Reproducible Longitudinal Assessment of Protein Function Annotation Models
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Motivation: Protein function prediction is a challenging task and an open problem in computational biology. The Critical Assessment of protein Function Annotation (CAFA) is a triennial, community-driven initiative that provides an independent, large-scale evaluation of computational methods for protein function prediction through time-delayed benchmarking experiments. CAFA has played a key role in highlighting high-performing methodologies and fostering detailed analysis and exchange of ideas. However, outside the periodic CAFA challenges, there is no platform for the continuous evaluation of newly developed methods and tracking performance as function annotations accumulate. Results: Here we introduce the Longitudinal Assessment of Protein Function Annotation Models server (LAFA) as a persistent benchmarking system for protein function prediction methods. LAFA provides a continuous evaluation of containerized function prediction methods, enabling up-to-date and robust comparative assessment of method performance under evolving ground truth. LAFA accelerates methodological iteration, supports reproducibility, and offers a more dynamic and fine-grained view of progress in protein function prediction. Code and Data Availability: LAFA is available at https://functionbench.net/. Detailed evaluation results can be found at https://github.com/anphan0828/CAFA_forever

title: Two types of averaging principles for multiplicative stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equations with fast oscillations
text:
Title: Two types of averaging principles for multiplicative stochastic Korteweg-de Vries equations with fast oscillations
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In this paper, we study averaging principles for stochastic KdV equations perturbed by a fast oscillating term generated by a stochastic reaction-diffusion equation in $H^s(\mathbb{R})$, $ s\geq 0$. When dealing with multilinear estimates of the nonlinear terms in the stochastic KdV type equation, two kinds of workspace are both effective. The classical workspace can help us prove the averaging principle in the $L_ω^2$ sense, but it has more restrictions on the noise kernel and the conservation structures. When we use a new workspace without homogeneous low frequency restrictions, only the regularity conditions and the $L_x^2$ conservation structure is needed. Correspondingly, because there is no moment estimate of the solution, we can only prove the perturbed equations converge to an averaging equation in the probability sense. Our works may have important reference value, because it not only provides a new perspective to handle dynamical problems of stochastic dispersive model, but also compare it with the classical method.

title: Through Ups and Downs: the Transient Lensing Behaviour of SIDM halos undergoing Core Collapse
text:
Title: Through Ups and Downs: the Transient Lensing Behaviour of SIDM halos undergoing Core Collapse
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) haloes can become extremely dense following gravothermal core collapse, motivating their use as explanations for unusually concentrated gravitational lenses. Using an emulator calibrated on gravothermal fluid calculations, we investigate whether increasing central density necessarily strengthens lensing. We follow initially Navarro-Frenk-White (NFW) haloes through core formation and collapse deep into the short-mean-free-path regime, and compute finite-source magnifications, critical curves, and source-plane lensing cross sections for isolated spherical haloes with elastic, velocity-independent self-interactions, including external shear in selected calculations. Lensing strength evolves non-monotonically: it initially decreases during core formation, rises during early collapse, and generally declines at later stages despite continued growth of the central density. This decline accompanies the emergence of a dense inner core whose mass and radius decrease within a more extended, lower-density core. Time-averaged enhancement relative to NFW haloes depends on the lensing statistic, halo concentration, and interaction cross section. Generalized NFW haloes with central cusps $ρ\propto r^{-γ}$ with $γ\geq 2$ always have larger lensing efficacies than core-collapsed SIDM haloes of equal mass and are therefore poor proxies, including in terms of the demographics (size and radial thickness) of arcs and Einstein rings. The core collapse stage at which SIDM haloes are optimal lenses coincides with the epoch at which the characteristic core surface density is close to critical, which typically occurs during the early stages of core collapse. These results demonstrate that central density alone is insufficient to characterize SIDM lensing and that its evolving mass distribution must be modelled explicitly.

title: Imaging spin entanglement with a scanning tunneling microscope
text:
Title: Imaging spin entanglement with a scanning tunneling microscope
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Artificial spin arrays assembled on surfaces enable atomic-scale studies of quantum correlations. Here we establish a hierarchy of connections between spin inelastic electron tunneling spectroscopy (IETS) and entanglement in spin-$1/2$ systems. We first show that the number of spectroscopically active transitions in a spin-$1/2$ dimer serves as an entanglement witness. Using the leading-order tunneling conductance for the tip placed on spin $i$, $dI(i)/dV$, we then relate spectral moments $\mathcal{M}^{(n)}(i)=\int V^n(d^2I(i)/dV^2)\,dV$ to quantum correlations. The zeroth moment probes the one-tangle in systems with a gapped, nondegenerate ground state. For rotationally invariant Heisenberg systems, the first moment yields thermal spin correlators $\langle\boldsymbol S(i)\cdot\boldsymbol S(j)\rangle$, enabling reconstruction of nearest-neighbor concurrence and spatial imaging of entanglement in spin chains. It also provides access to the internal energy and magnetic specific heat, both usable as entanglement witnesses. Applying this approach to experimental IETS data from nanographene spin chains, we find good agreement with theory. We further discuss how the second moment probes longer-range correlations and the inverse moment relates to local spin susceptibility. For spin-$1/2$ trimers, we connect inter-multiplet inelastic spectral weight to genuine tripartite entanglement quantified by the concurrence fill. Finally, we reconcile the local character of IETS with its sensitivity to nonlocal entanglement through an analogy with digital quantum circuits, where Hamiltonian evolution implements multiqubit operations. These results establish IETS as a tool for quantifying and imaging entanglement in engineered on-surface spin systems.

title: Cosmological constraints on extra radiation and early dark energy with lepton asymmetry and varying quark masses
text:
Title: Cosmological constraints on extra radiation and early dark energy with lepton asymmetry and varying quark masses
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We investigate cosmological constraints on extra radiation and axionlike early dark energy (EDE), allowing primordial lepton asymmetry or light-quark-mass variation during big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). We combine Planck CMB, DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ supernovae, and primordial helium and deuterium measurements. When both extra radiation and lepton asymmetry are allowed, we obtain $N_{\rm eff}=3.27\pm0.16$, $ξ=0.017\pm0.011$, and $H_0=69.24\pm0.92\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$. A positive lepton asymmetry compensates the helium increase caused by extra radiation, allowing a higher inferred Hubble constant even with the LBT helium measurement, which agrees with standard BBN. For EDE, primordial-abundance measurements instead restrict the higher baryon densities associated with larger EDE fractions, which reduce the predicted deuterium abundance. Allowing lepton asymmetry does not relax this restriction. In contrast, a positive light-quark-mass variation increases deuterium and compensates this reduction, permitting larger EDE fractions and a higher inferred Hubble constant. The same variation leaves the extra-radiation constraint nearly unchanged. We also find that allowing lepton asymmetry relaxes the 95\% upper limit on the summed neutrino mass from $0.0640\,{\rm eV}$ to $0.0777\,{\rm eV}$ in the extra-radiation model.

title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
text:
Title: Distribution Shift Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery using Machine Learning Models
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Remote sensing imagery acquired by Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) supports wide range of applications; however, deploying machine learning (ML) models on resource-constrained aerial platforms introduces challenges beyond predictive accuracy, particularly when deployment data differ from the distributions observed during training. Such shifts are common in remote sensing due to geographic, sensor, seasonal, and other visual variations. A practical solution is to equip deployed models with mechanisms that detect emerging distribution shifts and support subsequent responsive actions. This paper presents an empirical case study of three open-source detection tools: (i) Alibi-Detect; (ii) NannyML; and (iii) PyTorch-OOD. Using cross-dataset remote-sensing shifts, we evaluate both detection effectiveness and computational latency of these tools. Our results reveal differences in detection behavior and processing cost across methods and implementations, highlighting trade-offs between detection capability and response-time. These findings motivate further work toward lightweight, and latency-aware monitoring mechanisms for resource-constrained systems.

title: Potentials of individual atoms by convergent beam electron diffraction
text:
Title: Potentials of individual atoms by convergent beam electron diffraction
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

In convergent beam electron diffraction (CBED) on two-dimensional (2D) materials, the intensity distributions within the individual CBED spots map the local atomic arrangements within the probed region. In this study we demonstrate that the average intensities within the CBED spots essentially depend on the scattering parameters by a single atom, thus, offering the possibility of the direct measurement of such parameters. Scattering potential of an individual atom can be approximated by the Gaussian function and its parameters, the standard deviation and the maximal phase shift, can be recovered from the ratio of the intensities in the zero- and higher orders spots in CBED pattern. In order to demonstrate this, we simulated CBED patterns and extracted the atomic scattering parameters from such patterns. In the simulated examples, no weak phase object approximation is applied and the proposed method provides accurate results even for materials with large phase shifts up to 1.5 rad, as for example tungsten. The scattering parameters recovered from the experimental CBED patterns of graphene and twisted graphene-hBN structure show good agreement with the theoretically obtained values.

title: Nonlinear optimal stopping and domineering claims
text:
Title: Nonlinear optimal stopping and domineering claims
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study nonlinear optimal stopping and domineering claims in a Brownian--Poisson filtration, under a nonlinear evaluation induced by a Lipschitz BSDE driver satisfying a comparison condition. A nonlinear domineering claim is a strong $\mathcal{E}^f$-martingale dominating the reward process at every stopping time. We first establish the existence of such claims for every optional reward in $\mathcal{S}^2$. For left-limited, right-upper semicontinuous rewards, we prove a local dual representation at every stopping time: the nonlinear optimal stopping value equals the essential infimum of the values of all domineering claims defined on the remaining stochastic interval. This infimum is attained by a claim constructed from the associated reflected BSDE. We further show that a global domineering claim attains the value at a prescribed stopping time if and only if the reflection processes have accumulated no increase up to that time, with the appropriate endpoint convention. When the reward is right-upper semicontinuous in $\mathcal{E}^f$-expectation and the family of contact times is nonempty, its essential infimum is optimal. Under strict comparison, we also establish a necessary contact condition for optimality. No convexity assumption on the driver is required.

title: Edge dynamics of covariant higher-rank Chern-Simons theory of fractons
text:
Title: Edge dynamics of covariant higher-rank Chern-Simons theory of fractons
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We study the covariant higher-rank Chern-Simons theory of fractons in 2+1 dimensions in the presence of a planar boundary. The differential generator associated with the scalar gauge symmetry singles out a single scalar Ward combination of the functional field equations. Its zeroth and first normal moments give two integrated boundary identities. The zeroth moment yields a traceless rank-two current obeying a fractonic double-divergence conservation law and a higher-rank Kac-Moody algebra. The first moment makes the normal-tangential field $w_i=h_{2i}$ explicit and yields an ordinarily conserved vector current with a standard $U(1)$ Kac-Moody algebra. Functional differentiation also produces a mixed equal-time bulk-boundary commutator between $w_1$ and $h_{11}$: it is non-vanishing at finite normal distance and vanishes in the intrinsic boundary limit. The equal-time commutators of the boundary current with the spatial components of the gauge-invariant field strength vanish, so microcausality is satisfied; when the boundary parameters are such that the two boundary sectors decouple, its retarded response vanishes at all times. Locally, the boundary constraints are solved by $w_i=\partial_iχ$ and $h_{ij}=\partial_i\partial_jξ+η_{ij}φ$. When the boundary parameters are such that the two sectors decouple, the induced action is the direct sum of a chiral boson in the $w_i$ sector and a higher-rank sector in which $φ$ is auxiliary and $ψ=\partial_1ξ$ is the propagating field. The latter has a non-chiral Luttinger description on its positive-energy branch and admits a chiral reduction. The boundary conditions determine the velocity and positivity branch of the $w_i$ mode, while the compatibility analysis in the $h_{ij}$ sector selects the positive-energy branch. On the positive-energy branch the two chiral modes co-propagate with orientation opposite to the sign of $κ$.

title: UMA-Inverse: Ligand-Conditioned Protein Inverse Folding with a Distogram-Supervised Dense Pair Encoder
text:
Title: UMA-Inverse: Ligand-Conditioned Protein Inverse Folding with a Distogram-Supervised Dense Pair Encoder
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Designing protein sequences that bind specific ligands benefits from an inverse-folding model conditioned on full ligand geometry. We present UMA-Inverse, which replaces the sparse graph backbone of LigandMPNN with a dense pair-representation encoder: a six-block PairMixer (triangle multiplication, no triangle self-attention or sequence track) refines all residue-residue and residue-ligand atom pairs, supervised by an auxiliary distogram objective, and an autoregressive decoder attends over ligand atoms through a learned, position-specific readout of the pair tensor. The model is compact ($\sim$3.3 M parameters). On the LigandMPNN test splits it reaches 56.1%/55.1%/35.3% interface recovery (small-molecule/metal/nucleotide). It trails LigandMPNN, but by less than the published numbers suggest: re-run under our identical protocol, LigandMPNN scores 59.8/64.4/53.3 (vs. published 63.3/77.5/50.5). In a pocket-fixed setting the redesigns are confidently folded and ligand-binding-competent under Boltz-2 cofolding, again modestly behind LigandMPNN. Its distinctive property is representational: the dense encoder propagates ligand identity to residues far beyond the interface, where LigandMPNN's signal decays. We offer UMA-Inverse as a compact baseline for ligand-conditioned inverse folding that trails LigandMPNN in accuracy, together with a characterization of how a dense all-pairs encoder distributes ligand information.

title: Worldsheet skeins and block decomposition of quivers
text:
Title: Worldsheet skeins and block decomposition of quivers
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Following the knot-quiver correspondence, we investigate quiver counterparts of the HOMFLYPT skein relations by interpreting link invariants in terms of holomorphic worldsheets and their multicover contributions. Extending this framework to more general worldsheet geometries, we conjecture that, up to quiver equivalence, the adjacency matrix of the quiver associated with any link in a skein triple admits a block decomposition whose diagonal blocks are quiver adjacency matrices associated with the other two links. We verify this conjecture in numerous examples.

title: RadRef: A Reference-Free Metric for Radiology Report Generation
text:
Title: RadRef: A Reference-Free Metric for Radiology Report Generation
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

AI-generated radiology reports are usually evaluated by comparison with a radiologist-authored reference, leaving no way to score them when no reference exists. We introduce RadRef, a reference-free metric that scores report claims against image-derived beliefs over a clinical finding vocabulary, weighted by relevance to the clinical indication. On ReXVal, RadRef achieves 73.1% agreement on non-tied same-radiograph report pairs with radiologist rankings, comparable to leading reference-based metrics overall. It is also competitive on false findings and has its clearest relative result on omissions (missed findings). We further evaluate 100 model-generated and 100 radiologist-authored reports from 100 MIMIC-CXR studies, all independently annotated by two board-certified radiologists. On omissions, RadRef attains Kendall's tau-b = 0.295, against 0.386 between the two readers themselves, and no compared metric differs significantly from RadRef on this target. The same image-grounded representation provides a false-finding readout, RadRef-FF, with tau-b = 0.32 on ReXVal and 0.29 in the reader study, without requiring a reference. Controlled perturbations confirm that RadRef depends on the radiograph, report, and clinical indication. RadRef enables image-grounded evaluation before a radiologist-authored reference exists, supporting quality monitoring of report-generation systems in clinical settings, and complements reference-based metrics when one is available.

title: Engineering a digital acoustic black hole
text:
Title: Engineering a digital acoustic black hole
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We show how to design and build an analogue black hole as a synchronous digital circuit. We define the sound speed, the flow and the horizon of such a circuit in terms of its own logic, and realise one on a field-programmable gate array, where the black hole is probed electrically with a signal generator and an oscilloscope. We measure the stability of the horizon, its causal cone, the ringdown and rotational superradiance. A single flipped bit inside the horizon leaks out by an amount that falls exponentially with depth. Digital circuits thus form a reconfigurable class of gravitational analogues and realise an analogue black hole as a cellular automaton.

title: Elasticity of polycrystalline davemaoite constrains its grain size in the lower mantle
text:
Title: Elasticity of polycrystalline davemaoite constrains its grain size in the lower mantle
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Earth's lower mantle hosts large low shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) beneath Africa and the Pacific, but their origin remains debated. Davemaoite, a major lower-mantle mineral, has been proposed as a contributor to these anomalies; however, its experimentally measured shear modulus is approximately 30% lower than first-principles predictions, a longstanding discrepancy between theory and experiment. Here, using million-atom machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations, we show that nanoscale grain-boundary disorder, invisible to conventional x-ray diffraction, can reconcile this gap. Introducing 5.8 vol% disordered regions reduces the shear and bulk moduli by 37% and 12%, respectively. This shear-selective softening can reproduce LLSVP-like seismic anomalies in basalt-rich assemblages, but only at disorder levels corresponding to grain sizes smaller than those expected in the lower mantle. Combining the disorder-elasticity relationship with seismic constraints, we derive a minimum davemaoite grain size of approximately 100 nm. This limit is consistent with mantle grain growth models and with attenuation-based evidence for coarse-grained LLSVPs.

title: Accelerating dynamic polarizability calculations of organic molecules using equivariant graph neural networks
text:
Title: Accelerating dynamic polarizability calculations of organic molecules using equivariant graph neural networks
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Predicting the dynamic polarizability tensor of organic molecules is essential for simulating light-matter interactions in optoelectronic devices, yet conventional quantum-chemical methods such as time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) are computationally expensive and limit large-scale screening. We present an equivariant graph neural network architecture that predicts frequency-dependent, complex-valued dynamic polarizability tensors directly from readily available molecular information, such as 3D geometry and UV-vis spectra. The model learns to approximate the shape and magnitude of the dynamic polarizability tensor, capturing both dispersive and absorptive features that define the molecular optical response. We evaluate the model on molecules from both the QM9 dataset and the Harvard organic photovoltaic dataset using various metrics, including the earth mover's distance, which is suitable for comparing spectral quantities. For both datasets, the model successfully reproduces the main features of the dynamic polarizability tensor and generalizes across diverse molecules. To assess the applicability, we further validated the model using a downstream workflow to calculate the optical properties of organic photovoltaic devices. We used the model-predicted polarizabilities to perform device-level optical simulations, yielding charge carrier generation rates in agreement with TD-DFT-based results ($R^2 = 0.94$). Our approach offers a promising complement, or even an alternative, to conventional methods such as TD-DFT, enabling faster and more efficient screening of photoactive organic molecules for optoelectronic applications.

title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
text:
Title: A Cross-Scenario Survey and Analysis of Self-Evolving Multimodal Agents
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Recent work shows that multimodal agents increasingly self-improve without recurring human annotation. However, each self-improvement mechanism is designed and evaluated within a single scenario, leaving its preconditions unverified under cross-scenario transfer. This survey investigates the structural source of asymmetric mechanism transfer across four scenarios: multimodal reasoning, multimodal generation, GUI and Web navigation, and embodied manipulation. We first formalize the self-evolving multimodal agent by four criteria and a differentia of self-reference, and adopt the three-stage self-evolving loop of experience generation, feedback acquisition, and update consolidation as our analytical framework to position the scenarios along ceilings on rollout count and feedback fidelity. Comparing self-evolving with fixed loops within each scenario separates the limitations that the scenario imposes from those inherent in the self-evolving design. We then recast each mechanism as a trade-off that raises a scarce factor by presupposing a task-structural resource, such as output equivalence or checkable outcomes, and judge it portable, conditional, blocked, or redundant across scenarios. We attribute the asymmetry to divergent combinations of scarce factors and resources across opposite transfer directions, and identify the matched-budget measurements that could overturn these still untested verdicts.

title: Sharper Bounds for Graphical Two-Choice Allocation
text:
Title: Sharper Bounds for Graphical Two-Choice Allocation
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In graphical two-choice allocation, vertices are bins, and each arriving ball must be placed irrevocably at one endpoint of a uniformly random edge. The objective is to keep the maximum-minus-minimum load gap small at every time. On cycles, endpoint-local monotone rules incur polynomial gaps at long time horizons, whereas global rules can achieve polylogarithmic gaps. We prove a joint exponential-moment inequality for the orthogonal contrasts of a binary partition tree, controlling all contrasts along a root-to-leaf path simultaneously. Applied to the Bansal--Feldheim strategy, it improves the gap on every $κ$-edge-connected $d$-regular graph from $O((d/κ)\log^4 n\log\log n)$ to $O((d/κ)\log^3 n\log\log n)$. We give an explicit strategy on the $n$-cycle with expected gap $O(\log^2 n)$ uniformly over deterministic times and exponential tails at each such time. An Euler-tour projection yields $O(\bar d\log^2(2M))$ for every connected graph with $M$ edges and degree-proportional capacities. For lower bounds, we introduce a stochastic cut workload: the expected largest normalized overload forced by the requests, plus an indivisibility term. For every online integral strategy, the supremum over time of the expected gap is at least one sixth of this benchmark. Regular rings of cliques attain $Ω((d/κ)\log n)$ along an explicit family, improving the prior additive lower bound. With unequal capacities, the workload need not control the gap: one family has constant relative cut slack, bounded workload and gap $Ω(\log\log n)$; another has workload at most $20$ but forces gap $Ω(\log n)$ even for clairvoyant fractional allocations that remain irrevocable.

title: Sharp potential and Brenier map $W_2$-stability for log-concave sources
text:
Title: Sharp potential and Brenier map $W_2$-stability for log-concave sources
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study stability of Brenier potentials and maps under changes of the target measure. Let $κ>0$, for a full support $κ$-strongly log-concave source $ρ$, possibly with a non-smooth potential, the normalized transport potentials satisfy \[ \|u_μ-u_ν\|_{L^2(ρ)}\leqslant\sqrt{2/κ}\,W_2(μ,ν) \] for arbitrary targets with finite second moments. The proof controls normalized Laguerre cell barycentres by their mass derivatives and centers the potential velocity to remove unbounded source cell locations. Bounded variation interpolation then yields the sharp map exponent $1/3$ for targets in a common compact set, \[ \left\Vert T_μ-T_ν\right\Vert _{L^{2}(ρ)}\leqslant \operatorname{Const} \cdot W_{2}\left( μ,ν\right) ^{1/3}. \] Sharpness of the exponents for both the potential and Brenier map stability are established.

title: Minimal-Action Discrete Schrödinger Bridge Matching for Peptide Sequence Design
text:
Title: Minimal-Action Discrete Schrödinger Bridge Matching for Peptide Sequence Design
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Generative modeling of peptide sequences requires navigating a discrete and highly constrained space in which many intermediate states are chemically implausible or unstable. Existing discrete diffusion and flow-based methods rely on reversing fixed corruption processes or following prescribed probability paths, which can force generation through low-likelihood regions and require countless sampling steps. We introduce Minimal-action discrete Schrödinger Bridge Matching (MadSBM), a rate-based generative framework for peptide design that formulates generation as a controlled continuous-time Markov process on the amino-acid edit graph. To yield probability trajectories that remain near high-likelihood sequence neighborhoods throughout generation, MadSBM 1) defines generation relative to a biologically informed reference process derived from pre-trained protein language model logits and 2) learns a time-dependent control field that biases transition rates to produce low-action transport paths from a masked prior to the data distribution. We finally introduce guidance to the MadSBM sampling procedure towards a specific functional objective, expanding the design space of therapeutic peptides; to our knowledge, this represents the first-ever application of discrete classifier guidance to Schrödinger bridge-based generative models.

title: Simulating Nonlinear Resistive Networks using a Behavioral Splitting
text:
Title: Simulating Nonlinear Resistive Networks using a Behavioral Splitting
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

An operator splitting method is developed for computing operating points of nonlinear resistive networks. Our behavioral formulation separates the device laws from Kirchhoff's laws and casts simulation as a zero-finding problem. Branch port resistances then provide a diagonal preconditioner for the relaxed Peaceman-Rachford iteration in scattering variables. Each iteration requires solving independent scalar equations and a linear system with a fixed weighted Laplacian matrix. Convergence is established for maximal monotone device laws when an operating point exists. Contractive branch reflections also yield a linear convergence bound independent of network topology. Numerical experiments on crossbar arrays illustrate the computational advantages.

title: Mutant invasion in stochastic individual-based models with cyclic resident dynamics
text:
Title: Mutant invasion in stochastic individual-based models with cyclic resident dynamics
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

When a resident community oscillates, can a rare mutant invade, and with which probability? We study a multitype birth-and-death process with interactions, in which population sizes are of the order of a carrying capacity $K$, and whose large-population limit, as $K\to\infty$, has a hyperbolically stable limit cycle for the $D-1$ resident types. We introduce a single individual of a new type. We prove that, as long as the mutant population is smaller than $\varepsilon K$ for a small $\varepsilon>0$, the resident population sizes divided by $K$ stay close to a moving point of the cycle, whose asymptotic phase moves by at most $O(\varepsilon)$ per period. We deduce that, for large $K$, the mutant dies out quickly if its growth rate averaged over one period, $f(\bar{\mathbf n})$, is negative, and that it invades with positive probability, in a time close to $\ln K/f(\bar{\mathbf n})$, if $f(\bar{\mathbf n})$ is positive. This justifies a criterion used heuristically in ecology for decades. The invasion probability, unlike $f(\bar{\mathbf n})$, depends on the phase of the cycle at which the mutant arises. We give it explicitly through Kendall's formula, and show that its average over the cycle, weighted by the birth rate of the mutant, equals $f(\bar{\mathbf n})$. In predator-prey, competitive and mutualistic examples, the invasion probability varies by a factor between $2$ and $600$ along the cycle, and individual-based simulations agree quantitatively with the theory. After invasion, the oscillations may vanish, persist on a cycle of higher dimension, or give way to chaotic coexistence.

title: Crossover duality for the quantum long-range Ising chain: perturbation theory around the short-range endpoint and a DMRG test
text:
Title: Crossover duality for the quantum long-range Ising chain: perturbation theory around the short-range endpoint and a DMRG test
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We propose a weakly coupled description of the long-range transverse-field Ising chain near its short-range crossover at $s_*=7/4$, where the couplings decay as $r^{-1-s}$. The Ising conformal field theory is coupled to an instantaneous Gaussian field through $σχ$, extending the classical long-range Ising duality to quantum chains. The equal-time interaction generates a stress-tensor deformation that causes the velocity to run and renormalizes the dynamical critical exponent $z$. Conformal perturbation theory gives $z=1-0.720\,δ+O(δ^2)$, $1/ν=(1+z)/2+O(δ^2)$, and $ω=δ+O(δ^2)$, with $δ=s_*-s$. DMRG calculations on periodic chains of up to $128$ sites provide a consistency test using theoretical inputs for $1/ν$ and $ω$. After accounting for slow finite-size corrections, static and dynamical estimates of $z$ agree, supporting the crossover expansion at $s=1.5$ and a two-sided Padé interpolation at $s=1$, $1.25$, and $1.5$.

title: Theory of the charge response of the boron-vacancy spin in monolayer hexagonal boron nitride
text:
Title: Theory of the charge response of the boron-vacancy spin in monolayer hexagonal boron nitride
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

The boron vacancy $V_{\mathrm{B}}^{-}$ in hexagonal boron nitride is a leading two-dimensional spin sensor, but the microscopic connection between nearby charge positions and its spin Hamiltonian remains poorly understood. Calculations for carbon and oxygen donors 3.85--8.08 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ away show that direction matters, not only distance. In the frozen lattice, reversing a carbon donor's azimuth at 4.35 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ (C1 to C1m) more than halves $|E|$ and turns its axis across the mirror line. The ratio is 0.467 with the Perdew--Burke--Ernzerhof (PBE) functional, against 1 for distance alone. A field-plus-gradient model fitted to six donor configurations, including C1 but excluding C1m, predicted a ratio of 0.443 before C1m was calculated. Heyd--Scuseria--Ernzerhof hybrid statics give 0.432 and PBE relaxation 0.600.
