Epidemic waves are often shaped by uncertain external drivers, such as environmental variability or behavioral and policy changes, that can randomly amplify or dampen transmission. Capturing this randomness requires models whose dynamics evolve under time-varying, stochastic influences. In this paper, we introduce a stochastic Susceptible-Asymptomatic-Symptomatic-Removed (SuASR) framework that embeds random external factors directly into the epidemic mechanism through an extended continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC). The proposed framework is flexible enough to represent epidemic dynamics both with reinfection and with infection-induced immunity, depending on the epidemiological setting under study. Unlike standard Markovian epidemic models, our formulation explicitly tracks two concurrent infectious sources (asymptomatic and symptomatic), yielding coupled infection pathways and substantially richer transient behavior. A key contribution is analytical tractability, where we derive computable expressions for the joint distribution of asymptomatic and symptomatic infection-event counts and develop tools tailored to extreme-outbreak risk, including the distribution of the maximum infectious burden. These results enable probabilistic quantification of epidemic severity beyond mean trajectories, providing direct estimates of the likelihood of rare but consequential surges. We validate the model through extensive sensitivity analysis and an application to the H1N1 influenza epidemic, illustrating how stochastic external influences reshape outbreak profiles, total infections from both sources, and the probability of extreme epidemic scenarios

title: Robust Domain-Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
text:
Title: Robust Domain-Mixture Scheduling for Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) merges the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers, such as mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following, into a single compact student. Since all domains share a limited training budget, how to allocate it across domains directly determines the quality of distillation. Existing methods allocate the budget by each domain's learning progress, but offer no guarantee for lagging domains. We therefore introduce distributionally robust optimization (DRO) into MOPD to prioritize the worst-performing domain. However, the per-domain training signals are estimated from a few rollouts and are inherently noisy, so directly applying DRO mistakes noise for the worst case, lets occasional spikes hijack the budget, and protects inherently hard domains rather than truly regressing ones. To address these issues, we propose RDS-MOPD, which keeps the DRO objective and redesigns its three parts: it shifts the allocation only when differences clearly exceed the noise, bounds the influence of any single anomaly, and defines the worst case as the regression from each domain's own best level, all with theoretical guarantees. Experiments show that RDS-MOPD outperforms recent competing methods and ranks first on most mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction-following benchmarks.

title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
text:
Title: Beyond Truncation? Entailment-Licensed Elision and the Limits of Semantic Preservation in LLM Decoding
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Instruction-tuned large language models (LLMs) answer at greater length than a request needs. We ask whether a training-free controller inside the decoding loop can remove that surplus while preserving content, judged against the simplest possible baseline: truncating the model's own answer to the same length. An entropy-gated logits processor removes 25.5-34.9% of tokens on MT-Bench development questions and 19.9-34.2% on a sealed test split within pre-registered BERTScore non-inferiority margins, yet we prove and confirm by audit that its output is always a prefix of the unmodified answer: the saving is truncation. A survey of 23 training-free mechanism families finds none that selects content better than truncation without oracle labels. We therefore introduce Entailment-Licensed In-Decoding Elision (ELIDE), which, at each sentence boundary, withholds a span from the reader only when a natural-language inference model judges it entailed by the text already shown, while leaving the model's generation unchanged. ELIDE beats matched-length truncation on three model families, but reading 936 of its elisions on 670 public prompts shows that 59% harm the answer, a failure that no automatic measure detects. Scoping the licence to its discourse unit reduces the harmful share to about one elision in ten on two fresh tests.

title: Free energy of the Hopfield model
text:
Title: Free energy of the Hopfield model
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We identify the limit of the free energy of the Hopfield model with independent symmetric Bernoulli patterns, for every temperature and loading ratio. A Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation reduces the problem to that of identifying the limit free energy of a bipartite spin glass with $\pm 1$ and spherical spins. One key difficulty is that the patterns, which become the coupling coefficients in the bipartite model, are Bernoulli instead of Gaussian, and the limit free energy is sensitive to the law of these coefficients. We show that the model is in fact equivalent to one involving Gaussian patterns and also subject to a finite number of Bernoulli random fields. We then solve this model by adapting the techniques recently introduced to identify the limit free energies of spin glasses with either $\pm 1$ or spherical spins.

title: PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
text:
Title: PriorTilt: Decoding quantum LDPC codes with sparse perturbations of belief propagation priors
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Although belief propagation (BP) is a widely adopted decoder for classical low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes, its accuracy is limited in the quantum setting. We introduce \PriorTilt{}, a variant of BP obtained by selectively perturbing a small fraction of its prior log-likelihood ratios using offsets determined by recent posterior and outgoing-message statistics, while preserving the same message-passing rules. We compare \PriorTilt{} with Relay-BP and beam search decoders for circuit-level decoding of three benchmark codes. \PriorTilt{} achieves a lower logical error rate (LER) than both baselines at every tested data point. For the $[[144,12,12]]$ Gross code BB144 at noise rate $p=10^{-3}$, the LER reductions reach $4.3\times$ relative to Relay-BP and $3.1\times$ relative to the beam search decoder. At $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} has lower mean decoding times than Relay-BP on all three codes and achieves mean decoding speedups of approximately $2.6\times$--$3.0\times$ over the beam search decoder. For BB144 at $p=10^{-3}$, \PriorTilt{} achieves an LER approximately $610\times$ lower than the standard min-sum BP decoder with the same iteration budget, while perturbing fewer than $0.5\%$ of its priors per round on average.

title: Detection times are not local observables in quantum field theory
text:
Title: Detection times are not local observables in quantum field theory
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Detection times are routinely recorded in quantum experiments. We show that, under natural covariance and consistency requirements, the observables describing these times cannot be algebraically localized in any bounded spacetime region, even when the records themselves are localized. This challenges the identification of algebraic localization with the physical localization of measurements and shows why microcausality alone does not establish non-signalling for measurements in quantum field theory.

title: An unstructured finite-volume Helmholtz method with perfectly matched layers for heterogeneous two-phase acoustics
text:
Title: An unstructured finite-volume Helmholtz method with perfectly matched layers for heterogeneous two-phase acoustics
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

This paper presents a cell-centred unstructured finite-volume method for time-harmonic two-phase acoustics. A volume-fraction representation supplies density and acoustic compressibility. Face fractions average available neighbouring planar interface cuts independently of velocity direction, retaining the established one-field face-density closure. Cartesian complex-coordinate stretching provides perfectly matched layers (PMLs). Real-imaginary splitting yields a real-valued block system, discretized with corrected non-orthogonal fluxes and consistent boundary contributions. Verification covers homogeneous waves, layered gas-liquid transmission with PML truncation, baffled-piston radiation with Kirchhoff far-field reconstruction, and resolved rigid-sphere radiation forces. Homogeneous-wave pressure converges at approximately second order on orthogonal meshes and on meshes with non-orthogonal interiors and orthogonal boundary cells. Reconstructed velocity converges at approximately second order on orthogonal meshes and with an observed order of about 1.7 on the latter mesh family. Under aligned refinement, the layered case's relative whole-domain complex-pressure $L_2$ error decreases to $2.657\times10^{-4}$. The resolved-sphere force differs from the Gorkov prediction by at most 1.5% over the tested Rayleigh size range. The results quantify the accuracy and current limitations of the heterogeneous Helmholtz-PML formulation.

title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
text:
Title: Prune, Don't Merge: Expert Compression of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs on Multilingual Production Tasks
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Mixture-of-Experts language models are cheap to run per token but expensive to hold in GPU memory, which drives the cost of serving them in production. One-shot expert compression shrinks them after a single calibration pass. Its two current state-of-the-art methods are REAP for expert pruning, which deletes the least salient experts, and REAM for expert merging, which merges them into the most salient ones. Both have been evaluated only on academic benchmarks. We compare the two on five multilingual production tasks of a web-hosting company, from classification to the generation of marketing HTML email templates, with two 30B-parameter models (Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 and the hybrid Mamba-attention Nemotron-3.5-Lightning) at 25% and 50% of experts removed and the same calibration data. Pruning wins: on the same rows, REAP is significantly better in 16 of 20 comparisons and REAM in 2. At 25%, REAP keeps 93.6% of Qwen3-30B's generative quality and REAM 62.5%, although on benchmarks the two are within a point for the same model. The damage concentrates in the output contract rather than the content: 89.8-95.2% of each significant loss on email templates comes from hard-gate failures such as invalid JSON, broken mobile layouts and runaway generation, and most failed non-English domain descriptions copy the prompt's English opening phrase. Cross-perplexity and logit divergence, two diagnostics from the REAP paper, also track production quality, as does the rate of repetition loops; n-gram diversity does not. We close with practical guidance for compressing MoE models for production.

title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
text:
Title: From Likelihood Convergence to Parameter Convergence in POMDPs
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Likelihood-based methods are widely used to learn the parameters of partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). While finite-sample guarantees for policy suboptimality exist for certain POMDP subclasses, analogous guarantees for parameter recovery remain less well understood. For any candidate POMDP parameter, we bound its parameter recovery error in terms of its likelihood gap to the ground truth, the structural conditioning of the observation and transition kernels, and the behavior policy used to collect data. The bound applies in both the undercomplete and overcomplete regimes, with the latter following naturally from the undercomplete analysis. Because the result applies to any sufficiently good candidate, it yields finite-sample guarantees for the maximum-likelihood estimator and any procedure producing a parameter with controlled likelihood gap. This is particularly useful for near-optimal learning in infinite-horizon POMDPs, where existing approaches largely rely on model-based planning with accurate transition and observation kernel estimates. The bound separates the contributions of the behavior policy and model, showing how data-collection choices, including action coverage, and their effects on mixing can accelerate parameter learning.

title: Rovibrational dynamics in strongly-coupled gas-phase methane
text:
Title: Rovibrational dynamics in strongly-coupled gas-phase methane
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Polaritons, the hybrid light-matter states formed when molecular transitions are strongly coupled to an optical cavity mode, appear to alter chemical dynamics, reactivity, and photophysics, though the mechanisms and reproducibility of these effects remain hotly debated. Nearly all reports in polariton chemistry rest on spectroscopic measurements of optical cavity transmission. Interpretation of these experiments therefore relies on understanding the linear and nonlinear spectroscopy of strongly-coupled systems. Working in the gas phase can dramatically simplify spectroscopic observables, as the intermolecular and environmental interactions that complicate the response of condensed-phase systems can be minimized. Our prior work introduced a platform for gas-phase molecular polaritons and demonstrated that linear cavity transmission spectra in the strong coupling regime are well described with classical Fabry-Pérot cavity physics. Here, we extend this platform to the nonlinear spectroscopy of cavity-coupled rovibrational transitions of methane. We monitor transient changes in the cavity transmission spectrum following optical pumping of intracavity molecules via an axis orthogonal to the longitudinal cavity axis. We find that the classical Fabry-Pérot cavity treatment quantitatively reproduces our transient spectra and allows for extraction of the collisional relaxation and transport timescales of intracavity molecules. We observe no difference in the dynamics of strongly-coupled methane versus free-space, non-cavity control experiments. This effort connects our gas-phase work to the much larger body of transient condensed-phase polariton spectroscopy and represents a step towards predictive understanding of molecular dynamics under strong coupling.

title: Patching Up Circuit Learning via Parameter Sharing
text:
Title: Patching Up Circuit Learning via Parameter Sharing
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Probabilistic circuits (PCs) have emerged as generative models guaranteeing tractable probabilistic inference. However, tractability comes at the price of larger model sizes than in other generative models. As such, to scale PCs to high-dimensional data such as images, previous work has devised several parameter sharing techniques as well as fast evaluation protocols that consider learning PCs on independent image patches. In this work, we revisit this practice to highlight a surprising learnability issue: models that assume independence counterintuitively can yield better likelihoods than models that do not. To break this apparent bottleneck and to scale PCs further, we introduce a recursive parameter sharing construction (RePA) that fosters efficiency without assuming independence. We show empirically that RePA can greatly reduce time and memory consumption while yielding competitive likelihoods. Inspired by these results, we further generalize the approach to data modalities that do not inherently exhibit patch-structure (NoPA), such as tabular data, showing similar efficiency improvements, with marginal changes in likelihoods and sample quality on seven tabular datasets. Code available at https://github.com/april-tools/RePA.

title: Protein Language Models Diverge from Natural Language: Comparative Analysis and Improved Inference
text:
Title: Protein Language Models Diverge from Natural Language: Comparative Analysis and Improved Inference
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Modern Protein Language Models (PLMs) apply transformer-based model architectures from natural language processing to biological sequences, predicting a variety of protein functions and properties. However, protein language has key differences from natural language, such as a rich functional space despite a vocabulary of only 20 amino acids. These differences motivate research into how transformer-based architectures operate differently in the protein domain and how we can better leverage PLMs to solve protein-related tasks. In this work, we begin by directly comparing how the distribution of information stored across layers of attention heads differs between the protein and natural language domain. Furthermore, we adapt a simple early-exit technique-originally used in the natural language domain to improve efficiency at the cost of performance-to achieve both increased accuracy and substantial efficiency gains in protein non-structural property prediction by allowing the model to automatically select protein representations from the intermediate layers of the PLMs for the specific task and protein at hand. We achieve performance gains ranging from 0.4 to 7.01 percentage points while simultaneously improving efficiency by over 10 percent across models and non-structural prediction tasks. Our work opens up an area of research directly comparing how language models change behavior when moved into the protein domain and advances language modeling in biological domains.

title: Unlabeled Echoes: Pseudo-Labels and Genus-Aware Smoothing for Bat Call Recognition
text:
Title: Unlabeled Echoes: Pseudo-Labels and Genus-Aware Smoothing for Bat Call Recognition
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Passive acoustic monitoring produces far more bat recordings than experts can label. We show that simple model-generated pseudo-labels turn this surplus into effective supervision. We compare pseudo-labeling with other semi-supervised learning methods on an 18-species European corpus using only 10% of its training labels, then transfer the strongest approaches to South African field audio containing nine bat taxa and a nuisance class. Pseudo-labeling outperforms the other semi-supervised learning methods on every European measure, recovering up to 61.5% of the gap to full supervision. It transfers to field audio with gains of 10.69 points in species accuracy and 4.96 points in species macro-F1. We also introduce genus-aware smoothing, which directs uncertain target mass toward congeneric species. Combined with uniform smoothing, it reaches 79.16 species macro-F1, 4.73 points above hard targets. Simple pseudo-labels are therefore highly effective at this ecological data scale, while genus-aware targets inject useful biological structure at no annotation cost. https://code4conservation.github.io/UnlabeledEchoes/

title: Experimental Collapse in Virophysics: Protocol-Resolved Observation, Inference, and Plaque-Assay Blindness
text:
Title: Experimental Collapse in Virophysics: Protocol-Resolved Observation, Inference, and Plaque-Assay Blindness
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Virological measurements are often treated as reports of virion structure, mechanics, dielectric response, infectivity, or titer. In practice, an experiment observes a protocol-conditioned projection of a richer latent virion--environment ensemble. This paper defines this process as experimental collapse within protocol-resolved virophysics. Its central object is the null-inclusive observation operator $P_{\mathrm{obs},t}^{\varnothing}(\,\cdot\mid E\,) = \mathcal{M}_{E,t}^{\varnothing}P_{\mathrm{ref},t}$, which maps a reference latent ensemble to the observed ensemble generated by protocol $E$, including null outcomes. The formulation separates latent-state transformation, detection weighting, readout, and non-observation, making protocol effects explicit components rather than bias terms. The framework introduces protocol-conditioned latent ensembles, collapse functionals, protocol blindness, observation equivalence, Fisher-information observability, inverse inference, and multi-protocol consistency. It identifies collapse mechanisms including preparation, surface immobilization, mechanical loading, field steering, medium filtering, amplification, censoring, and detection thresholds. As a worked example, the plaque assay estimates an effective protocol-conditioned infectious concentration $Λ_{\mathrm{PFU}}=\int_Ψπ_{\mathrm{PFU}}(x;E_{\mathrm{PFU}})n_{\mathrm{ref}}(x),dx$, rather than total particle concentration. This recovers the Poisson plaque-count model and PFU titer formula in the dilute regime; extensions to overdispersion, zero inflation, plaque merging, endpoint dilution, neutralization, and morphology-augmented readouts recast deviations as protocol-conditioned information. Thus, virological data are outputs of explicit protocol kernels, clarifying what measurements report, miss, and how complementary assays can infer hidden latent virion structures.

title: GIA: Germline-Informed Aging with AlphaGenome Finds Genetically Regulated CpGs
text:
Title: GIA: Germline-Informed Aging with AlphaGenome Finds Genetically Regulated CpGs
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Epigenetic clocks estimate age and aging-related phenotypes from DNA methylation at selected CpG sites, but the extent to which these inputs are influenced by germline genetic variation is unclear. Because methylation at many CpGs is genetically regulated, some between-person variation in clock estimates may reflect inherited genetic differences rather than aging-related change alone. Here we developed GIA (Germline-Informed Aging), a framework that maps CpGs selected from 13 published epigenetic clocks to blood methylation quantitative trait loci (meQTLs) and scores associated genetic variants with AlphaGenome. We show that clock CpGs were enriched for blood meQTLs relative to matched unused Illumina 450k probes (62.7% versus 39.6%; OR 2.57), across multiple clock families, suggesting that age-informative methylation sites are heavily influenced by germline genetic variation. Ranking by predicted chromatin effect isolated rs10190186, a cis-acting variant at FHL2 predicted to increase blood chromatin accessibility (ATAC +1.00; DNase +1.64) and FHL2 RNA (+0.30). This locus illustrates how inherited variation may shape methylation features repeatedly used by epigenetic clocks, motivating direct tests of whether such variants shift baseline clock estimates or longitudinal aging trajectories.

title: Forecast Value Add: Reward-Based Action Selection over Probabilistic Demand Forecasts
text:
Title: Forecast Value Add: Reward-Based Action Selection over Probabilistic Demand Forecasts
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Strong machine-learning ensembles capture much of the trend, seasonality, and known events in demand, yet they can still understate peaks, miss moving events, or mistake temporary changes for shifts in demand level. We address this gap by framing forecast refinement as a reward-driven decision problem. For each forecast period, we let an agent choose among values already produced by the ensemble: its base forecast, distribution-free bounds, quantiles, and a bias-corrected estimate. We evaluate these choices against context-matched historical periods, accounting for calendar position, recurring and moving events, trend, price, and promotions. We then apply a structural seasonal guard to constrain adjustments and record the model, agent, and planner contributions to every published value. We evaluate our approach across five retail, consumer-goods, and direct-to-consumer deployments over nine months. Our refined forecasts reduce mean WMAPE by 6.3% compared with the stacked machine-learning forecast for every customer, with gains reaching 16.7%, and achieve the lowest error in 35 of 45 customer-months. Compared with statistical forecasts, our approach reduces mean error by 18.7%. These results demonstrate that context-aware, auditable action selection can add forecast value beyond a strong ensemble.

title: Numerical integration of intracule pair densities with optimized multicenter grids
text:
Title: Numerical integration of intracule pair densities with optimized multicenter grids
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Intracule pair densities provide insight into electron correlation, but their routine analysis in extended systems is limited by the cost of numerical integration and the restriction of analytical methods to Gaussian basis functions. We present an efficient multicenter integration scheme for intracule densities and their moments. By adapting the topological fuzzy Voronoi cell formalism, we partition intracule space around interatomic displacement vectors, concentrating quadrature points near secondary density maxima that standard single-center grids poorly resolve. Benchmarks on linear alkanes show improved convergence with increasing molecular size, achieving relative errors below 0.02% in electron-electron repulsion energies with fewer quadrature points than single-center methods. The partitioning also enables the decomposition of global two-electron properties into spatial contributions associated with short- and long-range electron-pair separations. Coupling the multicenter grid with kernel density estimation reconstructs smooth radial intracule distributions at large interelectronic distances without the dense angular grids required by conventional surface integration. Validation on the S22 dataset supports the reliability of the method across diverse molecular systems. These developments facilitate intracule analysis in polyatomic systems and the investigation of electron correlation and dispersion interactions.

title: MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Synergistic Learning for Multi-Modal Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting
text:
Title: MicroBT: Centroid-Guided Synergistic Learning for Multi-Modal Micro Brain Tumor Segmentation and Counting
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Multi-modal brain tumor segmentation is essential for clinical diagnosis, radiotherapy planning, and longitudinal monitoring. While recent studies have achieved remarkable overall segmentation performance, they rely on overlap-based objectives that inherently favor large regions, causing sub-3 mm micro-lesions to be systematically suppressed during training. Moreover, existing pixel-level segmentation frameworks lack explicit instance-level modeling, leading to unreliable lesion counting that directly impacts clinical staging and therapeutic decisions. To address these challenges, we propose MicroBT, a unified multi-modal framework for micro brain tumor segmentation and counting. Our core insight is that a fundamental geometric property is inherently scale-invariant: regardless of size, each lesion possesses a well-defined centroid. Leveraging this, we first devise a centroid-anchored synergistic paradigm that utilizes predicted centroids as shared anchors to simultaneously condition dense segmentation and instance-level localization. To counteract the tumor size imbalance, we further devise a Volume-Calibrated Loss (VC-Loss) that adaptively amplifies the gradient contribution of micro-lesions, alongside a Size-Aware Curriculum Optimization (SACO) that stabilizes multi-task training by establishing global representations before progressively unlocking fine-grained localization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MicroBT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly on metastases, where micro-lesion ($\leq 3$ mm) localization precision improves by approximately 7% and counting estimation errors decrease by approximately 26%. The code is available at https://github.com/leonlou921/MicroBT.

title: A Simple Approach to the Complexity of Mean Field Ising Spin Glasses
text:
Title: A Simple Approach to the Complexity of Mean Field Ising Spin Glasses
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

The geometry of spherical spin glasses is relatively well understood, thanks in large part to the Kac-Rice formula. However, this formula does not directly apply to discrete spin systems, and much less is known mathematically about the geometry of Ising spin glasses. In this paper, we present a simple method for counting local optima and gapped states in a broad class of discrete spin glasses. To illustrate its scope, we compute the annealed complexities ("configurational entropies," in the physics language) of mixed Ising spin glasses with potentials, such as external fields, and of the Ghatak-Sherrington model. These computations recover several existing results in the mathematics and physics literature as special cases. We can also compute energy-constrained complexity, finding a critical energy threshold analogous to the spherical case, but for gapped states of pure Ising spin glasses. Finally, we use our method to establish a form of disorder persistence for gapped states, identifying a transition between $3$-spin and $4$-spin glasses.

title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
text:
Title: A Theory of Policy Optimization in Post-Training: Coverage Collapse and Reference Resets
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Policy optimization is central to language model post-training, yet principled guidance remains limited. We revisit its theoretical foundations to identify algorithms that learn near-optimal policies using total samples and gradient steps governed by the base model's response coverage, a measure of how readily it generates optimal responses. We call such algorithms coverage-preserving. This guarantee captures the goal of amplifying capabilities accessible through sampling from the base model. (1) Coverage collapse. REINFORCE, the basis for PPO and GRPO, can drive the probability of optimal responses to near zero, even as reward improves. This coverage collapse stalls optimization, and convergence can require exponentially many steps despite good initial coverage. The failure arises even with exact gradients and persists under KL regularization to the base model. (2) Reference resets. We show that repeatedly resetting the KL reference to the most recent policy mitigates coverage collapse. We formalize this intervention in Approximate Policy Mirror Descent (APMD), a meta-algorithm that approximately solves a sequence of KL-regularized RL subproblems. APMD enables stronger regularization, making each subproblem easier to solve, while reference resets allow convergence to global optimality. (3) Coverage-preserving algorithms. For softmax linear policies over pretrained features, we use APMD to establish the first global convergence guarantees showing that widely used families of post-training algorithms are coverage-preserving. These include stylized PPO and GRPO variants with explicit KL regularization and reference resets, and squared-loss algorithms that implement them implicitly, including those used to train the Kimi models. These results clarify how regularization, clipping, and objective choice affect the sampling and optimization costs of post-training.

title: ARCHER: Amortized cross-specimen pose estimation for cryo-electron microscopy
text:
Title: ARCHER: Amortized cross-specimen pose estimation for cryo-electron microscopy
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) pose estimation is traditionally solved anew for each dataset, where iterative refinement is done from scratch while the estimator learns to store the molecule in its weights. In this work, we show that pose inference is a generalizable, specimen-agnostic operation when conditioned explicitly on a reference volume. We introduce ARCHER, an amortized contrastive classifier that models the pose posterior over a discrete rotation grid. Trained across a variety of protein structures, it operates zero-shot without retraining per structure. This transferability is grounded in Fourier-space information mechanics, where all specimen dependence is captured by the reference structure's power spectrum and spatial extent. ARCHER achieves a median angular error of 5.0° on 100 held-out test structures and 2.5° on experimental particles, matching dedicated estimators within 0.16 Å in 3D reconstruction. Crucially, downstream conformational signal is preserved. The leading conformational coordinate correlates at 0.97 with deposited benchmarks, faithfully reconstructing free-energy basins and mobile domains. These results overall demonstrate that cryo-EM pose estimation can be generalized across different structures.

title: Maximal correlation and optimal transformations of probability distributions in tensor-train format: a variational algorithm
text:
Title: Maximal correlation and optimal transformations of probability distributions in tensor-train format: a variational algorithm
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The correlation between two subsystems $A$ and $B$ of a many-body system is usually measured through a pair of observables chosen in advance. The Hirschfeld-Gebelein-Rényi maximal correlation removes the choice: it is the largest correlation coefficient between any function of the configuration of $A$ and any function of the configuration of $B$, and the two functions that reach it, the optimal transformations, are the observables that carry the correlation. Both follow from a singular value decomposition (SVD) of the joint distribution normalized by its marginals, a matrix whose dimension is the number of configurations. We show that this SVD can be computed variationally for a classical distribution of discrete variables, such as the Boltzmann distribution of a spin model, given in the tensor-train (matrix-product) format, without ever forming the matrix. The optimal transformations are sought as tensor trains; each step updates a single core in closed form, and the inverse of a small matrix contracted from the distribution and the remaining cores performs the division by the marginals core by core. Every iterate is a feasible pair, so the objective is a lower bound on the maximal correlation that increases monotonically, and the cost grows linearly with the number of variables. The algorithm reproduces the exact SVD on small systems, recovers the known nonlinear optimal transformations of synthetic distributions of up to ten angular variables ($10^{15}$ configurations), and, for the bipartite antiferromagnetic model with $2^{32}$ configurations, returns an optimal transformation that is a function of the group magnetization, linear above the transition and sign-like below it: the staggered order parameter is read off from the distribution instead of being postulated.

title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
text:
Title: Beyond Passive Imitation: On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation for Language Models
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Continual pre-training (CPT) adapts large language models (LLMs) to specialized domains, yet its standard next-token prediction (NTP) objective treats every corpus token as a fixed target, regardless of its utility to the current model. In a controlled study on the same 1B-token mathematical corpus, we observe sharply different outcomes across base models: NTP improves Llama-3.2-3B's performance on mathematical benchmarks but substantially degrades Qwen3-1.7B-Base's performance, indicating that, under a fixed training recipe, the same training sequences can have model-dependent effects. To address this problem, we introduce On-Policy Mid-Training Distillation (OPMD), which reformulates mid-training from offline text imitation into active, query-driven knowledge acquisition. At selected anchor positions, OPMD samples trajectories from the evolving student policy and applies dense token-level reverse-KL rewards from a frozen teacher, training the model on states it actually visits rather than only on ground-truth prefixes. This on-policy objective reduces the training-generation mismatch of teacher-forced NTP. On MATH-500 and Minerva, OPMD improves the Qwen student over its base performance and outperforms the evaluated NTP baseline, which degrades on both benchmarks. OPMD integrates into CPT pipelines without added inference-time overhead and offers a model-aware alternative to passive domain adaptation.

title: Phase Transitions in Unsupervised Feature Selection
text:
Title: Phase Transitions in Unsupervised Feature Selection
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Identifying minimal and informative feature sets is a central challenge in data analysis, particularly when few data points are available. Here we present a theoretical analysis of an unsupervised feature selection pipeline based on the Differentiable Information Imbalance (DII). We consider the specific case of structural and physico-chemical features describing a set of proteins. We show that if one considers the features as coordinates of a (hypothetical) statistical physics model, this model undergoes a phase transition as a function of the number of retained features. For physico-chemical descriptors, this transition is between a glass-like phase when the features are few and a liquid-like phase. The glass-like phase exhibits bimodal order-parameter distributions and Binder cumulant minima. In contrast, for structural descriptors the transition is less sharp. Remarkably, for physico-chemical descriptors the critical number of features identified from the DII coincides with the saturation of downstream binary classification performance. These results provide a principled, unsupervised criterion for minimal feature sets in protein classification and reveal distinct mechanisms of criticality across different feature types.

title: Comments on: "Optimized thermal control of a dual-wavelength-resonant nonlinear cavity"
text:
Title: Comments on: "Optimized thermal control of a dual-wavelength-resonant nonlinear cavity"
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

This comment addresses the publication [Appl. Opt. 65, 7090 (2026)] which targets an alleged ``optimization'' of a patented invention conceived by the author. The invention had introduced a multi-temperature management scheme for a dual-wavelength-resonant nonlinear cavity that optimized the crystal temperature around the beam waist for phase-matching, while utilizing independently adjustable temperatures in other regions of the same crystal to simultaneously satisfy the double-resonance condition. A foundational form of this invention was initially utilized by co-author H. Vahlbruch without the author's prior knowledge during the construction of the squeezed-light laser for the Virgo gravitational wave detector. In their publication, the three authors now propose a variant that reduces the maximum achievable temperature differential. Here, I demonstrate that this approach does not constitute an optimization but, on the contrary, represents a regression that dismantles the invention. In general, a high-quality implementation of this invention fundamentally depends on maximizing the achievable temperature differential. Only then can the problematic phase differences---introduced by dielectric coatings, Gouy phase shifts, and suboptimal poling lengths at the crystal facets---be effectively compensated for, particularly in short crystals. If desired, smaller temperature differences can always be selected dynamically anyway.

title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
text:
Title: Causal Integrated Gradients: Scalable Feature Attribution Along Causal Paths
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Existing feature attribution methods that account for feature dependencies do not scale to high dimensions. We propose causal integrated gradients (CIG) and causal expected gradients (CEG), which extend integrated gradients to incorporate prior causal structure among input features while retaining its computational efficiency and, under conditions on the causal graph, its axiomatic guarantees. In many settings, some causal structure between features is already known, for example, that a transcription factor causally regulates a target gene's expression. Yet existing gradient-based methods cannot exploit this structure, instead crediting a feature's downstream effects over its true upstream cause, such as ranking the target gene above the transcription factor that regulates it. Our key idea is to embed this causal structure by routing the integration path along the causal graph. The method thereby decomposes each feature's attribution into a direct effect and effects mediated through its causal descendants. We evaluate CIG in three settings of increasing realism. First, on a synthetic benchmark with a known causal model, CIG's attributions best match the ground-truth causal effect from Pearl's do-calculus, matching the accuracy of causal Shapley values at a fraction of the computational cost. Second, on simulated single-cell gene expression data with a known gene regulatory network (Dyngen), CIG most accurately recovers the transcription factors driving the simulation. Third, on real interferon-$β$ stimulation data, where only an approximate causal graph is available, CIG better prioritizes the transcription factors driving the measured response than DeepSHAP and integrated gradients. Together, these results show that incorporating causal structure into gradient-based attributions recovers upstream drivers that existing methods miss, without sacrificing scalability.

title: Mechanism-resolved phase-field fracture of composite shells with a certified admissible constitutive operator
text:
Title: Mechanism-resolved phase-field fracture of composite shells with a certified admissible constitutive operator
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Phase-field models of fracture in fibre-reinforced shells are usually formulated against a single closed-form stored energy, so that the stress, consistent tangent and plane-stress condensation are derived and verified for that expression alone. Here the constitutive law enters instead as a replaceable operator. The Green-Lagrange strain of a geometrically exact Reissner-Mindlin shell is pulled back through the Cholesky factor of the reference metric and resolved on four mutually orthogonal invariants with an exact closure identity, making the separation into fibre, inter-fibre and interaction channels a change of basis rather than a modelling assumption. On a curved midsurface, the metric, Cholesky factor and fibre direction vary through the thickness through the shifter I - zeta b, and the invariants inherit that dependence. The tension-compression split, channel degradation, plane-stress condensation, consistent tangent and finite-element assembly are all expressed in the channel potentials and their derivatives, allowing either closed-form or learned operators. The fibre-transverse interaction energy is stored once and degraded by the product of the fields whose mechanisms it couples. Six conditions define admissible operators; the two linear invariants are proved convex in the deformation gradient, the geometric tangent is shown independent of the material tangent, and the plane-stress condensation is regular wherever the residual stiffness is positive. A three-tier protocol certifies the algebra, solver state and admission of a state as training data. Numerical studies on notched IM7/8552 shells verify the discretisation in thin and curved regimes and show that fibre orientation governs the damage envelope and load capacity, while curvature drives a through-thickness fracture asymmetry that a single midsurface field cannot represent.

title: Unveiling the Influence of Graphitic Nanocarbon Structures, Defects, and Surface Functional Groups on Supercapacitive Performance in LiTFSI Electrolyte
text:
Title: Unveiling the Influence of Graphitic Nanocarbon Structures, Defects, and Surface Functional Groups on Supercapacitive Performance in LiTFSI Electrolyte
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

When investigating the performance of supercapacitors (SCs), it was found that they offer high-power density and long life but are limited in capacity and energy density. Water-in-salt electrolytes, i.e., 21___m lithium bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl) imide (LiTFSI), offer a solution by expanding the electrochemical window compared to a diluted aqueous environment. While significant research has been dedicated to improving these electrolytes, the impact of carbon properties on energy storage remains relatively underexplored. This study investigated the influence of carbon structures, defects, and surface functional groups on supercapacitive performance in LiTFSI electrolytes. For this purpose, a series of carbon materials, including carbon nano-onions and porous conductive carbon black (ENSACO), were synthesized and systematically modified by oxidative and reductive thermal treatments. Our results indicated that higher specific surface area and active surface area improve the ion adsorption and capacitance, while specific oxygen functionalities, such as carboxylic and anhydride groups, were found to significantly enhance capacitance. Furthermore, crystallinity and graphitic characteristics play a role in capacitance, with smaller graphene domains and greater disorder promoting ion storage. The study demonstrates a direct correlation between carbon microstructure and electrochemical behavior, providing insights into the rational design of carbon electrodes in high-performance SCs.

title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
text:
Title: The Geometry of Multitask Learning: Sharp Rates for Shared Subspace Estimation
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Learning a shared subspace in multitask learning is an important statistical problem, yet exact rates remain poorly understood in many of the formal settings considered in the literature. To address this gap, which arises from limitations of existing upper-bound techniques, we propose a general multitask lemma. The lemma provides sufficient conditions for fast subspace estimation in generic multitask settings, in the form of geometric conditions on the task regression functions and their estimators. We subsequently show that the multitask lemma yields sharp minimax rates---previously unknown---for linear regression and classification in the regimes considered, and rates matching up to logarithmic factors for additive-noise regression.

title: Overcoming the limitations of body-ordered potentials for atomistic machine learning
text:
Title: Overcoming the limitations of body-ordered potentials for atomistic machine learning
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Machine-learning interatomic potentials have become indispensable tools in atomistic simulations. The most popular models rely heavily on physical priors, such as locality, smoothness and symmetry, that are assumed to improve the accuracy and transferability of the trained models. However, recent evidence suggests that, in the data-rich regime, unconstrained models that learn symmetry from the data can achieve very competitive accuracy and computational efficiency, without sacrificing stability and generalization power. Many equivariant symmetric architectures historically rely on the assumption that the interatomic potential can be approximated well by a convergentcluster expansion, i.e., a decomposition in terms associated to atomic pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and higher-order tuples. We describe an architecture that incorporates locality, smoothness, and symmetry priors, but that -- thanks to a computationally efficient tensor product formulation -- does not assume low-order truncation of the body-ordered series.

title: Soft-confinement approximation of no-flux McKean-Vlasov dynamics
text:
Title: Soft-confinement approximation of no-flux McKean-Vlasov dynamics
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study the approximation of the no-flux McKean-Vlasov equation on a bounded convex domain by a whole-space equation with quadratic confinement of strength $λ^{-1}$ outside the domain. For a smooth bounded interaction kernel and a common bounded initial density with square-integrable gradient, we establish an $O(λ^{1/4})$ approximation rate. The estimate controls the $L^2$ density error uniformly on every finite time interval and the gradient error in space-time $L^2$. Without interaction, a spectral gap independent of $λ$ yields the $O(λ^{1/4})$ rate uniformly in time for the density error and uniformly over all unit time intervals for the gradient error. With interaction, we construct a counterexample showing that even weak convergence can fail to be uniform in time.

title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
text:
Title: Compression of turbulent flow data through an extended space-time correlation: certification against the modal energy budget
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The fidelity of direct numerical simulation now outpaces the storage and data-movement capacity available for the resulting fields. We present an open, distributed, GPU-accelerated low-rank compression framework for large turbulent flow databases. We assess it using two direct numerical simulations of a controlled diffusion compressor cascade under laminar and turbulent inflow conditions. Compression is formulated using a correlation operator over space and time, which is two orders of magnitude larger than that of snapshot POD. Its dominant range is extracted with a randomized range finder based on communication-avoiding hierarchical QR. The compressed databases are evaluated through a hierarchy of increasingly strict diagnostics, from instantaneous reconstruction and second-order statistics to the modal turbulent kinetic energy budget and its nonlinear interscale transfer. The budget terms are far more sensitive to compression than fieldwise or one-point errors. They remain accurate at conservative compression and degrade sharply once the retained energy is relaxed. The near-wall dissipation and the interscale transfer degrade the most and set the admissible compression level. An aggressive reduction preserves every one-point statistic to within a few per cent while corrupting both by an order of magnitude more. The dissipation error is confined to the viscous sublayer and grows with the development of the boundary layer. It is carried by the high-order modes. For both inflows, the linear budget terms scale with the discarded energy to the power $0.8$ and the triadic transfer to a power above one.

title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
text:
Title: Towards Out-of-Distribution Uncertainty Quantification for Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials via Pre-Training
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Informative uncertainty quantification (UQ) is essential for the practical deployment of machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), as it provides insight into their reliability across chemical space. Although numerous post-hoc uncertainty estimation methods for MLIPs have recently been proposed, most have been trained in low-data regimes, restricting their applicability to narrow domains of interest. Inspired by the emergence of foundational MLIPs, we propose pre-training uncertainty estimators on large, diverse datasets to enable broader applicability. We pre-train several UQ models on large materials science datasets to quantify the uncertainty of different MLIPs, and evaluate their performance on both in-distribution and out-of-domain (OOD) adsorption-energy predictions. We find that pre-trained uncertainty estimators provide viable zero-shot uncertainty estimates across multiple datasets, while fine-tuning consistently yields positive correlations between predicted uncertainty and prediction error, even on the most challenging datasets. These results lay the groundwork for foundational UQ models for MLIPs, ultimately facilitating their deployment in practical settings by providing users with a priori information about model reliability and applicability.

title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
text:
Title: HumanSightBench: A Benchmark for Human Visual Perception in MLLMs
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on knowledge-intensive and reasoning-based vision-language benchmark datasets, but still struggle to solve the visual questions that people can solve easily. Evaluating the differences between MLLMs and human-level visual perception is challenging due to end-to-end evaluation which combines various skills, or because we are uncertain if individual items are valid. Specifically, observed errors may reflect visual perception, language priors, background knowledge, question ambiguity, and underspecified answers. Our guideline for HumanSightBench is that we construct items that are human-easy by construction and model-hard by evaluation. HumanSightBench contains 2,876 visual questions with short answers across 7 top-level perceptual categories and 21 subcategories. We only include items that pass five inclusion gates: question clarity, answer uniqueness, visual grounding, human solvability, and text-only shortcut filtering. According to the protocol, errors are defined as incorrect answers on human-validated visual tasks with the evaluated interface. The inclusion gates are intended to reduce confounds from ambiguity and external knowledge. The best pass@3 score is 65.6% across eight evaluated MLLMs. No evaluated model exceeds 27.5% on Counting. These results identify capability gaps that are hidden by overall scores and can help future training experiments and held-out evaluation.

title: DiscKosky: Efficient Genealogical Constraints from Sector-By-Sector Critical Point Counting
text:
Title: DiscKosky: Efficient Genealogical Constraints from Sector-By-Sector Critical Point Counting
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We present DiscKosky, a new Mathematica package for efficiently generating genealogical constraints on the sequential discontinuities of Feynman integrals. DiscKosky works by tracking the solutions to the critical point equations associated with a Feynman integral; by identifying which of these critical points cease to exist in a given kinematic limit, we can associate each Landau singularity with a set of on-shell sectors. The hierarchical principle then forbids sequential discontinuities with respect to singularities that are associated with incompatible sets of on-shell propagators. In rare cases, this algorithm fails to make predictions due to the appearance of higher-dimensional critical varieties---nevertheless, we show that this phenomenon can sometimes be used to identify non-repeating discontinuities, which can be computed at most once in a Feynman integral. We illustrate the power of DiscKosky by applying the package to a broad class of Feynman integrals, including two-loop five-point integrals with one and two massive legs, and three-loop examples that go beyond the current computational frontier. DiscKosky can also be used to probe the analytic properties of more general classes of Euler integrals, which we illustrate by considering several examples that arise in the context of cosmological correlators.

title: Fisher-Glass Learning: Classification Bounds and Subpopulation Audits
text:
Title: Fisher-Glass Learning: Classification Bounds and Subpopulation Audits
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Accurate classifiers can fail when background cues change without altering the correct labels. Predictive performance alone does not quantify how much task information remains after accounting for such nuisance variation. Here we extend the Fisher-glass framework to connect nuisance-adjusted information with local classification difficulty and subpopulation auditing. We derive lower bounds on local minimax excess classification risk under explicit distinguishability and decision-separation conditions, alongside statistical audits accounting for estimation error and regularization. On Waterbirds, a feature-based diagnostic of task-background alignment selects an accurately classified group, with selection frozen before held-out evaluation. Across five training seeds, background replacements preserving the extracted bird foreground and labels yield 93.2% accuracy when background type is preserved and 40.6% when it changes, a controlled difference of 52.6 percentage points. Separately, search using task labels and a fixed nuisance direction identifies an independently evaluated population with 98.8% membership-weighted accuracy and low estimated projected predictive Fisher information. Training and acquisition experiments show that information gains and predictive gains can diverge. These findings support joint assessment of predictive performance, information under declared nuisance models and controlled sensitivity when diagnosing vulnerability and evaluating model improvements.

title: Stochastic Geometrically Exact Beams: Continuous-Time Geometric Principles and Variational Discretizations
text:
Title: Stochastic Geometrically Exact Beams: Continuous-Time Geometric Principles and Variational Discretizations
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Geometrically exact beams naturally arise in physical phenomena and engineering practice for modeling flexible structures, such as soft robotic manipulators and DNA structures. To the best of our knowledge, there appear to be no geometric integrators for stochastic geometrically exact beams in a variational formulation. In this paper, we introduce variational principles for the dynamics of stochastic geometrically exact beams, in both continuous- and discrete-time settings. By introducing perturbations via stochastic potentials and stochastic kinematics, we derive the equations of motion from a variational viewpoint. The resulting stochastic geometric integrators simultaneously discretize time and space in a parallel manner, which provides a distributed computational framework for solving the stochastic dynamics of complex beam systems. In particular, the proposed integrators are shown to be a stochastic extension of the well-known deterministic staggered leapfrog scheme for the wave equation, and also a stochastic extension of Yee's scheme for spatially one-dimensional computational electromagnetism. Numerical results are shown to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approaches.

title: PLUMED-JAX: GPU-native enhanced sampling for atomistic simulations
text:
Title: PLUMED-JAX: GPU-native enhanced sampling for atomistic simulations
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

We present PLUMED-JAX, an AI-assisted adaptation of selected PLUMED collective variables, umbrella sampling, and metadynamics for JAX-based atomistic simulations, developed using gpt-6.1-sol with reasoning effort set to high within the Codex harness. Integration with JAX-MD supports compiled molecular dynamics, batched replicas, walkers sharing a bias, and execution across multiple graphics processing units. We validate the framework against PLUMED and exact free energy benchmarks, and demonstrate applications to butane, silicon crystallization, and lithium transport, with severalfold improvements in computational throughput for both classical forcefields and machine learning interatomic potentials.

title: Rigidity of the Peres-Virág class
text:
Title: Rigidity of the Peres-Virág class
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

Consider the hyperbolic Gaussian analytic function (GAF) \begin{equation*} F_{\mathbb{D}}(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty }ξ_{n}z^{n},\qquad |z|<1, \end{equation*} where the $ξ_{n}$ are independent standard complex Gaussian variables. Peres-Virág theorem tells that the distribution of the zeros of $F_{\mathbb{D}}(z)$ is provided by a Determinantal Point Process (DPP). We prove that $F_{\mathbb{D}}(z)$ is the only GAF whose zeros are determinantal with a Hermitian kernel, up to multiplication by a zero-free holomorphic function and a one-to-one holomorphic change of variable, with a \ non-degeneracy condition imposed to exclude trivial cases. The proof identifies a geometric property of GAF's with (local) determinantal zeros: the metric defined by the first intensity must have constant curvature $-4$.

title: A Free-Field Realization of Boundary Symmetries in Discrete Jackiw--Teitelboim Gravity
text:
Title: A Free-Field Realization of Boundary Symmetries in Discrete Jackiw--Teitelboim Gravity
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We investigate a finite-periodic Miura free-field realization of the classical Virasoro--dilaton sector relevant to sl(2,R) Jackiw--Teitelboim (JT) gravity. Starting from a single logarithmic Cartan field, we use the established discrete Miura map and its free-field Poisson bracket to construct the lattice spin-two current. The dilaton is then realized as a periodic composite of the same Cartan variables, selected by an inhomogeneous difference equation and its monodromy condition. This construction yields an explicit induced mixed Poisson bracket without postulating an independent dilaton bracket. We examine the associated transfer problem and quadratic adjoint invariant, and test the finite Fourier algebra against the continuous Virasoro--dilaton transformation, in which the dilaton has conformal weight minus one. The construction supplies a free-field counterpart of the JT boundary transformation laws; it does not by itself identify the Miura Poisson structure with the canonical BF boundary-charge algebra.

title: Enabling Domain-Specific Atomistic Models: A Machine Learning Potential for the Solid Acid Family
text:
Title: Enabling Domain-Specific Atomistic Models: A Machine Learning Potential for the Solid Acid Family
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Machine-learned interatomic potentials trained across the periodic table have made atomistic simulation broadly accessible, and specializing them to a single compound class is widely expected to improve accuracy. Yet examples remain scarce, and fewer still surpass universal models in speed or reach a higher level of electronic-structure theory. Here we present a potential that is universal within the class of water-free solid-state hydrogen-bond network mediated proton conductors rather than across chemistry and a database of 4.4 million first-principles configurations spanning 55 materials. It surpasses leading general-purpose potentials across this domain, recovering measured activation energies and the ordering of anion rotational dynamics that those models miss; agreement on static structure does not imply agreement on transport. Accuracy falls for compositions far from the training set but stays competitive for close structural relatives, and a higher level of electronic-structure theory is reached with a few hundred additional configurations per material. We further introduce a compact variant carrying a fifth of the parameters, faster still and yet more accurate than every general-purpose model tested. It sustains more than a quarter of a million atoms on a single graphics processor, placing grain boundaries and the transition into the highly conducting phase within reach, and making a quantum treatment of the protons affordable. Reference accuracy and accessible system size thus become largely independent, offering a template for other compound classes.

title: A stochastic chemical system in contact with reservoirs
text:
Title: A stochastic chemical system in contact with reservoirs
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In this paper we analyse the behaviour of a non-reversible stochastic chemical system obtained as an approximation of a stochastic chemical system in which the concentration of some chemicals is higher than the concentration of the other chemicals. The master equation associated with this approximated system is characterised by a discrete part, modelling the reactions among chemicals that have low concentration, by a transport term and a diffusion term. The transport-diffusion terms describe the fluctuations in the concentration of abundant chemicals. The model contains a second order term is of order ε, that describes the fluctuation in the concentrations of the abundand substances. We prove that the master equation has a spectral gap that is independent on $ε$ and we analyse in detail the asymptotics of the solution to the master equation as $ε\to 0$.

title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
text:
Title: How Do AI Agents Waste Your Money?
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

AI agents may consume massive tokens across a wide range of tasks, but how many of those tokens are really necessary? Although prior work has shown that agents can incur unexpectedly high token costs, we still lack a systematic way to identify and measure token waste. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for measuring token waste across heterogeneous agent systems. Our framework records and normalizes complete agent trajectories, identifies removable spans using an LLM-as-a-Judge (LLMaJ), and maps the identified text spans back to the original trajectory for token-level measurement. We validate the identified waste through direct interventions by removing marked spans, resuming agent execution, and measuring changes in task outcomes and subsequent actions. In online pruning experiments, we remove 41-46% of the model's reasoning while largely preserving task performance across two distinct agent benchmarks. Using this framework, we analyze agents across multiple settings. Our analysis shows that token waste has a system-level structure that aggregate token usage alone cannot reveal. First, waste varies more across tasks and agent settings than across models. Second, reasoning and visible execution can exhibit different waste patterns. Third, different harnesses can introduce distinct sources of inefficiency even under the same model and task. Overall, our framework transforms token waste into an actionable optimization signal, enabling researchers and practitioners to train more efficient models, design better reasoning strategies, and optimize agent harnesses toward reducing unnecessary computation rather than merely reducing token usage.

title: Optical and Ultraviolet Emission from the Gas Photoionized by Gaia BH3: Archival Constraints and Predictions for the 2029 Periastron
text:
Title: Optical and Ultraviolet Emission from the Gas Photoionized by Gaia BH3: Archival Constraints and Predictions for the 2029 Periastron
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Gaia BH3, a $32.7\,M_\odot$ black hole (BH) on an 11.6-yr, $e=0.73$ orbit around a metal-poor giant at $\approx590$ pc, accretes from its wind. Neither its mass-loss rate $\dot M_{\rm w}$ nor the fraction of captured gas reaching the BH is known. We ask whether optical and ultraviolet lines from gas photoionized by the hot flow are observable and what they reveal. Unlike X-ray and radio data, they count the ionizing photons the gas absorbs and trace its density and velocity. With Cloudy we compute the H$α$ and He II 4686 emission of the wind and inflow along the orbit for $\dot M_{\rm w}=10^{-11}$-$10^{-8}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$, Eddington ratios $f_{\rm Edd}=10^{-8}$-$10^{-5}$ and wind speeds of 30 (slow) and 100 km s$^{-1}$ (fast), and test each model against archival UVES and ESPRESSO spectra. $f_{\rm Edd}$ mainly sets the lines; in dense models they come from gas falling freely onto the BH, spread over thousands of km s$^{-1}$. The archival spectra exclude $\dot M_{\rm w}>2\times10^{-9}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$ at $f_{\rm Edd}=2\times10^{-6}$ and $>2.6\times10^{-10}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$ at $10^{-5}$ (95%, slow wind), Eddington ratios already excluded by the apastron Chandra limit, $f_{\rm Edd}<7.6\times10^{-7}$. Of two simulated campaigns, only 25 epochs around the 2029 periastron go beyond existing limits. For a slow wind, whose capture rate is constant, a $\ge5σ$ H$α$ detection would imply an accretion state 2-3 times above the 2024 limit. For a fast wind, whose captured fraction rises 14-fold toward periastron, the campaign detects $\dot M_{\rm w}\simeq10^{-8}\,M_\odot\,{\rm yr^{-1}}$ for $f_{\rm Edd}\gtrsim1.2\times10^{-6}$, which the apastron limit allows. Below the Chandra limit, a slow wind produces no detectable line.

title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
text:
Title: Understanding Mixture-of-Experts Language Models Beyond Expert Boundaries
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

In Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, the nature of expert specialization remains controversial. Reports of domain-associated expert preferences contrast with analyses attributing routing primarily to token identity or syntactic patterns. To clarify these differing accounts, we look beyond expert-level routing to investigate the neuron-level organization of domain-specialized computation using Routing-Aware Magnitude Profiling (RAMP), a measure developed for this analysis. Using mixed-domain calibration data, we identify domain-specialized neuron sets with 58-74% overlap across multi-source samples of the same domain, compared with 15-24% across domains. To understand how this organization evolves during training, we trace neuron importance throughout pre-training and post-training across three fully open MoE families. Neuron importance continues to reorganize between pre-training checkpoints despite comparatively stable expert-level importance rankings, while post-training largely preserves neuron rankings. Building on these neuron-level perspectives, we further introduce RAMP-based Pruning (RAMPr) to select neurons across experts for balanced multi-domain capability preservation. At 75% neuron retention, RAMPr preserves average 91-98% of original full performance across six models. At 50% retention, our pruning method can reduce resident GPU memory by 36-43% and improves batched prefill throughput by 17-39% effectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/ydyjya/Neuron-Level-Specialization-in-MoE

title: Bayesian Inversion Beyond the Generator's Range: Reducing Non-physical Constraints from Generative Neural Networks
text:
Title: Bayesian Inversion Beyond the Generator's Range: Reducing Non-physical Constraints from Generative Neural Networks
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

To address non-uniqueness in geophysical inversions, Generative Neural Networks (GNNs) are often used to parameterise geological or other prior information in a lower-dimensional space (the so-called latent space), thereby reducing the number of inversion parameters. However, the training samples that represent this information are then always incorrect, because Earth structure is not intrinsically low-dimensional, and all GNNs are subject to training errors. Consequently, even when solutions are mapped back to the original higher-dimensional space, they inherit this imperfection and remain restricted to a low-dimensional manifold. From a mathematical point of view, latent space inversion thus fails fundamentally: generally, it can not even reproduce the best, higher-dimensional approximation to the true Earth. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an `escaping prior' distribution, which provides the necessary freedom to find solutions beyond the manifold of GNN-generated solutions, while still using the GNN as a guide. We use a hierarchical Bayesian approach to adapt the strength of prior information to the observed data and synthetic forward function $\textit{a posteriori}$. We illustrate our method on low-dimensional problems where the escaping prior is defined over a 1D manifold in 2D space. We then compare our approach with standard latent space and model space inversions using a uniform prior distribution in synthetic tomography problems, ranging from simple to more geologically realistic cases. Furthermore, we tested scenarios where the true solution is either far from or close to the manifold. In each case, our escaping prior shows significantly better results than the alternatives. It results in solutions beyond each GNN's generative capabilities, solutions which include the best possible model, and clearly demonstrates the limitations of latent space inversion.

title: Disentangling multispecific antibody function with graph neural networks
text:
Title: Disentangling multispecific antibody function with graph neural networks
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Multispecific antibodies offer transformative therapeutic potential by engaging multiple epitopes simultaneously, yet their efficacy is an emergent property governed by complex molecular architectures. Rational design is often bottlenecked by the inability to predict how subtle changes in domain topology influence functional outcomes, a challenge exacerbated by the scarcity of comprehensive experimental data. Here, we introduce a computational framework to address part of this gap. First, we present a generative method for creating large-scale, realistic synthetic functional landscapes that capture non-linear interactions where biological activity depends on domain connectivity. Second, we propose a graph neural network architecture that explicitly encodes these topological constraints, distinguishing between format configurations that appear identical to sequence-only models. We demonstrate that this model, trained on synthetic landscapes, recapitulates complex functional properties and, via transfer learning, has the potential to achieve high predictive accuracy on limited biological datasets. We showcase the model's utility by optimizing trade-offs between efficacy and toxicity in trispecific T-cell engagers and retrieving optimal common light chains. This work provides a robust benchmarking environment for disentangling the combinatorial complexity of multispecifics, accelerating the design of next-generation therapeutics.

title: From Non-Thermal to Thermal: Cosmological Imprints of Self-Interacting Secluded Dark Matter
text:
Title: From Non-Thermal to Thermal: Cosmological Imprints of Self-Interacting Secluded Dark Matter
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Dark matter (DM), secluded from the Standard Model (SM), can attain internal thermalization through self-interactions. We investigate the thermalization of a real scalar DM field with a quartic self-coupling, initially produced from the perturbative decay of the coherently oscillating inflaton field during reheating. The thermalization process has been studied numerically by solving Boltzmann equation of the DM momentum distribution function in presence of $2\rightarrow2$ DM elastic self-scatterings. In the absence of number-changing processes, the thermalized dark sector is characterized by a temperature and a nonzero chemical potential, determined by the inflaton mass and the reheat temperature. We find that if the inflaton mass is greater (smaller) than the reheat temperature, the DM temperature can be greater (smaller) than the SM temperature during Big Bang Nucleosynthesis, without violating any cosmological constraints. This is realized with a negative (positive) chemical potential for the DM temperature greater (smaller) than the SM one. Depending on DM production history, we can achieve the lower limit on the DM mass much below than in warm DM scenarios. The thermalization via self-scatterings tends to suppress the DM co-moving free-streaming length, compared to the non-thermal scenario without any collisions. Consequently, the lower limit on the DM mass weakens approximately by $40\%$ for a suitable choice of quartic self-coupling than in the non-thermal scenario. We obtain the lower limits on the thermal DM mass to be $2.2\times10^{-10}$ GeV and $0.47$ GeV for reheat temperatures, $5\times 10^6$ GeV and $5$ MeV respectively, while the inflaton mass is set at $10^3$ GeV.

title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
text:
Title: How Much Is Left Matters: False Positives and False Negatives in Partial-Prompt Contamination Tests
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Partial-prompt completion, where a model receives the first part of a benchmark problem and is checked for whether it reproduces the rest, is a widely used test for benchmark contamination. We audit this test on seven open-weight models using MATH-500 and recent AIME 2025/2026 problems, which serve as true negatives. Memorization flags depend strongly on how much text remains: for every model, problems with at most 8 leftover words are flagged several times more often than problems with at least 25 (31.5% vs. 5.5% for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and half to three-quarters of all ROUGE-based flags come from short leftovers. On true negatives, a ROUGE-L >= 0.75 threshold flags up to 6.7% of problems at a 60% prefix, and at an 80% prefix even exact match flags 8.6% (pooled over models; 6.2% on AIME 2026, which postdates every model), against 0% at 40-60%. The test also misses contamination upstream: models distilled from Qwen2.5-Math, whose base is heavily flagged in prior work, show almost no model-specific recall. Calibrating each model against models from other families removes most flags while isolating a consistent Qwen2.5-specific signal at every prefix length. We recommend length-stratified reporting, prefixes of at most 60%, style-matched post-cutoff controls, and cross-family calibration.

title: System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety
text:
Title: System Prompts Affect Response Bias More Than Discriminability in LLM Safety
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language model safety evaluations often focus on a compliance-refusal tradeoff: models should refuse unsafe requests without refusing safe ones. We argue that this misses a broader form of prompt-conditioned task selection, where the same request can elicit different behaviors depending on the system prompt. We investigate this using a controlled evaluation crossing eight safety-task prompt families with three clarity levels across HarmBench, XSTest, and IHEval. Holding benchmark items fixed, we evaluate 13 models and use signal detection theory to distinguish two possibilities: whether models become better at telling safe from unsafe requests (discriminability), or simply more willing to refuse (response criterion). We find substantial differences in discriminability across models, but system prompts primarily shift the willingness to refuse, with smaller and less consistent effects on discriminability. Increasing prompt clarity makes models more willing to refuse without reliably improving their ability to distinguish safe from unsafe requests. Beyond refusal, prompt families also shift responses among six distinct behavioral policies, including clarification and safe help.
