In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held-out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.

title: Exact sampling beyond Fock inputs and linear optics: photon-number superpositions, photonic matrix-product states, adaptive and non-linear circuits
text:
Title: Exact sampling beyond Fock inputs and linear optics: photon-number superpositions, photonic matrix-product states, adaptive and non-linear circuits
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Clifford and Clifford's algorithm samples single-photon boson sampling exactly, one output mode at a time, by adding the input photons in a uniformly random order. We extend this construction to other input states and to adaptive and non-linear circuits. It applies whenever non-negative weights on output prefixes and input sets satisfy one marginal identity, a set-chain lemma: the random-order sampler is then exact at one weight evaluation per candidate mode, and it gives the posterior over the hidden input set. We build four exact samplers on it. For sources in a superposition of vacuum and one photon, the weights are rectangular permanents on an offset input set, and the cost has the exponent of single photons under loss. For photonic matrix-product states of bond dimension $χ$, a gap-by-gap Kraus contraction turns each weight into a short sum of squared amplitudes. For adaptive linear optics, the chain starts from the posterior given the adaptive counts and rejects chains that contradict them. For a single-mode non-linear phase the identity fails, and rejection from linear branches is exact with acceptance $1/\|c\|_1^2$. All four samplers agree with strong simulation on small instances, and cost models put adaptive sampling with up to three adaptive modes within $10\%$ of single photons and a non-linear site at $\varphi=π/2$ at about $4\times$.

title: Quasi-Normal Modes and thermalization in integrable Quantum Field Theories from the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz
text:
Title: Quasi-Normal Modes and thermalization in integrable Quantum Field Theories from the Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

We propose a Thermodynamic Bethe Ansatz (TBA) approach for describing thermalization in integrable quantum field theories. The exponential damping and oscillations when approaching thermal equilibrium can be understood as the analogs of quasi-normal mode (QNM) frequencies of black hole perturbations within the framework of holography. Holographic intuitions and some general properties of thermal Green's functions motivate the existence of such a TBA formulation, as well as lead to the imposition of a nonstandard analytical structure on the QNM TBA, while comparison with integrable form-factor expansions fixes the remaining ingredients. We conjecture the QNM TBA to be equivalent to performing an all-order resummation of secular terms in a thermal form factor expansion of retarded 2-point correlation functions. We compare the predictions with tensor network simulations of the E8 deformation of Ising CFT at nonzero temperature. We conjecture that the QNM TBA framework should also be applicable for describing out-of-equilibrium approach to Generalized Hydrodynamics (GHD).

title: Persistent local Laplacian prediction of protein-ligand binding affinities
text:
Title: Persistent local Laplacian prediction of protein-ligand binding affinities
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Accurate prediction of protein-ligand binding affinity remains a central challenge in structure-based drug discovery. The effectiveness of machine learning models critically depends on the quality of molecular descriptors, for which advanced mathematical frameworks provide powerful tools. In this work, we employ a novel mathematical theory, termed the persistent local Laplacian (PLL), to construct molecular descriptors that capture localized geometric and topological features of biomolecular structures. The PLL framework addresses key limitations of traditional topological data analysis methods, such as persistent homology and the persistent Laplacian, which are often insensitive to local structural variations, while maintaining high computational efficiency. The resulting molecular descriptors are integrated with advanced machine learning algorithms to develop accurate predictive models for protein-ligand binding affinity. The proposed models are systematically evaluated on three well-established benchmark datasets, demonstrating consistently strong and competitive predictive performance. Computational results show that the PLL-based models outperform existing approaches, highlighting their potential as a powerful tool for drug discovery, protein engineering, and broader applications in science and engineering.

title: Phase Transitions for Random Least Common Multiples with Memory
text:
Title: Phase Transitions for Random Least Common Multiples with Memory
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study the least common multiple of a random subset of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ when the selection follows a correlated Bernoulli process with memory. The copying rule preserves the marginal retention probabilities and creates a genealogical forest. At fixed density, the logarithmic least common multiple exhibits a fluctuation phase transition at the memory parameter $a=1/2$. The boundary limits depend on how genealogical families are distributed among the divisibility classes carrying the leading arithmetic weight. Our proofs combine the von Mangoldt representation with a reduction to large primes. At fixed density, an exact expansion separates an innovation martingale from a memory term. An asymptotic projection onto the retained count identifies the contribution of memory. Marked point-process convergence and estimates for rare genealogical families give the boundary limits.

title: Flow-based conditional cardiac anatomy generation for virtual cohorts
text:
Title: Flow-based conditional cardiac anatomy generation for virtual cohorts
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Cardiac digital twin research is moving from subject-specific anatomical replicas toward virtual cohorts that represent clinically relevant population subgroups. Yet access to representative imaging-derived anatomy datasets remains limited by cohort size, subgroup sparsity, and data-sharing constraints. Conditional generative models could help address this gap, but virtual cohorts are useful only if they preserve realistic, metadata-dependent anatomical variability. Existing cardiac anatomy generators largely rely on conditional variational autoencoders (cVAEs), which couple representation learning and metadata conditioning through a shared regularized latent prior. We introduce CAN-FLOW, a two-step Conditional ANatomy generation framework based on normalizing FLOWs that first learns geometry-only latent representations of diffeomorphic cardiac shape momenta and then models their sex-, age-, and body-mass-index-dependent distribution with a conditional normalizing flow. We trained CAN-FLOW on 2,208 healthy UK Biobank subjects and compared it with cVAEs across regularization strengths. CAN-FLOW generated plausible stochastic biventricular anatomies that better reproduced clinical phenotype distributions, metadata-dependent trends, subgroup variability, point-cloud coverage, and high-dimensional shape variability. Together, these results establish CAN-FLOW as a shareable framework for generating realistic, stochastically varying, metadata-conditioned biventricular anatomies for virtual cohort construction and in silico clinical trial workflows.

title: AI-guided deep visual proteomics reveals recurrence-associated morpho-molecular signatures within triple-negative breast cancers
text:
Title: AI-guided deep visual proteomics reveals recurrence-associated morpho-molecular signatures within triple-negative breast cancers
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Outcome informed AI can localize prognostically relevant regions in digital pathology, but directly characterizing the molecular basis of these spatial predictions remains challenging. Here, we developed an outcome informed, AI-guided deep visual proteomics framework that uses recurrence-risk heatmaps to guide physical tissue sampling and mass spectrometry-based spatial proteomics in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC). In 156 patients, high- and low-risk regions coexisted within the tumor compartment and showed distinct nuclear and architectural features, indicating intratumoral variation beyond broad tissue identity. Guided by these maps, we physically isolated and profiled 46 AI-defined high- and low-risk tumor regions from two recurrent cases. High-risk regions were enriched for mitotic programs, whereas low-risk regions showed immune- and antigen-presentation-associated programs. We used proteins that consistently differed between high- and low-risk regions to construct a 13-protein composite. The composite showed a significant effect to discriminate highly recurrent patients from less recurrent patients in an expanded TNBC cohort, while the corresponding transcript-based score showed a similar trend in METABRIC. Integrating the protein composite with the H&E-derived risk score improved out-of-bag discrimination, increasing the C-index from 0.679 to 0.739 and the 5-year time-dependent AUC from 0.675 to 0.770. These findings establish outcome-informed H&E risk maps as spatial guides for molecular discovery, extending prognostic AI from prediction toward direct biological interrogation of recurrence-associated tissue states.

title: Gas-phase chemistry of $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_3^+$: a key building block for carbon mass growth in space
text:
Title: Gas-phase chemistry of $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_3^+$: a key building block for carbon mass growth in space
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

The gas-phase chemistry of $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_3^+$ plays a central role in the growth of carbonaceous species across a wide range of environments, from combustion systems to interstellar media. However, the presence of multiple isomers, primarily the linear propargyl cation and the cyclic cyclopropenyl cation, has so far prevented the determination of reliable isomer-specific reaction kinetics. In this work, we combine tunable vacuum-ultraviolet (VUV) photoionization with controlled ion--molecule reaction measurements to selectively produce and probe the reactivity of $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_3^+$ isomers. By employing a titration approach, we extract isomer-specific reaction rate coefficients and branching ratios for reactions of $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_3^+$ with $\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{H}_4$, $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_4$, and $\mathrm{C}_3\mathrm{H}_6$. Our results demonstrate a strong contrast in reactivity: the most stable cyclic isomer is found to be essentially unreactive under the investigated conditions, whereas the linear isomer exhibits efficient and diverse chemistry leading to the formation of larger hydrocarbon ions. In particular, the formation of $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5^+$ is observed, providing an important intermediate in pathways toward aromatic species. These findings help resolve long-standing ambiguities in previously reported rate coefficients and provide new quantitative constraints for kinetic and astrochemical models. More broadly, this work highlights the importance of isomer-specific chemistry in carbon growth processes and demonstrates the effectiveness of VUV-based photoionization methods for disentangling complex reaction networks in the gas phase.

title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
text:
Title: Matriarchy Classics: A Computational Approach to Swap Only Gendered Words in Classic Novels
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

This paper proposes a trustworthy computational method to gender-swap public domain novels, with programmatic guarantees that only gendered words are inverted and all other words are left unchanged. This may seem like a simple task, but both large language models and naive rule-based methods fail to complete it. The proposed method includes a custom whitespace-preserving tokenizer, gender-swap mappings across plural and possessive forms, pronoun handling, and a character renaming strategy. It shortens the time required to gender-swap a novel from weeks of manual labor to minutes. The method is demonstrated on two public-domain novels. Pride and Prejudice is transported to matriarchal Regency England, where inheritance flows through daughters, mothers rule the household, and a frantic Mr. Bennet is determined to secure advantageous marriages for his sons. The Great Gatsby pivots to a matriarchal Jazz Age where newly-rich Ms. Gatsbee throws lavish parties in the hopes of reuniting with her lost love, David, who is now married to the violent Thelma Buchanan. Gender-swapped novels could serve as useful tools to investigate the gender biases of readers, authors, societies, and AI systems.

title: Steerable Single-step Retrosynthesis with Electron-pushing Discrete Flow Matching and Feynman-Kac Steering
text:
Title: Steerable Single-step Retrosynthesis with Electron-pushing Discrete Flow Matching and Feynman-Kac Steering
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Expert chemists perform retrosynthetic analysis in a strategic manner, where each reaction in a route is employed with a specific purpose, combined with mechanistic reasoning represented as electron-pushing arrows to visualize how bonds are formed or broken via electron redistribution. Yet contemporary single-step retrosynthesis models exhibit neither of these properties: their learned reaction distribution is fixed to that of the training data, and reactions are predicted via de-novo generation of the precursors or molecular graph edits, omitting the electron redistribution that governs the chemical transformations. We introduce Verso MAELLE, the first electron-pushing-based single-step retrosynthetic model, representing disconnections as continuous-time Markov chains (CTMC) comprised of edits in the electron space, and is trainable using a discrete flow matching formulation. Being a generative model, Verso MAELLE is optionally steerable at inference time through the Feynman-Kac (FK) framework, using rewards that promote certain types of disconnections. We show that besides in-distribution learning, Verso MAELLE can be steered toward cyclization reactions which are scaffold-constructive but underrepresented in the training corpus, via a ring-breaking reward. As a proof of concept, we show how the electron-pushing reasoning, learned from patented data, combined with a domino incentivizing reward, could steer Verso MAELLE toward creative and strategic disconnections, demonstrated on the key domino sequence that was used to synthesize Punctaporonin U, a complex natural product of the sesquiterpene family.

title: A Benchmark and Layered Evaluation Protocol for Evidence-Grounded Shared Belief Updating in Connected Robotics
text:
Title: A Benchmark and Layered Evaluation Protocol for Evidence-Grounded Shared Belief Updating in Connected Robotics
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Connected physical systems fuse observations from robots, IoT sensors, and edge-AI modules into a shared account of the world, yet most evaluations score only the final answer or action and cannot tell whether a method attributed the evidence, updated its belief, handled contradictions, and justified its decision. We argue that shared reasoning in Connected Robotics should be evaluated as an evidence-to-belief trajectory, and introduce the Connected Robotics Evidence Graph (CREG) Benchmark to make that trajectory measurable. CREG comprises 350 deterministically generated scenarios across seven regimes (justified revision, belief preservation, relation association, contradiction onset and resolution, stale/delayed evidence, and source reliability), each exposing a normative posterior reference at every evidence prefix, validated by an independent log-odds checker and screened by a blinded expert audit. Nine representation conditions separate relation content from serialization, ordering, and metadata. Evaluating four open-weight instruction models and six transparent fusion baselines yields three findings. First, entity grounding accounts for a substantial part of the weak-model deficit. Second, deleting semantic relations costs 15.3 points of strict belief-state accuracy on relation-dependent scenarios (Holm-corrected p<0.001), but an information-matched structured list outperforms the full graph and shuffling the graph does not hurt: relation content matters where required, while graph serialization confers no consistent advantage. Third, belief accuracy is strongly non-monotonic along the evidence sequence, with mid-trajectory failures that endpoint-only evaluation cannot detect. All scenarios, references, prompts, metrics, and analysis code are released for offline, hardware-free reproduction.

title: Probing the Seed Effect of Supermassive Primordial Black Holes with Weak Gravitational Lensing
text:
Title: Probing the Seed Effect of Supermassive Primordial Black Holes with Weak Gravitational Lensing
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We investigate the cosmological implications of supermassive primordial black holes (PBHs) as a component of dark matter (DM), focusing on their seed effect on large-scale structure formation. In contrast to the Poisson effect associated with the discrete distribution of PBHs, the seed effect arises because PBHs act as early gravitational seeds, accreting surrounding DM and developing dense DM spikes to form dressed PBHs. These structures enhance the matter power spectrum, particularly on small scales. We model their contribution within the halo-model framework under two prescriptions for DM accretion: an optimistic scenario (Case 1) and a conservative scenario (Case 2), which predict different modifications to the 1-halo term. We constrain the PBH abundance using weak-lensing measurements from the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 (DES Y3), performing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo analysis to derive upper limits on the PBH fraction $f_{\rm PBH}$, as a function of the PBH mass $M_{\rm PBH}$. We find that weak lensing places competitive constraints on supermassive PBHs, with the upper limits on $f_{\rm PBH}$ becoming progressively stronger toward higher PBH masses. Case 1, which predicts more efficient DM accretion and hence a larger enhancement of the matter power spectrum, yields stronger constraints than Case 2; in particular, it excludes $f_{\rm PBH}\gtrsim10^{-4}$ for $M_{\rm PBH}\gtrsim10^{10} M_\odot$. We further forecast the sensitivity of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) using mock weak-lensing data and find that the constraints could improve by approximately two orders of magnitude. Our results establish weak gravitational lensing as a sensitive probe of the seed effect of supermassive PBHs and demonstrate its potential to complement other cosmological and astrophysical searches.

title: Identifying Neural State Changes due to Gain versus Off-Manifold Displacement
text:
Title: Identifying Neural State Changes due to Gain versus Off-Manifold Displacement
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Memory segmentation is thought to arise from rapid decorrelation in neural activity, often quantified by Euclidean distance or cosine angle. Although these metrics detect a transition, they do not reveal how the new state relates to the repertoire represented by the neural manifold. This matters because neuromodulators that drive state transitions also alter excitability, and learning may repurpose existing representations or create new ones. Here, I introduce a geometric decomposition that separates changes attributable to gain modulation of a nearby manifold state from movement within the manifold and genuine off-manifold displacement. The approach uses the radial axis of neural population activity to partition the normal space of a local manifold region. A central challenge is identifiability: given only a static reference manifold and a single test state, neither the state from which a perturbation began nor its gain magnitude and mechanistic decomposition can generally be recovered uniquely. I therefore formulate identifiability as a cascade of geometric gates specifying when each component can be interpreted. The gates distinguish structural failures, including the absence of a local chart or incorrect intrinsic dimensionality, from estimation error and systematic bias caused by reference sampling, tangent-frame error, gain-axis misalignment, anchor displacement, and poor ratio conditioning. Simulations show that neighborhood size, curvature, sampling density, ambient dimension, and noise act through a small set of geometric quantities. The framework specifies when assignments to gain or novelty are identifiable, how they become biased, and which diagnostics reveal the relevant failure regime. By quantifying the nature rather than only the magnitude of neural state change, it provides a clear, readily interpretable framework for evaluating mechanisms of neural state transitions.

title: Universal Curve Counting in Calabi-Yau 4-folds
text:
Title: Universal Curve Counting in Calabi-Yau 4-folds
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Recently, Pardon introduced a universal curve counting framework, which allows him to show that curve counting on 3-folds is "generated" by local curves (in a precise sense). We implement this universal curve counting program for Calabi-Yau 4-folds, where a significant technical difficulty comes from the dependence of the virtual dimension on the genus, which leads to more complicated generators than just local curves. Our main techniques are combinations of deformation-theoretic and homotopy-theoretic methods with an adaptation of Pardon's generic transversality results, which allow us to establish a full set of (computable) generators for CY4 curve counting. As a result, we prove (a slight correction of) the Gromov-Witten/Pandharipande-Thomas correspondence with primary descendents for CY4-folds, formulated by Cao, Maulik, and Toda. From this, we additionally obtain integrality of Gopakumar-Vafa style invariants for CY4-folds, as conjectured by Klemm-Pandharipande.

title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
text:
Title: Augmented Lagrangian methods with telescopic subproblems for MPCCs and cardinality constraints with general constraints: constraint-preserving swaps and B-stationarity
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We consider optimization problems with general equality and inequality constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints, which include complementarity constraints. In the augmented Lagrangian method that we consider, the bounds and the cardinality constraints are kept in the subproblems, which are solved by the Telescopic Method. The limit points of this method are B-stationary, without constraint qualifications, if the penalty parameters remain bounded, but not in general. The reason is that the swaps of the Telescopic Method pass through points at which the constraints have different values, and the corresponding variation of the penalty term grows with the penalty parameter. With unbounded penalty parameters and a derivative test outside the current face, the feasible limit points at which a linear independence constraint qualification holds are M-stationary for MPCCs. We modify the swaps, by means of a scaled Newton restoration, so that they preserve the values of the constraints, and we prove that every feasible limit point at which this constraint qualification holds is then B-stationary (S-stationary for MPCCs), whatever the behavior of the penalty parameters. Counterexamples show that the modification is necessary, even with exact solutions of the subproblems, and that the constraint qualification cannot be weakened to one of Mangasarian-Fromovitz type. In the MacMPEC collection, the method found certified S- or B-stationary points in 185 of the 193 instances, more than Algencan and the regularization method of Scholtes. In experiments with cardinality-constrained portfolios and sparse principal component analysis, the constraint-preserving swaps improved the original swaps and the methods applied to complementarity reformulations.

title: The second reconstruction transition for random graphs from 2-neighborhoods
text:
Title: The second reconstruction transition for random graphs from 2-neighborhoods
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We prove that, with high probability, the Erdős--Rényi random graph $G(n,p)$ is reconstructible up to isomorphism from the multiset of its rooted induced 2-neighborhoods whenever $p\geq n^{-3/4}(\log n)^3$. Together with the non-reconstructibility result of Johnston, Kronenberg, Roberts and Scott, our result locates the second reconstruction transition at the scale $p=n^{-3/4}$ up to polylogarithmic factors, resolving a question they posed. Our proof relies on a global rigidity argument exploiting 5-cycle constraints.

title: Native point defects in rock-salt and wurtzite MnSe: formation energies across the growth window and spin splitting in the A-type order
text:
Title: Native point defects in rock-salt and wurtzite MnSe: formation energies across the growth window and spin splitting in the A-type order
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Manganese selenide grows both as rock-salt $α$-MnSe, a type-II antiferromagnet, and as metastable wurtzite w-MnSe, whose magnetic order has not been measured. We compute the neutral Mn and Se vacancies and the two antisites of both polymorphs with density functional theory plus a linear-response Hubbard $U$, between the Se-rich limit bounded by MnSe$_2$ and the Mn-rich limit set by the measured formation enthalpy. In $α$-MnSe the Mn vacancy is lowest over most of the window (0.92 eV under Se-rich conditions), consistent with its p-type conduction. In w-MnSe, the Se antisite is lowest under Se-rich conditions, narrowly in the A-type order and clearly in the stripe order, and the Se vacancy is lowest under Mn-rich conditions. The Se vacancy has nearly the same formation energy in both polymorphs, whereas defects that change the number of Mn atoms differ by 0.4-1.1 eV, although DFT+$U$ places wurtzite below rock salt, contrary to experiment. A spin-degenerate stripe order lies 14 meV per formula unit below the altermagnetic A-type order of w-MnSe, and the formation energies shift between these orders by up to 0.24 eV, most for the Mn vacancy. Three of the four defects leave an uncompensated moment of 3-5 $μ_\mathrm{B}$. In the A-type order, band unfolding shows that the sign-reversing splitting of the most strongly split band, about 230 meV and 3 eV below the valence-band maximum, keeps its peak height within the 8% scatter of the analysis at 3% defects, while points on its shoulders move by up to about 70 meV. Band-edge states are not resolved.

title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
text:
Title: On Lipschitz Explosion in Deep Neural Networks with Normalization: Consequences for Optimization and Adversarial Robustness
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Can a network look stable at every layer and still be exponentially unstable as a whole? The Lipschitz constant of a neural network is a basic stability quantity appearing in optimization guarantees, generalization bounds, and robustness certificates. Deep networks naturally admit two such notions, input Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to data perturbations, and parameter Lipschitzness, measuring sensitivity to weight perturbations. We prove that, for deep networks with normalization layers, with batch normalization as the canonical example, both Lipschitz constants can grow exponentially with depth and hence with parameter dimension, even under strong per-layer norm control such as $\|W_\ell\|_2\le 1$, and already for linear activations. Thus, a mechanism widely used to stabilize training can create severe worst-case instabilities that are invisible locally, i.e., from layerwise norm bounds alone. Parameter-Lipschitz explosion turns Lipschitz-dependent nonsmooth optimization guarantees into exponential-in-dimension bounds for deep normalized networks, while input-Lipschitz explosion makes worst-case Lipschitz-based generalization and robustness certificates vacuous. The latter also yields a concrete rank-separation mechanism for adversarial vulnerability. The theory predicts that perturbations introducing new singular directions should be amplified much more strongly than perturbations at the same noise level that remain within the input's original singular subspace. Experiments on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 support this prediction, showing that rank-creating perturbations cause substantially sharper drops in accuracy, confidence, and margins than same-subspace perturbations.

title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling
text:
Title: All reweighted paths lead to Rome: Unification of reweighting schemes for stratified path sampling
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Path sampling-based stratification algorithms such as Transition Interface Sampling (TIS) enable the evaluation of kinetic rate constants and mechanisms of complex molecular rare event transitions. By sampling only short dynamical trajectories, TIS allows constructing an estimate of the unbiased dynamics by reweighting the interface path ensembles. In the past decades several methods have been developed and applied to achieve such path reweighting, based on statistically optimal use of the trajectory data. Why and how this reweighting exactly works has been underexplored up to now. Here we discuss several different schemes to compute the reweighted path ensemble (RPE), notably point-wise matching, Weighted Histogram Analysis Method (WHAM), Multistate Bennett Acceptance Ratio (MBAR), variance based reweighting (VBR) and survival analysis reweighting (SAR). We show that except for the point-wise matching the other methods are leading to the same outcome, and in fact can be seen as identical. Moreover, the SAR links to a well-established nonparametric maximum-likelihood estimator of product-limit form. This allows a synthesis of all path reweighting schemes, identifying the common underlying nature. All schemes follow from this common origin. We illustrate the reweighting with some simple examples, and show that care has to be taken when applying WHAM, if the number of interfaces and histogram bins do not match.

title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method
text:
Title: Local Metrics for Exact Streaming on Curvilinear Lattices: A Curvilinear D3Q27 Cumulant Lattice-Boltzmann Method
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

A three-dimensional curvilinear lattice-Boltzmann method is introduced for simulations on smoothly deformed grids while retaining exact one-to-one streaming on a uniform computational lattice. The coordinate transformation is represented locally through a metric-Gaussian equilibrium and a Christoffel-connection source in moment space. A dynamically reconstructed homogeneous-state perturbation streaming procedure preserves homogeneous physical states on warped meshes without interpolation in the advection step. The method is implemented on a D3Q27 lattice with a cumulant collision operator, while the geometric construction remains compatible with other local collision models. The formulation is assessed using two sets of tests. First, static non-orthogonal warped-cube cases validate the bulk curvilinear solver through a convected helical shear wave, the Taylor--Green vortex, and Arnold--Beltrami--Childress flow. These tests verify viscous decay, clean freestream preservation, vortex-breakdown dynamics, and the nonlinear inertial--pressure balance induced by geometric acceleration. Second, wall-bounded and moving-boundary demonstrations assess the boundary-compatible extension through warped plane Poiseuille flow, arbitrary Lagrangian--Eulerian (ALE) peristaltic pumping, and a two-way fluid--structure interaction (FSI) case with added-mass frequency shift. The results show that the proposed curvilinear LBM avoids interpolation-based transport, reduces geometry-locked numerical modes, preserves global mass and momentum to round-off accuracy in the tested warped periodic cases, and extends to wall-bounded ALE/FSI configurations with conservative treatment of mass and physically consistent momentum exchange.

title: Localization of generators of Markov processes via the Dynkin operator
text:
Title: Localization of generators of Markov processes via the Dynkin operator
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In this article, we consider a Feller process whose resolvent has the strong Feller property. Using the Dynkin operator of this process, we define local realizations of the generator on an open subset $U$ of its state space. In particular, this allows us to describe the generator of the process killed upon leaving a regular, open subset $U$ as a realization of a maximal operator subject to Dirichlet boundary conditions. Besides the definition via the Dynkin operator, we also consider other possible definitions of such a local realization: a definition in terms of the unkilled semigroup, a definition based on approximation with elements of the generator and a probabilistic definition using martingales. Under mild additional assumptions, we prove that all these definitions are equivalent.

title: OASIS: A Fast Dynamical Halo Finding Algorithm
text:
Title: OASIS: A Fast Dynamical Halo Finding Algorithm
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

In recent work (García et al. 2023), we advocated for defining a dynamical halo as the collection of particles that orbit their self-generated potential. Here we introduce the Orbiting-mass ASsIgnment Scheme (OASIS), a fast energy-based algorithm for constructing dynamical halo catalogs. Using single-snapshot information, OASIS achieves $\simeq 9\%$ scatter in orbiting mass estimates relative to the SPARTA particle-tracking algorithm. As an illustration of the applications enabled by OASIS, we use the Quijote and Erebos simulation suites to show that the $z=0$ dynamical halo mass function is nearly universal with respect to cosmology, and that it is well described by a modified Press-Schechter form with an effective collapse threshold $δ_{\rm sc} = 1.54$ at intermediate masses. However, this description fails at high masses.

title: A GPU-efficient local ADER finite-difference method for compressible-flow DNS
text:
Title: A GPU-efficient local ADER finite-difference method for compressible-flow DNS
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Algorithm design tailored to graphics processing units (GPUs) can substantially improve the efficiency of computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Efforts to adapt CFD solvers to GPUs often focus on spatial discretization, while time advancement commonly relies on multistage Runge--Kutta (RK) methods. However, these RK methods require repeated residual evaluations and full-domain operations, increasing the cost of compressible-flow direct numerical simulation (DNS). To reduce this overhead, we develop a local arbitrary high-order derivatives (ADER) finite-difference method that couples a compact ten-point quadratic predictor to a conservative central corrector through operator matching. With two quadrature nodes, one Picard correction, and selective dissipation, smooth convective tests recover third-order convergence under fixed-CFL refinement and near-seventh-order spatial behavior when background spatial error dominates. Temporal states remain kernel-local, and halo communication overlaps interior computation. Tests of smooth advection, periodic turbulence, and wall-bounded flows assess accuracy and flow statistics. On a $302^3$-node viscous Taylor--Green benchmark without heat conduction, throughput reaches 230.87 million node updates per second on one V100 GPU in double precision, 1.944 times that of spatially matched three-stage Runge--Kutta integration. Weak-scaling efficiency reaches 99.44\% from 4 to 32 V100 GPUs at 1.812 billion nodes.

title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
text:
Title: Think or Remember: The Exchange Rate of Agentic Inference
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Agents built on reasoning models resend their growing transcript at every call. Two transacting parties, not the model, decide what that costs: the client keeps or edits messages; the server decides whether earlier reasoning returns in the prompt and what its cache reuses. We define a cost model whose counts match an instrumented engine exactly; the architecture charges $c$ per token processed and $β$ per pair attended. Their ratio $P^*=c/β$ is an exchange rate between thinking and remembering: per token, processing dominates below this context length, a thinking regime, and attention above it, a memory regime. A policy change has a mechanical cost, incurred even if the agent writes the same tokens, and a behavioral one: it writes different tokens, changing cost and outcome. Serving alone can flip which policy is cheaper: on recorded Qwen3-8B ScienceWorld runs, dropping earlier reasoning costs 1.74 times keeping it when the server reuses generated states and 0.34 times when it reuses nothing. In live reruns, dropping it cuts correct HotpotQA answers by 9-23 percentage points on four models, at lower point-estimate cost. Comparing context policies means comparing systems: architecture and serving set the cost of the history kept and the work it induces.

title: Delayed Convergence of S-Parameter Sensitivities to Design Parameters in FDTD Simulations
text:
Title: Delayed Convergence of S-Parameter Sensitivities to Design Parameters in FDTD Simulations
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

In the finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) method, the sensitivities of S-parameters to design parameters come from discrete Fourier transforms of responses ending at a simulation time T. We show that, when a design parameter moves a resonance, the sensitivity converges later than the S-parameter. For a single mode with field decay time $τ$, the truncation error of the sensitivity is $(1+T/τ)e^{-T/τ}$, against $e^{-T/τ}$ for the resonant part of the S-parameter, so a 1% sensitivity error needs $T \geq 6.6τ$ instead of $4.6τ$. Automatic differentiation, the discrete adjoint and finite differences on the same run carry this error, so their agreement cannot reveal it. In three solvers, with no fitted parameter, the estimate predicts the simulated error within 4% at cavity resonances with $Q$ of 1000-7000; at lower $Q$ the error is larger. On a cavity whose slowest mode is weakly coupled, common end criteria leave $|S_{11}|$ within 0.5 dB of a 1.3 dB dip but its sensitivity 10-72% in error. A matrix-pencil extrapolation inside the differentiable computation recovers the sensitivity on a cavity with field probes from a run 66 times shorter. In a single-pole filter loop with a symmetric objective, truncation leaves the maximum of the objective in place, and the optimizer reaches the resonance of a full run despite the wrong gradient. With two coupled poles, the truncated objective moves the optimum: on runs of $1τ$ it over-couples by $Δk \approx 1.24/Q$, and an equal-ripple objective still shifts it by about $0.2\barα$ at $3τ$, but not at $4.6τ$.

title: Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
text:
Title: Bridging Gaps with Tensor Networks: From the Haldane Gap and Beyond
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Proofs generated by large language models are often difficult to understand, generalize, or formalize directly. Here we verify, digest, and formalize OpenAI's computer-assisted proof of a uniform gap in the periodic spin-1 Heisenberg chain using tensor-network diagrams and Lean 4. Reading the partition-function network along space and imaginary time shows how finite-ring bounds propagate across doubled lengths and inverse temperatures to all longer even rings, sharpening the spin-1 bound from the same finite inputs by a factor of 19 to $Δ_L > 0.0729$ for all even $L \geq 36$. We identify reflection positivity as the general condition behind the proof and certify uniform gaps in seven additional spin chains and ladders. More broadly, digesting machine-generated proofs into transparent physical mechanisms yields sharper bounds, broader theorems, and reusable formal verifications.

title: Density and Current Fluctuations for Run-and-Tumble Particles With and Without Interactions
text:
Title: Density and Current Fluctuations for Run-and-Tumble Particles With and Without Interactions
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study density and current fluctuations in a one-dimensional gas of run-and-tumble particles (RTPs), whose intrinsic velocities switch between two opposite values at a constant rate. We consider particles with and without pair interactions, including regularized Riesz gases, and also obtain corresponding results for Brownian particles. By linearizing the Dean-Kawasaki (DK) equations around a homogeneous stationary state, we compute density correlations and the variance of the integrated current through the origin. For repulsive Riesz interactions decaying as $1/|x|^s$ with $s>0$, this variance grows at long times as $t^{1/2}$ for $s>1$, but as $t^{s/(1+s)}$ for $0<s<1$. Starting from the same DK description, but retaining the Poisson statistics of direction reversals, we derive a macroscopic fluctuation theory (MFT) for RTPs with smooth pair interaction potential, which allows to compute the large time large deviation of the time integrated current. We show that, in the absence of interactions, the MFT saddle point equations can be solved explicitly using a generalized Cole-Hopf transform. This allows to recover and generalize previous results for the current distribution obtained by microscopic calculations, for RTPs with annealed or quenched step initial conditions. Beyond these distributions, MFT allows to compute the optimal density histories producing a prescribed current through the origin. We find that these density profiles, for both RTPs and Brownian particles, exhibit a nontrivial space-time structure. We also study stationary current fluctuations on an interval connected to reservoirs. Finally, we analyze the MFT equations perturbatively in the interaction. In both the infinite-line and reservoir geometries, we obtain explicit first-order corrections to the current generating functions for short-range interacting RTPs and Brownian particles.

title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
text:
Title: A complete analytical characterization of optimal collision-free motion for two robots
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Collision-free motion planning for multi-agent robotic systems remains an active research area because of the complexity of coordinating robot trajectories, with applications ranging from coordinated drone shows to autonomous operations on land, in the air, and on water. Importantly, the analytical difficulty of nonconvex collision-avoidance constraints has so far driven the development of exclusively numerical methods. We derive a complete analytical characterization of the optimal trajectories for two robots with zero initial and final velocities, under double-integrator dynamics and a squared-acceleration objective. We prove that these trajectories belong to eight distinct contact families and determine which family applies for each configuration of initial and final positions. We analyze the geometrical properties of the optimal trajectories and provide a numerical algorithm for computing them. These insights have already been adopted to improve the performance of numerical methods for multi-agent motion planning by several orders of magnitude.

title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
text:
Title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
text:
Title: Mechanistic Interpretability Needs a Logic of Inference
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Neural networks are increasingly studied not merely as predictive systems, but as complex systems whose internal computations are themselves objects of scientific inquiry. Recent progress in mechanistic interpretability (MI) has made it possible to identify neurons, features, circuits, population structures, and dynamical patterns associated with model behavior. As these tools improve, attention is shifting from what can be observed inside a model to how those observations support mechanistic explanations. We examine the parallel efforts of neuroscience and MI to address this question and identify recurring inferential bottlenecks when inferring mechanisms from complex neural systems. We propose five principles and organize them into a recursive logic for a more rigorous procedure of mechanistic inference. These principles provide a framework that supports scientific discovery in two senses: it helps turn local interpretability findings into cumulative knowledge of mechanisms within models, and it makes those mechanisms sufficiently precise to generate testable hypotheses about domains beyond the models. Evidence beyond MI is ultimately required to establish what model mechanisms reveal about the world.

title: Optimal summary statistics to constrain w0waCDM with the DESI BGS
text:
Title: Optimal summary statistics to constrain w0waCDM with the DESI BGS
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is the first stage-4 spectroscopic instrument installed on the 4-m Mayall Telescope at Kitt Peak National Observatory in Arizona. It contains 5000 robotically positioned fibers, allowing the measurement of as many galaxy spectra in one observation (~20 minutes). The data acquisition (2021--2028) aims at constraining the cosmological parameters, and especially the parameters describing the evolution of the dark energy with time. However, standard clustering analysis based on 2-point statistics only capture the Gaussian information of the matter density field, while the analytical models used to match these statistical probe are limited to quasi-linear scales, as they are based on perturbation theory. Therefore, the non-Gaussian and non-linear information of the density field is not exploited. To go beyond these limitations, several alternative clustering methods have been developed that rely on a simulation-based pipeline. In this presentation, we focus on the DESI Bright Galaxy Survey, a magnitude-limited sample of bright galaxies in the redshift range of 0.1 < z < 0.4. We present how accessing the non-linear and non-Gaussian information of the density field allows around 40% improvement on the constraints of some $Λ$CDM parameters. We are also extending the method to constrain w0waCDM in order to improve DESI's sensibility at low redshift where the Universe is dominated by dark energy.

title: PyCC: A Reference Quantum Chemistry Python Package for Education, Validation, and Rapid Prototyping
text:
Title: PyCC: A Reference Quantum Chemistry Python Package for Education, Validation, and Rapid Prototyping
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

PyCC is a Python-based quantum chemistry package that emphasizes coupled cluster and related methods. Developed over the last five years, PyCC's purpose is to provide a clear reference implementation that will serve as a validation suite for production code, a platform for rapid prototyping and testing of new methods, and an educational resource for newcomers to the field. The package covers both closed- and open-shell single-determinant references in spatial- and spin-orbital formulations for the coupled cluster hierarchy through triples-including methods such as CC3, as well as for MP2 and CI methods. PyCC provides a broad range of molecular properties such as analytic first and second energy derivatives including gradients, Hessians, polarizabilities and atomic polar tensors, as well as non-energy-derivative properties, such as velocity-gauge atomic polar tensors and diagonal Born-Oppenheimer corrections, plus dynamic linear response functions, and excitation energies. The package includes a number of unique capabilities, such as real-time CC propagation (up through CC3), atomic axial tensors for simulating vibrational circular dichroism spectra at the MP2 and CI levels, and local correlation methods including perturbation-aware correlation domains. The code is designed around a shared Wavefunction base and a method-agnostic derivative layer that enables a new method to inherit the full property set once it supplies its reduced densities and their first-order responses. PyCC is fully open source and available on GitHub under the BSD 3-clause license.

title: Multi-excited random walks on general trees
text:
Title: Multi-excited random walks on general trees
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study multi-excited random walks on infinite locally finite trees. The model is described by placing a stack of ``cookies'' at each vertex, with one cookie consumed on each successive visit. As long as cookies remain, the walk is in an excited regime and makes nearest-neighbour steps according to a prescribed sequence of biases. Once the stack is exhausted, the walk is in a non-excited regime and moves uniformly among the neighbouring vertices. The model is closely connected to foraging ecology, where repeated visits to a location can deplete local resources and thereby influence the attractiveness of that location for future visits. We prove that the process exhibits a sharp phase transition between recurrence and transience. The critical threshold is determined by the branching-ruin number of the tree, which is equal to the Hausdorff dimension of the tree's boundary under a suitable metric. Our result substantially extends Zerner's recurrence-transience criterion for multi-excited random walks on $\mathbb Z$ [Probab. Theory Related Fields 133 (2005)] to general trees.

title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Title: Clinical predictions using artificial intelligence in neurosurgery and its subspecialties: a systematic review and meta-analysis
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Artificial intelligence models for clinical prediction are proliferating across neurosurgery, but their aggregate discriminative performance, distribution along the care pathway and methodological quality are unclear. We systematically reviewed and meta-analysed these studies in neurosurgery and its subspecialities along with their risk of bias appraisal. We performed a PRISMA search for peer-reviewed original studies using AI to predict a clinical outcome in neurosurgical populations. Metrics were pooled using random effects modelling. Each study was classified as diagnostic, prognostic or forecasting and was assigned an evidence level. Clinical prediction task sub-stratification analysis was performed. Risk-of-bias was assessed using PROBAST. 1063 studies were included. Across 451 studies reporting AUC, pooled discrimination was 0.86, ranging from 0.84 (spine) to 0.87 (neuro-oncology), with extreme heterogeneity. Performance varied by clinical pathway stage, highest for diagnosis, grading and molecular tasks and lowest for post-operative tasks. Only 51 studies were using prospective data with external validation, whereas 619 rested on internal validation alone or no validation. 89 percent studies were at high risk-of-bias, driven by the analysis domain. AI models report high performance across all the neurosurgical subspecialities, concordant across AUC, accuracy, sensitivity and specificity and robust to risk-of-bias stratification. Performance is highest for imaging-anchored diagnostic tasks and lowest at decision-facing post-operative stage. However, the literature is dominated by optimism-prone, internally-validated and poorly calibrated models with extreme heterogeneity. External validation, calibration analysis and reporting guidelines adherence remain prerequisites for clinical adoption.

title: Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape: A Field-Theoretic Approach to Fluctuation-Induced Tumor Relapse
text:
Title: Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape: A Field-Theoretic Approach to Fluctuation-Induced Tumor Relapse
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Classical mathematical oncology employs deterministic mean-field models predicting that sufficiently high chemotherapy doses drive tumor density to zero. We show that this apparent cure is an artifact of neglecting demographic fluctuations. We construct a nonequilibrium stochastic PK-PD field theory combining a two-compartment pharmacokinetic model with a stochastic tumor-immune sector in the Doi-Peliti formalism, then map it to coupled multiplicative Langevin equations via the Martin-Siggia-Rose/Janssen-De Dominicis approach. In immune-depleted sanctuary sites, the dynamics reduce to a time-dependent Feller diffusion whose Fokker-Planck equation yields an analytical survival functional: demographic noise implies a strictly nonzero relapse probability for tumor micro-clusters under high-dose chemotherapy. Standard bolus administration acts as a nonselective annihilation process, driving immune fields into an absorbing state and creating a spatially immune-depleted vacuum that enables fluctuation-induced relapse -- Stochastic Pharmacokinetic Escape. We derive quantitative conditions under which metronomic dosing and adjuvant immunotherapy suppress this stochastic window of vulnerability. A model-agnostic analysis of 1461 longitudinal patient records shows that the majority of evaluable lesions exhibit a nadir followed by measurable regrowth rather than monotonic elimination; fitting the model's drift functional to these trajectories reproduces this pattern quantitatively, and a direct test of the predicted demographic-noise scaling law reveals size-dependent noise largest at the smallest observed tumor volumes, consistent with the proposed mechanism.

title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability
text:
Title: Heavy tails in Gaussian-process surrogates: process-level profiling degeneracy versus observation-level identifiability
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

In this article, we study heavy-tailed alternatives to Gaussian-process surrogates, namely Student-$t$ processes, $α$-stable processes and Gaussian processes with heavy-tailed noise. These are Gaussian scale mixtures, and the position of the mixing variable decides whether the tails can be learned from a single realization. For process-level mixtures with a free amplitude, the profile likelihood of the mixing law is data-free and is maximized by the Gaussian law, the plug-in predictive is a data-free transformation of the Gaussian-process predictive, and no estimator can be consistent for the mixing law over the model along one path. For observation-level mixtures with symmetric $α$-stable noise, the tail index is identifiable. Further, for one-dimensional inputs under fixed-domain asymptotics with $α_0<2$ and compact hyperparameter sets, a cross-fitted plug-in estimator and the Laplace marginal-likelihood estimate computed at the global posterior mode attain the efficiency bound of the model with a known regression function, also for Matérn-$5/2$ sample paths. We also characterize small-sample failures of the Laplace approximation as folds of a posterior-mode branch and give a diagnostic. Finally, in a repeated Bayesian optimization study, observation-level tails reduced regret under gross outliers, as did Student-$t$ noise, and no degradation was detected under Gaussian noise.

title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
text:
Title: One-shot Distributed Learning via Weighted Averaging with Server-side Information
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Distributed learning has drawn considerable attention due to its capability of learning from distributed data without aggregating raw observations. However, frequent exchange of model updates can become the main bottleneck of communication. Therefore, one-shot approaches where each worker fits a local model and sends it to the server to aggregate emerge. It is known that averaging can achieve the so-called pooled-data mean squared error (MSE) order of a hypothetical node that has access to data from the server and all the workers, and performs empirical risk minimization (ERM) on it. However, when the number of workers increases too fast compared to the local sample size, nonzero local estimation bias prevents averaging from achieving this order. In this paper, we study whether independent server data can overcome this limitation. We consider $m$ workers with $n$ observations each and a server with $p$ observations, all i.i.d., giving $N=mn+p$ observations in total. Under certain regularity conditions, a pooled-data ERM achieves MSE of order $\mathcal O(N^{-1})$. We analyze deterministic nonnegative averaging of convex-loss M-estimators, with equal worker weights and the server's own estimator included. Under our assumptions, including nonzero local bias of order $n^{-α}$, $α\geq1$, sample-size weighted averaging achieves the pooled-data MSE order whenever $m=\mathcal O(n^{2α-1})$. Above this worker scale, it does so if and only if $p=Ω(nm\cdot m/n^{2α-1})$. Hence, server-only estimation, whose MSE is of order $\mathcal{O}(p^{-1})$, can achieve pooled-data order while sample-size weighting fails. Analytical examples and synthetic experiments illustrate when averaging matches the pooled-data MSE order, complemented by CIFAR-10 experiments comparing aggregation strategies with linear and nonlinear classifiers.

title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
text:
Title: Regularization vs. Convolution in Kernel-Based Hypothesis Testing
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

The maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) test is a popular nonparametric test on general domains. Two lines of work have studied its optimality through structurally different approaches. The first, a convolution approach on $\mathbb{R}^d$, uses translation-invariant kernels with a shrinking bandwidth and is minimax optimal over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation; the second, a regularization approach on general measurable spaces, uses spectral regularization of the kernel covariance operator and is minimax optimal over Hellinger- and $χ^2$-separated alternatives. In this paper, we study the regularization approach over Sobolev balls under $L^2$-separation, which reveals the connection between the two approaches. We show that, with a translation-invariant kernel on $\mathbb{R}^d$, both are ways of meeting a single condition on the kernel's spectral density: the spectral regularized discrepancy captures the $L^2$-separation $Δ$ of a Sobolev alternative of smoothness $s$ as soon as the regularization parameter $λ$ is below the spectral density on frequencies up to $Δ^{-1/(2s)}$. A kernel with a shrinking bandwidth $h$ meets this condition with $λ\asymp h^d$, and under this coupling the constant regularizer, which gives the MMD test itself, attains the Sobolev minimax rate. This explains, from a spectral perspective, the need for a shrinking bandwidth in the convolution approach. With a non-constant spectral regularizer, our analysis requires the bandwidth to shrink only when the spectral density decays faster than any polynomial, as for the Gaussian kernel. Thus, for Matérn and Laplace kernels, a fixed bandwidth with $λ\to 0$ attains the Sobolev minimax rate. Finally, an adaptive test over a grid of bandwidths and regularization parameters is minimax optimal, up to a $\log\log$ factor, over both classes without prior knowledge of the smoothness.

title: Conformal Bootstrap Unblocked
text:
Title: Conformal Bootstrap Unblocked
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We develop a novel conformal bootstrap formulated directly in terms of conformal symmetry, reflection positivity, and crossing symmetry, without explicitly relying on the operator product expansion or conformal blocks. By constructing Gram matrices from states created by pairs of local operators and imposing spectral constraints through conformal generators, we obtain a hierarchy of semidefinite programs that directly constrain correlation functions. We demonstrate the method in one to three dimensions, obtaining correlator and spectral bounds that capture generalized free field behavior and reproduce the characteristic Ising kinks in two and three dimensions. We further show that joint positivity of states at different insertion configurations naturally constrains correlators away from self-dual kinematics.

title: The "Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery" Workshop: A Community Roadmap for the Future of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory After the LSST
text:
Title: The "Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery" Workshop: A Community Roadmap for the Future of the Vera C. Rubin Observatory After the LSST
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

The NSF-DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory will complete its ten-year Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) in the mid-2030s. Its 8.4 m aperture and 9.6 square degree field of view give it an étendue unmatched by any facility planned for that era. The Rubin 2036: Opportunities for Discovery workshop (KIPAC/SLAC, 3-5 August 2026) brought together approximately 100 participants to discuss Rubin's future after LSST. This paper summarizes the workshop's structure and discussions across five working groups. The continued-surveying group explored a machine-learning foundation model pretrained on Rubin imaging for detection, deblending, and classification. The cadence group considered allocating post-LSST observing time and strategies for transiting exoplanets, Type Ia supernova cosmology, time-delay cosmography, and second-scale transients. The filter group explored broadband, medium-band, and narrowband filters for photometric redshifts, high-redshift large-scale structure, AGN reverberation mapping, Galactic archaeology, and emission-line imaging. The multi-messenger group explored follow-up of next-generation gravitational-wave and neutrino sources, including standard sirens, kilonovae, and Galactic supernovae. The technology group organized options by cost and lead time, including fast readout, new filters, a faster shutter, and summit edge computing. Cross-cutting topics included AI/ML, Chilean and Latin-American co-leadership, satellite megaconstellations, and weather and climate trends at Cerro Pachón. White papers and workshop talks are available through https://zenodo.org/communities/rubin2036workshop/ and https://rubin-observatory.github.io/Rubin-Beyond-LSST/pages/Rubin2036proceedings/.

title: Sudden disappearance of a bright exciton in solid helium
text:
Title: Sudden disappearance of a bright exciton in solid helium
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Excitons, bound electron-hole pairs, are investigated extensively in optical spectra, where their wave vector is considered to be vanishing. Excitonic spectra as a function of wave vector are much less explored, both theoretically and with measurements of the loss function. Here, we uncover a striking angular dependence of excitonic spectra for the prototypical case of solid helium, where a prominent excitonic peak is completely suppressed for a momentum transfer in certain directions. The effect is entirely due to the electron-hole exchange interaction. This phenomenon leads to a counter-intuitive effect close to Bragg points, where an infinitesimal change of direction of wave vector is sufficient to change the spectrum dramatically. We explain in which way the nature of excitons makes such a scenario possible. We discuss the pressure dependence, point to experimental evidence for our findings, and predict under which circumstances dramatic angular dependencies may also be found in other materials.

title: GPCR Ligand Bioactivity Prediction with Physics-Informed Dual-State Query Learning
text:
Title: GPCR Ligand Bioactivity Prediction with Physics-Informed Dual-State Query Learning
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Predicting the bioactivity profiles of small molecules against G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) is a challenge in drug discovery. Although deep learning has accelerated the prediction of binding affinities, existing approaches often struggle to distinguish between functional efficacies because they neglect dynamic conformational equilibria. Furthermore, structure-based methods are frequently limited by the scarcity of high-resolution active-state crystal structures and the indistinguishability of conformational states in static representations. To bridge the gap between black-box prediction and biophysical reality, we propose Dual-State Query (DSQ), a physics-informed multimodal architecture that explicitly embeds the Monod-Wyman-Changeux (MWC) model of allostery within a neural network. Unlike conventional models that rely on explicit 3D structures, DSQ utilizes learnable orthogonal queries to extract disentangled representations of active and inactive receptor states. These latent representations are governed by a novel neural MWC gating module, which mathematically derives the probability of receptor activation from thermodynamic competition between ligand-state affinities and the receptor's intrinsic conformational energy barrier. A contrastive ranking objective is also introduced to enforce differential affinity constraints, ensuring physical consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DSQ outperforms other baselines, particularly for the agonist subset. Additional homology-stratified, temperature-sensitivity, perturbation, clustering, and efficiency analyses show that DSQ provides useful thermodynamic inductive bias, while also exposing a clear limitation on low-homology receptors. The code is available at https://github.com/jiankliu/DSQ.

title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
text:
Title: Agentic Distributional Regression: Conditional Density Estimation through Agent-Written Programs
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Artificial intelligence offers statisticians a new paradigm for modelling and analysing complex datasets. Agents based on large language models can reason about data and automate key stages of the statistical modelling workflow, from model fitting to validation. In this paper we propose a method that uses such an agent to estimate the conditional density of a response given a vector of covariates from an iid sample. The agent examines the sample, chooses a model for the conditional distribution of the response and the procedure to fit it, and returns the estimator as a short computer program. The program is built from a library of probability distributions. The returned law can therefore be a parametric distribution, a mixture or a multivariate factorization, with distribution parameters given by explicit formulas in the covariates. We call this approach agentic distributional regression (ADR). Unlike in the classical approach, the statistician no longer chooses the estimator, but asks an agent to build one. Treating the returned program as a random conditional density estimator, we derive a finite-sample error bound under assumptions on the number of admissible models and on the accuracy of the agent's fit, and an oracle inequality for the selection of a model among fitted candidates using independent validation data. Finally, assuming that, as the sample size grows, the agent selects the same smooth parametric model with probability tending to one and fits it accurately, we show that the estimated parameters are asymptotically normal. In simulation studies, on twelve real datasets and on a new dataset whose responses postdate the agents' training data, ADR with Claude Opus 5.5 has the best average performance among the existing methods from the statistical literature with which it is compared.

title: Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation
text:
Title: Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.

title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
text:
Title: How Much Conversation History Does an AI Agent Need?
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

How does using less conversational history change reader-token use and benchmark scores? We examine this question on 1,100 BEAM questions. We held the retrieval ranking and reader constant across five fixed passage budgets, and mean assigned scores rose as the passage budget grew. The score gain per additional token became smaller at the upper tested budgets. Answerable questions generally received higher scores with more context. Pooled abstention scores sometimes rose as the passage budget shrank. We also tested message retention in a controlled task with explicit conversational-state targets and compared retained user messages with token-matched recency. Qwen matched the full state more often for direct requirements when user messages were retained. Its full-state matching declined when answers depended on references to earlier offers. Mistral produced near-floor results across the retention conditions. A scoring audit leaves the correctness of BEAM answers unresolved. These experiments characterize the token and score consequences of the tested memory budgets. Reliable budget selection depends on retaining the evidence each question requires and validating the measure used to assess answer quality.

title: NuPaD: A Generative AI Framework for Fostering Deep Learning in Subatomic Physics
text:
Title: NuPaD: A Generative AI Framework for Fostering Deep Learning in Subatomic Physics
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education has introduced a critical pedagogical paradox: while these systems possess extraordinary capacity for information retrieval and synthesis, their default operational mode of supplying immediate, unprompted answers actively undermines the cognitive processes upon which genuine scientific understanding is built. This paper presents NuPaD (Nuclear \& Particle Physics -- Deep Learning Tutor), a novel pedagogical framework designed for the graduate-level subatomic physics curriculum. For such advanced courses, instruction naturally shifts toward inquiry-driven, problem-based learning, making it an ideal environment to use GenAI to explore complex, open-ended physical questions rather than merely querying established facts. The framework consists of three tightly coupled and easy-to-use components: a primary agent instruction file that enforces a structured problem-based learning protocol, a purpose-built textbook optimized for precise parsing by privacy-preserving local GenAI, and a concise companion file that bridges the knowledge gap between the textbook and GenAI, alongside a comprehensive dynamic skill set for specialized tasks. We explain in detail the architectural principles of the modular NuPaD framework, the design philosophy of the Markdown-native textbook format, and the underlying GenAI regulation principles. By redefining the interaction loop between student and model, this framework transforms GenAI from a passive answer engine into an active, personalized tutor, ensuring that it accelerates rather than bypasses the development of deep learning and scientific reasoning.

title: Spectral measures and sharpness of quantum speed limits
text:
Title: Spectral measures and sharpness of quantum speed limits
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Quantum speed limits bound the time required for a given state to evolve into a given subspace of the Hilbert space under specific energy constraints. We prove that for several standard orthogonalization time bounds, the unique spectral measure associated with the initial vector that saturates the bound is a sum of two Dirac measures. Furthermore, we constrain the families of spectral measures that come arbitrarily close to these bounds and construct examples with measures which are purely absolutely continuous and purely singular continuous with respect to the Lebesgue measure. As a complementary perspective, we discuss the geometric intuition behind quantum speed limits provided by the numerical range of the evolution operator.

title: Many Brains, One Geometry: A Shared Visual-Semantic Space for Cross-Dataset fMRI Decoding
text:
Title: Many Brains, One Geometry: A Shared Visual-Semantic Space for Cross-Dataset fMRI Decoding
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Visual decoding from fMRI is typically siloed by participant and experiment, obscuring whether heterogeneous neural measurements can be organized within a common computational geometry. Here we introduce BRAID-fMRI (Brain Representation Alignment across Individuals and Datasets), a shared CLIP-supervised decoding framework. BRAID-fMRI uses a single ROI-wise Transformer with optional participant conditioning across eight visual-fMRI datasets comprising 93 dataset-specific participant entries, 430,007 single-trial responses and 162,839 unique stimuli. Regional brain activity is aligned with 512-dimensional CLIP ViT-B/32 representations using a multi-positive contrastive objective that treats repeated stimuli across participants and datasets as positives. BRAID-fMRI supports retrieval across seven evaluation datasets. On eight matched participant entries, it achieves 35.0 +/- 11.1% Top-10 accuracy, exceeding the observed mean accuracy of the two evaluated baselines - the MindEye-style pooled-CLIP decoder (27.1 +/- 5.1%) and ridge regression (21.1 +/- 9.1%) - and attaining the highest observed accuracy for seven of eight entries. In separately trained participant-agnostic models, expanding the source pool increased target-dataset holdout accuracy by up to 92.1% relative to the initial source-training condition. The learned space preserves graded semantic structure, while ablations and saliency highlight ventral and early visual cortex and category-specific motion and attentional systems. These results support scalable cross-dataset decoding into a common CLIP-aligned space, with model sensitivity concentrated in ventral and early visual inputs.

title: Recovering Missing Degrees of Freedom in Simulation-Trained Field-Level Generative Models
text:
Title: Recovering Missing Degrees of Freedom in Simulation-Trained Field-Level Generative Models
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Simulation-trained generative models are emerging as a powerful framework for field-level inference in cosmology, particularly in strongly nonlinear regimes where analytical approaches become intractable.
