On the worldsheet, cancelling the fermionic boundary terms requires introducing a specific closed two-form in the boundary action, and its contribution to the bosonic boundary conditions reproduces precisely these worldvolume fields. We then construct field-dependent reflection matrices that lift the boundary conditions to gluing conditions for the Cagnazzo--Zarembo Lax connection and describe displacements along geodesics normal to the brane. The resulting double-row monodromy matrix generates infinitely many conserved charges, which establishes the classical integrability of the open superstring for any mixture of fluxes. In AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$, these branes are expected to be dual to conformal interfaces in a deformation of the symmetric product orbifold of T$^4$.

title: On phases of 4d $Spin/SO$ Yang-Mills theories
text:
Title: On phases of 4d $Spin/SO$ Yang-Mills theories
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We study the low-temperature phase diagrams of $Spin(N)/SO(N)_\pm$ Yang-Mills theories as functions of the $θ$-parameter. In particular, for every even integer $N\geq 4$, we find a phase diagram consistent with the center/CP mixed anomaly, via the technique of mixed gauge theory. The resulting phase diagrams are in perfect agreement with the phase diagrams of $Spin(N)/SO(N)_\pm$ super Yang-Mills theory softly broken by a small gaugino mass. In the case of $Spin(4k)$ Yang-Mills for an integer $k\geq 2$, only two phases appear in the phase diagram, while in the $Spin(4)$ case the phase diagram contains four SPT phases protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_2\times \mathbb{Z}_2$ center symmetry. In the case of $Spin(4k+2)$ Yang-Mills for a positive integer $k$, the phase diagram contains four SPT phases protected by the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ center symmetry.

title: Cosmological Backreaction and the Separate Universe Conjecture: Dynamical volume partitioning of Newtonian cosmologies
text:
Title: Cosmological Backreaction and the Separate Universe Conjecture: Dynamical volume partitioning of Newtonian cosmologies
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

We provide a description of general Newtonian cosmologies for collisionless matter in terms of an exact and dynamical volume partitioning of global realizations of Newtonian models. Employing the formalism for the description of cosmological backreaction, an interaction between the inhomogeneities of the formation of structures in the Universe and their average properties can be analyzed. Our results can be regarded as a tool for many potential applications in the context of Newtonian simulations, but they also provide an exact way to assume analytical properties of the universe models on regional scales in conformity with global integral constraints on their average properties. We discuss approaches in relation to `separate Universe conjectures' in the literature and examine their consistency with the exact partitioning framework. In particular, using the Average Expansion Rate Approximation (AvERA) as an example, we show that identifying locally assigned Friedmannian rates with physical regional expansion rates is constrained by the global Newtonian 3-torus condition. Alternatively, when the simulation cells are interpreted as non-material control volumes, Reynolds transport introduces mass flux and flux-backreaction terms, so that their dynamics is not in general that of independent Friedmann domains. We also discuss the corresponding consistency conditions for stable clustering prescriptions.

title: Resonant electroweak clouds around Schwarzschild black holes
text:
Title: Resonant electroweak clouds around Schwarzschild black holes
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We construct nonlinear electroweak clouds around Schwarzschild black holes in the bosonic Weinberg-Salam theory. These configurations are supported by harmonically time-dependent charged gauge fields, while their energy-momentum tensor remains static. Regularity at the horizon imposes a resonance condition relating the field frequency to the horizon electrostatic potential. Unlike linear clouds, these solutions exhibit a finite mass and electric charge gap, and exist only up to a maximal horizon size. We obtain both magnetic and electric clouds, including spherically symmetric and dipolar configurations, which reduce to electroweak balls in the vanishing-horizon limit. We also report a new family of dipolar electroweak balls, which can be energetically favoured over their spherical counterparts at fixed electric charge. Our results, obtained in the probe limit for electroweak couplings away from their measured values, establish a new realization of nonlinear resonant vector hair in a non-Abelian gauge-Higgs theory.

title: Advancing Alzheimer's Disease Treatment: Synergistic Ligand Combinations Targeting BACE1 via Multi-Ligand Simultaneous Docking
text:
Title: Advancing Alzheimer's Disease Treatment: Synergistic Ligand Combinations Targeting BACE1 via Multi-Ligand Simultaneous Docking
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Alzheimer's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by memory loss, cognitive decline, and behavioral changes, primarily affecting the elderly. Current treatments focus on symptom management as no therapies effectively halt or reverse disease progression. Newer therapies targeting BACE1, a key enzyme in amyloid plaque formation, have shown promise in clinical trials, though they have been limited by side effects and insufficient efficacy in slowing cognitive decline. This is the first study where multi-ligand simultaneous docking (MLSD) was employed to identify potential synergistic inhibitor combinations from among thousands of small molecules that could yield better results than the current phase-III inhibitors of BACE1. The recent phase III drugs such as Atabecestat, Elenbecestat, Lanabecestat, and Verubecestat were considered to be standards for comparison in this study. A library of small molecules with known IC50 values against BACE1 was filtered for flagging Pan-Assay Interference (PAINS) and "Brenk" compounds. Single-ligand docking revealed individual ligand interactions with the protein, forming the basis for creating ligand pairs tested in MLSD. Among these combinations, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3656158, CHEMBL4078427 and CHEMBL3695732, Verubecestat and CHEMBL3656158, and CHEMBL4078427 and Lanabecestat demonstrated excellent binding affinity of -19.90 kcal/mol, -18.45 kcal/mol, -18.07 kcal/mol, and -17.67 kcal/mol with the protein, which is significantly greater than those of phase-III inhibitors, along with inter-ligand interactions indicative of a synergistic effect. These findings underscore the transformative potential of MLSD in identifying synergistic compound interactions, paving the way for novel combination therapies in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease.

title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
text:
Title: TCSExam: Evaluating Frontier LLMs on the Full Range of TCS Research
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Can large language models (LLMs) advance theoretical computer science and resolve its long-standing open conjectures? To study progress toward this goal, we introduce TCSExam, a unified framework and benchmark covering the full range of TCS research. It evaluates theorem proving, solver engineering, and constructions alongside direct attempts to resolve open conjectures, capturing both concrete research accomplishments and progress toward long-standing research goals. TCSExam-Full contains 100 expert-reviewed tasks, with submissions checked by the Lean kernel or an executable task checker. TCSExam-Lite selects 20 tasks, five per track, reducing the number of task attempts by 80% at the same per-attempt budget. We evaluate eight agents on Full and nine on Lite. The TCSExam Index combines all four tracks: GPT-6 Astra leads Full (71.9), and Opus 5.5 leads Lite (72.3). Full and Lite rankings are strongly aligned across eight shared agents (Spearman's $ρ=0.93$), supporting Lite as a compact, discriminative benchmark. The evaluations yield improved solver outputs and mathematical constructions, together with independently verified special cases and bounds from open-conjecture attempts. TCSExam provides an extensible framework with task sources, Docker build recipes, and evaluation tools for reproducible use.

title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
text:
Title: Benchmarking Large Language Models on Heterogeneous Cognitive and Biomedical Knowledge Graphs: The Role of Graph Grounding in Multi-Hop Reasoning and Hallucination Mitigation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in biomedical and cognitive neuroscience, but their ability to reason reliably over heterogeneous knowledge graphs (KGs) remains unclear. We benchmark five LLMs (GPT-5.1, Gemini 2.0 Pro, Llama 3, Qwen, and BioGPT) across five KGs: DrugBank, NeuroSynth, Cognitive Atlas, Brain Map, and GDPKG. We introduce a multitier query dataset to evaluate reasoning depth and factual accuracy under KG-aware (graph-grounded) and KG-agnostic conditions. Inter-annotator agreement was substantial, with Cohen's kappa of 0.781 (range: 0.753-0.807) and Fleiss' kappa of 0.77. Results show that general-purpose models, particularly GPT-5.1 and Gemini 2.0 Pro, generally outperform domain-specific models on multi-hop and high-level reasoning tasks, although performance declines as query complexity increases. KG grounding reduces hallucination rates across all evaluated models. Contrary to our initial hypothesis, domain-specific models do not consistently outperform general-purpose models on specialized tasks without graph grounding. These findings highlight the value of combining broad language-model capabilities with structured domain knowledge. We provide practical guidance for selecting LLM-KG integration strategies based on task complexity and computational constraints, and discuss hybrid neurosymbolic architectures for personalized medicine, cognitive disorder diagnosis, and explainable AI.

title: A Post-Quantum Interactive Hashing Theorem
text:
Title: A Post-Quantum Interactive Hashing Theorem
Domain: Quantum Physics (quant-ph)

Interactive hashing, introduced by Ostrovsky, Venkatesan, and Yung [OVY93], is a building block in many cryptographic protocols, including perfectly hiding commitments from one-way permutations [NOVY92]. Its multi-output generalization is a key ingredient in constructions of statistical zero-knowledge arguments for NP and statistically hiding commitments from arbitrary one-way functions [NOV06,HR07]. In this note, we give a post-quantum security proof for this multi-output interactive hashing protocol with arbitrary relations.

title: Decoupling Across Dimensions
text:
Title: Decoupling Across Dimensions
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

We present a prescription for identifying decoupled sectors of 4d SCFTs obtained from compactifications of branes. Central to our analysis is the comparison of anomaly polynomials obtained via field-theoretic reduction versus anomaly inflow. Our flagship examples are the 4d $\mathcal{N}=1$ SCFTs obtained by compactifying the 6d $(1,0)$ theory from M5-branes probing a $\mathbb{C}^2/\mathbb{Z}_2$ orbifold singularity on a torus with flux. The anomaly polynomial of the interacting fixed point is known to decompose into the $T^2$ reduction of the 6d anomaly polynomial, plus a contribution from flip fields introduced to remove operators from the spectrum. Adopting the inflow perspective, the contribution from the flipped sector is obtained as the difference between inflow anomaly polynomials in the singular and resolved geometries, which we efficiently compute using equivariant localization. Helpfully, the 4d SCFTs admit two dual quiver gauge theory descriptions: $Y^{p,q}$ quiver gauge theories, and class $\mathcal{S}_2$ necklace quivers obtained from trinions. We study the interacting and decoupled sectors on both sides of the duality and construct an explicit map between their chiral rings, identifying a range of parameter space for which the quivers flow to apparently different interacting fixed points. Each chiral ring generator is furthermore matched to an M2-brane wrapping a 2-cycle in the resolved M-theory geometry.

title: Multi-Step Performance Estimation for Gradient Descent under the Polyak Lojasiewicz Condition
text:
Title: Multi-Step Performance Estimation for Gradient Descent under the Polyak Lojasiewicz Condition
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Gradient descent is a fundamental algorithm in machine learning and statistical inference. Performance estimation provides a systematic framework for obtaining sharp convergence bounds through semidefinite programming. We study the worst-case performance of constant-stepsize gradient descent over the class of $L$-smooth functions satisfying the $μ$-Polyak--Łojasiewicz (PŁ) inequality. We formulate the $N$-step objective-gap analysis as a semidefinite programming (SDP) relaxation based on pairwise smoothness constraints and pointwise PŁ inequalities. Since an exact interpolation condition for smooth PŁ functions is not currently available, the resulting SDP provides a valid upper bound on the true worst-case performance. We solve a reduced SDP retaining only consecutive-pair smoothness constraints analytically for every horizon $N$ and every stepsize $t\in(0,2/L)$. The solution exhibits three stepsize regimes. For $0<t\leq 1/L$ and $1/L<t\leq \sqrt{3}/L$, the reduced and full pairwise SDPs have the same optimal value, and the one-step SDP contraction factor tensorizes to a geometric $N$-step rate. For $\sqrt{3}/L<t<2/L$, the reduced-SDP value is nongeometric in the horizon: an initial transient phase is followed by eventual geometric decay. The resulting asymptotic contraction factor is tight for the full pairwise SDP and strictly improves the bound obtained by recursively applying the one-step estimate. Explicit primal and dual feasible solutions certify the results, with numerical SDP experiments guiding their construction. Our results show that analyzing several iterations together can give a better convergence bound than repeatedly applying the sharp one-step SDP bound in the Regime III.

title: Basis Functions for Time-Dependent Kohn-Sham Inversion
text:
Title: Basis Functions for Time-Dependent Kohn-Sham Inversion
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Floquet theory provides insight into the inversion of time-dependent Kohn-Sham density functional theory. Specifically, mathematical derivations show that the fundamental frequencies of a time-dependent wavefunction solution are the leading-order harmonics for the TD-KS state. Numerical tests of the resulting ansatz in 1D and 3D for atomic and molecular cases demonstrate its utility. In particular, low $L_{2}$ errors in the time-dependent density and longitudinal current were found, even though currents were not an explicit optimization objective. In all, the proposed inversion ansatz provides exchange-correlation potentials from time-dependent wavefunctions, is highly interpretable, and may significantly help in the development of nonadiabatic density functionals.

title: Deterministic Oracle Complexity for Goldstein Stationarity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Constraints
text:
Title: Deterministic Oracle Complexity for Goldstein Stationarity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Constraints
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We consider the deterministic oracle complexity of finding a $(δ,ε)$-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function under constraints. The problem is posed in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $d$ denotes the dimension; constraints are specified either by a closed feasible set or by a single explicit inequality. For closed feasible sets that are star-shaped with respect to an interior ball, including all convex bodies, we use a resisting-oracle construction to show that every deterministic algorithm needs $Ω(ε^{-2})$ objective-oracle calls in the worst case when $d\gtrsimε^{-2}$ and $δ\lesssimε$. For explicit inequalities satisfying uniform Goldstein constraint qualification and strict feasibility, finding Goldstein KKT stationary points requires exponentially many oracle calls in $d$ in the worst case, even at fixed stationarity accuracy. This exponential dependence holds under dimension-independent constraint regularity and strict-feasibility bounds, with a sufficiently small neighborhood radius and complementary slackness error. The result covers common constraints such as ball and box constraints and also allows nonconvex feasible regions. For convex coercive constraints with a Slater point, the resisting-oracle argument also gives an $Ω(ε^{-2})$ oracle-call bound in the same dimension and radius regime while allowing a larger complementary slackness error. These results hold for all deterministic algorithms using a local oracle, whether or not the returned point was queried. Each constructed objective has a strictly feasible global minimizer; the lower bounds therefore concern the information required to find stationary points, not their existence.

title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
text:
Title: Finite-Sample LTI System Identification from a Misspecified Finite Model Set
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

We consider the problem of finite-sample identification of an unknown LTI system from a finite hypothesis class. In contrast to existing results that assume the hypothesis class contains the true system, we consider the misspecified setting, where the true system does not belong to the hypothesis class. We first characterize the resulting estimation target and its dependence on the data-generation scheme. We then establish a finite-sample lower bound on the failure probability that any identification algorithm must incur. Finally, we analyze the robustness of an existing exponential weighting-based identification algorithm to the misspecification and derive a finite-sample upper bound on its failure probability. Our results illustrate when using a misspecified finite hypothesis class can provide an advantage over identification without prior knowledge of the candidate systems.

title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
text:
Title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
text:
Title: Treating the Model as an Untrusted Component: Deterministic Policy Enforcement, Human Approval and Taint Tracking Against Prompt Injection in Tool-Using Agents, with Validation on Open-Weights Models
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Tool-using LLM agents act on instructions embedded in the data they read, so prompt injection is a structural rather than a prompt-wording problem. We compare in-prompt defences (hardened prompts, spotlighting, LLM detectors) with deterministic enforcement outside the model (four reference monitors of increasing strength), human approval and taint tracking, judged by one effect-based oracle independent of every defence in an executable environment of 13 tasks and 12 tools, with argument-fuzzing attackers and severity-weighted harm. In an evaluation with real open-weights models (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Qwen2.5-7B; 156 attack episodes per defence and model), the models proposed the attacker's call in 64% and 84% of attack episodes behind the task-bound monitor, which admitted 1.3% and 7.7%; guardrail effects depended on the model (a prompt guardrail moved obedience from 67% to 65% and from 86% to 55%, spotlighting plus a detector to 12% and 0%) against static attacks. Simulation with an assumed model covers what no real run did: under the assumed erosion law a persistent adaptive attacker or a compromised model drives every guardrail stack to 100.0% attack success, whereas the task-bound monitor holds severe actions at 0.0%; its residual (harm 0.69/10) falls by 62% under taint-triggered human review, and a human layer without a deterministic monitor fails against approval spamming unless each episode has a deterministic approval budget. Implementation quality matters: a naive monitor admits 18 of 33 effective attack variants, a hardened one 6 and a capability-bound one 1. The real-model evidence is limited to two open-weights models and static attacks, the human-approval and taint results are simulation-only, and the larger model's detector stack contradicts the assumed erosion law. Code, data, a two-rater oracle audit and a notebook for repeating the real-model evaluation are provided.

title: PROTOCOL: Late Interaction Retrieval for Protein Homolog Search
text:
Title: PROTOCOL: Late Interaction Retrieval for Protein Homolog Search
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Protein homology search underlies function annotation, structure prediction, and evolutionary analysis, but remains challenging in the "twilight zone," where global sequence similarity is weak and classical alignment methods lose sensitivity. Protein language models provide context-aware representations that could improve alignment sensitivity in this regime. However, prior protein embedding-based retrieval pipelines often pool these representations into a single vector, potentially obscuring local motifs, domains, or conserved residues that reveal remote homology. We introduce ProtoCol, a model which represents proteins as sets of residue embeddings and uses ColBERT-style late interaction to test whether residue-level comparison improves homolog retrieval. ProtoCol encodes proteins independently, keeps candidate representations pre-computable, and scores candidates with MaxSim over residue embeddings. On SCOPe superfamily and Pfam clan benchmarks, ProtoCol outperforms sequence-composition, alignment-based, pooled PLM, and trained single-vector baselines, supporting late interaction as an effective retrieval layer for remote homology search.

title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets
text:
Title: The importance of tensor handling and implementation of physics-informed DeepONets
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) reduce or eliminate the need for large labelled datasets by enforcing governing equations during training. Physics-informed Deep Operator Networks (PI-DeepONets) extend this approach to learning solution operators, enabling rapid prediction across families of problems. Despite these advantages, we show that their application to higher-dimensional problems remains limited by the computational cost of training. To address this issue, we propose a modified PI-DeepONet architecture that reduces this cost by removing redundancy in how the Branch network processes input functions across collocation points. The proposed formulation is mathematically equivalent to the original architecture but reduces input tensor sizes and the number of Branch network evaluations. We analyse the computational complexity of both architectures and derive theoretical scaling laws for training time with respect to the number of collocation points and input functions. The proposed architecture is evaluated on 1D, 2D, and 3D linear advection problems. In all cases, it achieves comparable predictive accuracy to the original PI-DeepONet while consistently reducing training time. In 2D experiments, a maximum speed-up of $3.75\times$ is observed, with empirical training-time scaling agreeing with the predicted linear dependence on collocation points and input functions. Furthermore, training a 3D model on an NVIDIA A100 GPU is only feasible using the proposed architecture, as the original formulation exceeds memory limits. These results demonstrate that careful consideration of how PI-DeepONets are implemented can yield substantial gains, enhancing the practical performance of PI-DeepONets and enabling their application to otherwise intractable physics-informed learning problems.

title: Federated Affine Variational Inequalities: Exact Averaging and Complexity Limits
text:
Title: Federated Affine Variational Inequalities: Exact Averaging and Complexity Limits
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We study the classical Local Stochastic Extragradient method (Local SEG) for monotone variational inequalities under intermittent communication, where devices perform several local oracle calls between synchronization rounds. For affine monotone mean operators, including nonsymmetric bilinear saddle systems, we prove that equal device averaging commutes pathwise with both stages of the stochastic extragradient update. Local trajectories may therefore drift apart while their mean follows a centralized stochastic-extragradient recursion driven by averaged noise. The identity remains valid when individual oracle realizations are nonlinear and query dependent. Under conditionally centered oracle errors that are conditionally independent across devices within each stage, the reduction yields a restricted weak-gap rate that uses the local sequential depth for deterministic progress and the aggregate oracle budget across devices for variance reduction. When every device makes at least two local oracle calls per communication round, the bound contains no additional mixed client-drift term and is also attained by a terminal-only aggregation schedule. An affine Gaussian lower bound matches the depth and sample dependences before statistical saturation for distributed zero-respecting algorithms; its statistical component applies to arbitrary randomized algorithms. A complementary lower bound for feasible distributed zero-respecting methods shows that bounded geometry and query-dependent noise can create an additional communication-locality obstruction. These results delineate the exact-averaging regime of unconstrained affine Local SEG and a complexity boundary that arises under active feasibility constraints.

title: Transformer-Based Active Learning for Data-Efficient Vaccine Epitope Selection in PRRS
text:
Title: Transformer-Based Active Learning for Data-Efficient Vaccine Epitope Selection in PRRS
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

High-fidelity molecular docking simulations can produce biologically relevant estimates of epitope-receptor binding affinity but are computationally expensive and therefore limit the number of candidates that can be screened for vaccine design. In this work, we evaluate machine learning (ML) approaches where variants of active learning are used to classify instances of high binding affinity between 9-mer epitopes and a well-conserved swine leukocyte antigen (SLA) receptor in the context of Porcine Reproductive and Respiratory Syndrome (PRRS). We use an internally generated dataset of 80 epitope-SLA docking affinities, each requiring more than 48 hours of high-performance computing (HPC). Multiple model families (linear, MLP, CNN, and a small transformer) are trained under strict low-data conditions within a pool-based active learning loop. In each case, optimal model configurations are identified by conducting large-scale hyperparameter optimization over the combined space of model architecture, training configuration, acquisition policy, and ensemble decision rules. To mitigate the effects of data subsample selection, each candidate configuration is evaluated by averaging performance over many randomized and balanced training and validation data subsets. Across experiments, transformer-based sequence models consistently emerged as the best-performing architecture, with active incremental learning yielding significant improvement over a baseline random sample acquisition strategy. Under moderate training data availability (N=30), the optimized ML-model configuration outperforms a standard baseline trained on twice the amount of data. Under higher training data availability (N=60), the same configuration achieves a peak accuracy of 86.8%, consistent with an upper bound of 85% classification accuracy based on two independent estimates of conformational noise.

title: Quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance
text:
Title: Quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

We present the concept of quadrature-detected zero-to-ultralow-field nuclear magnetic resonance (QD ZULF NMR). Two orthogonal sensors, atomic optically pumped magnetometers, are used to separately detect components of oscillating sample magnetization, which are then combined into a quadrature signal. This approach enables the distinction of positive and negative resonance frequencies with respect to the laboratory frame---such that absolute signs of gyromagnetic ratios can be determined. In addition, QD ZULF NMR reduces peak density and overlap compared to ZULF NMR with single-axis detection, while providing richer information about nuclear-spin dynamics. As an illustration, we present experimental $J$-spectra for thermally polarized [$^{13}$C]-formic acid and [$^{13}$C]-methanol, compounds commonly used in ZULF NMR which represent XA and XA$_3$ spin systems, respectively. A theoretical framework describing QD ZULF NMR signals is provided.

title: Regime-Aware Coupled Orchestration of Neural Operator Specialists for Multiphysics Dynamics
text:
Title: Regime-Aware Coupled Orchestration of Neural Operator Specialists for Multiphysics Dynamics
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Real-world physics often unfolds over a variety of characteristic lengths and time scales. These non-uniformities are among the main reasons numerical simulations remain expensive when used predictively on practical systems: the same computational domain can contain smooth transport, vortical structures, thin interfaces, reaction fronts, and rapidly relaxing regions. Neural operators are attractive surrogates for such problems. However, a single architecture is still expected to represent all these local behaviours with a single set of weights and a single inductive bias. In this work, we introduce the regime-aware coupled neural orchestrator (RCNO), a framework that learns to distribute and connect a library of local operator specialists in space and time. For every patch, an orchestrator builds a causal query from the current fields, neighbouring halo values, local regime features, patch identity, activity level, and case parameters. The nine expert embeddings exchange two rounds of query-conditioned message passing before an edge-biased cross-attention stage produces a dispatch distribution that can be evaluated sparsely. Local predictions are assembled into a global field and projected onto system-specific physical constraints. A seam-aware extension additionally learns residual corrections across internal patch interfaces. We apply the same orchestration architecture to two qualitatively different systems: reacting flow and Cahn-Hilliard-Navier-Stokes (CHNS) dynamics. The results show that useful operator specialisation exists across local regimes, that the advantage of conditional composition increases as the spatial decomposition becomes finer, and, on reacting flow, that explicitly treating patch interfaces improves continuity, PDE consistency, and rollout accuracy.

title: Ignoring Blow-Ups for Approximations
text:
Title: Ignoring Blow-Ups for Approximations
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

It is well known that for SDEs with non-Lipschitz coefficients, the Euler scheme can fail to converge in an Lp sense. It is also widely observed that convergence fails only due to rare explosive trajectories, that distort the expectation. In this work we demonstrate that almost any method of removing these rare explosive trajectories leads to convergence in a suitable strong and weak sense. We apply this framework to coefficients that grow faster than linearly at infinity and Lennard-Jones type coefficients that explode like a reciprocal power on a compact set.

title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
text:
Title: Beyond the Transcript: Measuring and Improving the Use of Acoustic Information in Audio Language Models
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Audio language model benchmarks provide comprehensive evaluation across diverse tasks. However, some tasks can be answered from the transcript or even the question alone, and benchmark scores can therefore confound acoustic understanding with language modeling ability. We distinguish lexical tasks, for which the transcript usually suffices, from global-attribute and within-recording-structure tasks, which require the model to analyse the recording beyond its words, either as a whole, for properties such as the speaker and emotion, or within it, for patterns such as stress and intonation. We evaluated 19 open models and Gemini 3.1 Pro on 92 tasks from 6 benchmarks and estimated the recording gain, the accuracy advantage of the original recording over references that retain its words, by comparing the recording with synthetic readings of its transcript and by adding it to the transcript. On attribute and structure tasks, the open models fall behind Gemini by 28.6 and 41.9 percentage points, and about half or more of each deficit lies in the recording gain. Nevertheless, linear probes in Gemma-4 12B and Qwen2.5-Omni-7B show that the acoustic information needed for answering is already readable in early language-model layers, while the readout of many cues declines in the layers that follow. We therefore constructed training data and trained LoRA adapters in these layers, with a content anchor, which raises attribute and structure accuracy by 12.8 to 44.4 points in the two models and keeps mean lexical accuracy within 1 point of the base model. Most of the improvement appears as larger recording gains. These results suggest that training improves the use of acoustic information that the models already encode.

title: Efficient Simulation of Gate Leakage Currents in Ultra-scaled Transistors from First Principles
text:
Title: Efficient Simulation of Gate Leakage Currents in Ultra-scaled Transistors from First Principles
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

To ensure high electrostatic integrity in ultra-scaled field-effect transistors (FETs), thin gate dielectric layers are typically needed, potentially giving rise to (strong) leakage currents. Being able to model this effect is therefore crucial. Here, we show how gate leakage currents can be computed at the ab initio level in WS$_2$-hBN FETs by extending the well-established quantum transmitting boundary method (QTBM). Two main challenges are tackled: (i) the calculation of the open boundary conditions (OBCs) for the gate contacts and (ii) the solution of the resulting sparse linear system of equations A x = b where the matrix A possesses an unstructured sparsity pattern. We demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms the state of the art and can be readily applied to simulate transistors with gate lengths exceeding 25 nm.

title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
text:
Title: Prediction with Foundation Models under Deployment Budgets
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Foundation models can supply predictions for a downstream task that draw on knowledge from extensive pretraining, but they differ in task-specific accuracy and query cost. We develop a framework that improves prediction for the task under a budget on the average query cost per input, using training data to learn which models to query and how to combine their outputs with features available without querying. The first method queries the same models for every input; the second lets them vary across inputs and uses Q-learning to decide which model to query next and when to stop. For the first method, we show that several individually inaccurate outputs can jointly outperform the best single one. It attains the minimax rate when the regression function depends on the outputs only through models within the budget. Otherwise, any method within the budget can be forced to a slower rate, which the first method attains. For the second method, we show when varying the queried models across inputs strictly improves on querying the same models for every input, and bound its prediction risk and average cost in finite samples. In simulations and a multimodal laptop price application, both methods outperform existing methods.

title: SMO: Compiling Natural Language Skills into Graphs of Reusable State-Move-Outcome Bricks
text:
Title: SMO: Compiling Natural Language Skills into Graphs of Reusable State-Move-Outcome Bricks
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Large language model agents increasingly rely on reusable natural-language skills, yet growing skill collections remain accumulations of isolated text artifacts that are difficult to compare, deduplicate, and compose. We argue that the reusable content of a skill lies not in its surface wording but in its procedural transitions: which operation to execute under a given state and which observable outcome to produce. Based on this observation, we propose State-Move-Outcome (SMO), a compilation-like framework that decomposes raw skills into reusable procedural bricks and organizes admitted bricks as an externalized symbolic structure. When compiling a skill, SMO first retrieves and composes existing bricks, dynamically connects them through Outcome-to-State conditions, and creates a candidate brick only for an uncovered procedure; the candidate becomes reusable only after validation and admission. Experiments on SkillsBench v1.1 demonstrate that SMO represents 232 rawSkills from 87 underlying tasks with 95 shared bricks, reducing the corresponding skill representations from 366,472 to 149,154 tokens--a $\mathbf{59.3}\times$ reduction and $\mathbf{2.46}\times$ compression. Across 232 skill-conditioned evaluation instances, SMO raises the average task score from $\mathbf{0.6379}$ to $\mathbf{0.7478}$ and increases 5/5 Pass instances from $\mathbf{138}$ to $\mathbf{164}$, while matching or outperforming rawSkill on $\mathbf{208}$ of $\mathbf{232}$ instances. It also reduces average runtime token consumption by $\mathbf{38.38\%}$. These results show that compiling natural-language skills into shared procedural units can jointly improve skill reuse, representation efficiency, and downstream execution.

title: Early onset of the hot circumgalactic medium around Milky Way galaxies
text:
Title: Early onset of the hot circumgalactic medium around Milky Way galaxies
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Hot coronae are key regulators in Milky Way (MW)-type galaxy formation and are thought to emerge once a galaxy's dark matter halo crosses a critical mass threshold, $M_{\mathrm{vir}}\sim10^{12} {\mathrm{M}}_\odot$, so that accretion shocks can heat infalling gas to virial temperatures, $T_{\mathrm{vir}}$. Here we investigate the roles of stellar feedback and accretion shocks in establishing the circumgalactic medium (CGM) around MW-mass galaxies using the VINTERGATAN cosmological simulation suite. We find that stellar feedback drives the early formation of a hot CGM, with $T_{\mathrm{CGM}}\sim T_{\mathrm{vir}}$. By contrast, in feedback-free simulations, accretion shocks alone do not produce a CGM with comparably high average temperatures at early epochs ($z>2$), independent of gas metallicity. We show that CGM virialisation (defined when halo-gas cooling time exceeds the free-fall time) begins with the emergence of a hot corona ($T>10^5$ K) that can appear as early as $z\approx3$ at virial radius, $R_{\mathrm{vir}}$, when feedback is included. This is much earlier than predicted by accretion-shock theory or feedback-free models ($z\lesssim1$). While accretion shocks alone produce an inside-out virialisation pattern, feedback can alter this behaviour, driving a rapid transition ($\lesssim0.5$ Gyr) that is either outside-in or nearly simultaneous throughout the halo. Finally, these early-forming coronae are largely stable from formation through to the present day, but can appear to evolve simply because the definition of $R_{\mathrm{vir}}$ grows with time. This 'CGM pseudo-evolution' is analogous to the pseudo-evolution of dark matter haloes and should be taken into account when interpreting the evolution of hot coronae.

title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
text:
Title: LLM Validation Makes Minimal-Pair Benchmarks Easier for Language Models
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Minimal-pair benchmarks are only as good as their labels, and LLMs are an obvious substitute for costly human validation. We test it on BLiMP (English) and QFrBLiMP (Quebec French), the two public minimal-pair datasets releasing every forced-choice human judgment. Three LLMs validate by forced choice, by rating, and as a panel, scored against human panels of one, three and five judges in two pre-registered phases. On BLiMP, forced-choice validators agree with held-out human majorities more often than five-judge panels, yet catch far fewer pairs whose label humans reject than one judge does. By point estimate, no validator is worth more than one judge. The errors are not random. On both datasets, across 10 open LMs, human-supported pairs that the pre-registered LLM filter flags are 18.9 points harder than those it accepts, in all 70 LM-validator combinations, and harder than pairs a single human judge flags. Filtering thus removes items on which LMs fail but humans do not, raising accuracy more than random removal. A protocol frozen before any output replicates the gap and the lift on Dutch BLiMP-NL. LLM validation makes minimal-pair benchmarks easier for the models they are meant to test; we release code, validator outputs and item-level scores.

title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
text:
Title: Sparse concept attribution for histomorphological hypothesis generation from whole-slide classifiers
Domain: Quantitative Methods in Biology (q-bio.QM)

Histology images contain rich morphological information and can provide insights into pathological processes. However, deriving hypotheses relating morphological phenotypes to clinical attributes is bottlenecked by a manual image interpretation step. Here, we demonstrate that this process can be automated through interpretable deep learning. We present SCOPE, a method to interpret slide-level classifiers by combining pathology-specific vision--language models with sparse concept attribution onto a generalist histomorphological concept bank. To measure whether such explanations recover known morphology, we introduce MorphoRecoveryBench, a benchmark of seven tasks with pathologist-curated reference descriptions. On this benchmark, dense concept attribution is indistinguishable from a random baseline, whereas sparse attribution recovers substantial known morphology; decomposing the pooled slide embedding reaches similar explanation correctness at a fraction of the computational cost. Post-hoc interpretation of whole-slide classifiers can thus generate morphological hypotheses at scale, for expert validation.

title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
text:
Title: Safeguarding Agentic AI in Radiology Workflows: A Multimodel Evaluation of Rule-based and Large Language Model-based Verification
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Purpose: To estimate how often tool-using large language model (LLM) agents record clinically relevant false or unsupported information in simulated radiology documentation and how much safeguards applied before each action reduce these errors. Materials and Methods: In this simulation study (October 2026), 48 synthetic, radiologist-reviewed base scenarios covered finding communication, tumor board preparation and follow-up management. Forty-three also had a misleading-information variant (91 variants). Six LLM agents (Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.1-Sol, GLM-5.3, MiniMax M3, Gemma-4-31B, Qwen3.8-27B) completed each variant with permissions only, deterministic rules, and rules plus a locally run LLM checker (1638 episodes). The primary outcome was at least one executed high-severity violation per episode. Risk differences were estimated per agent at base-scenario level and, exploratorily, pooled across agents, with analyses of document access and blocks. Results: With permissions only, 7.3%-27.1% of episodes had a high-severity violation (pooled across agents, 19.4%). Pooled, it was 16.7% with rules (-2.8 percentage points; 95% CI: -6.1, 0.5) and 13.2% with rules plus the LLM checker (-6.2; 95% CI: -9.5, -3.0). Adding the LLM checker to rules changed it by -3.5 (95% CI: -6.3, -0.7). No difference between agents was detected (P = .43), and task success did not decrease detectably. In misleading variants, agents opened the altered document in 83% of episodes regardless of error, and 58% of erroneous statements cited it. Most blocked actions (64%-68%) would not have caused a violation and were returned for revision. Conclusion: Layered safeguards reduced but did not prevent high-severity errors. Errors after misleading information reflected misjudged rather than missed information.

title: Generalizing Causal Decision-Making: Markov Equivalence, Transportability and Counterfactuals
text:
Title: Generalizing Causal Decision-Making: Markov Equivalence, Transportability and Counterfactuals
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Structural causal bandits use causal knowledge to guide exploration when reward mechanisms are unknown. This paper extends the approach to partially known causal structure, information from other environments, and realizable counterfactual actions. First, we develop graphical criteria for minimal intervention sets under Markov equivalence and characterize possibly-optimal minimal intervention sets for maximal ancestral graphs. A search algorithm finds sets that are possibly optimal in at least one graph represented by a partial ancestral graph. Second, we derive target reward bounds from source distributions through partial transportability, accounting for non-manipulable variables. Dominance relations provide further bounds for action pruning and restricted exploration, with a regret guarantee under valid prior bounds. Third, we formulate counterfactual structural causal bandits over actions supported by specified experimental capabilities. Graphical characterizations of minimality and possible optimality yield algorithms that remove equivalent or dominated choices while preserving an optimal action. Experiments with specified structural causal models examine how these reductions and transferred bounds affect learning. Together, these results clarify how causal knowledge and experimental capabilities determine which actions merit exploration and guide learning within the retained action space.

title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics
text:
Title: First-Principles Calculations of the Electron-Hole-Pair Creation Energy in Semiconductors and Dielectrics
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

We present first-principles calculations of the electron-hole-pair creation energy in semiconductors and dielectrics, focusing in particular on AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2. We have employed density functional theory (DFT) to calculate the band structure, density-functional perturbation theory to obtain the phonon dispersion, and time-dependent DFT (TDDFT) to calculate the electron energy loss function (via the dielectric function). We performed full-band Monte Carlo simulations of electron thermalization for energies up to ~100 eV and calculated the average energy required to excite an electron-hole pair. We calculated pair-creation energies of approximately 12.2, 6.5, 7.3, 3.10, and 16.7 eV/pair for AlN, 3C-SiC, 4H-SiC, Si, and SiO2, respectively. These values are in good agreement with measured data, with the largest discrepancy being that of Si (about 14.9% lower than the accepted experimental value of ~3.6 eV/pair). To improve the agreement for Si, we used the GW approach and the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) to calculate the quasiparticle shifts of the electronic band structure and the dielectric function, respectively. Finally, using the GW/BSE data, we calculated a creation energy of ~3.50 eV/pair. We find that the marked improvement in the accuracy of the calculated creation energy, when using the GW/BSE approach, is primarily attributable to the slight decrease in the magnitude of the electron energy-loss function when using the GW/BSE approach for energies below ~10-15 eV. Overall, it is clear that the competition between phonon emission and ionization near the intersection of the phonon scattering and ionization rates is largely responsible for determining the value of the creation energy, with the other major factor being the location and shape of the plasmon peak in the energy-loss function.

title: Sequential versus fully conditional specification for tree-based synthesis of health data
text:
Title: Sequential versus fully conditional specification for tree-based synthesis of health data
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Disseminating synthetic data in place of original ones is a promising way to enforce privacy while complying with open science principles, especially in the healthcare domain. To keep pace with the rate at which researchers collect such data, there is a need for fast and flexible synthesis procedures. A popular class of such procedures is based on models of conditional distributions induced by decision trees. Such models can be combined into a synthetic distribution following two main approaches: sequential specification and fully conditional specification. However, there is currently no recommendation on which specification to use to optimize the risk-utility tradeoffs. In this work, we use both specifications to synthesize medical datasets by combining tree-based models of conditional distributions. We compare the quality of the resulting synthetic data using several metrics of risk and utility. Our results indicate no general superiority of either specification over the other. Sequential synthesis seems sensitive to the ordering of the variables, while the fully conditional specification involves more hyperparameters and incurs higher computational costs, which may limit its suitability for off-the-shelf synthesis procedures.

title: A pressure-based coupled general synthetic iterative scheme for rarefied gas flow simulation
text:
Title: A pressure-based coupled general synthetic iterative scheme for rarefied gas flow simulation
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

This work develops a pressure-based coupled (PBC) GSIS. Within each GSIS iteration, a conventional kinetic solver advances the velocity distribution function, from which non-equilibrium constitutive relations are extracted. A PBC macroscopic solver then solves the steady macroscopic synthetic equations: continuity and momentum equations are solved as a coupled pressure-velocity system under fixed temperature, followed by a segregated temperature solve. A boundary treatment is constructed to maintain strict consistency between kinetic boundary fluxes and macroscopic boundary conditions throughout the macroscopic iterations. The proposed method is validated against direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) data across multiple three-dimensional test cases, including tube-to-vacuum flows, a dynamic gas lock configuration for EUV lithography, divertors in nuclear fusion, and sphere flow at Mach numbers up to 10. Numerical results demonstrate that our GSIS-PBC preserves asymptotic-preserving properties and yields satisfactory accuracy across continuum-to-transitional flow regimes. For low-speed near-continuum internal flows, GSIS-PBC delivers wall clock time speed-ups of up to two orders of magnitude compared with the conventional iterative scheme, and substantially outperforms the original density-based GSIS for challenging low-Mach internal flow problems. For nuclear-fusion divertor flows, GSIS-PBC is faster than the DSMC by four orders of magnitude.

title: Causal Discovery Grounding and the Naturalness Assumption
text:
Title: Causal Discovery Grounding and the Naturalness Assumption
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Standard causal discovery postulates that structure can be described by a directed acyclic graph (DAG), which can be partially reconstructed by using the faithfulness principle. According to this principle, conditional independencies in the observational distribution correspond exactly to those encoded in the unknown DAG. However, such algorithms are challenged by the fact that, without even stronger assumptions, approximate failures of faithfulness are empirically undistinguishable from exact ones. This leaves an inferential gap which can lead to major implications to causal effect identification. We introduce a different perspective, not reliant on exact independencies. By considering the specialized problem of discovering whether unmeasured confounding can be ruled out for a particular cause-effect pair, we introduce a principle we call naturalness, in which the strength of observational associations bounds the strength of causal dependencies. The bounding function is unknown, with degrees of freedom not present in faithfulness. We model uncertainty about this function using a Bayesian framing which allows for the use of experiments from separate studies, grounding an adaptive causal discovery principle on historical experimental data. We demonstrate its usefulness in partial identification of causal effects, and discuss how the promising results can motivate new principles for general causal discovery.

title: Identities, Not Pairs: Distribution-Free False-Accept Control for Embedding-Based Verification
text:
Title: Identities, Not Pairs: Distribution-Free False-Accept Control for Embedding-Based Verification
Domain: Statistical Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Embedding-based verification often calibrates a false-accept threshold from all impostor pairs among $m$ identities, although these pairs share identities. We characterize a worst-case limit: when hub identities score highly against a fraction $ρ$ of the population, a calibration-only threshold with marginal false-accept rate (FAR) at most $α$ under every identity-exchangeable law reaches the hub score on hub-free calibration sets with probability at most $(m+2)α/(2ρ)$. Uniformly accepting near that score at levels well below $ρ/m$ therefore requires trial information. We propose COVE, which ranks the trial pair among all $N=\binom{m+2}{2}$ pairs formed by augmenting the calibration units with the probe and reference. Under identity exchangeability, its marginal FAR is at most $\lfloorαN\rfloor/N$, with first possible acceptance at $1/N=O(1/m^2)$. The rule also retains this guarantee with a fixed symmetric cohort-normalized score using an independent cohort. On 6 benchmarks and 8 frozen encoders, realised FAR was consistent with the exact bound. Where both valid calibration-only baselines accepted nothing, COVE retained a median $100\%$ of the sampled oracle's true-accept rate over reliable comparisons. In contrast, an empirical quantile over dependent pairs reached 2.87$\,α$ FAR, and a binomial upper confidence bound over pairs missed its nominal 95\% conditional-FAR target in up to 55\% of calibration draws. Symmetric CSLS raised COVE's true-accept rate by up to 4.3-fold in the tested settings. The code is available in https://github.com/salimkhazem/Cove.git

title: Which Acoustic Features Survive Compression? Tracker-Estimated First-Formant Statistics for Codec-Robust Audio DeepfakeDetection
text:
Title: Which Acoustic Features Survive Compression? Tracker-Estimated First-Formant Statistics for Codec-Robust Audio DeepfakeDetection
Domain: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Audio deepfake detectors that work well on clean lab recordings often degrade after telephone or platform compression. This paper asks a specific question: which low-dimensional acoustic descriptors stay informative after codec degradation? We screen 36 utterance-level features(formants, PNCCs, LFCCs, prosody) on ASVspoof 2019 data and test on the official ASVspoof 2021 LA set across seven codec conditions. Of 33 statistically significant descriptors, only four show large practical separation (|r| >0.5, bootstrap 95% CIs), all first-formant (F1) measures, highly redundant (PC1: 79% variance). The payoff is stability: the 36-feature SVM degrades 14 pp under codec mismatch (9.5%-23.5% EER), while the four-feature RBF-SVM degrades only 5.9 pp (17.0%-22.9%). The F1 subset varies 3.4 pp across conditions versus 13.1 pp for the full set. F1 differences persist after controlling for speaker identity (p greater than 10^10, mixed-effects model). The results suggest that physically interpretable F1 statistics offer a compact, codec-stable diagnostic signal that may complement higher accuracy neural detectors.

title: Direct real-space imaging of sign-reversal superconducting state by scanning Josephson tunneling
text:
Title: Direct real-space imaging of sign-reversal superconducting state by scanning Josephson tunneling
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Phase-sensitive experiments based on Josephson tunneling have been considered as a pivotal method to determine the pairing symmetry in high-temperature (high-Tc) cuprate superconductors. However, in iron-based superconductors, traditional phase-sensitive experiments face setbacks because of the complexity of pairing symmetry in multiband systems. Here, using scanning Josephson tunneling microscopy (SJTM), we report the half-unit-cell periodic Josephson tunneling modulations in monolayer high-Tc Fe(Te,Se) film epitaxially grown on SrTiO3(001). The Josephson tunneling almost vanishes along the lines connecting next-nearest-neighbor Fe atoms under an s-wave superconducting tip. Combined with single-particle tunneling spectra showing the full superconducting gap, our experimental results are consistent with the sign-reversal nodeless d-wave pairing symmetry. Our findings provide sub-unit-cell scale superconducting phase information for understanding the mechanism of high-Tc superconductivity. We anticipate our work as a starting point for atomically resolved Josephson interference experiments using SJTM in various unconventional superconductors.

title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
text:
Title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
Domain: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision. Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals. Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision. Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI. Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.

title: Alter-excitons in Altermagnets: Symmetry, Splitting and Dispersion
text:
Title: Alter-excitons in Altermagnets: Symmetry, Splitting and Dispersion
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Magnetism provides a fertile platform for discovering emergent quantum phenomena governed by symmetry. Recent developments of spin-space-group (SSG) theory have revealed altermagnets as a distinct class of nonrelativistic collinear magnets with unconventional spin-dependent electronic structures. Here, we demonstrate that altermagnetic symmetry imposes fundamentally different constraints on electronic and excitonic excitations. Although the quasiparticle and two-body Hamiltonians possess identical SSG symmetries, we find that symmetry-protected degeneracies present in the electronic band structure can be intrinsically lifted in the exciton spectrum at specific momenta. This splitting arises solely from the many-body nature of excitons and does not require spin-orbit coupling or noncollinear magnetic order. Combining symmetry analysis with many-body perturbation theory, we predict a novel class of spin-split excitonic quasiparticles, termed alter-excitons, and reveal their characteristic dispersions in altermagnetic systems. Our results establish excitons as a sensitive probe of hidden spin-space symmetries and uncover a new route toward symmetry-engineered many-body phenomena in collinear magnets.

title: Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics: An eT-i-PI Interface for Ab Initio Cavity Born-Oppenheimer Dynamics and Joint Nuclear-Photon Path-Integral Sampling
text:
Title: Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics: An eT-i-PI Interface for Ab Initio Cavity Born-Oppenheimer Dynamics and Joint Nuclear-Photon Path-Integral Sampling
Domain: Chemical Physics (physics.chem-ph)

Simulating molecules in quantum electrodynamic (QED) cavities requires a consistent description of electronic response, nuclear motion, and electromagnetic-field fluctuations. Here, I present Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics, an interface connecting eT and i-PI for atomistic simulations of finite molecular systems coupled to a single photon mode. The code evaluates a self-consistent cavity Born-Oppenheimer Hartree-Fock (CBO-HF) energy surface and supports classical-nuclei dynamics under canonical (NVT) and microcanonical (NVE) ensembles, as well as canonical joint nuclear-photon path-integral sampling including nuclear quantum effects (NQEs). A fixed-displacement gradient correction provides nuclear and photon forces consistent with the same energy surface as the photon coordinate evolves independently. OpenMP threading, concurrent bead evaluations, and analysis utilities support practical simulations. Water-monomer benchmarks assess both dynamical propagation and equilibrium sampling. Energy-derivative checks and NVE timestep tests demonstrate consistent force evaluation and integration, while path integral molecular dynamics (PIMD) simulations with PILE-L thermostatting reproduce analytic finite-bead photon second moments, including their centroid and internal contributions, within sampling uncertainties. At the tested parameters, cavity coupling produces a small but statistically resolved increase in photon fluctuations, while changes in mean molecular geometry remain within sampling uncertainty. The resulting Cavity-QED Molecular Dynamics framework enables controlled investigations of how coupled quantum fluctuations of matter and the electromagnetic field influence molecular equilibrium properties within the CBO-HF approximation, providing a foundation for future studies of cavity-modified hydrogen bonding, vibrational spectra, and molecular polaritonic phenomena.

title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
text:
Title: Say Shibboleth: Fingerprinting the LLMs and Harnesses Behind Agentic Attacks
Domain: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

We study the fingerprinting of agentic cyberattacks. Our objective is to reliably infer information about the attacker's configuration, such as LLM version and harness, from telemetry. To achieve this, we introduce a technique we call shibboleth traps: modular honeypot services designed to elicit discriminative behaviors from agentic attackers. The traps make informative interactions a condition for obtaining resources the agent seeks, eliciting model declarations and characteristic writing without requiring a successful prompt injection. To achieve harness fingerprinting, we introduce general mechanisms to indirectly probe peculiar execution behaviors of harnesses. These probes reveal how a harness masks secrets in tool output, enforces command time limits, and schedules tool calls, using only the effects visible in subsequent requests. We show that combined declarative and behavioral inference distinguishes among 15 candidate models with an average 90% top-1 accuracy, with behavioral classifiers evaluated on held-out harnesses or task families. In a separate experiment across four harnesses, fixed probe rules identify the correct harness with 92% accuracy. When instructed to conceal their identity, agents still leave useful behavioral evidence even as their declarations become uninformative.

title: Implicit DeepReach Without Implicit Differentiation
text:
Title: Implicit DeepReach Without Implicit Differentiation
Domain: Optimization and Control (math.OC)

We consider the problem of approximating backward reachable and reach-avoid tubes for high-dimensional nonlinear systems whose Hamiltonians require numerical optimization over constrained controls and disturbances. Existing neural Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability methods alleviate the dimensionality bottleneck of grid-based solvers, but evaluating Hamiltonians without closed-form expressions introduces an additional computational challenge. We show that, under suitable assumptions, the gradients required for value-function training can be computed without differentiating through the inner optimization problem. Specifically, we establish an envelope-type gradient identity for the saddle point Hamiltonian, under which the optimal control and disturbance enter backpropagation as constants without gradient tracking. This enables end-to-end neural HJ reachability with numerically evaluated Hamiltonians while avoiding both solver unrolling and implicit differentiation. We demonstrate the accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed approach on nonlinear reachability and reach-avoid problems of different scales.

title: Uniqueness and full coverage in $k$-neighbor graphs
text:
Title: Uniqueness and full coverage in $k$-neighbor graphs
Domain: Probability (math.PR)

We study the number of infinite clusters in the $2dp$-neighbor graph on $\mathbb Z^d$, $d\ge2$, in which every vertex independently selects $\lfloor 2dp\rfloor$ of its nearest neighbors uniformly at random, and one more with probability $2dp-\lfloor 2dp\rfloor$. The model has negatively correlated edges and, for $1\le2dp\le2d-1$, neither finite energy nor insertion or deletion tolerance. We prove that the undirected graph has at most one infinite cluster for every $p\in [0,1]$, and that in the planar case the same holds for forward and strong forward clusters of the directed graph when $p\in[1/2,1]$. We further exhibit a second phase transition: for $p\ge(d+1)/(2d)$ the open cluster of the origin is almost surely the whole lattice, and for $p>(d+1)/(2d)$ any two vertices of a box are connected inside the box of twice the size with probability exponentially close to one. In particular, the percolation function is continuous but not analytic on the supercritical interval $(p_c,1]$. Finally, we prove that the full-coverage phase transition at $p_f = (d+1)/2d$ is of order $2^d$.

title: Heavy quark thermalization using phonon-heavy quark EFT
text:
Title: Heavy quark thermalization using phonon-heavy quark EFT
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

The description of heavy quarks inside the QGP medium, especially at low momenta, remains challenging from first principles, due to large coupling strength and gluon occupation numbers. An alternative way to formulate a description in terms of perturbative degrees of freedom is the interaction of the heavy quarks with the collective excitations of the medium in the form of phonons. This description is derived as an effective field theory (EFT) and therefore allows for a natural occurring power counting of the allowed interactions. This EFT has already been established in our previous work, where we have derived the phonon-heavy quark interactions and calculated their thermal scattering cross section. In this work, we use these results, together with the heavy quark expansion, to calculate the heavy quark drag coefficient. Subsequently, we compare our results with the drag coefficient obtained from AdS/CFT calculations to determine the previously unknown Wilson coefficients for the quark-phonon coupling. Finally, we will use these coefficients to solve the Boltzmann equation for the heavy quark distribution, studying its thermalization in the QGP via soft phonon interactions.

title: Relativistic N-body simulations with mass-varying neutrinos
text:
Title: Relativistic N-body simulations with mass-varying neutrinos
Domain: Cosmology and Extragalactic Astrophysics (astro-ph.CO)

Recent cosmological data provide weak hints for smaller masses than what is required by neutrino-oscillation experiments, motivating investigations into variation of the neutrino masses with cosmic time. Here we study a model where the neutrinos couple to a quintessence field that acts as dark energy. We compute structure formation using fully dynamical and relativistic N-body and lattice simulations, with nonlinear field evolution and a weak-field metric expansion. Similar to previous studies, we find the generic appearance of neutrino lumps, but observe them to be highly dynamical and spinning. We study several models where the effective dark energy, including nonlinear effects of the scalar field on the cosmic expansion, can show phantom crossing. The relativistic physics available in our simulation framework can help distinguish such models from LCDM, through observations of neutrino and dark energy properties, and slip between the gravitational potentials due to anisotropic stress. The rich phenomenology offered by mass-varying neutrinos motivates further exploration and development of the simulation techniques.

title: Effect of Electric Charge on Biotherapeutic Transport, Binding and Absorption: A Computational Study
text:
Title: Effect of Electric Charge on Biotherapeutic Transport, Binding and Absorption: A Computational Study
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

This study explores the effects of electric charge on the dynamics of drug transport and absorption in subcutaneous injections of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs). We develop a novel mathematical and computational model, based on the Nernst-Planck equations and porous media flow theory, to investigate the complex interactions between mAbs and charged species in subcutaneous tissue. The model enables us to study short-term transport dynamics and long-term binding and absorption for two mAbs with different electric properties. We examine the influence of buffer pH, body mass index, injection depth, and formulation concentration on drug distribution and compare our numerical results with experimental data from the literature.

title: PepALD: Macrocyclic Peptide Generation via Autoregressive Latent Diffusion
text:
Title: PepALD: Macrocyclic Peptide Generation via Autoregressive Latent Diffusion
Domain: Biomolecules (q-bio.BM)

Macrocyclic peptides are promising therapeutic candidates for intracellular targets, but their design requires simultaneous control over non-natural monomer chemistry, ring topology, membrane permeability, and target binding. Existing SMILES- or HELM-string generative models either operate in long atom-level sequence spaces or treat monomers as symbolic tokens with limited chemical grounding. We introduce PepALD, an Autoregressive Latent Diffusion (ALD) foundation model for \textit{de novo} macrocyclic peptide generation. The model represents HELM monomers with structured chemical embeddings, generates each residue through context-conditioned diffusion in chemically informed latent space, predicts R-group-aware ring closures during autoregressive generation, and aligns the denoiser to affinity rewards using winner-protected diffusion-adapted preference optimization. In silico experiments demonstrate PepALD's generation quality and reward-optimization performance against representative peptide generation baselines.

title: Multiloop Unitarity from Airy Zeros
text:
Title: Multiloop Unitarity from Airy Zeros
Domain: High Energy Physics - Theory (hep-th)

Hidden zeros are non-trivial cancellations that make amplitudes or integrands vanish on specific kinematic loci away from propagator poles. They have been shown to uniquely determine tree amplitudes and one-loop surface integrands in $\Tr(φ^3)$ theory, without assuming factorization. Here we extend both the zeros and the uniqueness results to two, three and four loops at arbitrary multiplicity. We show that two types of zeros naturally enter the all-loop problem. First, tree-level zeros extend to all loop orders and fix relative weights within families of subgraphs attached to vacuum ``loop cores.'' We then show that Kontsevich's matrix Airy function can be used to generate a rich structure of loop level zeros that fix the relative weights of the loop cores themselves. The relative factorization and cut data required by unitarity therefore follow from the combination of tree and Airy loop zeros. These results bring within reach the emergence of unitarity to all orders in perturbation theory.

title: Spin swapping mediated by spin-orbital textures in centrosymmetric multiorbital materials
text:
Title: Spin swapping mediated by spin-orbital textures in centrosymmetric multiorbital materials
Domain: Materials Science (cond-mat.mtrl-sci)

Spin swapping converts a primary spin current into a secondary one by interchanging its flow and spin-polarization directions, attributed to spin-orbit scattering or spin-band splitting. Here we uncover a fundamentally distinct route to spin swapping arising from the orbital degree of freedom in the spin pumping to centrosymmetric multiorbital materials \textit{without spin-band splitting}. When the dynamical proximity ferromagnet injects a longitudinal spin current flowing normal to the interface, spin-orbit-entangled orbital textures redirect the injected spins into longitudinal and transverse orbital currents. Their subsequent conversion back to the spin sector generates transverse spin currents with propagation and polarization directions swapped relative to the primary spin current. The swapping efficiency achieves $50\%$ for Ge and Si. Governed by a fourth-rank tensor constrained by crystalline symmetry and without requiring spin-orbit scattering or inversion symmetry breaking, our finding reveals spin-orbital textures as hidden intermediate channels of spin swapping with unexplored material choices and functionalities.

title: A $θ$-implicit hybrid particle-in-cell algorithm for kinetic simulations of magnetized plasmas
text:
Title: A $θ$-implicit hybrid particle-in-cell algorithm for kinetic simulations of magnetized plasmas
Domain: Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC) models with kinetic ions and an inertialess electron fluid are widely used to simulate magnetized plasmas at ion scales, but explicit time advances are constrained by the whistler-wave CFL condition $\dt \propto Δx^2$, and the sub-cycling and artificial dissipation used to mitigate it carry accumulating costs. We present a $θ$-implicit hybrid PIC algorithm, implemented in the open-source GPU-capable code WarpX, in which fields and particles are advanced as a single nonlinear system solved by a particle-suppressed Jacobian-free Newton--Krylov method: the particles are nonlinearly eliminated, the electric field of the generalized Ohm's law is the sole unknown, and mass matrices remove all particle operations from the linear iterations. The electron pressure is advanced inside the nonlinear solve, and the scheme satisfies a discrete energy law whose single dissipation term vanishes at $θ= 1/2$ and damps only temporally under-resolved modes for $θ> 1/2$. The advance reproduces parallel and perpendicular wave dispersion including the ion Bernstein modes, conserves total energy to machine roundoff where the explicit advance heats secularly, does not develop the cold-beam finite-grid instability, and reproduces the $m=0$ instability of a Bennett pinch in RZ geometry.
